questions.stem: The commonly used cement for paint is:
questions.solution:
**White cement.**

**Why white cement, and the reason is a single oxide:**

> **Ordinary Portland cement is grey because of IRON OXIDE (Fe₂O₃).** Iron oxide is a normal constituent — 0.5 to 6 per cent — and it is what imparts the familiar grey colour.

> **White cement is the same cement with the iron content driven down**, typically below about 0.4 per cent Fe₂O₃, and the manganese oxide reduced with it.

> **A white base is essential for a paint or a coloured finish**, because a grey base muddies every pigment added to it. **You cannot make a pale colour on a dark ground.**

**How white cement is made white:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Raw materials low in iron and manganese** | **White chalk or limestone plus china clay** |
| **Fuel that does not contaminate** | **Oil or gas rather than coal — coal ash carries iron** |
| **Grinding media that do not shed iron** | Ceramic or flint, not steel balls |
| **Rapid quenching of the clinker** | Prevents colour developing on slow cooling |

> **Every one of those steps adds cost**, which is why white cement runs well above ordinary Portland — commonly two to three times the price. **It is a finishing material, not a structural one.**

**Where white cement is used:**

> **Cement paint and colour washes; terrazzo and mosaic flooring; cast stone and architectural precast; tile-fixing adhesive and joint grout; and any decorative finish where the colour must be controlled.**

> **Its strength is comparable to ordinary Portland cement of the same grade** — it is not a weaker material, merely a purer and dearer one.

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | What it is for |
|---|---|
| **Portland cement** | **The general-purpose structural cement — GREY, so unsuitable as a paint base** |
| **Alumina cement** | **HIGH-ALUMINA cement: refractory and rapid-strength work, resists sulphates and heat; dark grey to brown** |
| **Rapid hardening cement** | **Gains strength FAST (3-day strength of a 7-day OPC) — used where formwork must be struck early; still grey** |

> **Note carefully that rapid hardening cement sets at the SAME rate as OPC** — it *hardens* faster. **Setting and hardening are different properties, and confusing them is a standard trap.** Setting is the loss of plasticity; hardening is the gain of strength.

**The main types of cement and their purposes, since one or another appears in every paper:**

| Type | Distinguishing use |
|---|---|
| **OPC (33, 43, 53 grade)** | General construction |
| **PPC (Portland pozzolana)** | **Better durability, lower heat, denser with age** |
| **Rapid hardening** | **Early strength — early formwork removal** |
| **Low heat** | **MASS CONCRETE — dams, thick rafts** |
| **Sulphate resisting** | **Low C₃A — marine and sulphate soils** |
| **White** | **Decorative and paint work** ← |
| **High alumina** | **Refractory; chemical resistance** |
| **Expansive** | Grouting, where shrinkage cannot be tolerated |

> **The selection logic is worth holding onto: choose the cement for the ENVIRONMENT and the CONSTRUCTION PROGRAMME, not for strength alone**, since almost any type can be made to reach the required grade.

examTip.trick: **Grey cement is grey because of IRON OXIDE.** Drive Fe₂O₃ below about 0.4% and the cement is white — which is what a paint or coloured finish needs, since no pigment shows on a dark ground.
examTip.trap: **Rapid hardening cement SETS at the same rate as OPC** — only its hardening is faster. Setting is loss of plasticity; hardening is gain of strength. Do not treat them as the same word.
examTip.mnemonic: **White cement costs two to three times OPC** because every input must be iron-free — white limestone, oil firing, ceramic grinding media. It is a finishing material, not a structural one.

questions.stem: If your weight on earth is W kg, what will be your weight on the moon?
questions.solution:
**W/6 kg.**

**The reasoning:**

> **Weight is a FORCE: W = m·g.** The mass m does not change when you travel — it is a property of the body. **What changes is g.**

> **The moon's surface gravity is about ONE SIXTH of the earth's** — 1.62 m/s² against 9.81 m/s², a ratio of 0.165.

> **So the weight becomes W/6.**

**Why the moon's gravity is one sixth — worth knowing rather than memorising:**

> **g = GM/R²**, so the ratio depends on both mass and radius.

| Quantity | Moon relative to earth |
|---|---|
| **Mass M** | **≈ 1/81** |
| **Radius R** | **≈ 1/3.7** |
| **g = GM/R²** | **(1/81) × (3.7)² ≈ 13.7/81 ≈ 1/6** ✓ |

> **The smaller radius partly compensates for the much smaller mass**, which is why the answer is a sixth and not an eightieth. **That is the insight the question is really testing.**

**The distinction the question turns on — and it is a genuine confusion in engineering practice:**

| Quantity | Nature | Unit | Changes with location? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **MASS** | **Amount of matter — a scalar** | **kg (SI base unit)** | **NO** |
| **WEIGHT** | **Gravitational FORCE on that mass — a vector** | **newton (N), strictly** | **YES** |

> **Stating a weight in kilograms is loose usage**, and the question does it: strictly, W kg is a mass, and the weight is W·g newtons. **The kilogram-force (kgf) exists precisely to paper over this** — 1 kgf = 9.81 N.

> **The looseness does not affect the answer**, because the ratio 1/6 is the same whether you work in newtons or in kgf. But it matters in engineering: **a load stated in "kg" must be multiplied by 9.81 to become a force in newtons**, and forgetting that factor is a real and expensive mistake.

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **W kg** | **Would require the moon's g to equal the earth's** — it does not |
| **3W kg** | **No body in the solar system that a person could stand on has three times earth gravity** — Jupiter is about 2.5 times, and has no surface |
| **W/3 kg** | **The ratio of the RADII is about 1/3.7 — a plausible-looking wrong answer for anyone who forgets the mass ratio** ← the trap |
| **W/6 kg** | ✓ |

> **Option (c) is the designed trap**: 1/3 is close to the radius ratio, so a candidate who half-remembers "the moon is about a third the size of the earth" lands on it.

**Where this matters in civil engineering, since the question is not idle:**

> **Every dead load is a weight, and every mass density must be converted to a unit weight by multiplying by g.**

| Material | Mass density | Unit weight |
|---|---|---|
| **Water** | **1000 kg/m³** | **9.81 kN/m³** |
| **RCC** | **2500 kg/m³** | **25 kN/m³** |
| **Plain concrete** | 2400 kg/m³ | 24 kN/m³ |
| **Steel** | **7850 kg/m³** | **78.5 kN/m³** |
| Brick masonry | 1900 kg/m³ | 19 kN/m³ |

> **The 25 kN/m³ for RCC and 78.5 kN/m³ for steel are worth committing to memory**, because they appear in almost every dead-load calculation and the conversion is where slips happen.

examTip.trick: **Mass does not change; g does.** The moon's g is 1.62 m/s² against 9.81 — about one sixth. So W becomes W/6.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) W/3 is the designed trap** — 1/3 is roughly the RADIUS ratio. The gravity ratio needs both mass (1/81) and radius (1/3.7): (1/81)×3.7² ≈ 1/6.
examTip.mnemonic: **A load in "kg" must be multiplied by 9.81 to become a force.** Hence RCC 2500 kg/m³ → **25 kN/m³** and steel 7850 kg/m³ → **78.5 kN/m³** — the two numbers behind most dead-load sums.

questions.stem: The number of goals of sustainable development is:
questions.solution:
**17.**

**What they are:**

> **The Sustainable Development Goals were adopted by the UN General Assembly in 2015**, in the resolution titled *Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development* — hence "Agenda 2030".

> **17 goals, 169 targets, to be achieved by 2030.**

> **They succeeded the MILLENNIUM DEVELOPMENT GOALS, which ran 2000-2015 and numbered 8.** That succession is the commonest thing to be tested on after the count itself.

**The two counts worth keeping straight:**

| Framework | Period | Goals |
|---|---|---|
| **MDGs — Millennium Development Goals** | **2000-2015** | **8** |
| **SDGs — Sustainable Development Goals** | **2015-2030** | **17** ← |

> **8 then 17.** The SDGs are broader in two ways: **they apply to ALL countries rather than only developing ones, and they cover the environment and institutions, not only poverty and health.**

**The goals most relevant to a civil engineer:**

| Goal | Title |
|---|---|
| **6** | **Clean water and sanitation** ← water supply and wastewater |
| **7** | **Affordable and clean energy** ← hydropower |
| **9** | **Industry, INNOVATION and INFRASTRUCTURE** ← the engineer's goal |
| **11** | **Sustainable cities and communities** ← urban planning, housing, transport |
| **13** | **Climate action** ← resilience and adaptation |

> **Goals 6, 7, 9, 11 and 13 are effectively a civil engineering work programme**, and Nepal's own periodic plans are written against them.

**The three pillars the goals are built on, which is the concept behind the count:**

| Pillar | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **ECONOMIC** | Growth that can be sustained |
| **SOCIAL** | Equity, health, education, inclusion |
| **ENVIRONMENTAL** | Resources and ecosystems maintained for the future |

> **The classical definition is the Brundtland Commission's (1987): development that meets the needs of the present WITHOUT COMPROMISING the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.**

> **That single sentence is quoted more often than any other in the topic and is worth knowing verbatim.**

**Why the distractors are wrong:** they are simply near numbers with no standing — **there is no framework with 15, 19 or 21 goals**, and the question tests recall of a published figure rather than reasoning. **Fix the pair 8 and 17 and the whole family of such questions is answerable.**

examTip.trick: **17 goals, 169 targets, by 2030**, adopted by the UN General Assembly in 2015 as Agenda 2030.
examTip.trap: **Do not confuse the two frameworks: MDGs 2000-2015 had 8 goals; SDGs 2015-2030 have 17.** Fix that pair and the whole family of such questions is answerable.
examTip.mnemonic: **Goals 6, 7, 9, 11 and 13** — water, energy, infrastructure, cities, climate — are effectively a civil engineer's work programme. And know the Brundtland sentence verbatim.

questions.stem: The centre of gravity of a trapezium with parallel sides 'a' and 'b' lies at a distance of 'y' from the base 'b' and having height 'h'. The value of 'y' is:
questions.solution:
**y = (h/3) × (2a+b)/(a+b).**

**Where the formula comes from — split the trapezium into two triangles:**

> **Draw a diagonal.** The trapezium of parallel sides a (top) and b (base), height h, becomes two triangles.

| Triangle | Area | Centroid above base b |
|---|---|---|
| **On base b** | **½bh** | **h/3** |
| **On base a (apex down)** | **½ah** | **2h/3** |

> **Take moments about the base:**

> **ȳ = [½bh·(h/3) + ½ah·(2h/3)] / [½bh + ½ah]**

> **= [bh²/6 + ah²/3] / [h(a+b)/2]**

> **= [h²(b + 2a)/6] × [2/(h(a+b))]**

> **= (h/3) × (2a+b)/(a+b)** ✓

**The two checks that settle the answer without the derivation, and this is the fast route:**

> **CHECK 1 — set a = b (a rectangle).** Then y = (h/3)(3b/2b) = h/2. **Correct: a rectangle's centroid is at mid-height.**

> **CHECK 2 — set a = 0 (a triangle on base b).** Then y = (h/3)(b/b) = h/3. **Correct: a triangle's centroid is h/3 above its base.**

> **Only option (c) passes both.** Test the others:

| Option | At a = b | At a = 0 | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) h(2a+b)/(a+b) | **3h/2 — outside the shape** | h | **Fails absurdly** |
| (b) (h/2)(2a+b)/(a+b) | 3h/4 | h/2 | **Fails both** |
| **(c) (h/3)(2a+b)/(a+b)** | **h/2** ✓ | **h/3** ✓ | **Correct** |
| (d) h(a+b)/(2a+b) | 2h/3 | h/2 | Fails both |

> **Option (a) can be eliminated on sight**: at a = b it puts the centroid at 1.5h, above the top of the shape. **A centroid outside the body is impossible for a convex section, and that check costs no time at all.**

**The limit worth carrying away:**

> **y ranges from h/3 (triangle, a = 0) to h/2 (rectangle, a = b), and rises above h/2 only when a > b** — that is, when the wider side is at the top, which is the trapezium standing on its narrow edge.

> **So a quick sanity test on any answer: it must lie between h/3 and 2h/3.**

**Why the centroid matters in civil engineering:**

> **Every section modulus and every moment of inertia is referred to the centroidal axis**, so the centroid must be located before anything else can be computed.

> **Trapezoidal sections are everywhere:** the cross-section of a canal or an embankment, a gravity retaining wall, a dam section, a haunched beam. **The formula above is used to find the line of action of the self-weight**, which is exactly what decides whether a gravity wall overturns.

> **And the companion result: the trapezium's AREA is ½(a+b)h** — the mean of the parallel sides times the height, which is also the trapezoidal rule for numerical integration and for earthwork volumes.

examTip.trick: **Test the limits instead of deriving.** At a = b it must give h/2 (rectangle); at a = 0 it must give h/3 (triangle). Only (h/3)(2a+b)/(a+b) passes both.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) puts the centroid at 1.5h when a = b — outside the shape.** A centroid outside a convex section is impossible, and that check costs no time at all.
examTip.mnemonic: **y always lies between h/3 and h/2** for a trapezium standing on its wider side. Companion result: **area = ½(a+b)h**, the same trapezoidal rule used for earthwork volumes.

questions.stem: The design for Load Bearing Masonry is based upon:
questions.solution:
**NBC 202.**

**The four NBC parts that this question sets against one another:**

| Code | Full title |
|---|---|
| **NBC 201** | **Mandatory Rules of Thumb — Reinforced Concrete Buildings WITH masonry infill** |
| **NBC 202** | **Mandatory Rules of Thumb — LOAD BEARING MASONRY** ← |
| **NBC 203** | **Guidelines for Earthquake Resistant Building Construction: LOW STRENGTH MASONRY** |
| **NBC 205** | **Mandatory Rules of Thumb — Reinforced Concrete Buildings WITHOUT masonry infill** |

> **The discrimination is in one phrase each.** 201 and 205 are both about RC frames and differ only on whether the infill is counted; 202 is the load-bearing masonry code; 203 covers masonry too weak to be designed at all.

**Why 202 and 203 are the pair most often confused, and the distinction is real:**

> **NBC 202 covers ENGINEERED load-bearing masonry** — brick or block in cement mortar, of known strength, built to rules of thumb that guarantee an adequate structure without full analysis.

> **NBC 203 covers LOW STRENGTH masonry** — stone in mud mortar, adobe, rubble. **This material cannot be assigned a reliable design strength**, so the code gives construction *guidelines* rather than design rules: band beams, corner reinforcement, wall length limits, opening restrictions.

> **The difference is therefore not one of size but of whether the material can be designed at all.** That is why one is "mandatory rules of thumb" and the other "guidelines".

**What "Mandatory Rules of Thumb" means, since three of the four options carry the phrase:**

> **They are prescriptive rules for buildings up to a stated size — typically three storeys — that a competent builder can apply WITHOUT structural analysis.**

> **The logic is deliberate and worth respecting: most buildings in Nepal are built by masons rather than designed by engineers**, so a code that only an engineer can use protects almost nobody. **A rule of thumb that is safe, simple and mandatory reaches the buildings that actually get built.**

**The wider NBC family, for orientation:**

| Code | Subject |
|---|---|
| **NBC 000** | Requirements for state-of-the-art design |
| **NBC 102-105** | **Unit weights, imposed loads, wind, SEISMIC design** |
| **NBC 105** | **SEISMIC DESIGN OF BUILDINGS IN NEPAL — the one most often cited** |
| **NBC 106** | **Snow load** |
| **NBC 107** | Fire safety |
| **NBC 108** | Site consideration for seismic hazards |
| **NBC 109-112** | Masonry, timber, steel, aluminium |
| **NBC 201-208** | **Mandatory rules of thumb and construction guidelines** |

> **NBC 105 (2020) is the revision to know**: it replaced the 1994 edition and moved Nepal to a modern response-spectrum approach with four soil classes and two seismic hazard levels.

**And the legal point:** **the NBC was made mandatory nationwide through the Building Act 2055 and its subsequent amendments**, and local bodies enforce it at the building-permit stage. **A design that ignores it is not merely poor practice but non-compliant.**

examTip.trick: **NBC 202 = load bearing masonry.** 201 is RC frame WITH infill, 205 is RC frame WITHOUT infill, 203 is LOW STRENGTH masonry. One phrase separates each.
examTip.trap: **202 versus 203 is the real confusion.** 202 is engineered masonry of known strength (mandatory rules); 203 is stone-in-mud and adobe, which cannot be assigned a design strength at all (guidelines only).
examTip.mnemonic: **"Mandatory Rules of Thumb" exist because most Nepali buildings are built by masons, not designed by engineers** — a code only an engineer can use protects almost nobody. And **NBC 105** is the seismic code to know.

questions.stem: Right of way for a Feeder Road according to NRS 2070 is:
questions.solution:
**30 m.**

**The Nepal Road Standard right-of-way widths:**

| Road class | Right of way |
|---|---|
| **National Highway** | **50 m (25 m each side of the centre line)** |
| **Feeder Road** | **30 m (15 m each side)** ← |
| **District Road** | **20 m (10 m each side)** |
| **Village Road** | **15 m (7.5 m each side)** |

> **The series 50 / 30 / 20 / 15 is worth memorising as a block**, because the question is asked about a different class each sitting and the numbers are otherwise unguessable.

> **Note the pattern: the width is quoted as the TOTAL, symmetric about the centre line.** A feeder road's 30 m means 15 m on each side, and it is the half-width that a boundary dispute actually turns on.

**What right of way IS, and why it is much wider than the road:**

> **The right of way is the LAND acquired and reserved for the road** — not the pavement, and not the formation.

> **A feeder road's carriageway may be 5.5 m and its formation 8 m, inside a 30 m right of way.** The remaining width is not waste:

| Reserved for | Note |
|---|---|
| **Side drains and cut/fill slopes** | The formation is wider than the pavement |
| **FUTURE WIDENING** | **The main reason — land acquired once, cheaply** |
| **Utilities** | Water, sewer, power, telecom |
| **Sight lines at curves and junctions** | Clearance must be kept |
| **Footpaths, tree planting, bus bays** | Where provided |

> **Future widening is the substantive purpose.** Acquiring a 30 m corridor while the land is agricultural costs a fraction of acquiring 10 m more once buildings line the road. **Every road where this was not done is now impossible to widen at reasonable cost — a lesson visible in most Nepali towns.**

**The road hierarchy behind the numbers:**

| Class | Function |
|---|---|
| **National Highway (H)** | **Connects regions and international borders; the primary network** |
| **Feeder Road (F)** | **Connects district headquarters and important centres TO the highway network** ← |
| **District Road (D)** | Within a district, connecting rural areas to feeder roads |
| **Village Road (V)** | **Local access; the lowest class** |

> **A feeder road "feeds" the highway network** — that is the mnemonic and it also explains the width: it carries district-level traffic and is a realistic candidate for future upgrading, so the reserve is generous.

**The related widths, since they are asked alongside:**

| Element | Typical NRS value |
|---|---|
| **Carriageway, single lane** | **3.75 m** |
| **Carriageway, intermediate lane** | 5.5 m |
| **Carriageway, two lane** | **7.0 m** |
| **Shoulder** | 1.0-2.5 m by class |
| **Camber, bituminous surface** | **2.0-2.5 %** |
| Camber, gravel | 3.0-4.0 % |

> **Do not confuse the right of way with the FORMATION WIDTH or the carriageway width** — the three are nested, and each question names one specifically. **Reading which one is asked is half the mark.**

examTip.trick: **Memorise the block: 50 / 30 / 20 / 15 m** for National Highway / Feeder / District / Village. The numbers are unguessable otherwise and one of them is asked every sitting.
examTip.trap: **Right of way is not the carriageway or the formation** — the three are nested and each question names one specifically. A feeder road's 5.5 m carriageway sits inside a 30 m right of way.
examTip.mnemonic: **A feeder road "feeds" the highway network.** The wide reserve exists for FUTURE WIDENING — buy the corridor while the land is farmland, because once buildings line the road it cannot be afforded.

questions.stem: When bleaching powder is added to water, its pH value:
questions.solution:
**Increases.**

**The chemistry:**

> **Bleaching powder is calcium hypochlorite, Ca(OCl)₂**, containing about 30-35 per cent available chlorine.

> **It is a CALCIUM salt of a weak acid (hypochlorous acid), so it hydrolyses to give an ALKALINE solution:**

> **Ca(OCl)₂ + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + 2HOCl**

> **The calcium hydroxide raises the pH.** Bleaching powder solution is typically pH 10.5 to 11.

> **So adding bleaching powder RAISES the pH.**

**The contrast that makes this worth testing — chlorine gas does the opposite:**

| Chlorinating agent | Effect on pH | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Chlorine gas, Cl₂** | **LOWERS pH** | **Cl₂ + H₂O → HOCl + HCl — hydrochloric acid is produced** |
| **Bleaching powder, Ca(OCl)₂** | **RAISES pH** | **Releases Ca(OH)₂ — a base** ← |
| **Sodium hypochlorite, NaOCl** | **RAISES pH** | Releases NaOH |

> **That is the whole point of the question: the same disinfectant element, opposite pH effects, depending on the compound it is delivered in.** Gas acidifies; the hypochlorite salts alkalise.

**Why the pH matters so much in disinfection — this is the substantive engineering:**

> **Chlorine in water exists as two species in equilibrium:**

> **HOCl ⇌ H⁺ + OCl⁻**

| Species | Disinfecting power |
|---|---|
| **HOCl (hypochlorous acid)** | **80 to 100 times MORE effective** |
| **OCl⁻ (hypochlorite ion)** | Much weaker |

> **The split is governed by pH**, with the changeover around pH 7.5:

| pH | Dominant species | Disinfection |
|---|---|---|
| **< 7.5** | **HOCl predominates** | **STRONG** |
| 7.5 | About 50:50 | Moderate |
| **> 8.5** | **OCl⁻ predominates** | **WEAK** |

> **So raising the pH weakens the disinfection**, and this is the practical consequence of using bleaching powder rather than gas: **at high pH the same residual chlorine kills far less.**

> **Disinfection is therefore most effective at a LOWER pH**, and where the raw water is already alkaline the dose must be increased or the contact time extended. **Recommended practice keeps the pH below about 8 for effective chlorination.**

**Why option (d) is the closest distractor:**

> **"Depends on characteristics of water" is superficially attractive** because the *magnitude* of the pH change certainly depends on the water's buffering capacity — a hard, well-buffered water will shift less than a soft one.

> **But the DIRECTION does not depend on it.** Adding a base raises the pH of any water; only the size of the rise varies. **The question asks what happens to the pH, not by how much**, so (b) is right and (d) is a hedge.

**And a practical note on bleaching powder:** **it is unstable, losing available chlorine on storage — roughly 1 to 5 per cent a month, faster in heat and damp.** So the dose must be based on a fresh determination of available chlorine, not on the nominal 30-35 per cent. **Assuming the label figure on old stock is a common cause of under-dosing and of an outbreak that the plant records show as adequately chlorinated.**

examTip.trick: **Bleaching powder releases Ca(OH)₂ — a base — so pH RISES** (to about 10.5-11). But **chlorine GAS gives HCl and LOWERS pH.** Same element, opposite effects.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) hedges.** Water characteristics affect the SIZE of the pH change, not its DIRECTION. Adding a base raises the pH of any water.
examTip.mnemonic: **HOCl is 80-100× stronger than OCl⁻**, and the split turns at pH 7.5 — so raising the pH WEAKENS disinfection. Keep pH below about 8 for effective chlorination.

questions.stem: In what direction does the buoyant force on an object immersed in a liquid act?
questions.solution:
**Vertically upward.**

**Why upward — the reason is the pressure gradient:**

> **Pressure in a fluid at rest increases with depth: p = ρgh.**

> **So the pressure on the BOTTOM of a submerged body is greater than on its TOP**, because the bottom is deeper.

> **The net pressure force is therefore upward**, and its magnitude is the difference — which works out to the weight of the fluid displaced.

> **ARCHIMEDES' PRINCIPLE: F_B = ρ_fluid × g × V_displaced**, acting vertically upward through the centroid of the displaced volume.

> **The horizontal pressure forces cancel**, because at any given depth the pressure is the same on both sides — which is why the resultant is purely vertical.

**The two centres, and the distinction is the whole of stability theory:**

| Point | Definition |
|---|---|
| **CENTRE OF GRAVITY (G)** | **Centroid of the BODY's mass — where the weight acts** |
| **CENTRE OF BUOYANCY (B)** | **Centroid of the DISPLACED FLUID — where the buoyant force acts** |

> **They coincide only if the body is of uniform density and fully submerged.** For a floating body they never coincide, and their relative position decides whether the body is stable.

| Case | Condition for stability |
|---|---|
| **Fully submerged body** | **B ABOVE G** |
| **Floating body** | **METACENTRE M above G** (B may be below G) |

> **The floating case is the subtle one**: a ship's centre of buoyancy is well below its centre of gravity, yet it is stable — because when it heels, B shifts sideways and the metacentre M ends up above G, generating a righting moment.

**The three floating conditions:**

| Relation | Result |
|---|---|
| **Weight > buoyancy at full submergence** | **SINKS** |
| **Weight = buoyancy at full submergence** | **Neutrally buoyant — floats at any depth** |
| **Weight < buoyancy at full submergence** | **FLOATS, displacing only part of its volume** |

> **A floating body displaces fluid of weight exactly equal to its own weight** — which is why a steel ship floats: the hull encloses enough air that the *average* density is below water's.

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Vertically downward** | **That is the WEIGHT, not the buoyant force** — the two oppose |
| **Towards centre** | **Confuses buoyancy with a central/gravitational attraction** — buoyancy has no such tendency |
| **Anywhere** | **A resultant pressure force in a fluid at rest can only be vertical**, since horizontal components cancel at equal depth |

> **Option (c) is the interesting distractor** because it sounds like it invokes the earth's centre. **But the direction of buoyancy is set by the pressure gradient, which is itself vertical** — so buoyancy is *anti-parallel* to gravity, not directed toward any centre.

**Where buoyancy governs civil engineering design, since the question looks abstract:**

> **UPLIFT on a submerged or below-water-table structure is buoyancy**, and it is a routine cause of failure.

| Situation | The buoyancy problem |
|---|---|
| **Empty underground water tank, high water table** | **FLOATS UP and cracks — check uplift with the tank EMPTY** |
| **Basement raft below the water table** | Net uplift must be resisted by weight or anchors |
| **Buried pipeline in saturated soil** | Empty pipe can float; needs anchor blocks |
| **Caisson or well foundation during sinking** | Buoyancy reduces the effective sinking weight |
| **Gravity dam** | **Uplift under the base reduces the effective weight and the FOS against overturning** |

> **The empty-tank case is the classic examination and site error**: the tank is checked full, when the critical case is empty and the ground saturated. **A structure must be checked in every state it will pass through, not only its service state.**

examTip.trick: **Pressure rises with depth, so the bottom is pushed harder than the top** — the resultant is upward and equals the weight of fluid displaced. Horizontal components cancel at equal depth.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) "towards centre" invokes the wrong physics.** Buoyancy is set by the vertical pressure gradient, so it is anti-parallel to gravity, not directed at any centre.
examTip.mnemonic: **Check an underground tank for uplift EMPTY, not full** — the empty tank in saturated ground floats and cracks. Buoyancy is the uplift term in basements, buried pipes and dam bases alike.

questions.stem: Which of the following is called an inverted siphon?
questions.solution:
**Depressed sewer.**

**What a depressed sewer is:**

> **A depressed sewer is a length of sewer dropped BELOW the normal grade line to pass under an obstruction** — a stream, a subway, a large pipe, a depression in the ground.

> **It runs FULL and under PRESSURE**, unlike an ordinary sewer which flows partly full by gravity.

> **It is called an "inverted siphon" because the profile looks like a siphon turned upside down** — dipping down where a siphon rises up.

**Why the name is technically wrong, and the source states the distinction:**

| | **TRUE SIPHON** | **INVERTED SIPHON (depressed sewer)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Profile** | **Rises above the hydraulic grade line** | **Dips BELOW it** |
| **Hydraulic gradient line** | **BELOW the flow line (pipe)** | **ABOVE the flow line** |
| **Pressure in the pipe** | **NEGATIVE — below atmospheric** | **POSITIVE — above atmospheric** |
| **Needs priming?** | **Yes** | **No** |

> **A true siphon works on negative pressure and must be primed; a depressed sewer works on positive pressure and never needs priming.** They are hydraulically opposite, which is why the name is a misnomer that has simply stuck.

> **"Depressed sewer" is the correct term, and modern texts prefer it.**

**The design problem a depressed sewer creates, and why it is disliked:**

> **It cannot be self-cleansing at low flow.** An ordinary sewer is sized so that the velocity at the minimum flow still reaches about 0.6 m/s and scours the invert. **A depressed sewer runs full at every flow, so the velocity falls with the discharge** — and at night flow it may drop far below self-cleansing.

> **Silt and grit then settle in the low point, exactly where they cannot be reached.**

**The standard remedy:**

| Measure | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **TWO OR MORE PARALLEL BARRELS of different size** | **Small barrel takes dry-weather flow at scouring velocity; larger ones cut in as flow rises** ← the key device |
| **Inlet chamber with a weir arrangement** | Distributes flow between barrels automatically |
| **Design velocity at least 0.9-1.2 m/s** | Higher than an ordinary sewer, to compensate |
| **Inlet and outlet chambers with access** | So each barrel can be rodded and flushed |
| **Provision for flushing** | Because settlement is inevitable |

> **The multiple-barrel arrangement is the answer to the low-flow problem**, and it is what distinguishes a properly designed depressed sewer from a pipe simply dipped under a river.

**Why the distractors are wrong — each names a sewer classified by its POSITION IN THE NETWORK, not by its profile:**

| Option | What it is |
|---|---|
| **LATERAL sewer** | **The smallest — collects from individual house connections** |
| **Main / branch sewer** | **Receives several laterals** |
| **TRUNK sewer** | The largest, receiving mains |
| **OUTFALL sewer** | **Carries the whole flow from the network to the treatment works or disposal point** |

> **These four form a size hierarchy: lateral → branch/main → trunk → outfall.** A depressed sewer is not a member of that hierarchy at all — **it is a length of ANY of them that happens to dip under an obstruction.** So the question is testing whether the candidate reads the classification correctly, and the four options are deliberately drawn from two different classification schemes.

examTip.trick: **A true siphon RISES above the hydraulic grade line and runs at negative pressure; a depressed sewer DIPS below it and runs at positive pressure.** Hydraulically opposite — the name "inverted siphon" is a misnomer that stuck.
examTip.trap: **Lateral, main and outfall classify a sewer by POSITION IN THE NETWORK; depressed classifies it by PROFILE.** The options are drawn from two different schemes on purpose.
examTip.mnemonic: **It runs full at every flow, so velocity falls with discharge and it cannot be self-cleansing** — hence TWO OR MORE PARALLEL BARRELS of different size, the small one scouring at dry-weather flow.

questions.stem: Building material made from rock is:
questions.solution:
**Stone.**

**The distinction the question is drawing:**

> **Stone is rock.** It is quarried, dressed and used — **its mineral structure is unchanged from the rock mass it came out of.** No manufacture, no chemical transformation.

> **That is what "made from rock" means in the strict sense the question intends: a NATURAL building material.**

**Why the distractors are wrong, and each for a different reason:**

| Option | Made from | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **Brick** | **CLAY — a soil, moulded and BURNT at 900-1200 °C** | **Not rock. Clay is a weathering product, and firing changes it chemically** |
| **Cement** | **Limestone and clay, CALCINED at about 1450 °C** | **Limestone IS a rock — but the product is a manufactured chemical, not the rock** |
| **All of these** | — | **Requires all three to be rock; brick disqualifies it outright** |

> **Option (c) cement is the genuinely arguable one, and worth taking seriously.** Its principal raw material is limestone, which is a rock. **But calcination decomposes the limestone (CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂) and the clinker minerals formed are new compounds that do not exist in the parent rock.** Cement is a manufactured product whose raw material is rock — not a material *made from* rock in the sense of stone.

> **The test that separates them cleanly: could you recover the original rock? For stone, you never left it. For cement, the chemistry is irreversible.**

**Natural versus artificial building materials:**

| Natural (used as found) | Artificial (manufactured) |
|---|---|
| **Stone** | **Brick** |
| **Timber** | **Cement, concrete** |
| **Sand, gravel, natural aggregate** | **Steel, glass, plastics** |
| Clay, lime (raw) | **Lime and cement after burning** |
| Bitumen (natural asphalt) | **Refined bitumen, tiles, blocks** |

> **The classification matters more than it looks: natural materials vary from source to source and must be TESTED batch by batch**, while manufactured materials are made to a specification and can be accepted on a certificate. **That difference drives the whole quality-control regime for each.**

**Since stone is the answer, the rock classification worth knowing:**

| Class | Formation | Building examples |
|---|---|---|
| **IGNEOUS** | **Solidified magma** | **Granite, basalt, trap** |
| **SEDIMENTARY** | **Deposited and compacted** | **Sandstone, limestone, shale** |
| **METAMORPHIC** | **Altered by heat and pressure** | **Marble (from limestone), slate (from shale), quartzite, gneiss** |

> **The metamorphic pairs are the ones examined: limestone → marble, shale → slate, sandstone → quartzite, granite → gneiss.**

**And the requirements of a good building stone, since they follow directly:**

| Property | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Crushing strength** | **Not less than about 100 N/mm² for structural work** |
| **Water absorption** | **Below 5 % — high absorption means frost and salt damage** |
| **Appearance and texture** | Uniform, fine-grained, free of cracks and cavities |
| **Durability, hardness, toughness** | Resists weathering and abrasion |
| **Dressing** | Should work easily without shattering |

> **Water absorption is the most diagnostic single test for durability**, because almost every mechanism that destroys stone — freezing, salt crystallisation, chemical attack — needs water to get inside it first.

examTip.trick: **Stone IS rock — quarried and dressed, chemically unchanged.** Brick is burnt clay; cement is calcined limestone, a manufactured chemical. Only stone is used as found.
examTip.trap: **Cement is the arguable distractor** — its raw material IS a rock. But calcination is irreversible and the clinker minerals do not exist in limestone. The test: could you recover the parent rock?
examTip.mnemonic: **Natural materials must be TESTED batch by batch; manufactured ones can be accepted on a certificate.** And **water absorption below 5%** is the single most diagnostic durability test for stone.

questions.stem: Nepal Engineering Council is:
questions.solution:
**An autonomous body.**

**What the Nepal Engineering Council is:**

> **The NEC was constituted under the NEPAL ENGINEERING COUNCIL ACT, 2055 BS (1998 AD)** as an **AUTONOMOUS and corporate body**, with perpetual succession and its own seal, able to sue and be sued in its own name.

> **Autonomous means it is created BY statute and governs itself under that statute**, rather than being a department of a ministry taking instructions through the civil service chain.

> **It is a statutory regulator — the standard model for a professional council worldwide.**

**Why autonomy is essential to what a council does, and this is the substance of the question:**

> **The council's central function is to decide who may practise engineering and to remove those who practise it badly.**

> **Both decisions must be made on PROFESSIONAL grounds and must be seen to be free of political direction.**

> **A regulator that could be instructed whom to license, or whom not to discipline, would be worthless** — its register would carry no information. **Autonomy is therefore not a privilege granted to the profession but the condition on which the register means anything.**

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

| Option | Why not |
|---|---|
| **Government body** | **The NEC is not a ministry department.** Its members are not civil servants, and it is not funded from the ordinary budget line — it raises its own fees |
| **NGO** | **An NGO is a PRIVATE, voluntary association with no statutory powers.** The NEC's powers to license and to discipline exist only because an Act granted them |
| **None of these** | Autonomous is a recognised category and is the correct one |

> **The government/autonomous distinction is the one worth getting right**, and the test is simple: **a government body exercises the government's own authority through the executive; an autonomous body exercises authority granted directly to it by statute.**

> **The link to government is real but limited: the Government of Nepal APPROVES the council's rules and regulations, and appoints some members.** That is oversight, not control of day-to-day decisions — and it is why the previous question in this paper about who approves the rules has a different answer from this one.

**The council's principal functions:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **REGISTRATION of engineers** | **Maintaining the register — the core function** |
| **The LICENSE EXAMINATION** | **The gate to registration for graduate engineers** |
| **Recognition of academic qualifications** | Which degrees qualify; inspecting institutions |
| **CODE OF ETHICS and professional conduct** | Setting standards of practice |
| **DISCIPLINARY action** | **Warning, suspension or removal from the register** |
| Advising government | On engineering education and practice |

> **The register is the instrument through which every other function operates.** Recognition of a degree matters because it leads to the register; the code of ethics matters because breach of it leads to removal from the register. **The council's real power is the power to strike a name off.**

**And the practical consequence:** **an unregistered person may not practise as an engineer or use the title**, and signing drawings or certifying work without registration is an offence under the Act. **That is why the license examination exists and why it matters.**

examTip.trick: **AUTONOMOUS body, constituted under the Nepal Engineering Council Act 2055.** Created by statute and governing itself under that statute — the standard model for a professional regulator.
examTip.trap: **Government body versus autonomous body is the discrimination.** A government body exercises the executive's authority; an autonomous body exercises authority granted directly to it by an Act.
examTip.mnemonic: **Autonomy is the condition on which the register means anything** — a regulator that could be told whom to license would produce a register carrying no information. Its real power is the power to strike a name off.

questions.stem: The height of the headlight above the road surface is:
questions.solution:
**0.75 m.**

**The three standard sight-distance heights, which must be held together:**

| Height | Value | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| **DRIVER'S EYE above road** | **1.2 m** | **Stopping and overtaking sight distance** |
| **OBJECT height above road** | **0.15 m** | **Stopping sight distance** |
| **HEADLIGHT height above road** | **0.75 m** | **VALLEY (sag) curve design at night** ← |
| Oncoming vehicle height | 1.2 m | Overtaking sight distance |

> **1.2 / 0.15 / 0.75 is the set to memorise**, and each is used in a different formula. **Substituting the wrong one is the standard error in this topic.**

> **The headlight beam is also taken to spread 1° upward from the axis**, which is the second number in the sag-curve formula.

**Why the headlight height matters only for VALLEY curves — this is the reasoning:**

| Curve | The night-time problem |
|---|---|
| **SUMMIT (crest) curve** | **NONE — the road surface itself blocks the line of sight, and it does so equally by day and night. Daytime sight distance governs** |
| **VALLEY (sag) curve** | **The headlight beam shines UP into the air as the vehicle enters the dip, so the lit length of road ahead is shortened. NIGHT governs** ← |

> **That asymmetry is the key idea.** On a crest, sight distance is limited by the pavement; at night the headlights still light whatever the driver could have seen. **On a sag, the driver can see plenty by day — the limitation appears only in the dark, when the visible road is whatever the beam happens to fall on.**

> **So a valley curve is designed for HEADLIGHT SIGHT DISTANCE**, and the governing criterion is that the beam must reach at least the stopping sight distance ahead.

**The four criteria for a valley curve, in the order they are checked:**

| Criterion | Note |
|---|---|
| **HEADLIGHT sight distance** | **Usually GOVERNS** ← |
| **Comfort (centrifugal acceleration)** | Rate of change of grade limited, typically 0.6 m/s³ |
| **Drainage** | The low point must drain |
| **General appearance** | Smooth profile |

> **Headlight sight distance almost always governs the length**, so it is the calculation to do first.

**And for a summit curve, by contrast, the governing criteria are:**

> **Stopping sight distance (minimum), or overtaking/intermediate sight distance where overtaking must be provided** — using eye 1.2 m and object 0.15 m, both daytime values.

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **0.3 m** | No standard height; too low for any vehicle's lamps |
| **0.5 m** | Plausible-looking but not the standard value |
| **0.75 m** | ✓ |
| **1 m** | **Close to the DRIVER'S EYE height of 1.2 m — the trap for anyone who conflates the two** |

> **Option (d) is the designed trap**: a candidate who remembers only "about a metre" reaches for it, having confused the eye height with the lamp height. **The lamp is well below the eye, which is exactly why the beam and the line of sight differ and why the sag curve needs its own criterion.**

**A note on the physical reality behind the figure:** **0.75 m is a design abstraction, not a measurement of any particular car.** Real headlamp heights range from about 0.6 m on a low car to over 1 m on a truck. **The standard picks a value that is safe for the common case and then relies on the 1° upward beam spread to cover the spread of real vehicles.**

examTip.trick: **Memorise the set 1.2 / 0.15 / 0.75 m** — driver's eye, object, headlight. Each belongs to a different formula, and substituting the wrong one is the standard error here.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) 1 m is the trap** — it is near the DRIVER'S EYE height of 1.2 m. The lamp sits well below the eye, which is precisely why a sag curve needs its own criterion.
examTip.mnemonic: **Headlight height matters only for VALLEY curves.** On a crest the pavement blocks sight equally day and night; in a sag the beam shines up into the air, so NIGHT governs. Plus a 1° upward beam spread.

questions.stem: Khosla's theory can be used for calculating which of the following?
questions.solution:
**Uplift pressure and exit gradient.**

**What Khosla's theory does:**

> **It gives the flow pattern BELOW the impervious floor of a hydraulic structure founded on permeable soil**, by treating the seepage as potential flow and solving it with the theory of complex variables.

> **From that flow pattern two design quantities follow directly:**

| Quantity | What it decides |
|---|---|
| **UPLIFT PRESSURE under the floor** | **The THICKNESS of the floor** — it must be heavy enough not to be lifted |
| **EXIT GRADIENT at the downstream end** | **Safety against PIPING** — the depth of the downstream cut-off |

> **Those are the two things the theory is for, and they are exactly what option (a) names.**

**Why Khosla superseded Bligh, and this is the substance of the topic:**

| | **BLIGH'S CREEP THEORY** | **KHOSLA'S THEORY** |
|---|---|---|
| **Assumption** | **Head is lost UNIFORMLY along the creep path** | **Solves the actual potential flow field** |
| **Vertical vs horizontal path** | **Treated as equally effective** | **VERTICAL cut-offs are FAR more effective** |
| **Basis** | Empirical | **Mathematical (conformal transformation)** |
| **Verdict** | Superseded — unsafe in places, wasteful in others | **Standard practice** |

> **Bligh's central error was treating a metre of vertical sheet pile as equal to a metre of horizontal floor.** Khosla showed vertical cut-offs are much more effective at killing the exit gradient — which is why modern weirs use **deep sheet-pile or concrete cut-offs at the ends rather than long horizontal aprons.**

> **And Khosla's second finding, from the Panjnad weir investigations, was that intermediate sheet piles are almost useless** — they lie in a region of low pressure gradient and do very little. **Only the END cut-offs earn their cost.** That single result changed weir design.

**How the theory is applied — the method of independent variables:**

> **A complex floor with several sheet piles is broken into a set of SIMPLE standard forms** (a straight horizontal floor with a pile at the upstream end, at the downstream end, or at an intermediate point), each of which has a closed-form solution.

> **The pressures from the simple forms are then CORRECTED for three effects:**

| Correction | For |
|---|---|
| **Mutual interference of piles** | One pile alters the field near another |
| **Thickness of the floor** | The solution is for a floor of zero thickness |
| **Slope of the floor** | Where the floor is not horizontal |

> **The corrections are applied with sign, and getting a sign wrong is the commonest arithmetic error in the method.**

**The exit gradient formula and its safe values:**

> **G_E = (H/d) × 1/(π√λ)**, where H is the head, d the depth of the downstream cut-off, and λ a function of the floor length to depth ratio.

| Soil | Safe exit gradient |
|---|---|
| **Shingle** | **1/4 to 1/5** |
| **Coarse sand** | **1/5 to 1/6** |
| **Fine sand** | **1/6 to 1/7** |

> **The finer the soil, the LOWER the permissible gradient**, because fine particles are lifted more easily. **Note that d appears in the denominator: the way to make a weir safe against piping is to drive the downstream cut-off DEEPER.**

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

> **Option (b), seepage pressure, is the closest and is worth a careful answer.** Uplift pressure *is* the seepage pressure acting on the underside of the floor, so the terms overlap. **But "seepage pressure" alone omits the exit gradient — and the exit gradient is the half of the output that prevents piping, which is the failure mode that destroys weirs.** Option (a) names both, so it is the fuller and correct answer.

> **Option (d), "all of the mentioned", would be right if (b) named something additional to (a).** It does not; it names a subset. **A candidate who reaches for "all of the above" without checking whether the options are independent is caught here.**

examTip.trick: **Khosla gives two outputs: UPLIFT PRESSURE (which sets the floor thickness) and EXIT GRADIENT (which sets the downstream cut-off depth against piping).**
examTip.trap: **"All of the mentioned" is wrong because option (b) is a SUBSET of (a), not an addition to it.** Check whether the options are independent before reaching for an all-of-the-above.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bligh treated vertical and horizontal creep as equal; Khosla showed vertical cut-offs dominate — and that INTERMEDIATE piles are nearly useless.** Only the END cut-offs earn their cost.

questions.stem: The relation between Manning's 'n' and Chezy's 'C' is given by (where R = hydraulic mean depth):
questions.solution:
**C = R^{1/6}/n.**

**The derivation, which is two lines:**

> **Manning:  V = (1/n) R^{2/3} S^{1/2}**

> **Chezy:  V = C √(RS) = C R^{1/2} S^{1/2}**

> **The same velocity, so equate them:**

> **C R^{1/2} S^{1/2} = (1/n) R^{2/3} S^{1/2}**

> **The S^{1/2} cancels on both sides — which is the point of the relation, since it means the equivalence holds at ANY slope:**

> **C = (1/n) R^{2/3 − 1/2} = (1/n) R^{1/6}**

> **C = R^{1/6}/n** ✓

> **The exponent is simply 2/3 − 1/2 = 4/6 − 3/6 = 1/6**, and that subtraction is the whole question.

**Why the two formulas differ at all:**

| | **CHEZY (1769)** | **MANNING (1889)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Form** | **V = C√(RS)** | **V = (1/n) R^{2/3} S^{1/2}** |
| **Roughness measure** | **C — not dimensionless, and it VARIES with R** | **n — nearly CONSTANT for a given surface** |
| **Practical value** | Historically first | **Preferred, because n can be tabulated** |

> **This is the real reason Manning displaced Chezy.** Since C = R^{1/6}/n, **Chezy's C depends on the hydraulic radius** — so a value of C measured in one channel cannot be carried to a channel of different size. **Manning's n can be, which is why every textbook table lists n and not C.**

| Surface | Manning's n |
|---|---|
| **Smooth cement plaster** | **0.010-0.013** |
| **Concrete lining** | **0.013-0.017** |
| **Brick lining** | 0.015 |
| **Earth channel, clean and straight** | **0.018-0.025** |
| **Earth channel, weedy or winding** | **0.025-0.040** |
| Natural stream with boulders | 0.040-0.070 |

> **0.013 for concrete and about 0.025 for a clean earth channel are the two values worth remembering** — most canal problems use one or the other.

**A dimensional note that explains why n looks odd:**

> **Manning's equation is NOT dimensionally homogeneous.** For it to give SI units, n carries dimensions of s/m^{1/3}.

> **This is why the numerical value of n differs between SI and FPS units**, and why the equation is sometimes written V = (1/n)R^{2/3}S^{1/2} in SI but V = (1.486/n)R^{2/3}S^{1/2} in feet and seconds. **Using an SI n in an FPS formula, or the reverse, is a factor-of-1.5 error.**

**Why the distractors are wrong, and a note on the printed options:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **R^{1/6}/n** | ✓ |
| **R^{2/3}/n** | **The Manning exponent used directly — the trap for anyone who forgets to subtract Chezy's 1/2** |
| **R^{1/3}/n** | **Would follow from 2/3 − 1/3, a slip in the subtraction** |

> **Option (b) is the designed trap**: 2/3 is the exponent a candidate has just been staring at in Manning's equation, so writing C = R^{2/3}/n feels natural. **The whole content of the question is remembering that Chezy already carries R^{1/2}, so only the DIFFERENCE remains.**

**And the definition, since the stem uses a loose term:** **R is the HYDRAULIC RADIUS — the wetted area divided by the wetted perimeter.** The stem calls it the "hydraulic mean depth", which is standard older usage for the same quantity. **For a wide rectangular channel R approaches the flow depth y, and that approximation is what makes wide-channel problems quick.**

verification.notes: Duplicate option removed. The source paper printed options (c) and (d) identically as R^(1/3)/n, leaving the question with only three distinct choices. Option (d) has been replaced with "None of the above". The keyed answer is unchanged - (a) R^(1/6)/n, which the source's own derivation confirms.

examTip.trick: **Equate the two velocities and the slope term cancels.** C R^{1/2} = (1/n) R^{2/3}, so the exponent is just 2/3 − 1/2 = **1/6**. That subtraction is the whole question.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) R^{2/3}/n is the trap** — it is the Manning exponent used directly. Chezy already carries R^{1/2}, so only the DIFFERENCE survives.
examTip.mnemonic: **C = R^{1/6}/n shows why Manning displaced Chezy: C depends on channel SIZE, n does not.** Which is why every table lists n — 0.013 concrete, 0.025 clean earth channel.

questions.stem: When was Pharping Hydropower established in Nepal?
questions.solution:
**1911.**

**The facts:**

> **Pharping (originally the Chandrajyoti Hydro-electric Power Station) was commissioned in 1911 AD (1968 BS)**, built under Prime Minister Chandra Shamsher Jang Bahadur Rana — whose name it carried.

> **It was inaugurated by King Prithvi Bir Bikram Shah on 22 May 1911**, marked by switching on lights at Tundikhel, Kathmandu.

> **Installed capacity 500 kW.** It is **the FIRST hydropower plant in Nepal and among the earliest in Asia.**

**Why the date is worth knowing beyond recall:**

> **1911 places Nepal remarkably early.** For comparison, the world's first hydroelectric plant was 1882 (Appleton, Wisconsin), and India's first was 1897 (Darjeeling). **Nepal was only fourteen years behind India and less than thirty years behind the world.**

> **The plant ran for decades and has been preserved as a LIVING MUSEUM** — much of the original equipment survives in place.

**Nepal's hydropower milestones, which is what the question is really sampling:**

| Year | Plant / event | Capacity |
|---|---|---|
| **1911** | **Pharping (Chandrajyoti) — the FIRST** | **500 kW** ← |
| 1936 | Sundarijal | 640 kW |
| 1965 | Panauti | 2.4 MW |
| **1967** | **Trishuli** | **21 MW** |
| 1982 | Devighat | 14.1 MW |
| **1985** | **Kulekhani I — Nepal's only STORAGE plant** | **60 MW** |
| **1995** | **Marsyangdi** | **69 MW** |
| **2002** | **Kali Gandaki A — the largest for many years** | **144 MW** |
| 2016 | Chameliya, Kulekhani III | — |
| **2021-22** | **Upper Tamakoshi — the largest to date** | **456 MW** |

> **Two entries carry engineering significance rather than mere size: Kulekhani is Nepal's ONLY reservoir (storage) plant**, every other being run-of-river; **and Upper Tamakoshi is the largest and was built substantially with domestic finance.**

> **The storage point is the one to hold onto.** Nepal's rivers carry far less water in the dry season than in the monsoon, so **a run-of-river plant's dry-season output collapses to a fraction of its installed capacity.** Only storage can move monsoon water into the winter, and Nepal has essentially one such plant — which is why winter load-shedding was a structural problem rather than a maintenance one.

**The potential figures, since they accompany this topic:**

| Figure | Value |
|---|---|
| **Theoretical potential** | **~83,000 MW** |
| **Technically feasible** | **~45,000 MW** |
| **Economically feasible** | **~42,000 MW** |

> **The 83,000 MW figure comes from Dr Hari Man Shrestha's 1966 doctoral study** and is quoted in almost every policy document since. **Note how little of it is developed** — which is the context in which the whole hydropower syllabus sits.

**Why the distractors are wrong:** **1907, 1915 and 1919 are near dates with no standing.** The question tests a single recalled fact, and **the anchor to fix is 1911, 500 kW, Pharping, Chandra Shamsher.**

examTip.trick: **1911, Pharping (Chandrajyoti), 500 kW, under Chandra Shamsher** — Nepal's first hydropower plant, and among the earliest in Asia.
examTip.trap: **Do not confuse it with Sundarijal (1936, 640 kW)**, the second plant, which is the other early name that appears in options.
examTip.mnemonic: **Kulekhani (60 MW) is Nepal's ONLY storage plant** — everything else is run-of-river, whose dry-season output collapses. That single fact explains why winter shortage was structural, not a maintenance failure.

questions.stem: The unconfined compression test is carried out on:
questions.solution:
**Clay.**

**Why the test only works on clay:**

> **In an unconfined compression test the sample stands UNSUPPORTED — the confining pressure is zero — and is loaded axially until it fails.**

> **That is only possible if the sample can stand up by itself, which requires COHESION.**

> **A sand or gravel sample with no confining pressure simply collapses into a heap** before any load can be applied. It has friction but no cohesion, and friction needs confinement to mobilise.

> **So the test is restricted to SATURATED COHESIVE soils — clays.** For those the apparent angle of shearing resistance φ_u is taken as zero, and the whole strength is cohesion.

**The result and how it is read:**

> **With σ₃ = 0 and σ₁ = q_u (the unconfined compressive strength), the Mohr circle passes through the origin.**

> **For φ_u = 0 the failure envelope is horizontal, so:**

> **c_u = q_u / 2**

> **The UNDRAINED COHESION IS HALF THE UNCONFINED COMPRESSIVE STRENGTH.** That one relation is the whole output of the test and is asked constantly.

**Consistency classified from q_u — the field correlation worth knowing:**

| Consistency | q_u (kN/m²) | Field identification |
|---|---|---|
| **Very soft** | **< 25** | **Squeezes between the fingers** |
| **Soft** | 25-50 | Easily moulded by the fingers |
| **Medium** | 50-100 | Moulded by strong finger pressure |
| **Stiff** | 100-200 | **Indented by the thumb** |
| **Very stiff** | 200-400 | Indented by the thumbnail |
| **Hard** | **> 400** | Difficult to indent at all |

> **These are useful precisely because they can be applied on site with no equipment**, and a borehole log that disagrees with the driller's fingers deserves a second look.

**Why option (a) silt is the closest distractor, and it deserves care:**

> **Silt occupies the boundary.** A saturated, plastic silt has some apparent cohesion and can sometimes be tested; a non-plastic rock-flour silt cannot stand unsupported at all.

> **So the honest position is that the test applies to CLAYS reliably and to plastic silts marginally.** The question asks for the soil the test is *carried out on*, and the standard answer — the one every code and text gives — is clay. **Option (c) is right; option (a) is right only in a qualified way that the question does not offer.**

**How the test sits among the shear tests:**

| Test | Confinement | Drainage | Suits |
|---|---|---|---|
| **UNCONFINED compression** | **None** | Undrained | **Saturated clay only — quick and cheap** |
| **Direct shear (box shear)** | Normal stress applied | Drained | **Sand and gravel** |
| **TRIAXIAL (UU, CU, CD)** | **Controlled cell pressure** | **Controlled** | **Any soil — the reference test** |
| **VANE shear (field)** | In situ | Undrained | **SOFT clay in situ** |

> **The triaxial test is the general one and the unconfined test is its degenerate case with σ₃ = 0.** So the unconfined test gives one point where the triaxial gives an envelope — which is its limitation and the reason it is used for classification and quick checks rather than for design of anything important.

> **And its practical value is speed: minutes rather than days**, on a sample straight from the tube. **For a preliminary assessment of a clay site that is often exactly what is wanted.**

examTip.trick: **The sample must stand unsupported, which needs COHESION.** Sand and gravel collapse into a heap with no confinement — friction needs confinement to mobilise. So: clay.
examTip.trap: **Silt is the boundary case** — plastic silt can sometimes be tested, non-plastic rock flour cannot stand at all. The standard answer every code gives is clay.
examTip.mnemonic: **c_u = q_u/2** — undrained cohesion is HALF the unconfined compressive strength, since σ₃ = 0 and φ_u = 0. That single relation is the test's whole output.

questions.stem: The minimum clear cover for a column is:
questions.solution:
**25 mm — but only under a stated exception, and the distinction is the whole question.**

**What IS 456:2000 clause 26.4.2.1 actually says:**

> **For a longitudinal reinforcing bar in a column, the nominal cover shall in no case be less than 40 mm, nor less than the diameter of the bar.**

> **EXCEPT: in columns of minimum dimension 200 mm or under, whose reinforcing bars do not exceed 12 mm, a nominal cover of 25 mm may be used.**

> **So the GENERAL requirement is 40 mm, and 25 mm is the ABSOLUTE MINIMUM permitted anywhere in a column.**

> **The stem asks for the MINIMUM, and 25 mm is the minimum. The keyed answer is right on the wording used.** But a candidate who reads the question as "the cover for a column" will answer 40 mm — and would be right on that reading.

**Read the stem carefully, because both numbers are correct answers to different questions:**

| Question asked | Answer |
|---|---|
| **"Nominal cover for a column"** | **40 mm** |
| **"MINIMUM clear cover for a column"** | **25 mm (small columns, bars ≤ 12 mm)** ← as keyed |
| "Cover for a column bar of 40 mm diameter" | **40 mm — never less than the bar diameter** |

> **This is the kind of question where the mark turns on one word.** The word is "minimum".

**The nominal cover table, since the whole set is examined:**

| Member | Nominal cover |
|---|---|
| **SLAB** | **15 mm (20 mm where bars exceed 12 mm)** |
| **BEAM** | **25 mm** |
| **COLUMN** | **40 mm** |
| **FOOTING** | **50 mm** |
| Foundation cast directly on soil | **75 mm** |

> **15 / 25 / 40 / 50 is the block to memorise**, and notice that options (b), (c) and (d) of this question are exactly the column, footing and cast-against-earth values — **the distractors are the neighbouring rows of the same table.**

**Why cover increases down that list — the logic, which makes the numbers memorable:**

> **Cover does two jobs: it protects the steel from CORROSION, and it gives the bar its BOND and FIRE resistance.**

> **The more aggressive the environment and the more critical the member, the more cover.** A slab is thin, indoors, and lightly stressed; a footing sits permanently in damp ground; concrete cast directly against earth cannot even be placed to an accurate line, so it gets 75 mm.

> **A column gets 40 mm rather than a beam's 25 mm because a column carries the whole structure above it** — corrosion of column steel is a collapse mechanism, not a serviceability defect.

**And the exposure adjustment, which overrides all of the above:**

| Exposure | Nominal cover | Minimum grade |
|---|---|---|
| **Mild** | **20 mm** | M20 |
| **Moderate** | **30 mm** | M25 |
| **Severe** | **45 mm** | M30 |
| **Very severe** | **50 mm** | M35 |
| **Extreme** | **75 mm** | **M40** |

> **Exposure class governs where it demands more.** So a column in a severe marine exposure takes 45 mm, not 40 — **cover is decided by the more demanding of the member requirement and the exposure requirement, never by the member alone.**

**The site reality worth stating:** **cover is the single most commonly mis-built dimension in RCC work**, because it depends on cover blocks being placed and staying in place while concrete is poured and vibrated. **Insufficient cover is the leading cause of premature reinforcement corrosion**, and unlike most design errors it cannot be corrected afterwards.

verification.notes: Answer keyed (a) 25 mm and the source's own explanation supports it: IS 456:2000 cl. 26.4.2.1 permits 25 mm in columns of minimum dimension 200 mm or under with bars not exceeding 12 mm, while the general nominal cover for a column is 40 mm. The stem's word "minimum" is what makes 25 mm correct; read as "nominal cover for a column" the answer would be 40 mm. The distinction is set out in full in the solution rather than smoothed over.

examTip.trick: **The word is "MINIMUM".** IS 456 cl. 26.4.2.1: general nominal cover for a column is 40 mm, but 25 mm is permitted in columns of minimum dimension ≤ 200 mm with bars ≤ 12 mm — so 25 mm is the minimum.
examTip.trap: **Options (b), (c) and (d) are the neighbouring rows of the same table** — column 40, footing 50, cast-against-earth 75. Learn the block 15 / 25 / 40 / 50 and the distractors become obvious.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cover is decided by the MORE DEMANDING of the member requirement and the EXPOSURE requirement** — a column in severe exposure takes 45 mm, not 40. And cover never goes below the bar diameter.

questions.stem: No tension should develop at the base of a rectangular well foundation or at any horizontal section within the well. For no tension at the base, the resultant of P (total active thrust) and W (weight of soil and well above the base) must pass through the middle:
questions.solution:
**Middle third of the base.**

**Where the middle-third rule comes from — it is one line of algebra:**

> **A resultant of magnitude R acting at eccentricity e from the centroid of a base of width b produces:**

> **σ = R/A ± (R·e)/Z**, where for a rectangular base of unit length Z = b²/6 and A = b.

> **σ = (R/b)(1 ± 6e/b)**

> **For no tension the minimum stress must be ≥ 0:**

> **1 − 6e/b ≥ 0  ⟹  e ≤ b/6**

> **An eccentricity of b/6 either side of the centre defines a band of total width b/3, centred on the base — THE MIDDLE THIRD.**

> **So "e ≤ b/6" and "the resultant falls in the middle third" are the same statement.** The first is what you compute; the second is what you say.

**The stress distribution as the resultant moves out:**

| Position of resultant | e | Base pressure |
|---|---|---|
| **At the centre** | **0** | **UNIFORM, R/b** |
| **Within the middle third** | **< b/6** | **Trapezoidal, all compression** |
| **At the edge of the middle third** | **= b/6** | **TRIANGULAR — zero at one edge, 2R/b at the other** |
| **Outside the middle third** | **> b/6** | **TENSION would be required at the far edge — so the base LIFTS and the contact area shrinks** |

> **Note what happens at e = b/6: the maximum pressure is 2R/b, exactly TWICE the uniform value.** So merely reaching the limit of the middle third has already doubled the peak bearing pressure — which is why the rule protects the soil as well as the joint.

**Why tension cannot be allowed, and this is the physical reason rather than a convention:**

> **A footing, a well kerb or a masonry joint cannot TRANSMIT TENSION.** There is no bond across the soil-concrete interface, and none across a mortar joint in the long term.

> **So if the analysis calls for tension, the base does not stretch — it SEPARATES.** The contact area reduces, the pressure on the remaining contact rises sharply, and the analysis that predicted the tension is no longer valid.

> **That is why "no tension" is a design requirement and not merely a preference: crossing it invalidates the calculation itself.**

**The same rule under three other names, all worth recognising:**

| Context | Statement of the same rule |
|---|---|
| **Well and shallow foundations** | **Resultant within the middle third of the base** ← |
| **Gravity retaining walls** | **Resultant within the middle third — no tension at the heel** |
| **Gravity dams** | **No tension at the heel with reservoir full; at the toe when empty** |
| **Masonry columns and chimneys** | **e ≤ b/6, the "rule of the middle third"** |
| **Circular base of diameter D** | **e ≤ D/8, not D/6 — the shape factor differs** |

> **The circular case is the one that catches people.** For a circle Z = πD³/32 and A = πD²/4, so the limit is **e ≤ D/8.** **The middle-third rule is specific to a RECTANGLE, and applying it to a circular well base is a real error.**

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Middle half** | **Would permit e = b/4, giving σ_min = (R/b)(1 − 1.5) — decidedly negative. Tension** |
| **Middle third** | ✓ |
| **Middle quarter** | **e ≤ b/8 — SAFE but unnecessarily strict; it is the CIRCULAR limit, misapplied** |
| **"Middle of the base"** | Means e = 0, uniform pressure — safe but a requirement no design could meet |

> **Option (c) is the interesting distractor**, because b/8 is a real limit — for a circular base. **A candidate who remembers both rules but not which shape each belongs to will pick between (b) and (c) at random.** Rectangle → third; circle → quarter (D/8 each side of centre).

examTip.trick: **σ = (R/b)(1 ± 6e/b), so no tension needs e ≤ b/6** — a band of total width b/3 about the centre. "e ≤ b/6" and "middle third" are the same statement.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) middle quarter is a REAL limit — for a CIRCULAR base (e ≤ D/8).** The middle-third rule belongs to a RECTANGLE. Applying one shape's rule to the other is a genuine error.
examTip.mnemonic: **At e = b/6 the peak pressure is already 2R/b — twice uniform.** And tension is barred not by convention but because a base that cannot pull SEPARATES, which invalidates the calculation itself.

questions.stem: In a two-dimensional flow, the components of the velocity along the X-axis and the Y-axis are u = ax² + bxy and v = cxy + dy². What should be the condition for the flow field to be continuous?
questions.solution:
**(2a+c)x + (b+2d)y = 0.**

**The continuity equation for two-dimensional incompressible flow:**

> **∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 0**

> **Note the pairing carefully: u is differentiated with respect to x, and v with respect to y.** Getting that wrong is the only way to fail this question.

**The differentiation:**

> **u = ax² + bxy**

> **∂u/∂x = 2ax + by**  (treat y as constant)

> **v = cxy + dy²**

> **∂v/∂y = cx + 2dy**  (treat x as constant)

> **Add them:**

> **(2ax + by) + (cx + 2dy) = 0**

> **Collect the x and y terms:**

> **(2a + c)x + (b + 2d)y = 0** ✓

**Where each distractor comes from — every one is a specific slip, which is what makes this a good question:**

| Option | The mistake that produces it |
|---|---|
| **(a+b)x + (c+d)y = 0** | **Differentiating nothing — just collecting the printed coefficients** |
| **(a+c)x + (b+d)y = 0** | **Dropping the factor 2 from BOTH squared terms** |
| **(2a+b)x + (c+2d)y = 0** | **Differentiating u by x but v by x as well — the wrong pairing** ← |
| **(2a+c)x + (b+2d)y = 0** | ✓ |

> **Option (c) is the designed trap and the most instructive.** It is what you get from ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂x, that is, from differentiating both components with respect to the same variable. **The whole content of the continuity equation is that each velocity component is differentiated along ITS OWN direction.**

**What the condition means physically:**

> **Continuity is CONSERVATION OF MASS.** For an incompressible fluid, whatever flows into an element must flow out of it, so the net rate of volume change is zero.

> **∂u/∂x is the rate at which the flow stretches in x; ∂v/∂y the rate in y.** If the flow stretches in one direction it must contract in the other by the same amount, or mass is being created.

> **Here the condition is not satisfied identically** — it holds only where (2a+c)x + (b+2d)y = 0, which is a straight line through the origin. **So the given field is NOT a valid incompressible flow everywhere; it is valid only along that line, unless the coefficients themselves satisfy 2a + c = 0 and b + 2d = 0.**

> **That second reading is the more useful one: for the field to be continuous EVERYWHERE, the coefficients must satisfy c = −2a and b = −2d.** The question as worded asks for the condition, and the expression is it.

**The full family, since the examiner may ask any member:**

| Case | Continuity equation |
|---|---|
| **2D incompressible, steady or unsteady** | **∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 0** |
| **3D incompressible** | **∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y + ∂w/∂z = 0** |
| **3D compressible, unsteady** | **∂ρ/∂t + ∂(ρu)/∂x + ∂(ρv)/∂y + ∂(ρw)/∂z = 0** |
| **Cylindrical, 2D axisymmetric** | ∂(r·v_r)/∂r + ∂(r·v_z)/∂z = 0 |

> **Note that the incompressible form has NO time term** — incompressibility makes the continuity equation a constraint on the velocity field at every instant, not an evolution equation. **Which is why an unsteady incompressible flow still satisfies exactly the same equation as a steady one.**

**And the companion test that is often asked alongside:** **a flow is IRROTATIONAL if ∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y = 0.** Continuity and irrotationality are independent conditions — **a flow can satisfy either, both, or neither**, and only a flow satisfying both admits a velocity potential as well as a stream function.

examTip.trick: **∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 0** — each component differentiated along ITS OWN direction. ∂u/∂x = 2ax + by, ∂v/∂y = cx + 2dy, giving (2a+c)x + (b+2d)y = 0.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) is what you get from ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂x** — differentiating both components with respect to x. The wrong pairing is the only way to fail this question.
examTip.mnemonic: **The incompressible continuity equation has NO time term** — incompressibility constrains the velocity field at every instant. So unsteady incompressible flow obeys exactly the same equation as steady.

questions.stem: Which type of open drain would be fully operative only in the rainy season?
questions.solution:
**Deep surface drains.**

**Why a deep surface drain is fully operative only in the rains:**

> **A deep surface drain does two jobs at once.** It carries the surface runoff delivered to it by the shallow drains, **and** it intercepts the sub-surface seepage water from the water table.

> **To take the seepage it is cut deep, and a CUNNETTE — a small subsidiary channel about 0.6 m deep — is formed along the centre of its bed.**

> **In the dry season only the seepage flows, and it is confined entirely within the cunnette.** The drain's main section carries nothing.

> **Only in the rains, when surface runoff arrives as well, does the full cross-section come into use.** Hence "fully operative only in the rainy season".

**Why the cunnette is there at all — it is a self-cleansing device:**

> **A large channel carrying a small flow runs at very low velocity and silts up.** The dry-season seepage spread thinly across a wide bed would deposit its load and choke the drain before the monsoon arrived.

> **Confining that small flow to a narrow deep cunnette keeps the velocity up and the channel scoured.**

> **The cunnette is LINED**, both to resist that higher velocity and to prevent weed growth — weeds in a drain bed are as effective an obstruction as silt.

> **This is the same design idea as the multiple barrels of a depressed sewer: give the small flow a small section so it keeps moving.**

**The drainage hierarchy, and how a system fits together:**

| Drain | Depth | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **Field / shallow surface drains** | **~0.5-1 m** | **Collect surface runoff from the fields; the finest network** |
| **DEEP surface drains (collector)** | **Deeper, with cunnette** | **Take runoff from shallow drains AND intercept sub-surface seepage** ← |
| **Main / outfall drain** | Deepest | Carries the whole flow to a river or natural depression |

> **Note that only the deep drain addresses the water table.** Shallow drains remove ponded water from the surface; **they do nothing about a high water table**, which is the actual cause of waterlogging and of salinity.

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Shallow surface drains** | **Operate whenever there is surface runoff, and carry nothing otherwise — they are not "partly operative", they are simply empty or full** |
| **FRENCH drains** | **NOT OPEN DRAINS AT ALL — a trench filled with graded stone (with or without a perforated pipe), covered over. Sub-surface, and works continuously** ← the category error |
| **"Drains"** | Not a class of anything |

> **Option (c) is worth separating properly, because the stem says "open drain" and a French drain is not one.** It is a **buried** drain: a stone-filled trench that conducts water through the voids between the stones. **It operates continuously, whenever there is water in the ground to conduct** — the opposite of a seasonal pattern.

> **So option (c) fails on two counts at once: wrong category (closed, not open) and wrong behaviour (continuous, not seasonal).**

**The problem all of this is solving — waterlogging:**

> **Waterlogging is the rise of the water table into the ROOT ZONE**, and it is caused most often by **seepage from unlined canals and over-irrigation** — that is, by the irrigation system itself.

| Consequence | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Roots suffocate** | **Air is displaced from the soil pores; roots need oxygen** |
| **SALINITY** | **Capillary rise brings dissolved salts up; evaporation leaves them at the surface** ← the permanent damage |
| Soil temperature falls | Delays germination |
| Cultivation impeded | Machinery cannot work saturated ground |

> **Salinity is the consequence that outlasts the drainage problem.** Water can be drained away in a season; **the salt left behind by years of capillary rise requires leaching and gypsum treatment, and some land is simply lost.**

> **Which is why drainage is not an optional adjunct to an irrigation scheme but part of it.** An irrigation project without drainage raises the water table it created and eventually salinises the land it was built to water — **a failure mode visible across large areas of the Indo-Gangetic plain.**

examTip.trick: **A deep surface drain carries seepage in the dry season and runoff as well in the rains.** The dry-season seepage is confined to the 0.6 m CUNNETTE, so only the monsoon brings the full section into use.
examTip.trap: **A French drain is not an open drain at all** — it is a buried stone-filled trench, and it works CONTINUOUSLY. Option (c) fails on both category and behaviour.
examTip.mnemonic: **The cunnette is a self-cleansing device** — a small flow in a big channel silts up, so confine it to a small lined section and keep the velocity up. Same idea as a depressed sewer's multiple barrels.

questions.stem: The most appropriate triaxial test to assess the long-term stability of an excavated clay slope is:
questions.solution:
**Consolidated drained (CD) test.**

**Why the drained test, and the reasoning is about TIME:**

> **The choice of triaxial test is decided by ONE question: will the pore pressures have dissipated by the time the critical loading occurs?**

| Timescale | Pore pressures | Test |
|---|---|---|
| **SHORT term (immediately after construction)** | **Have NOT dissipated — undrained** | **UU** |
| **LONG term (years later)** | **HAVE dissipated — drained** | **CD** ← |
| Intermediate / sudden change after consolidation | Partly dissipated | **CU** |
