> **The stem says LONG-TERM, so the answer is the drained test.** That is the whole logic, and it applies to every soil-mechanics test-selection question.

**Why an EXCAVATED slope is the classic long-term case — and this is the subtle part:**

> **Excavation UNLOADS the soil.** Removing the material above reduces the total stress, which generates **NEGATIVE excess pore pressures.**

> **A negative pore pressure means a HIGH effective stress and therefore HIGH strength — temporarily.**

> **As water is drawn in and the negative pressures dissipate, the effective stress FALLS and the strength FALLS with it.**

> **So a cut slope in clay is at its STRONGEST immediately after excavation and gets WEAKER with time.**

> **That is why cut slopes in clay fail years after they were made** — sometimes decades. The contractor leaves a stable slope; the failure belongs to the owner.

**Contrast with an EMBANKMENT, which is the mirror image:**

| | **CUT (excavation)** | **FILL (embankment on clay)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Total stress change** | **DECREASE** | **INCREASE** |
| **Excess pore pressure** | **NEGATIVE** | **POSITIVE** |
| **Strength immediately after** | **HIGH** | **LOW** |
| **Strength with time** | **FALLS** | **RISES** |
| **Critical case** | **LONG TERM — use CD** | **SHORT TERM — use UU** |

> **This pair is examined repeatedly and reasoned about rarely.** Fix it by remembering the sign of the total stress change, and everything else follows: **unloading gives suction which decays (getting worse), loading gives excess pressure which drains away (getting better).**

> **Hence: an embankment that survives its construction will survive; a cutting that survives its construction may not.**

**The three triaxial tests set out fully:**

| Test | Consolidation stage | Shear stage | Duration | Represents |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **UU (unconsolidated undrained)** | **Drainage NOT allowed** | **Drainage NOT allowed** | **5-10 minutes — the QUICK test** | **Rapid loading of low-permeability soil; end of construction** |
| **CU (consolidated undrained)** | **Drainage ALLOWED — consolidation occurs** | **Drainage NOT allowed** | Hours to days | **A soil consolidated under its load, then loaded suddenly — e.g. an earth dam on SUDDEN DRAWDOWN** |
| **CD (consolidated drained)** | **Drainage ALLOWED** | **Drainage ALLOWED, very slowly** | **The SLOW test — days to weeks** | **LONG-TERM stability; effective stress parameters c′ and φ′** ← |

> **The CD test is slow precisely because it must be**: the shear rate has to be slow enough that no excess pore pressure builds up at any stage, and in a clay that means weeks.

> **Its output is the EFFECTIVE STRESS parameters c′ and φ′**, which is what a long-term analysis needs. **CU with pore-pressure measurement gives the same parameters far faster, which is why it is the practical alternative** — but the question asks for the most appropriate test, and that is CD.

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Unconfined compression** | **Not a triaxial test at all** (σ₃ = 0), and gives only undrained strength |
| **Consolidated drained** | ✓ |
| **Unconsolidated undrained** | **Gives SHORT-term strength — the wrong end of the timescale** |
| **Consolidated undrained** | **The closest wrong answer: it gives effective parameters if pore pressure is measured, but the test itself is UNDRAINED and models a sudden change, not a long-term condition** |

> **Option (d) is the designed near-miss.** A candidate who remembers "consolidated" as the key word picks between (b) and (d) and must then decide on the second word. **The second word is the one that matters: DRAINED means long-term.**

examTip.trick: **One question decides every test-selection problem: have the pore pressures dissipated?** Long term = yes = DRAINED = CD. Short term = no = UU.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) CU is the near-miss** — "consolidated" is in both. The second word decides: DRAINED means long-term. CU models a sudden change after consolidation, such as sudden drawdown.
examTip.mnemonic: **A cut UNLOADS, giving suction that decays — so a clay cutting gets WEAKER with time. An embankment LOADS, and its excess pressure drains away — so it gets STRONGER.** Cut → long term critical; fill → short term.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not correct regarding CPM and PERT?
options: CPM and PERT use similar terminology but were developed independently
all of these statements are correct
questions.solution:
**"CPM is probabilistic in nature" is the incorrect statement.**

**The distinction:**

> **CPM is DETERMINISTIC. PERT is PROBABILISTIC.**

| | **CPM — Critical Path Method** | **PERT — Programme Evaluation and Review Technique** |
|---|---|---|
| **Time estimate** | **ONE duration per activity** | **THREE — optimistic, most likely, pessimistic** |
| **Nature** | **DETERMINISTIC** | **PROBABILISTIC** |
| **Orientation** | **ACTIVITY-oriented** | **EVENT-oriented** |
| **Suits** | **REPETITIVE work of known duration — construction** | **NOVEL work of uncertain duration — R&D, defence** |
| **Handles cost** | **YES — time-cost trade-off, crashing** | Not originally |
| **Developed** | **1957, DuPont (with Remington Rand)** | **1958, US Navy (Polaris programme)** |

> **The word "probabilistic" belongs to PERT alone**, and the question is testing exactly that one-word swap. **Option (a) states it correctly; option (b) is the same claim moved to the wrong method.**

**Why CPM can afford to be deterministic:**

> **It was built for CONSTRUCTION**, where the durations are known from experience. **How long to cast a slab of a given area is not a matter of speculation — a contractor has done it many times.**

> **PERT was built for the Polaris missile programme**, where many activities had never been performed by anyone. **A single duration estimate there would be a fiction, so three estimates and a distribution are honest about the uncertainty.**

> **So the difference is not one method being better but each matching its information.** Applying PERT's three estimates to routine concreting adds arithmetic and no knowledge; applying CPM's single estimate to genuine research understates the risk.

**The PERT arithmetic, since it is the examinable half:**

> **Expected time (beta distribution):**

> **t_e = (t_o + 4t_m + t_p) / 6**

> **Standard deviation:**

> **σ = (t_p − t_o) / 6**

> **Variance:  σ² = [(t_p − t_o)/6]²**

> **Along a path, VARIANCES add — never standard deviations:**

> **σ_path = √(Σσ²)**

> **That last point is the one most often got wrong.** Adding standard deviations overstates the spread badly; **it is the variances that are additive.**

> **The probability of completing by a date T is then read from the standard normal table with z = (T − T_e)/σ_path.**

**Why option (c) is correct, and therefore not the answer:**

> **CPM and PERT were indeed developed independently and almost simultaneously** — CPM at DuPont in 1957 for plant overhaul, PERT for the Navy in 1958 — **and they arrived at very similar network terminology by convergence rather than by borrowing.**

> **The two have since merged in practice.** Modern planning software offers PERT-style three-point estimates within an essentially CPM framework, and the term "CPM/PERT" is used for the combined technique. **So option (c) is a true statement, historically and practically.**

**Why option (d) is wrong:** it asserts all three are correct, which cannot stand once (b) is identified as false. **It is the standard "all of the above" that a candidate reaches for when unsure, and here it is simply the consequence of not spotting the swap in (b).**

**The vocabulary that both share, since option (c) refers to it:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **EST / EFT** | Earliest start / finish time (forward pass) |
| **LST / LFT** | Latest start / finish time (backward pass) |
| **TOTAL FLOAT** | **LFT − EFT: delay possible without delaying the PROJECT** |
| **FREE FLOAT** | Delay possible without delaying the FOLLOWING activity |
| **CRITICAL PATH** | **The longest path — and the path of ZERO total float** |
| Dummy activity | Shows dependence without consuming time or resource |

> **The critical path is the longest path through the network, and it is exactly the set of activities with zero float** — the two definitions are equivalent, and holding both makes most network questions immediate. **Its length is the shortest possible project duration**, which is the apparent paradox worth being comfortable with.

examTip.trick: **CPM is DETERMINISTIC; PERT is PROBABILISTIC.** The question is a one-word swap: option (a) states it correctly, option (b) moves it to the wrong method.
examTip.trap: **Along a path, VARIANCES add — never standard deviations.** σ_path = √(Σσ²). Adding standard deviations overstates the spread badly and is the commonest PERT error.
examTip.mnemonic: **CPM = DuPont 1957, construction, activity-oriented, handles cost. PERT = US Navy Polaris 1958, research, event-oriented, three estimates.** Each matches its information rather than being better.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a factor that affects compaction?
questions.solution:
**Texture of soil — as the standard list is written.**

**The four factors named in every text and in the source's own answer:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **WATER CONTENT** | **The dominant factor — dry density peaks at the OMC** |
| **COMPACTIVE EFFORT** | **More effort → higher max dry density and LOWER OMC** |
| **TYPE OF SOIL** | Gradation and plasticity govern the achievable density |
| **METHOD OF COMPACTION** | Kneading, rolling, impact and vibration give different results |
| **ADDITION OF ADMIXTURE** | Lime, cement, bitumen alter the compaction characteristics |

> **"Texture of soil" is not one of the standard headings — "TYPE of soil" is.** The question turns on that wording, and the source's own answer states it explicitly.

**Be clear about what is and is not being claimed here, because the distinction is a fine one:**

> **Soil TYPE demonstrably affects compaction**, and the standard list says so:

| Soil | Compaction behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Well-graded coarse soil with some fines** | **HIGHEST max dry density, LOW OMC** |
| **Excessive fines** | Max dry density decreases |
| **Poorly graded or uniform sand** | **LOWEST max dry density** |
| **Clay — density falls as plasticity rises** | **Heavy plastic clay: LOW max dry density, HIGH OMC** |
| Cohesive soils generally | High OMC |

> **In pedology, "texture" means the particle-size distribution — sand, silt and clay fractions — which is precisely what "type" covers.** On that reading texture *does* affect compaction, and the question would have no correct answer.

> **The question intends "texture" in the narrower sense of surface texture or feel**, distinct from gradation and plasticity, and on that reading it is genuinely not a listed factor. **The source is internally consistent, so the keyed answer stands** — but the discrimination is one of terminology rather than of physics, and it is worth saying so plainly rather than pretending the option is absurd.

**Why the other three are unambiguously factors:**

> **Water content (a) is the whole subject of the compaction curve.** Below the OMC the soil is too stiff to be worked into a dense state; above it, water occupies the space solids would have filled.

> **Method of compaction (a) — the source's own note is the useful one:** field compaction is kneading or rolling, laboratory compaction is dynamic impact, **so the laboratory test returns a HIGHER maximum dry density than a roller of nominally equivalent energy achieves.** That is why field compaction is specified as a percentage of the laboratory maximum rather than as an absolute density.

> **Admixtures (c) alter the soil itself** — lime flocculates a clay and raises its OMC; cement stiffens it. **This is the basis of soil stabilisation.**

**The compaction curve, which is the core of the topic:**

> **Plot dry density against water content and the result is a curve with a single peak.**

| Point | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **OMC — optimum moisture content** | **The water content at which max dry density is achieved** |
| **γ_d,max** | The peak dry density |
| **DRY side of optimum** | **Flocculated structure; higher strength, more brittle, prone to SWELLING** |
| **WET side of optimum** | **Dispersed structure; lower strength, more flexible, prone to SHRINKAGE** |
| **ZERO AIR VOIDS line** | **The theoretical S = 100% line — the curve can APPROACH but never reach it** |

> **The zero-air-voids line is the diagnostic check on any test result: a plotted point lying on or above it is an arithmetic error, not a very good result.**

> **And the dry-side/wet-side distinction has real design consequences.** A core for an earth dam is compacted slightly WET of optimum, to get a flexible, less permeable, non-cracking fill; **a road subgrade is compacted at or slightly dry of optimum for strength.** Same soil, different target, because the requirement differs.

**The two standard tests, since the numbers are examined:**

| Property | **IS Light (Standard Proctor)** | **IS Heavy (Modified)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Rammer weight** | **2.6 kg** | **4.9 kg** |
| **Height of fall** | **310 mm** | **450 mm** |
| **Layers** | **3** | **5** |
| **Blows per layer** | **25** | **25** |
| **Mould volume** | 1000 cc | 1000 cc |

> **Heavy compaction gives a HIGHER max dry density at a LOWER OMC** — the general rule that more effort shifts the peak up and to the left.

verification.notes: Keyed (b) and the source's own explanation states it: the standard list of factors is water content, compactive effort, TYPE of soil, method of compaction and addition of admixture, and the source concludes "the texture of the soil is not a factor that affects compaction". The discrimination is one of terminology - in the pedological sense texture means particle-size distribution, which is what "type" covers - and the solution says so explicitly rather than presenting the option as absurd.

examTip.trick: **The standard headings are water content, compactive effort, TYPE of soil, method of compaction, admixtures.** "Texture" is not one of them — the question turns on that single word.
examTip.trap: **In pedology "texture" means particle-size distribution, which IS what "type" covers.** The distinction here is terminology, not physics. Recognise it as a wording question and move on.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dam core: compact WET of optimum** (flexible, less permeable, does not crack). **Road subgrade: at or slightly DRY** (strength). Same soil, different target. And **no point can plot above the zero-air-voids line** — that is an arithmetic error.

questions.stem: The minimum diameter of a sewer generally adopted during design is:
questions.solution:
**150 mm.**

**Why there is a minimum at all — and it is not a hydraulic requirement:**

> **The hydraulic flow from a few houses would pass easily through a 100 mm pipe.** The minimum is set for reasons that have nothing to do with capacity.

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **BLOCKAGE by solids** | **Sewage carries rags, plastics, grit and other objects that no design anticipates. A 100 mm pipe blocks; a 150 mm pipe survives** ← the governing reason |
| **CLEANING and rodding** | Drain rods and cleaning equipment need the bore |
| **Manufactured sizes** | 150 mm is the smallest standard sewer size available |
| Tree roots and joint displacement | A larger bore tolerates more intrusion before blocking |

> **The controlling consideration is that a sewer must not block**, and the objects that block sewers are not proportional to the population served. **A lateral serving five houses meets the same rag as a trunk sewer does.**

> **So the minimum is set by what goes down the pipe, not by how much.**

**The available sizes, from the source's own note:**

> **150, 200, 300, 350, 400 mm and upward to about 1.6 m** — the standard commercial range.

> **Note that 250 mm is often skipped in practice**, the jump being from 200 to 300.

**The companion requirement — self-cleansing velocity — and the two must be satisfied together:**

| Velocity | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **MINIMUM (self-cleansing)** | **0.6-0.8 m/s** | **Below this, solids settle and the sewer silts up** |
| **MAXIMUM (non-scouring)** | **2.5-3.0 m/s** | **Above this, the invert erodes** |

> **A sewer must run FAST ENOUGH TO SCOUR at the minimum flow and SLOW ENOUGH NOT TO ERODE at the maximum.** Those two limits, plus the minimum diameter, are the three constraints of sewer design.

> **The tension between them is real and is the heart of the design problem**: the minimum diameter forces a large pipe on a small flow, and a large pipe on a small flow runs slowly. **Hence the slope of a small sewer is governed by the self-cleansing requirement, not by the ground profile** — a 150 mm sewer typically needs a gradient of about 1 in 150 to reach 0.6 m/s.

**Why sewers are designed to flow PARTLY FULL, since it follows:**

> **A sanitary sewer is designed to run at about half to three-quarters full at peak flow**, never full.

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **VENTILATION** | **The space above the water carries sewer gases away — essential, since H₂S is both corrosive and dangerous** |
| **Reserve for peak and future flow** | Flows are estimated, not known |
| **Free surface flow is stable** | A sewer running full becomes a pressure pipe, with surcharge risk at manholes |

> **The ventilation reason is the one to hold onto.** Hydrogen sulphide generated in stagnant sewage oxidises on the crown to sulphuric acid and destroys concrete pipes from the inside — **"crown corrosion"** — and a ventilated sewer with a scouring velocity is the defence against it.

**Interestingly, a sewer flowing at about 0.8 of full depth carries its MAXIMUM discharge:**

> **Because the wetted perimeter grows faster than the area as the pipe fills toward the crown**, the hydraulic radius peaks before the pipe is full. **Maximum velocity occurs at about 0.81 of the depth and maximum discharge at about 0.94** — so a sewer running full actually carries slightly LESS than one running nearly full. **A result that looks wrong and is not.**

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **100 mm** | **A house DRAIN size, not a public sewer — blocks too readily** ← the trap |
| **150 mm** | ✓ |
| **200 mm** | A standard size, but not the minimum |
| **300 mm** | Often the minimum for a *storm* sewer, where grit loads are higher — but not for a sanitary sewer |

> **Option (a) is the designed trap** because 100 mm *is* a real and common pipe size — **for the drain inside and immediately outside a building.** The distinction between a house drain and a public sewer is exactly what the question tests.

examTip.trick: **150 mm, and the reason is BLOCKAGE, not capacity.** The rags and grit that block sewers are not proportional to the population — a lateral meets the same rag as a trunk sewer.
examTip.trap: **100 mm is a real size — for a HOUSE DRAIN, not a public sewer.** That distinction is exactly what the question tests.
examTip.mnemonic: **Self-cleansing 0.6-0.8 m/s minimum, non-scouring 2.5-3.0 m/s maximum**, and design PARTLY FULL for ventilation — H₂S oxidising on the crown to sulphuric acid destroys concrete pipes from inside.

questions.stem: What is the formula for the velocity of the water jet at the inlet of a Pelton turbine? (H = net head acting on the Pelton wheel, Cv = coefficient of velocity of jet)
questions.solution:
**V = Cv √(2gH).**

**Where the formula comes from — it is Torricelli's result with a correction:**

> **Apply Bernoulli between the reservoir surface and the nozzle exit.** The whole net head H is converted to kinetic energy:

> **H = V²/2g  ⟹  V_theoretical = √(2gH)**

> **The actual jet is slightly slower because of friction in the penstock nozzle**, so a coefficient of velocity is applied:

> **V_actual = Cv √(2gH)**

> **For a well-designed Pelton nozzle Cv = 0.97 to 0.99** — the loss is small, which is why a Pelton nozzle is such an efficient device.

**Why the √(2gH) form is worth recognising instantly:**

> **Every free-discharge velocity in hydraulics has this form**, because they all come from converting a head to a velocity:

| Situation | Velocity |
|---|---|
| **Orifice under head H** | **Cv√(2gH)** |
| **Pelton jet from a nozzle** | **Cv√(2gH)** ← |
| Sluice outlet (free discharge) | Cd·A·√(2gH) for discharge |
| **Velocity of approach term** | **V²/2g is the head equivalent** |

> **√(2gH) is the velocity a body reaches falling freely through a height H** — which is the physical meaning, and why the factor 2 is there. **Dropping the 2, as option (a) does, is the same as forgetting that v² = 2gh.**

**Dimensional check, which settles the question without any theory:**

| Option | Dimensions | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **Cv√(gH)** | **√(m/s² · m) = m/s** ✓ | **Dimensionally OK — but the factor 2 is missing** |
| **Cv√(2gH)** | **m/s** ✓ | **Correct** |
| **2Cv√(2H)** | **√m — NOT a velocity** | **FAILS: g is missing entirely** |
| **2Cv·g·√H** | **m/s² · √m = m^{2.5}/s²** | **FAILS** |

> **Options (c) and (d) can be struck out on dimensions alone, in seconds.** That leaves a two-way choice on the factor 2 — **and dimensional analysis cannot settle a dimensionless factor, which is exactly why it must be remembered.**

**The Pelton design relations that go with it, since they are asked together:**

| Quantity | Relation |
|---|---|
| **Jet velocity** | **V = Cv√(2gH)** ← |
| **Bucket (peripheral) speed** | **u = φ√(2gH), with the speed ratio φ = 0.43-0.48** |
| **Ideal speed ratio** | **u = V/2 — half the jet speed** |
| **Jet ratio** | **m = D/d, usually 11-14** |
| **Number of buckets** | **Z = 15 + D/(2d) = 15 + m/2** |
| **Bucket deflection angle** | **165°, not 180°** |

> **The u = V/2 result is the important one and is genuinely derivable:** the power transferred to a moving bucket is maximum when the bucket moves at half the jet speed, because that is where the product of force and velocity peaks. **At u = 0 the force is maximum but no work is done; at u = V there is no force at all.**

> **And the 165° deflection rather than a full 180° is a practical compromise**: a full reversal would send the spent water straight back into the oncoming jet. **The 15° shortfall is what lets the discharged water clear the next bucket** — a small detail that costs a few per cent of theoretical efficiency and without which the machine would not work at all.

**Where the Pelton belongs:**

| Turbine | Head | Type |
|---|---|---|
| **PELTON** | **HIGH — above about 250 m, up to 1800 m** | **IMPULSE** |
| **Turgo, cross-flow** | Medium-high | Impulse |
| **FRANCIS** | **MEDIUM — 45 to 400 m** | **REACTION, mixed flow** |
| **KAPLAN / propeller** | **LOW — below about 60 m** | **REACTION, axial flow** |

> **The Pelton suits Nepal's high-head, low-flow mountain sites particularly well**, which is why it is the commonest turbine in the country's small and micro-hydro schemes.

examTip.trick: **V = Cv√(2gH)** — Torricelli with a friction correction. √(2gH) is the speed of free fall through height H, which is why the 2 is there. Cv = 0.97-0.99 for a Pelton nozzle.
examTip.trap: **Strike out options (c) and (d) on DIMENSIONS in seconds** — one omits g entirely, the other has g to the wrong power. That leaves the factor 2, which dimensions cannot settle and memory must.
examTip.mnemonic: **u = V/2 maximises power** — at u = 0 the force is greatest but no work is done; at u = V there is no force. And **buckets deflect 165°, not 180°**, so the spent water clears the next bucket.

questions.stem: The distance from the pivot to the rear leg in the Benkelman Beam test is:
questions.solution:
**1.66 m.**

**The geometry of the Benkelman beam:**

| Dimension | Value |
|---|---|
| **Total beam length** | **3.66 m** |
| **Pivot to PROBE tip** | **2.44 m** |
| **Pivot to DIAL GAUGE** | **1.22 m** |
| **Pivot to FRONT leg** | **0.25 m** |
| **Pivot to REAR leg** | **1.66 m** ← |

> **Note the ratio 2.44 : 1.22 = 2 : 1.** The probe arm is exactly twice the gauge arm, so **the dial reading is HALF the actual deflection and every reading is multiplied by two.** That is the single most important thing about the instrument's geometry.

> **The three legs form the reference frame**, and they must rest outside the deflected area — which is why the beam is long.

**What the test measures and how it is run:**

> **A loaded truck's rear dual wheel is placed over the test point, the probe inserted between the tyres, and the pavement's REBOUND as the truck moves away is measured.**

| Parameter | Standard value |
|---|---|
| **Axle load** | **8170 kg (80 kN)** |
| **Tyre pressure** | **5.6 kg/cm²** |
| **Reading positions** | **Initial (Do), intermediate at 2.7 m (Di), final at 9 m (Df)** |
| Result | **Rebound deflection, in mm** |

> **It measures REBOUND (elastic recovery), not the deflection under load.** The truck is driven away and the pavement springs back; that recovery is what the dial records.

**The corrections, which are the examinable part:**

> **True deflection D = 2(Do − Df)**, with the factor 2 from the lever ratio.

> **If (Di − Df) > 0.025 mm, the legs were themselves sitting on deflected pavement**, and a **LEG CORRECTION** is applied: D = 2[(Do − Df) + 2.91(Di − Df)].

> **Then two further corrections:**

| Correction | For |
|---|---|
| **TEMPERATURE correction** | **Standardised to 35 °C — bitumen is stiffer when cold, so a cold-weather deflection understates the true value** |
| **SEASONAL / moisture correction** | **The subgrade is weakest just after the monsoon; a dry-season test must be factored up** |

> **Both corrections matter more than they look.** A deflection measured in a cold, dry January and used untreated will make a weak pavement look adequate — **and the overlay designed from it will fail in the first monsoon.**

**What the answer is used for:**

> **The characteristic deflection = mean + 2 (standard deviations)** for a major road, or mean + 1 SD for lesser roads, computed over at least ten points on a homogeneous section.

> **That single figure, entered in the IRC 81 design chart with the traffic, gives the required OVERLAY THICKNESS.**

> **So the whole purpose of the test is STRENGTHENING design of an existing pavement** — it answers "how much overlay?" without excavating anything. **A high deflection means a weak pavement and a thick overlay.**

**Why the distractors are wrong — every one is another dimension of the same instrument:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **0.25 m** | **Pivot to FRONT leg** |
| **0.9 m** | Not a Benkelman dimension |
| **1.66 m** | ✓ **Pivot to rear leg** |
| **2.44 m** | **Pivot to PROBE tip — the most-quoted figure of the instrument** ← the trap |

> **Option (d) is the designed trap.** 2.44 m is the number a candidate is most likely to have memorised, because it is the probe arm and appears in the lever ratio. **The question deliberately asks for the one dimension that is not the famous one**, which is why the whole geometry has to be learned rather than a single figure.

**And the modern successor, worth a line:** **the Falling Weight Deflectometer (FWD)** applies an impulse load and measures a deflection *basin* with several sensors, from which the modulus of each layer can be back-calculated. **The Benkelman beam gives one number; the FWD gives a layer-by-layer diagnosis** — but the beam needs only a truck and two people, which is why it remains in use.

examTip.trick: **Learn the whole geometry: 3.66 total, 2.44 probe, 1.22 gauge, 0.25 front leg, 1.66 rear leg.** The 2.44 : 1.22 ratio is 2 : 1, so every dial reading is DOUBLED.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) 2.44 m is the trap** — the probe arm, the figure everyone memorises. The question asks for the one dimension that is not the famous one.
examTip.mnemonic: **It measures REBOUND, not deflection under load** — the truck drives away and the pavement springs back. Corrected to 35 °C and for season, then characteristic deflection = mean + 2SD → overlay thickness from IRC 81.

questions.stem: The vehicle distribution factor for a four-lane single carriageway road is:
options: The design should be based on 40 % of the commercial vehicles in both directions
The design should be based on 75 % of the commercial vehicles in both directions
The design should be based on 60 % of the commercial vehicles in both directions
The design should be based on 45 % of the commercial vehicles in both directions
questions.solution:
**40 % of the commercial vehicles in both directions.**

**The lane distribution factors:**

| Road type | Distribution factor |
|---|---|
| **SINGLE CARRIAGEWAY** | |
| Single-lane road | **1.00 — all traffic in one lane** |
| Two-lane road | **0.75** |
| Three-lane road | 0.60 |
| **Four-lane road** | **0.40** ← |
| **DUAL CARRIAGEWAY** | |
| Two-lane each way | **0.75 of the traffic in each direction** |
| Three-lane each way | 0.60 of each direction |
| Four-lane each way | 0.45 of each direction |

> **Notice how the factor falls as lanes are added — and why.** The design must be for the **MOST HEAVILY TRAFFICKED LANE**, since the pavement fails where the loading is greatest, not on average.

> **With one lane, every vehicle uses it: factor 1.0.** With four lanes, the traffic spreads, but not evenly — **heavy vehicles concentrate in the slow lane**, so the worst lane still carries far more than a quarter of the total. Hence 0.40, not 0.25.

**The critical distinction the options are built on:**

> **For a SINGLE carriageway the factor applies to the traffic in BOTH DIRECTIONS.**

> **For a DUAL carriageway it applies to the traffic in EACH DIRECTION separately.**

> **This is why 0.75 appears twice in the table with different meanings**, and why the option wording matters: **every option in this question ends "in both directions", so the question is unambiguously about a single carriageway.** A candidate who half-remembers "four lane → 0.45" is recalling the DUAL carriageway value and is caught.

> **Option (d) 45 % is exactly that trap.**

**Where the factor is used:**

> **In computing the CUMULATIVE STANDARD AXLES (CSA) for flexible pavement design:**

> **N = [365 × A × ((1+r)^n − 1)/r] × D × F**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **A** | **Initial commercial vehicles per day (CVPD), at the end of construction** |
| **r** | **Annual growth rate (minimum 5 % assumed if no data)** |
| **n** | **Design life — 10 to 15 years for flexible pavement** |
| **D** | **LANE DISTRIBUTION FACTOR** ← this question |
| **F** | **VEHICLE DAMAGE FACTOR — standard axles per commercial vehicle** |

> **Only COMMERCIAL vehicles count** — those above 3 tonnes laden. **Cars and two-wheelers are ignored entirely in pavement design**, because pavement damage rises roughly as the FOURTH POWER of axle load, and a car's contribution is negligible against a truck's.

> **That fourth-power law is the single most important idea in pavement design:** doubling an axle load multiplies the damage by about sixteen. **One overloaded truck can do the damage of many thousands of cars**, which is why axle-load control matters more to road life than traffic volume does.

**The vehicle damage factor, since it multiplies alongside D:**

| Terrain and traffic | VDF |
|---|---|
| **Plain / rolling, < 150 CVPD** | **1.5** |
| Plain / rolling, 1500-4500 CVPD | 4.5 |
| **Hilly, < 150 CVPD** | **0.5** |
| Hilly, 1500-4500 CVPD | 1.5 |

> **VDF should be measured by axle-load survey wherever possible**, because it varies enormously with the local pattern of overloading — and it is the term that most often makes a design inadequate. **Assuming a standard VDF on a route with heavy overloading is a design failure dressed as a code compliance.**

examTip.trick: **Single carriageway: 1 lane → 1.00, 2 → 0.75, 3 → 0.60, 4 → 0.40**, applied to traffic in BOTH directions. The factor falls with lanes because design is for the WORST lane, not the average.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) 45 % is the DUAL carriageway four-lane value**, applied per direction. Every option here says "in both directions", so the question is about a single carriageway.
examTip.mnemonic: **Pavement damage rises as the FOURTH POWER of axle load** — double the load, sixteen times the damage. Which is why only COMMERCIAL vehicles are counted and why axle-load control matters more than volume.

questions.stem: What quantity of binding wire is required for fixing one quintal of steel bars?
questions.solution:
**1 kg.**

**The standard allowance:**

> **Binding wire is taken as 0.9 to 1.3 kg per quintal (100 kg) of reinforcement steel** — that is, roughly **1 per cent by weight**, or **9 to 13 kg per tonne.**

> **The nearest option is 1 kg, and "about 1 % of the steel weight" is the figure to carry.**

> **The wire itself is 18 or 20 gauge annealed mild steel wire**, soft enough to twist by hand and to be cut with pliers.

**Why the answer is so small, which is what makes the distractors tempting:**

> **Binding wire only ties bars where they cross.** It carries no load and is not structural — **it merely holds the cage in position until the concrete sets.**

> **A few centimetres of thin wire per intersection, over a hundred kilograms of bars, comes to about a kilogram.** Options (b), (c) and (d) are five to twelve times too much and would represent a mass of wire visible in the cage.

> **The sanity check is worth doing: 10 kg of binding wire per 100 kg of steel would mean a tenth of the reinforcement by weight is tying wire. No cage looks like that.**

**Note on the unit, since "quintal" appears in Nepali and Indian estimating practice:**

| Unit | Value |
|---|---|
| **1 quintal** | **100 kg** |
| **1 metric tonne** | **10 quintals = 1000 kg** |

> **The word appears constantly in bills of quantities and rate analysis in the region**, and a candidate who does not know it cannot even read the question. **Reinforcement is commonly rated per quintal or per tonne, cement per bag of 50 kg.**

**The other standard allowances of the same kind, since they are examined as a family:**

| Item | Standard allowance |
|---|---|
| **BINDING WIRE** | **~1 kg per quintal of steel (9-13 kg/tonne)** ← |
| **Cover blocks** | By count; concrete or PVC |
| **Wastage of steel (cutting)** | **3-5 %** |
| **Wastage of cement** | **2-3 %** |
| **Bulking of dry sand** | **20-30 % — affects VOLUME batching** |
| **Cement bag** | **50 kg = 0.035 m³ (roughly 34.7 litres)** |
| **Dry volume of mortar/concrete** | **1.52 to 1.54 × wet volume** |
| **Steel in RCC, by volume** | **0.7-1.0 % slab, 1-2 % beam, 1-5 % column** |

> **The 1.54 factor for dry volume and the 0.035 m³ cement bag are the two most-used numbers in estimating**, and the bulking allowance is the one whose omission causes real trouble: **volume-batching damp sand without allowing for bulking delivers less sand than intended and a richer, more shrinkage-prone mix.**

**Where the figure is used in practice:**

> **It goes into the RATE ANALYSIS for reinforcement work**, alongside the steel itself, the cutting and bending labour, and the fixing labour.

> **A typical rate item for "supplying, cutting, bending, binding and placing reinforcement" is built up per quintal**, and binding wire is one small line in it. **Omitting it does not change a tender materially — but omitting the whole family of such small allowances does**, which is why the estimator's discipline is to include every one.

examTip.trick: **About 1 % of the steel weight — 0.9 to 1.3 kg per quintal, or 9-13 kg per tonne.** 18 or 20 gauge annealed wire, soft enough to twist by hand.
examTip.trap: **Sanity-check the distractors: 10 kg per quintal would make a tenth of the cage tying wire.** No cage looks like that. Binding wire carries no load and only holds position until the concrete sets.
examTip.mnemonic: **1 quintal = 100 kg; 1 tonne = 10 quintals.** Learn the allowance family with it: **steel wastage 3-5 %, cement 2-3 %, sand bulking 20-30 %, cement bag 0.035 m³, dry volume 1.54 × wet.**

questions.stem: Which among the following is not a type of non-destructive testing?
questions.solution:
**Compression test.**

**The definition that settles it:**

> **A non-destructive test leaves the member FIT FOR SERVICE afterwards.** The test may be repeated, and the tested item is the item that goes into the structure.

> **A compression test loads a specimen TO FAILURE.** The cube is crushed and destroyed — nothing could be more destructive.

> **So option (a) is the answer, and the reasoning needs no knowledge of the other three.**

**The two families:**

| **NON-DESTRUCTIVE** | **DESTRUCTIVE** |
|---|---|
| **Visual inspection** | **Compression test** |
| **Rebound hammer (Schmidt hammer)** | **Tensile test** |
| **Ultrasonic pulse velocity (UPV)** | **Flexure / modulus of rupture** |
| **Penetration (Windsor probe)** | **Impact test (Charpy, Izod)** |
| **Pull-out test** | **Hardness test** (leaves an indent) |
| **Radiography / radioactive methods** | **Fatigue test** |
| **Eddy current, magnetic particle, dye penetrant** | **Shear test** |
| **Half-cell potential (corrosion), cover meter** | **Core cutting** (semi-destructive) |

> **The pull-out test is the interesting boundary case**: it pulls an embedded insert out of the concrete, causing local damage that must be patched. **It is usually classed as non-destructive because the member survives, though "partially destructive" is the more honest label.** Core cutting is the same in a larger way.

**What each of the three genuine NDT options actually does:**

| Test | Principle | Tells you |
|---|---|---|
| **VISUAL** | **Look at it — the first and most valuable test** | **Cracks, spalling, honeycombing, rust staining, deflection** |
| **ULTRASONIC (UPV)** | **Time a pulse through the member; V = path/time** | **Uniformity, voids, cracks, and an INDICATION of strength** |
| **EDDY CURRENT** | **Induced currents disturbed by flaws — for METALS** | **Surface and near-surface cracks in conductors** |

> **Visual inspection deserves its place at the top of the list rather than being dismissed as trivial.** It is free, immediate, and finds most defects; **the instrumented tests are for quantifying what the eye has already found, or for looking where the eye cannot.**

**The UPV interpretation, since it is the NDT most often examined:**

| Pulse velocity (km/s) | Concrete quality |
|---|---|
| **> 4.5** | **Excellent** |
| **3.5 - 4.5** | **Good** |
| **3.0 - 3.5** | Medium / doubtful |
| **< 3.0** | **Doubtful — investigate** |

> **UPV measures a modulus, not a strength**, and the correlation to strength is affected by moisture, aggregate type, reinforcement position and age. **So UPV is excellent for comparing one part of a structure with another, and unreliable as an absolute strength figure.** That distinction is the standard misuse of the method.

**Why NDT matters in practice, since the topic looks academic:**

> **The cube test tells you about the concrete that went into the cube**, taken at the batching point, cured in a laboratory tank.

> **NDT tells you about the concrete that is actually IN THE STRUCTURE** — placed, compacted and cured on site, in the weather, by the people who were there that day.

> **Those two are not the same concrete, and the difference is precisely what matters.** A structure with excellent cube results and honeycombed columns is not a hypothetical. **Which is why acceptance rests on cubes but investigation rests on NDT.**

> **The combination most used is the rebound hammer (surface hardness) plus UPV (internal soundness)**, since together they distinguish a weak surface from a weak body — something neither can do alone.

examTip.trick: **Non-destructive means the member is FIT FOR SERVICE afterwards.** A compression test crushes the specimen — the definition alone settles it, with no knowledge of the other three needed.
examTip.trap: **Pull-out and core cutting are boundary cases** — they cause local damage that must be patched, so "partially destructive" is the honest label though they are usually grouped with NDT.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cubes tell you about the concrete that went INTO the cube; NDT tells you about the concrete IN THE STRUCTURE.** They are not the same concrete. UPV: >4.5 excellent, 3.5-4.5 good, <3.0 doubtful.

questions.stem: Khosla's safe exit gradient for the design of weirs will be the lowest for which of the following soil types?
questions.solution:
**Fine sand.**

**The safe exit gradient values:**

| Soil | Safe exit gradient |
|---|---|
| **Shingle** | **1/4 to 1/5  (0.25 to 0.20)** |
| **Coarse sand** | **1/5 to 1/6  (0.20 to 0.17)** |
| **Fine sand** | **1/6 to 1/7  (0.17 to 0.14)** ← **LOWEST** |

> **The pattern is the whole answer: the FINER the soil, the LOWER the permissible exit gradient.**

**Why finer soil demands a lower gradient — the physical reason:**

> **Piping begins when the upward seepage force on a soil grain at the exit equals the grain's submerged weight.**

> **A fine grain has a much smaller weight but a comparable surface for the seepage to act on**, so it is lifted by a gentler gradient.

> **Once the finest grains are washed out, the void left behind concentrates the flow, which removes more grains — the process is SELF-ACCELERATING.** That is why piping is a progressive failure and why the margin against it must be generous.

> **So the design gradient is lowest where the grains are lightest.** Fine sand is the most vulnerable of the three tabulated soils.

**Why option (b) gravels is the trap:**

> **Gravel is coarser still than shingle, so a candidate reasoning correctly about the trend would expect gravel to have the HIGHEST permissible gradient — not the lowest.** It is the opposite end of the series from the answer.

> **And gravel does not appear in the standard table at all**, because a weir founded on clean gravel has a different problem: **the permeability is so high that seepage quantity, not piping, governs.** The exit-gradient criterion is for sands and shingle.

> **So (b) is wrong twice over: wrong direction of the trend, and outside the table.**

**Where the criterion enters design — and the practical consequence:**

> **G_E = (H / d) × 1/(π√λ)**, where

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **H** | **Seepage head (upstream water level minus downstream)** |
| **d** | **DEPTH of the downstream cut-off (sheet pile) below the floor** |
| **λ** | **(1 + √(1 + α²))/2, with α = b/d, b the floor length** |

> **Note that d is in the DENOMINATOR.** So:

> **The way to reduce the exit gradient is to drive the DOWNSTREAM CUT-OFF DEEPER.**

> **That is the single most useful design conclusion in the topic.** Lengthening the floor helps a little through λ; deepening the end cut-off helps directly and strongly. **Khosla's finding that the downstream cut-off is what controls piping is the reason modern weirs are built with deep end cut-offs rather than long aprons.**

**The two distinct failure mechanisms of a weir foundation, since they are confused:**

| Failure | Mechanism | Guarded against by |
|---|---|---|
| **PIPING (undermining)** | **Seepage lifts and washes out soil at the exit; a channel forms backwards under the floor** | **EXIT GRADIENT criterion — deep downstream cut-off** |
| **UPLIFT (floor rupture)** | **Seepage pressure under the floor exceeds its weight; the floor cracks and lifts** | **Floor THICKNESS — t = (h/G−1), with h the residual head and G the specific gravity of concrete** |

> **Piping destroys the FOUNDATION; uplift destroys the FLOOR.** Both are computed from the same Khosla pressure distribution, and both must be checked — **a weir safe against one can fail by the other.**

> **And note the uplift formula's structure: the required thickness is the residual head divided by (G − 1), roughly h/1.4 for concrete.** So a residual head of 2 m needs about 1.4 m of floor — **which is why downstream floors of weirs are so massive, and why reducing the residual head by good cut-off design saves a great deal of concrete.**

**The safety factor in practice:** **the tabulated "safe" gradients already contain a factor of safety of 4 to 5 against the critical gradient**, which for most soils is about 1.0. **So a design at the tabulated value is not marginal — it is deliberately conservative, because the consequence of piping is total and sudden loss of the structure.**

examTip.trick: **The finer the soil, the LOWER the safe exit gradient.** Shingle 1/4-1/5, coarse sand 1/5-1/6, fine sand 1/6-1/7. A fine grain weighs little and is lifted by a gentler gradient.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) gravels is wrong twice** — coarser than shingle, so it would sit at the HIGH end of the trend, and it is not in the table at all (for gravel, seepage quantity governs, not piping).
examTip.mnemonic: **d is in the denominator of G_E = (H/d)·1/(π√λ)** — so the way to beat piping is to drive the DOWNSTREAM CUT-OFF DEEPER. That is why modern weirs have deep end cut-offs, not long aprons.

questions.stem: Kennedy's design consideration for canal design is based upon:
options: bed is unprotected, side slope is protected
bed is protected, side slope is unprotected
both bed and side slope are protected
both bed and side slope are unprotected
questions.solution:
**Bed is unprotected, side slope is protected.**

**What Kennedy assumed and why:**

> **Kennedy studied 22 reaches of the Upper Bari Doab Canal in 1895** and observed which channels neither silted nor scoured.

> **His central idea: the silt is held in suspension by EDDIES rising from the CHANNEL BED.**

> **So the bed is where the action is — it is the bed that must generate the eddies, and the bed that is therefore unprotected and free to interact with the flow.**

> **The SIDE SLOPES are taken as protected** (by vegetation, by the natural armouring of coarser material, or simply as contributing negligible eddy generation), so **they play no part in his analysis.**

> **That is exactly the assumption option (a) states, and it is the distinguishing feature of Kennedy's theory.**

**The theory itself:**

> **Critical velocity:  V_o = 0.55 m y^{0.64}**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **V_o** | **Critical velocity — the velocity at which silt is neither deposited nor scoured** |
| **y** | **DEPTH of flow (full supply depth)** |
| **m** | **CRITICAL VELOCITY RATIO (CVR) = V/V_o, allowing for silt grade** |

> **m > 1 for coarser silt than the Bari Doab's, m < 1 for finer.** Typical values 0.8 to 1.2.

> **The formula depends on DEPTH ONLY — not on width, not on slope.** That is the theory's power and its fatal limitation together.

**Why Kennedy's theory is incomplete, and Lacey's answer:**

> **Kennedy gives ONE equation** (plus Manning or Kutter for the velocity) **but the design has TWO unknowns — bed width B and depth y.**

> **So the solution is INDETERMINATE**: a trial-and-error procedure is needed, and the answer depends on an assumed bed-width-to-depth ratio. **Different engineers get different canals from the same data.**

| | **KENNEDY (1895)** | **LACEY (1930)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Silt held up by** | **Eddies from the BED only** | **Eddies from the ENTIRE WETTED PERIMETER** |
| **Equations given** | **One (critical velocity)** | **THREE — velocity, area, slope** |
| **Solution** | **Indeterminate; needs a trial B/y** | **DETERMINATE** |
| **Silt measure** | **CVR (m)** | **SILT FACTOR (f)** |
| **Regime concept** | Not defined | **Initial, true and final regime distinguished** |
| **Cross-section shape** | Trapezoidal, as built | **SEMI-ELLIPTICAL** |

> **Lacey's correction is the exact point on which this question turns.** Where Kennedy protects the sides and credits only the bed, **Lacey says the whole wetted perimeter generates eddies — which is both more physically reasonable and what makes his system determinate.**

> **Lacey's three equations:**

> **V = 0.639 √(f R)** ,  **A f² = 140 V⁵** ,  **S = f^{5/3} / (3340 Q^{1/6})**

> **With the silt factor f = 1.76 √(d_mm), d being the mean particle size in mm.**

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Bed unprotected, sides protected** | ✓ **Kennedy** |
| **Bed protected, sides unprotected** | **The exact reversal — a lined-bed channel, which is not a silt-transport theory at all** |
| **Both protected** | **That is a fully LINED canal** — no silt problem arises, so no regime theory is needed |
| **Both unprotected** | **Closest to LACEY's position** — the whole perimeter active ← the near-miss |

> **Option (d) is the designed near-miss, and it is the one to reason about.** "Both unprotected" is essentially Lacey's assumption. **A candidate who knows the Kennedy-versus-Lacey distinction gets this instantly; one who knows only "regime theory" is guessing between (a) and (d).**

**And the deeper point about regime theory generally:**

> **Both theories are EMPIRICAL, derived from Punjab canals in a particular alluvium**, and both are extrapolated well beyond that origin.

> **They are used because the alternative — a full sediment-transport analysis — needs data no designer has.** **But their limits should be honest:** a regime formula applied to a canal in a different silt, a different climate and a different discharge range is an educated guess, not a calculation.

> **Which is why a designed canal is always compared against a comparable EXISTING canal in the same region before it is built.**

examTip.trick: **Kennedy: eddies rise from the BED only, so the bed is unprotected and the sides are taken as protected and inactive.** V_o = 0.55 m y^{0.64} — depends on DEPTH alone.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) "both unprotected" is essentially LACEY's assumption** — the whole wetted perimeter generates eddies. Knowing which theory says which is the entire question.
examTip.mnemonic: **Kennedy gives ONE equation for TWO unknowns, so it is indeterminate and needs a trial B/y. Lacey gives THREE and is determinate.** That is why Lacey superseded him.

questions.stem: Hooke's Law holds good up to:
questions.solution:
**The limit of proportionality.**

**What Hooke's law actually states:**

> **Stress is DIRECTLY PROPORTIONAL to strain: σ = E ε.**

> **"Directly proportional" means a STRAIGHT LINE through the origin.** The moment the stress-strain curve departs from a straight line, the law no longer describes the material — even if the behaviour is still perfectly elastic.

> **The point where the curve ceases to be straight is, by definition, the LIMIT OF PROPORTIONALITY.**

> **So Hooke's law holds up to the limit of proportionality — and not one step beyond.**

**The four points in order, which is the whole content of the question:**

| Point | Definition | Order |
|---|---|---|
| **LIMIT OF PROPORTIONALITY (A)** | **End of the STRAIGHT LINE — σ ∝ ε ends here** | **1st** ← |
| **ELASTIC LIMIT (B)** | **End of full RECOVERY — beyond it, permanent set remains** | **2nd** |
| **UPPER YIELD POINT (C)** | **Onset of large plastic flow** | **3rd** |
| **Lower yield point (C′) → yield plateau (CD)** | Strain at nearly constant stress | 4th |
| **Strain hardening (DE)** | Stress rises again | 5th |
| **ULTIMATE point (E)** | **MAXIMUM stress the specimen carries** | 6th |
| **Fracture / breaking point (F)** | **Specimen separates — at a LOWER stress than ultimate** | Last |

> **For mild steel the limit of proportionality is at about 0.12 % strain, and fracture at 20 to 30 %** — so the elastic range is a tiny fraction of the total.

**Why option (d), the elastic limit, is the trap and deserves care:**

> **The elastic limit and the limit of proportionality are NOT the same point**, though they are very close together in mild steel and are often treated as identical in practice.

| | **Limit of proportionality** | **Elastic limit** |
|---|---|---|
| **Defines the end of** | **LINEARITY** | **RECOVERABILITY** |
| **Test for it** | **Is the graph still straight?** | **Does the specimen return to its original length on unloading?** |
| **Which comes first** | **THIS ONE** | Just after |

> **Between the two, the material is ELASTIC BUT NON-LINEAR** — it recovers fully, but σ is no longer proportional to ε.

> **That narrow band is exactly what the question is about.** Hooke's law is a statement about *proportionality*, not about *recovery* — so it fails at the first of the two points, not the second.

> **Rubber is the illustration that makes it obvious: rubber is highly elastic (it recovers completely) but grossly non-linear (its curve is nowhere straight). Rubber obeys the definition of elasticity and does not obey Hooke's law at all.**

**Why the other two are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Yield point** | **Well beyond both limits — large plastic flow is occurring; nothing is proportional there** |
| **Breaking point** | **The very end of the curve; the material has already necked and lost load-carrying capacity** |

**What the slope is, since it follows directly:**

> **E, YOUNG'S MODULUS, is the slope of the straight portion — tan θ.**

> **It is defined only over the linear range**, which is another way of saying that E exists only where Hooke's law holds.

| Material | E (GPa) |
|---|---|
| **Structural steel** | **200-210** |
| **Concrete (M25)** | **~25 (5000√f_ck in N/mm²)** |
| **Aluminium** | **70** |
| **Timber, along grain** | 8-15 |

> **Note that E for concrete is code-defined as 5000√f_ck** precisely because concrete has no straight portion worth speaking of — **the code specifies a secant modulus and calls it E, which is a convention rather than a measurement of a linear region.**

**And the two related moduli, since a full statement of Hooke's law needs them:**

| Modulus | Relation |
|---|---|
| **E — Young's (direct stress)** | σ = Eε |
| **G — rigidity (shear)** | **τ = Gγ**, and **G = E/[2(1+μ)]** |
| **K — bulk (volumetric)** | **K = E/[3(1−2μ)]** |

> **With μ ≈ 0.3 for steel, G ≈ 0.385E ≈ 80 GPa and K ≈ 0.83E.** And note **K → ∞ as μ → 0.5**, which is why a Poisson's ratio of 0.5 means an incompressible material — the theoretical upper limit.

examTip.trick: **Hooke's law is about PROPORTIONALITY, not recovery** — so it ends where the graph stops being straight: the limit of proportionality, which comes FIRST.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) elastic limit is the trap.** Between the two points the material is elastic but non-linear — recovers fully, but σ is not proportional to ε. **Rubber proves the difference exists.**
examTip.mnemonic: **Order: proportionality → elastic limit → upper yield → plateau → strain hardening → ULTIMATE → fracture** (fracture at a LOWER stress than ultimate). E is the slope, and exists only where the line is straight.

questions.stem: The effect of surcharge pressure on effective pressure is:
options: effective stress increases by surcharge load
effective stress decreases by surcharge load
questions.solution:
**Effective stress increases by the surcharge load.**

**Why — the principle of effective stress:**

> **σ′ = σ − u**

> **A surcharge is a load placed ON THE GROUND SURFACE** — a fill, a stockpile, a stack of material, a temporary embankment.

> **It adds directly to the TOTAL vertical stress σ at every depth below it.**

> **In the long term the pore pressure u returns to its original hydrostatic value**, so the whole surcharge appears in the effective stress:

> **σ′_new = σ′_old + q**, where q is the surcharge intensity.

> **Note that a UNIFORM surcharge of q over a wide area adds q at EVERY depth**, undiminished — unlike a footing load, which spreads and reduces with depth. **That is what makes surcharge such a useful tool.**

**The short-term qualification, which the honest answer must include:**

> **IMMEDIATELY after the surcharge is placed on a saturated clay, the pore pressure rises by very nearly q** and the effective stress barely changes at all.

> **The increase in effective stress happens as the excess pore pressure dissipates — that is, as CONSOLIDATION proceeds.**

| Time | Δσ | Δu | Δσ′ |
|---|---|---|---|
| **t = 0** | **+q** | **+q** | **≈ 0** |
| **Intermediate** | **+q** | Falling | Rising |
| **t = ∞** | **+q** | **0** | **+q** |

> **So the answer is correct as an end state, and the question is asking about the end state.** In a sand the dissipation is effectively instantaneous and the distinction does not arise.

**Why this matters — the surcharge is a deliberate engineering technique:**

> **PRELOADING (surcharge loading) is one of the standard ground-improvement methods for soft clay.**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Place a temporary fill HEAVIER than the future structure** |
| **2** | **Wait for consolidation — monitored with settlement plates and piezometers** |
| **3** | **REMOVE the surcharge** |
| **4** | Build the structure |

> **The settlement that would have occurred under the building has already been taken out of the ground before the building exists.** The clay is left overconsolidated with respect to the structure's load, so the remaining settlement is small and elastic.

> **And the reason the surcharge is made HEAVIER than the structure is subtle and important: it accelerates the primary consolidation AND pre-compresses the soil against SECONDARY consolidation (creep)**, which no amount of waiting under the structure's own load would remove.

> **Combined with VERTICAL DRAINS (sand drains or prefabricated band drains), the consolidation time is cut dramatically**, because the drainage path becomes horizontal and short instead of vertical and long — and consolidation time varies with the SQUARE of the drainage path.

**The other face of the same principle — surcharge behind a retaining wall:**

> **A surcharge behind a wall increases the LATERAL pressure too**, by K_a·q for an active case:

> **The pressure diagram gains a RECTANGULAR block of K_a·q over the full height**, on top of the usual triangle.

> **Its resultant acts at MID-HEIGHT (H/2), not at the third point** — so the surcharge raises the overturning moment more than its share of the force suggests. **Placing a spoil heap or parking heavy plant behind a completed retaining wall is a genuine and recurring cause of wall failure**, and it is why drawings carry a stated surcharge allowance.

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Increases** | ✓ |
| **Decreases** | **That is what EXCAVATION (unloading) does, or a RISE in the water table** |
| **Remains constant** | **True only at the instant of loading in a saturated clay — not the general answer** ← the partially-right option |
| **None of these** | — |

> **Option (c) is the interesting distractor** because it is momentarily true in a saturated clay, as set out above. **But "remains constant" as a general statement about the effect of surcharge on effective stress is wrong**, and the question asks for the effect, which means the outcome.

examTip.trick: **σ′ = σ − u.** A surcharge adds q to the TOTAL stress at every depth, undiminished. Once u returns to hydrostatic, the whole q appears in σ′.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) is momentarily TRUE in saturated clay** — at t = 0 the pore pressure takes the whole surcharge and σ′ barely moves. It becomes wrong as consolidation proceeds, which is what the question asks about.
examTip.mnemonic: **Preloading works because the settlement is taken out BEFORE the building exists** — and the fill is made heavier than the structure to pre-compress against creep too. Behind a wall, surcharge adds K_a·q acting at H/2, not H/3.

questions.stem: The rock rarely found in Nepal is:
questions.solution:
**Basalt.**

**Why basalt is rare in Nepal — the reason is tectonic:**

> **Basalt is an EXTRUSIVE igneous rock — solidified lava.** It requires VOLCANIC activity at or near the surface.

> **Nepal's geology is the product of CONTINENTAL COLLISION, not volcanism.** The Indian plate is being driven under the Eurasian plate, and the resulting geology is dominated by:

| Process | Rocks produced |
|---|---|
| **Uplift and metamorphism** | **Gneiss, schist, quartzite, slate, marble, phyllite** |
| **Marine sedimentation of the Tethys, later uplifted** | **LIMESTONE, dolomite, shale, sandstone** |
| **Erosion and deposition in the foreland basin** | **Siwalik SANDSTONE, mudstone, conglomerate** |
| **Deep intrusion** | **GRANITE — present in the High Himalaya** |

> **Notice what is absent from that list: extrusive volcanic rock.** A collision belt has no volcanic arc at the surface once the ocean between the plates has closed. **Hence basalt is a rarity in Nepal, while metamorphic and sedimentary rocks are everywhere.**

> **Granite, by contrast, is genuinely present** — the High Himalayan leucogranites are a well-known feature of the range. **So granite is not the answer, even though it is also igneous**, and the discrimination the question makes is between **INTRUSIVE (present) and EXTRUSIVE (rare)** igneous rock.

**Nepal's five geological zones, north to south — the framework the question sits in:**

| Zone | Character | Typical rocks |
|---|---|---|
| **Tibetan-Tethys Himalaya** | Marine sediments, uplifted | **Limestone, shale, sandstone** |
| **Higher Himalaya** | **High-grade metamorphic, with GRANITE intrusions** | **Gneiss, schist, quartzite, marble, granite** |
| **Lesser Himalaya (Midland)** | Low- to medium-grade metamorphic | **Slate, phyllite, schist, dolomite, quartzite** |
| **Siwalik (Churia)** | **Young, WEAK, poorly consolidated** | **Sandstone, mudstone, conglomerate** |
| **Terai** | **Alluvium — Quaternary, unconsolidated** | Sand, gravel, silt, clay |

> **The Main Boundary Thrust and the Main Central Thrust separate these zones**, and they are the structural features that make Nepali slopes unstable.

> **The SIWALIK zone is the one every Nepali civil engineer must know about.** It is geologically young, poorly cemented, and steeply dipping — **so it produces the country's worst landslides, its most difficult road cuttings and its least reliable foundation material.** A road built through Siwalik sandstone will need retaining structures and drainage that the same road through Lesser Himalayan quartzite would not.

**Why the other three are common:**

| Option | Where in Nepal |
|---|---|
| **Granite** | **Higher Himalaya intrusions — used as building and dimension stone** |
| **Sandstone** | **Abundant in the Siwaliks; widely used, though the weak Siwalik variety is poor stone** |
| **Limestone** | **Widespread in the Lesser and Tethys Himalaya — and the basis of Nepal's CEMENT industry** |

> **The limestone point is worth adding because it has economic weight:** Nepal's cement plants — Udayapur, Hetauda, and the newer private plants — exist because limestone is abundant. **A country without limestone must import cement or clinker; Nepal need not.**

**And the engineering use of each, since that is why a civil engineer studies rocks:**

| Rock | Engineering use |
|---|---|
| **Granite** | **Strong, durable dimension stone; aggregate; facing** |
| **Quartzite** | **Excellent aggregate — hard and inert** |
| **Limestone** | **Cement manufacture; lime; aggregate (though soluble)** |
| **Slate** | **Roofing and flooring — splits into thin sheets** |
| **Marble** | Decorative and facing work |
| **Sandstone** | Masonry, paving — quality varies enormously with the cement between the grains |
| **Basalt (where found)** | **Very good aggregate and road metal — hard and tough** |

> **The irony is worth noting: basalt is one of the BEST road aggregates there is, and Nepal has very little of it.** Which is part of why quartzite and river gravel dominate as aggregate sources in the country.

examTip.trick: **Basalt is EXTRUSIVE — it needs volcanism.** Nepal's geology is continental COLLISION: metamorphic and sedimentary rock, plus deep-seated granite. No volcanic arc, so no basalt.
examTip.trap: **Granite is also igneous but IS present** — the High Himalayan leucogranites. The discrimination is intrusive (present) versus extrusive (rare), not igneous versus not.
examTip.mnemonic: **Know the five zones north to south: Tethys, Higher Himalaya, Lesser Himalaya, SIWALIK, Terai.** The Siwalik is young, weak and steeply dipping — Nepal's worst landslides and hardest road cuttings.

questions.stem: What is the recommended formula for the top width of a very low dam?
questions.solution:
**0.2H + 3 (that is, H/5 + 3), with H the height of the dam in metres.**

**What governs the top width of a low earth dam:**

> **For a low dam the top width is NOT a stability requirement at all.** The section is already wide enough at the crest for any structural purpose.

> **It is governed by the MINIMUM ROADWAY WIDTH needed on the crest** — for construction plant during building, and for access and inspection afterwards.

> **Hence the formula's structure: a constant 3 m of minimum usable width, plus a modest allowance H/5 that grows with the dam's height.**

> **A = H/5 + 3 = 0.2H + 3**

**Check the formula at both ends, which is how to be sure of it:**

| Dam height H | Top width A = 0.2H + 3 |
|---|---|
| **5 m** | **4.0 m** |
| **10 m** | **5.0 m** |
| **20 m** | **7.0 m** |
| 30 m | 9.0 m |

> **Those are sensible crest widths for small dams — a single-lane track to a two-lane one.** The formula behaves reasonably over its intended range, which is a good sign.

> **Now test the distractors the same way, at H = 10 m:**

| Option | At H = 10 m | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **H + 3** | **13 m** | **Absurdly wide for a 10 m dam** |
| **0.2H + 3** | **5 m** ✓ | **Reasonable** |
| **0.2H** | **2 m** | **Too narrow to drive on, and gives ZERO width for a very low dam** |
| **H + 5** | **15 m** | **Worse than (a)** |

> **Option (c) fails on a limiting check that costs no effort: as H → 0 the top width → 0.** A dam cannot have zero crest width. **The presence of a CONSTANT term is essential, and that observation alone reduces the choice to (a), (b) or (d).**

> **Then options (a) and (d) both grow with H at full rate, giving 13 m and 15 m for a 10 m dam** — several times what any low dam needs. **Only (b) survives.**

**What the crest width is actually used for:**

| Purpose | Note |
|---|---|
| **Construction access** | **Compaction plant must be able to work and turn on the crest — this usually governs** |
| **Inspection and maintenance access** | For the life of the dam |
| **Freeboard against wave run-up and settlement** | The crest must stay above the reservoir |
| **Length of the seepage path through the crest** | Minor, but real |
| **A road, where one is provided** | Then the road standard governs, not the formula |

> **Construction access is the practical control.** A roller needs room to operate; **a crest narrower than the plant is a crest that cannot be compacted properly**, which defeats the purpose.

**The other crest dimensions of an earth dam, since they are asked alongside:**

| Element | Typical requirement |
|---|---|
| **FREEBOARD** | **Above the maximum water level: allowance for wave run-up plus settlement, commonly 1.5-3 m for small dams** |
| **CAMBER on the crest** | **Provided so that post-construction SETTLEMENT still leaves the crest level** |
| **Upstream slope** | 2:1 to 3:1 (H:V) |
| **Downstream slope** | 2:1 to 2.5:1 |
| **Free board for wave run-up** | Function of fetch and wind speed |

> **The camber is the detail worth knowing** — an earth dam settles for years after construction, so the crest is built with an upward camber that the settlement removes. **A dam built dead level ends up sagging in the middle, exactly where the water is deepest.**

**And the wider point about empirical formulae like this one:**

> **They are dimensional formulae — the 3 is metres and the 0.2 is dimensionless.** Substituting H in feet gives a meaningless answer, and this is the commonest error with such expressions.

> **They are also bounded by their derivation: "very low dam" means roughly under 30 m.** For a large dam the crest width is set by the roadway carried, by earthquake considerations and by the core detailing — **not by a formula.**

examTip.trick: **A = H/5 + 3 = 0.2H + 3.** The constant 3 m is the minimum usable crest width; the H/5 grows modestly with height. Top width of a low dam is a ROADWAY requirement, not a stability one.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) 0.2H gives ZERO width as H → 0** — impossible. That single limiting check eliminates it instantly, and (a) and (d) then give 13-15 m for a 10 m dam, which is absurd.
examTip.mnemonic: **Construction plant governs the crest width** — a crest narrower than the roller cannot be compacted. And the crest is built with **CAMBER**, because an earth dam settles for years and a level crest ends up sagging.

questions.stem: The standard loads used for calculation of CBR are:
options: 1870 kg at 2.5 mm penetration and 2555 kg at 5.00 mm penetration
1470 kg at 2.5 mm penetration and 2555 kg at 5.00 mm penetration
1570 kg at 2.5 mm penetration and 2055 kg at 5.00 mm penetration
1370 kg at 2.5 mm penetration and 2055 kg at 5.00 mm penetration
questions.solution:
**1370 kg at 2.5 mm and 2055 kg at 5.00 mm.**

**What the numbers are:**

> **They are the loads that a STANDARD CRUSHED STONE reference material requires to reach those penetrations.** They are the denominators of the CBR ratio, not results of the test.

> **CBR = (load carried by the test soil / standard load) × 100**

| Penetration | Standard load | Standard pressure |
|---|---|---|
| **2.5 mm** | **1370 kg** | **70 kg/cm²** |
| **5.0 mm** | **2055 kg** | **105 kg/cm²** |
| 7.5 mm | 2630 kg | 134 kg/cm² |
| 10.0 mm | 3180 kg | 162 kg/cm² |
| 12.5 mm | 3600 kg | 183 kg/cm² |

> **The first two are the ones used**, and **1370 / 2055 is the pair to memorise.** The plunger is 50 mm diameter, giving an area of 19.635 cm² — which is where the pressures come from.

**The rule that trips candidates, and it is the substance of the topic:**

> **Compute the CBR at BOTH 2.5 mm and 5.0 mm.**

> **Normally the 2.5 mm value is HIGHER, and that is the CBR reported.**

> **If the 5.0 mm value comes out higher, the test must be REPEATED.** If the repeat confirms it, the 5.0 mm value is reported.

> **The reason is that a higher 5 mm value usually indicates a surface irregularity or a poorly prepared top surface**, which depresses the early readings. **So the anomaly is treated as a signal of a test defect first and accepted as real only on confirmation.**

**How to eliminate the wrong options without recall, since the numbers are so similar:**

> **The pairs offered are 1870/2555, 1470/2555, 1570/2055 and 1370/2055.**

> **Notice the ratio.** For the real pair, 2055/1370 = 1.50 exactly.

| Option | Ratio | Note |
|---|---|---|
| 1870 / 2555 | 1.37 | |
| 1470 / 2555 | 1.74 | |
| 1570 / 2055 | 1.31 | |
| **1370 / 2055** | **1.50** ✓ | **The clean ratio** |

> **The exact 1.5 is not a coincidence** — it reflects the shape of the reference material's load-penetration curve. **Recognising it is a useful check when the four options differ by a hundred kilograms and memory is uncertain.**

**The test conditions, since they are examined together:**

| Condition | Value |
|---|---|
| **Plunger diameter** | **50 mm** |
| **Rate of penetration** | **1.25 mm per minute** |
| **Mould** | **150 mm diameter, 175 mm high** |
| **Surcharge weight** | **Simulating the pavement above — 2.5 kg annular weights** |
| **Soaking** | **96 hours (4 days) for the SOAKED CBR** |
| **Sieve** | **Material passing 20 mm** |

> **The 4-day soak is the condition that matters in design.** Nepal's subgrade is at its weakest just after the monsoon, so **the SOAKED CBR is what a pavement must be designed for** — an unsoaked value flatters the subgrade and produces a pavement that fails in its first wet season.

**Typical CBR values, for orientation:**

| Material | CBR (%) |
|---|---|
| **Poor clay subgrade** | **2-5** |
| **Fair subgrade** | 5-10 |
| **Good gravelly subgrade** | **20-30** |
| **Sub-base material** | **> 20-30** |
| **Base course (WBM/WMM)** | **> 80** |
| **Standard crushed stone (the reference)** | **100 by definition** |

> **The reference material is 100 % by definition** — that is what makes CBR a *ratio* rather than a strength. **And it is why CBR has no units and cannot be converted to a stress:** it indicates *relative* strength of paving materials, not absolute strength.

> **That limitation is the standard misunderstanding.** A CBR of 5 does not mean a bearing capacity; **it means the soil takes 5 % of the load the reference stone takes at the same penetration**, and its only legitimate use is entering a design chart calibrated against it — IRC 37 for flexible pavements.

examTip.trick: **1370 kg at 2.5 mm, 2055 kg at 5.0 mm** — the loads the reference crushed stone needs. Note the ratio is exactly **1.50**, which is a useful check when four options differ by a hundred kilograms.
examTip.trap: **Compute CBR at BOTH penetrations.** Normally 2.5 mm gives the higher value and that is reported; if 5 mm is higher the test must be REPEATED, because it usually signals a bad top surface.
examTip.mnemonic: **Design on the SOAKED (96-hour) CBR** — Nepali subgrade is weakest after the monsoon, and an unsoaked value flatters it. And CBR is a RATIO with no units: it cannot be converted to a bearing capacity.

questions.stem: A circular column section is generally not used in actual practice because:
options: It cannot carry the load safely
It is difficult to connect beams to the round sections
questions.solution:
**It is difficult to connect beams to the round sections.**

**Why the reason is CONSTRUCTABILITY, not structural performance:**

> **A circular column is structurally excellent.** Its radius of gyration is the same about every axis, so **it has no weak direction** — the buckling capacity is identical whichever way the load tries to bend it. **A rectangular column always buckles about its weak axis first.**

> **A circular column with helical (spiral) reinforcement is even credited with a 5 % HIGHER strength in IS 456**, because the spiral confines the core and the failure is more ductile.

> **So the objection is not to the column. It is to the JOINT.**

**What goes wrong at the joint:**

| Difficulty | Note |
|---|---|
| **Beam soffit and sides meet a CURVED face** | **No flat surface for the beam's formwork to seat against** |
| **Formwork is complex and non-reusable** | **A curved-to-flat junction must be cut for each case** |
| **Beam reinforcement anchorage** | **Bars entering a round core have varying anchorage lengths and awkward geometry** |
| **Slab and beam edges do not align** | Finishing, plastering and partition lines all become special details |
| **Column reinforcement congestion at the joint** | Circular bar arrangement fights the orthogonal beam steel |

> **Buildings are orthogonal.** Beams run in two perpendicular directions, walls are straight, slabs are rectangular. **A round column is the one non-orthogonal element in an orthogonal system, and every interface with it becomes a special detail.**

> **That is a cost and a source of site error, repeated at every floor and every column.** In a building with a hundred beam-column joints, a hundred awkward details is a real burden.

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Why not |
|---|---|
| **Uneconomical** | **Partly true, but only BECAUSE of the formwork and detailing — it is a consequence of (c), not an independent reason. On material alone a circular column is efficient** |
| **Cannot carry the load safely** | **Plainly false. Circular columns carry load perfectly well and are used wherever they are appropriate** |
| **Difficult to connect beams** | ✓ **The direct and primary reason** |
| **All of the above** | **Fails because (b) is false** |

> **Option (d) is the trap and the reasoning against it is clean: an "all of the above" cannot survive one false member, and (b) is false.** A candidate who accepts (a) as also true still cannot choose (d).

**Where circular columns ARE used, which proves the point:**

| Application | Why circular is chosen there |
|---|---|
| **BRIDGE PIERS** | **No beams frame in from the sides; and a round pier offers less obstruction to river flow and collects less debris** |
| **Piles** | Bored and driven piles are naturally circular |
| **Water tank staging** | Free-standing columns, no orthogonal framing |
| **Architectural columns in halls and porticos** | Appearance governs, and there are few connections |
| **Silos, chimneys, circular structures** | The structure itself is circular |

> **The pattern is unmistakable: circular sections are used wherever there are FEW OR NO beam connections.** Which confirms that the connection, not the column, is the objection.

> **The bridge pier case is the most instructive.** There the circular shape is positively advantageous — **it presents the same face to the flow whatever the direction of the current, which matters in a braided Himalayan river that changes its channel** — and there are no beams to frame in. **So the very reason circular sections are avoided in buildings is absent, and they become the preferred choice.**

**And the reinforcement note, since it follows:**

| Requirement | Circular column |
|---|---|
| **Minimum longitudinal bars** | **SIX (against four for a rectangular column)** |
| **Minimum bar diameter** | **12 mm** |
| **Lateral ties** | **Circular ties or HELICAL spiral** |
| **Strength bonus with helical reinforcement** | **1.05 × the axial capacity, per IS 456 cl. 39.4** |
| Minimum steel | **0.8 % of gross area** |
| Maximum steel | **6 %, practically limited to 4 % at laps** |

> **The six-bar minimum and the 1.05 factor are the two facts most often examined about circular columns**, and both reflect the same thing: **the shape works well when it is allowed to.**

examTip.trick: **The objection is to the JOINT, not the column.** A circular column has no weak axis and even gets a 1.05 strength bonus with helical reinforcement — but a round face gives beam formwork nothing flat to seat against.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) "all of the above" fails because (b) is false** — circular columns carry load perfectly well. One false member kills an all-of-the-above, regardless of the others.
examTip.mnemonic: **Circular sections ARE used where there are no beams: bridge piers, piles, tank staging, chimneys.** A pier's round face is even an advantage in a braided river that changes its channel. That proves the connection is the issue.

questions.stem: In a venturi meter, the velocity of the liquid at the throat is ... than that at the inlet.
questions.solution:
**Higher.**

**Two equations give the whole answer:**

> **CONTINUITY:  A₁V₁ = A₂V₂**

> **The throat area A₂ is smaller than the inlet area A₁, so V₂ must be LARGER.** The same volume must pass a smaller opening in the same time.

> **BERNOULLI:  p/ρg + V²/2g + z = constant**

> **Since the velocity head rises at the throat, the PRESSURE head must fall.** Energy is conserved, not created.

> **So the throat has the HIGHEST velocity and the LOWEST pressure in the meter.** Those two facts always travel together.

**How the meter turns that into a measurement:**

> **The pressure difference between inlet and throat is measured with a differential manometer**, and the discharge follows:

> **Q = C_d × [A₁A₂ / √(A₁² − A₂²)] × √(2gh)**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **h** | **The manometer head difference** |
| **C_d** | **Coefficient of discharge, 0.95 to 0.98 for a venturi** |
| A₁, A₂ | Inlet and throat areas |
