> **The whole device converts a pressure difference (easy to measure) into a velocity (hard to measure).** That is what a venturi meter is for.

**The geometry, and why it is asymmetric:**

| Part | Cone angle | Length | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Converging (entrance) cone** | **20° to 22°** | **SHORT** | **Accelerating flow does not separate, so it can be steep** |
| **Throat** | — | 0.25 to 0.5 D | Where the measurement is taken |
| **Diverging (exit) cone** | **5° to 7°** | **LONG** | **DECELERATING flow separates easily — the gentle taper prevents it** |

> **The asymmetry is the most instructive feature of the instrument and it is asked often.**

> **A decelerating flow has an ADVERSE pressure gradient — pressure rising in the direction of flow — and boundary layers separate under those conditions.** Separation would cause turbulence, energy loss and an unstable reading.

> **So the exit cone is made three or four times as long as the entrance cone**, purely to recover the pressure gently. **This is why the venturi has a low permanent head loss (about 10 % of the differential) while an orifice plate loses 50 to 60 %.**

**Comparison of the flow meters, since the choice is examinable:**

| Meter | C_d | Head loss | Cost | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **VENTURI** | **0.95-0.98** | **LOW (~10 %)** | **HIGH** | **Long, bulky; best where head is precious** |
| **Orifice plate** | **0.60-0.65** | **HIGH (50-60 %)** | **LOW** | Compact, cheap, easily changed |
| **Nozzle** | 0.93-0.98 | Medium | Medium | Intermediate |
| **Pitot tube** | — | Negligible | Low | **Measures POINT velocity, not discharge** |

> **The trade-off is clean: the venturi costs more and loses less.** On a long pumped main the pumping cost of an orifice plate's permanent head loss can exceed the price difference in a season.

**And the reason to care about the low pressure at the throat — CAVITATION:**

> **If the throat pressure falls to the liquid's VAPOUR PRESSURE, the liquid boils** and vapour cavities form, which then collapse violently downstream.

> **The damage is real: pitting of the throat, noise, vibration, and a meter reading that becomes meaningless because the flow is no longer single-phase.**

> **So the throat cannot be made arbitrarily small.** The area ratio is limited by the requirement that the throat pressure stay comfortably above vapour pressure at the maximum flow — **which is the same limit that governs a pump's suction lift and a turbine's setting.**

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Lower** | **That is the PRESSURE at the throat, not the velocity** ← the swap |
| **Remains same** | **Would violate continuity for a changing area** |
| **All of these** | Mutually contradictory options cannot all hold |

> **Option (b) is the designed trap and it is a good one**, because at the throat one quantity does go down. **The candidate must keep straight which: velocity UP, pressure DOWN.**

examTip.trick: **Continuity forces the velocity UP at the smaller throat; Bernoulli then forces the pressure DOWN.** Highest velocity and lowest pressure both occur at the throat, always together.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) is the swap** — the PRESSURE falls at the throat, not the velocity. Keep straight which quantity goes which way.
examTip.mnemonic: **Entrance cone 20-22° and short; exit cone 5-7° and long** — because DECELERATING flow separates under an adverse pressure gradient. That gentle recovery is why a venturi loses ~10 % against an orifice plate's 50-60 %.

questions.stem: When pipes are connected in series, then:
questions.solution:
**Discharge will be constant.**

**The two rules for pipes in series:**

> **Pipes in series (compound pipes) are pipes of DIFFERENT lengths and DIFFERENT diameters joined END TO END.**

> **RULE 1 — DISCHARGE:  Q₁ = Q₂ = Q₃ = Q**

> **The same water must pass through every pipe in turn. There is nowhere else for it to go.** This is simply continuity applied to a single path.

> **RULE 2 — HEAD LOSS:  h_L = h_{L1} + h_{L2} + h_{L3}**

> **The losses ADD**, because the water suffers each one after the other.

> **So: discharge common, losses additive.** That pair is the whole of series pipe analysis.

**The parallel case, which is the exact mirror image and must be held alongside it:**

| | **SERIES** | **PARALLEL** |
|---|---|---|
| **Arrangement** | **End to end, one path** | **Branches that rejoin** |
| **DISCHARGE** | **Q₁ = Q₂ = Q₃ = Q  (COMMON)** | **Q = Q₁ + Q₂ + Q₃  (ADDS)** |
| **HEAD LOSS** | **h_L = h_{L1} + h_{L2} + h_{L3}  (ADDS)** | **h_{L1} = h_{L2} = h_{L3}  (COMMON)** |

> **Notice the perfect exchange: what is common in one is additive in the other, and vice versa.** Learning them as a pair is far more reliable than learning either alone, and this symmetry is why the pair is examined so often.

> **The electrical analogy is exact and useful: discharge behaves like current, head loss like voltage, and pipe resistance like electrical resistance.** Series resistances add; parallel currents add.

**The important consequence for the parallel case, worth stating because it is counter-intuitive:**

> **In parallel, the head loss is the SAME in every branch even though the branches differ in length and diameter.**

> **So a long thin branch carries LESS flow than a short fat one — the flows distribute themselves so that every branch happens to lose the same head.** The distribution is an output of the analysis, not an input.

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Pressure will be low** | **Meaningless as stated — low compared with what? The pressure varies continuously along the line** |
| **Discharge will be more** | **More than what? Adding pipes in series adds resistance, so for a given head the discharge is LESS, not more** |
| **Pressure will be medium** | **Not a statement about anything** |
| **Discharge will be constant** | ✓ **The one option that states a definite, correct relation** |

> **Options (a) and (c) are vague by construction**, and recognising vagueness is itself a technique: **an option that does not say what it is being compared with cannot be a correct answer to a definite question.**

> **Option (b) is the substantive wrong answer and inverts the physics.** Two pipes in series are *more* resistive than either alone, so **the discharge under a given head falls.** A candidate might be thinking of the parallel case, where adding a branch does increase the total discharge.

**The equivalent-pipe method, since it is the practical use of all this:**

> **A series of pipes can be replaced by a single EQUIVALENT PIPE that carries the same discharge under the same total head loss.**

> **Using Darcy-Weisbach, h_f = fLQ²/(12.1 D⁵), so for series pipes:**

> **L_e/D_e⁵ = L₁/D₁⁵ + L₂/D₂⁵ + L₃/D₃⁵**

> **Note the FIFTH POWER of diameter.** This is the most consequential relation in pipe hydraulics:

| Change | Effect on capacity at the same head loss |
|---|---|
| **Diameter × 1.26 (one standard size up)** | **Discharge × 1.78** |
| **Diameter × 2** | **Discharge × 5.7** |
| **Diameter × 1.15** | Discharge × 1.44 |

> **A modest increase in diameter buys a large increase in capacity**, which is why the economic pipe size is almost always larger than the minimum hydraulically adequate one — the pumping energy saved over the pipe's life outweighs the extra pipe cost.

**And the loss terms, for completeness:**

| Loss | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Friction (Darcy-Weisbach)** | **h_f = fLV²/(2gD)** |
| **Entry** | 0.5 V²/2g |
| **Exit** | **1.0 V²/2g — the FULL velocity head is lost** |
| **Sudden enlargement** | **(V₁−V₂)²/2g** |
| Bend, valve, fitting | k V²/2g |

> **In a long pipeline the friction loss dominates and the minor losses are often neglected; in a short one with many fittings the opposite is true.** The rule of thumb is that minor losses matter when the pipe length is less than about 1000 diameters.

examTip.trick: **SERIES: discharge COMMON, losses ADD. PARALLEL: losses COMMON, discharges ADD.** A perfect exchange — learn them as a pair, never singly.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) inverts the physics.** Pipes in series add resistance, so for a given head the discharge FALLS. Adding a PARALLEL branch is what increases discharge.
examTip.mnemonic: **Capacity goes as D^{5/2} at fixed head loss** — one standard size up (×1.26 diameter) buys ×1.78 discharge. That fifth-power law is why the economic pipe is bigger than the minimum adequate one.

questions.stem: The rules and regulations of the Nepal Engineering Council are approved by:
questions.solution:
**The Government of Nepal.**

**The mechanism, and why it is not a contradiction of the council's autonomy:**

> **Under the Nepal Engineering Council Act, 2055, the Council FRAMES its rules and regulations — and the GOVERNMENT OF NEPAL APPROVES them.**

> **This is the standard pattern for delegated legislation everywhere.** A statutory body is given power to make subordinate rules, but those rules bind the public, so **a democratically accountable authority must approve them before they take effect.**

> **The council proposes; the government approves.** Neither step alone is sufficient.

**Why this does not conflict with the council being an AUTONOMOUS body:**

| Layer | Who decides | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **The ACT itself** | **PARLIAMENT** | Primary legislation — creates the council and its powers |
| **RULES and REGULATIONS under the Act** | **Council frames, GOVERNMENT approves** | **Subordinate legislation — binding on the public** ← |
| **Individual decisions under the rules** | **The COUNCIL alone** | **Registration, examination results, discipline — no government involvement** |

> **The distinction is between making general rules and applying them.** The government has a say in the first and none in the second.

> **That is precisely the right division.** Rules that bind every engineer in the country should not be made by the profession alone without public accountability; **but deciding whether a particular engineer should be struck off must be free of political influence, and it is.**

> **So autonomy is preserved where it matters — in decisions about individuals — and shared where accountability requires it.**

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Why not |
|---|---|
| **Government of Nepal** | ✓ |
| **Nepal Engineering Council** | **The council FRAMES them; it does not approve its own rules.** A body approving its own binding rules would be accountable to no one ← the near-miss |
| **Nepal Engineer's Association (NEA)** | **A PROFESSIONAL ASSOCIATION, not a regulator.** Voluntary membership, no statutory power ← the important distinction |
| **All of these** | Cannot stand once (b) and (c) are excluded |

> **Option (b) is the designed trap, and reasoning it out is instructive.** It feels natural to say an autonomous body approves its own regulations. **But the whole point of requiring external approval is that rules binding the public need someone accountable to the public to sanction them.** The council frames; it does not self-approve.

**Option (c) is worth separating carefully, because the two bodies are constantly confused:**

| | **NEC — Nepal Engineering Council** | **NEA — Nepal Engineers' Association** |
|---|---|---|
| **Nature** | **STATUTORY REGULATOR (Act 2055)** | **Voluntary PROFESSIONAL ASSOCIATION** |
| **Membership** | **COMPULSORY to practise** | **Voluntary** |
| **Function** | **Registration, licensing, discipline, standards** | **Advocacy, welfare, CPD, technical events, representing members** |
| **Can it stop you practising?** | **YES — by refusing or removing registration** | **NO** |
| **Whose interest does it serve?** | **The PUBLIC's** | **The MEMBERS'** |

> **The last row is the deepest distinction and the one to remember.** A regulator exists to protect the public from bad engineering; **an association exists to advance the interests of engineers.** Both are legitimate, and they are not the same job — which is exactly why they are separate bodies.

> **Where they conflict, the regulator must win**, and that is the reason a professional association cannot be the licensing authority.

**And a note on this paper:** **an earlier question in the same paper asks what KIND of body the NEC is (autonomous), and this one asks who approves its rules (the government).** The two answers look inconsistent and are not — **and a candidate who reads them as contradictory will get one of the two wrong.** The resolution is the table above: autonomy in individual decisions, government approval for general rules.

examTip.trick: **The council FRAMES the rules; the GOVERNMENT approves them.** Standard delegated legislation — rules binding the public need someone accountable to the public to sanction them.
examTip.trap: **This paper also asks what kind of body the NEC is (autonomous).** The two answers look contradictory and are not: **autonomy in decisions about INDIVIDUALS, government approval for GENERAL RULES.**
examTip.mnemonic: **NEC is a statutory REGULATOR protecting the PUBLIC; NEA is a voluntary ASSOCIATION advancing MEMBERS' interests.** Only one can stop you practising — which is why they must be separate bodies.

questions.stem: The percentage of magnesia in cement is:
questions.solution:
**1 to 3 per cent.**

**The full oxide composition of ordinary Portland cement:**

| Constituent | Percentage | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **LIME, CaO** | **60-65** | **Forms the calcium silicates and aluminates — the largest constituent** |
| **SILICA, SiO₂** | **17-25** | **Imparts STRENGTH** |
| **ALUMINA, Al₂O₃** | **3-8** | **Quick setting; excess weakens** |
| **IRON OXIDE, Fe₂O₃** | **0.5-6** | **Colour, hardness, strength** |
| **MAGNESIA, MgO** | **1-3** | **A small amount adds strength and hardness** ← |
| **Sulphur trioxide, SO₃** | **1-3** | **Excess causes UNSOUNDNESS** |
| **Calcium sulphate (gypsum)** | **0.1-0.5** | **RETARDS setting — added after burning** |
| Alkalis (Na₂O, K₂O) | 0.5-1.3 | Excess causes efflorescence and alkali-silica reaction |

> **Lime and silica together make up over 80 per cent of the cement**, and the two behave in opposite ways when out of specification.

**Why the magnesia limit matters — and it is a durability limit, not a strength one:**

> **MgO does not hydrate at the same rate as the other constituents.** Free magnesia hydrates **very slowly** to Mg(OH)₂, and that reaction involves a **VOLUME INCREASE.**

> **If the expansion happens after the concrete has hardened, it cracks the concrete from within — UNSOUNDNESS.**

> **So the limit is not there to keep the cement weak enough; it is there to keep a delayed expansion from destroying hardened concrete years later.** IS 269 caps MgO at 6 per cent maximum, and the practical range in good cement is 1 to 3, with the source noting that **it should not exceed 2 per cent to maintain strength.**

**The two unsoundness constituents, which travel together:**

| Constituent | Reaction | Test |
|---|---|---|
| **Free MAGNESIA (MgO)** | **Slow hydration with expansion** | **AUTOCLAVE test (Le Chatelier misses it)** |
| **Free LIME (CaO)** | **Slow hydration with expansion** | **LE CHATELIER test** |
| **Excess SO₃** | Delayed sulphoaluminate formation, expansion | Both |

> **The distinction between the two soundness tests is examinable and is often confused.** The **Le Chatelier test detects unsoundness due to free LIME**, and the **AUTOCLAVE test detects unsoundness due to free MAGNESIA** — because magnesia hydrates too slowly for the boiling-water Le Chatelier method to reveal it. **Steam under pressure is needed to force the reaction within a test's duration.**

**The effect of each constituent being out of range — the pattern is worth seeing whole:**

| If too much | If too little |
|---|---|
| **Lime: cement becomes UNSOUND and expands** | **Lime: cement is WEAK and sets too fast** |
| **Silica: strength develops SLOWLY** | Silica: strength is low |
| **Alumina: cement WEAKENS, sets too fast** | Alumina: setting is slow |
| **Magnesia: UNSOUNDNESS** | Magnesia: no harm |
| **SO₃: UNSOUNDNESS** | SO₃/gypsum: FLASH SET |

> **Notice that lime is the constituent where BOTH excess and deficiency are harmful, and in opposite ways** — excess gives unsoundness, deficiency gives weakness and quick setting. **That symmetry is a favourite examination point.**

**The Bogue compounds, since the oxides combine into them and the compounds are what actually behave:**

| Compound | Symbol | % | Contributes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Tricalcium silicate** | **C₃S** | **~50** | **EARLY strength (7 days); high heat** |
| **Dicalcium silicate** | **C₂S** | **~25** | **LATER strength (beyond 28 days); low heat** |
| **Tricalcium aluminate** | **C₃A** | **~10** | **FLASH SET if ungypsumed; HIGHEST heat; SULPHATE VULNERABILITY** |
| **Tetracalcium aluminoferrite** | **C₄AF** | **~10** | Little strength; colour |

> **C₃A is the compound that explains three separate specifications at once:** gypsum is added to control its flash set, **low-heat cement reduces it** for mass concrete, and **sulphate-resisting cement reduces it** because sulphate attack works through C₃A. **One compound, three cement types.**

**Why the distractors are wrong:** **3-5 and 4-6 are the neighbouring ranges of alumina and iron oxide respectively**, so a candidate who remembers the shape of the table but not which row is which will be caught. **The oxide list has to be learned as a set, in order, because the ranges overlap.**

examTip.trick: **Learn the oxide table in order: lime 60-65, silica 17-25, alumina 3-8, iron oxide 0.5-6, MAGNESIA 1-3, SO₃ 1-3, gypsum 0.1-0.5.** The distractors here are the neighbouring rows.
examTip.trap: **Le Chatelier detects unsoundness from free LIME; the AUTOCLAVE test detects it from free MAGNESIA** — magnesia hydrates too slowly for boiling water to reveal it, so steam under pressure is needed.
examTip.mnemonic: **Lime is the one where BOTH excess and deficiency harm** — excess gives unsoundness, deficiency gives weakness and quick set. And **C₃A alone explains gypsum, low-heat cement and sulphate-resisting cement.**

questions.stem: The bearing capacity of cohesionless soil from a plate load test is:
questions.solution:
**Qu(f) = Qu(p) × Bf/Bp.**

> Where **Bf** is the width of the FOOTING, **Bp** the width of the test PLATE, and **Qu(p)** the ultimate bearing capacity measured on the plate.

**Why the capacity scales with width in SAND — and this is the physical reason:**

> **In a cohesionless soil the strength comes entirely from FRICTION, and friction needs CONFINING PRESSURE.**

> **A wide footing pushes its failure surface DEEPER into the ground**, where the overburden pressure is higher and the sand is therefore stronger.

> **A narrow plate mobilises only the weak, lightly confined sand near the surface.**

> **So the bearing capacity of sand INCREASES with the width of the loaded area**, and the scaling is linear in width. **Hence the direct ratio Bf/Bp.**

> **Since a real footing is always much wider than a 300-600 mm test plate, Qu(f) > Qu(p)** — the plate test UNDERSTATES the capacity of sand, and the correction increases it.

**The clay case is completely different, and the contrast is the whole point of the topic:**

| | **COHESIONLESS (sand)** | **COHESIVE (clay)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Strength from** | **FRICTION (needs confinement)** | **COHESION (independent of confinement)** |
| **Ultimate capacity** | **Qu(f) = Qu(p) × Bf/Bp — INCREASES with size** | **Qu(f) = Qu(p) — INDEPENDENT of size** |
| **SETTLEMENT at the same pressure** | **Sf = Sp × [Bf(Bp+0.3)/Bp(Bf+0.3)]²** | **Sf = Sp × Bf/Bp — increases with size** |
| **Which governs design?** | **Usually SETTLEMENT** | **Often bearing capacity, then settlement** |

> **The symmetry is elegant and worth noticing: in sand the CAPACITY scales with size; in clay the SETTLEMENT scales with size.**

> **For clay the answer would be option (d), Qu(p)** — the capacity is the same whatever the size, because c_u does not care about confining pressure. **So options (a) and (d) are the sand and clay answers respectively, and the question's word "cohesionless" is what selects between them.**

**Why the plate load test's limitation matters — the depth of influence:**

> **A loaded area influences the soil to roughly 1.5 to 2 times its own width.**

| Loaded area | Depth influenced |
|---|---|
| **300 mm test plate** | **~0.45 to 0.6 m** |
| **3 m footing** | **~4.5 to 6 m** |

> **This is the test's fundamental weakness, and it cannot be corrected by any formula.**

> **If a soft layer lies 2 m below the surface, the plate never feels it — but the footing sits on it.** The plate returns an excellent result and the building settles badly.

> **So the plate load test must ALWAYS be accompanied by a borehole to at least twice the footing width**, to confirm there is nothing unpleasant below the plate's reach. **A plate test alone is not a soil investigation.**

> **That is the honest limitation to state, and it is why the test has largely given way to SPT and CPT for anything important** — those sample or probe the full depth of influence.

**The test itself, for completeness:**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Plate size** | **300 to 750 mm square (or 300 mm circular)** |
| **Test pit width** | **At least 5 times the plate width** |
| **Plate seated at** | **The proposed foundation level** |
| **Load increments** | **About one fifth of the estimated safe load** |
| **Each increment held** | **Until settlement is less than 0.02 mm/min** |
| **Ultimate load read as** | **The point of shear failure, or the load at a settlement of one fifth the plate width** |

> **The requirement that the test pit be five plate widths across is often skipped and matters**: a narrow pit confines the plate laterally and inflates the result.

**Why the other distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **(Bp/Bf) × Qu(p)** | **The ratio INVERTED — would predict that a wide footing has LESS capacity than a small plate, which is backwards for sand** ← the trap |
| **2 Qu(p)** | An arbitrary factor with no basis; the ratio depends on the actual sizes |
| **Qu(p)** | **Correct for CLAY, not for sand** |

> **Option (b) is the designed trap** because the two symbols are easy to transpose. **The check is physical, not algebraic: a wide footing on sand must be STRONGER, so the footing width belongs on TOP.**

examTip.trick: **Sand's strength is FRICTION, which needs confinement, and a wide footing pushes its failure surface deeper into better-confined sand.** So capacity scales with width: Qu(f) = Qu(p)·Bf/Bp.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) has the ratio inverted, and option (d) is the CLAY answer** (capacity independent of size, since cohesion does not need confinement). The word "cohesionless" selects between them.
examTip.mnemonic: **In sand the CAPACITY scales with size; in clay the SETTLEMENT does.** And the plate's fatal limit: it influences only ~1.5-2 plate widths of depth, so a soft layer 2 m down is invisible to it. Always drill a borehole too.

questions.stem: For a simply supported beam, the bending moment diagram due to a point load is:
questions.solution:
**Triangular.**

**Why triangular — the degree argument, which answers every question of this kind:**

> **Between the support and the load there is no distributed load, so the shear force is CONSTANT.**

> **The bending moment is the integral of the shear force, so a constant shear integrates to a LINEAR moment.**

> **Two straight lines meeting at a peak under the load, returning to zero at each support: a TRIANGLE.**

**For a central point load W on a span L:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **Reactions** | **W/2 each** |
| **Shear force** | **+W/2 from A to C, then −W/2 from C to B — a step change AT the load** |
| **Maximum bending moment** | **WL/4, at mid-span** |
| **BMD shape** | **TRIANGLE, apex WL/4 at the centre** |

> **WL/4 is the number to have instantly**, and it is the single most-used bending moment result in structural engineering.

**The general rule that generates all the standard shapes — learn this and stop memorising diagrams:**

> **Each integration raises the degree of the curve by one.**

| Loading | Shear force diagram | Bending moment diagram |
|---|---|---|
| **Point load** | **Constant (rectangular), with a STEP at the load** | **LINEAR → TRIANGLE** ← |
| **Uniformly distributed load (udl)** | **Linear (triangular/trapezoidal)** | **PARABOLIC (2nd degree)** |
| **Triangular (linearly varying) load** | **Parabolic** | **CUBIC (3rd degree)** |
| **Applied couple/moment** | No change | **STEP jump in the BMD** |

> **The pattern: load → shear → moment, each one degree higher.** A point load is degree 0 in the shear, so degree 1 in the moment — a straight line, hence a triangle.

**The three companion relations, which make any diagram checkable:**

> **dV/dx = −w**  (the slope of the shear diagram is minus the load intensity)

> **dM/dx = V**  (the slope of the moment diagram is the shear force)

> **Therefore M is maximum where V = 0 or changes sign.**

> **The last one is the workhorse: to find the maximum moment, find where the shear crosses zero.** For a central point load the shear jumps straight through zero at the load, so the moment peaks exactly there.

**The standard maxima worth having memorised, since they are the currency of the subject:**

| Beam and load | Maximum BM | Maximum deflection |
|---|---|---|
| **SSB, central point load W** | **WL/4** | **WL³/48EI** |
| **SSB, udl w** | **wL²/8** | **5wL⁴/384EI** |
| **Cantilever, end point load W** | **WL** | **WL³/3EI** |
| **Cantilever, udl w** | **wL²/2** | **wL⁴/8EI** |
| **Fixed beam, udl w** | **wL²/12 at supports, wL²/24 at centre** | **wL⁴/384EI** |
| Fixed beam, central point load | **WL/8 at both supports and centre** | WL³/192EI |

> **Note how the fixed beam's udl deflection is exactly ONE FIFTH of the simply supported one** (wL⁴/384 against 5wL⁴/384) — the restraint at the ends is worth a factor of five in stiffness, which is asked elsewhere in this same paper.

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | What it would correspond to |
|---|---|
| **Rectangular** | **A constant moment — which happens only under PURE BENDING (equal end couples, or between two equal point loads)** ← the interesting one |
| **Square** | **Not a diagram description; a geometric shape name confused with "rectangular"** |
| **Triangular** | ✓ |
| **Line** | Would mean zero moment everywhere |

> **Option (a) is the instructive distractor**, because a rectangular BMD is a real thing: **the central region of a beam under two symmetric point loads carries constant moment and zero shear — pure bending.** That is exactly the arrangement used in the FOUR-POINT BENDING TEST for the modulus of rupture, precisely because it gives a region of uniform moment with no shear to complicate the failure.

> **So the candidate must attach each shape to its cause: point load → triangle; udl → parabola; two symmetric point loads → trapezium with a rectangular middle.**

examTip.trick: **No distributed load → constant shear → LINEAR moment → triangle.** Each integration raises the degree by one: point load gives a triangle, udl gives a parabola, triangular load gives a cubic.
examTip.trap: **A RECTANGULAR BMD is a real thing** — the constant-moment region between two symmetric point loads (pure bending), which is exactly why the four-point bending test is arranged that way.
examTip.mnemonic: **dM/dx = V, so M peaks where V crosses zero.** And have WL/4, wL²/8, WL and wL²/2 instantly — plus **fixed-beam udl deflection is exactly 1/5 of the simply supported value.**

questions.stem: How many types of river training works are there?
questions.solution:
**Three.**

**The classification by PURPOSE:**

| Type | Purpose | Typical works |
|---|---|---|
| **Training for DISCHARGE (high-water training)** | **Provide adequate waterway for the FLOOD discharge and control flooding** | **Levees, embankments, flood walls** |
| **Training for DEPTH (low-water training)** | **Concentrate the low-season flow to maintain NAVIGABLE or usable depth** | **Bandalling, groynes/spurs, dredging** |
| **Training for SEDIMENT (mean-water training)** | **Control the river's COURSE and the movement of its bed material** | **Guide banks, spurs, pitching, cut-offs** |

> **Three purposes, three types — and each corresponds to a different flow condition: high water, low water, mean water.** That is the memorable structure of the classification.

> **A single structure often serves more than one purpose**, which is why the classification is by objective rather than by hardware. **A spur can be built for depth or for sediment control depending on how it is placed.**

**The main structures themselves, since the count question is usually followed by one on these:**

| Structure | What it does |
|---|---|
| **GUIDE BANKS (Bell's bunds)** | **Guide the river through a bridge or headworks opening; protect the approach embankments** |
| **SPURS / GROYNES** | **Project into the flow to deflect it away from a bank, or to attract it** |
| **MARGINAL EMBANKMENTS (levees)** | Confine the flood within a defined width |
| **CUT-OFFS** | **Shorten the course by cutting through a meander loop, steepening the slope** |
| **PITCHING and revetment** | Armour a bank against direct attack |
| **Launching apron** | **Stone that falls into a developing scour hole and self-protects the toe** ← |
| **Bandalling** | Bamboo screens that concentrate low flow — cheap, temporary, and traditional |
| Artificial and closing dykes | Close off secondary channels |

> **The LAUNCHING APRON is the concept most worth understanding**, because it explains how river works survive at all. **Stone laid on the bed beyond the toe of a protection "launches" — slides down — as the bed scours, automatically covering the new slope.** The apron is deliberately designed to be destroyed in an orderly way. **A protection without a launching apron simply undermines and collapses.**

**The two kinds of spur, which is a favourite discrimination:**

| Spur | Points | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **REPELLING (pointing upstream)** | **Upstream, at about 60-70° to the bank** | **REPELS the flow away from the bank — the usual choice for bank protection** |
| **ATTRACTING (pointing downstream)** | **Downstream** | **ATTRACTS the flow toward the bank — used to hold a channel in a desired position** |
| **Deflecting (normal)** | At 90° | Local deflection only |
| **T-headed (Denehy's)** | With a head across the tip | Provides a longer line of defence |

> **The counter-intuitive one is worth fixing: a spur pointing UPSTREAM REPELS the flow.** The intuition that a structure points where it sends the water is exactly wrong.

**Why a river needs training at all, in Nepal in particular:**

> **Himalayan rivers are BRAIDED and carry enormous sediment loads**, and they change their channel from one monsoon to the next.

| Problem | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Meandering and bank erosion** | Land loss; villages and roads undermined |
| **Channel shifting** | **A bridge or an intake left dry while the river flows a kilometre away** |
| **Aggradation** | **The bed RISES, so the same discharge floods more — the Terai's characteristic problem** |
| Scour at structures | Bridge pier and abutment failure |

> **The aggradation problem is the one specific to this region and the hardest to solve.** A river that deposits its bed load in the Terai raises its own bed year on year, **so embankments must be raised repeatedly and the flood risk grows even without any change in rainfall.** Training works can guide such a river; they cannot stop it depositing.

**Why the distractors are wrong:** **2, 5 and 7 are near counts with no standing in the classification.** The question tests whether the three-purpose scheme has been learned as a scheme — **and a candidate who knows the three purposes (discharge, depth, sediment) can never be uncertain about the count.**

examTip.trick: **Three purposes, three types — and each matches a flow condition: DISCHARGE (high water), DEPTH (low water), SEDIMENT (mean water).** Know the scheme and the count follows.
examTip.trap: **A spur pointing UPSTREAM REPELS the flow** — the intuition that it sends water where it points is exactly backwards. Downstream-pointing spurs ATTRACT.
examTip.mnemonic: **The LAUNCHING APRON is designed to be destroyed in an orderly way** — stone slides down into the developing scour hole and covers the new slope. Protection without one simply undermines and collapses.

questions.stem: Which of the following IS standard codes has live or imposed load specified?
questions.solution:
**IS 875 (Part 2).**

**The five parts of IS 875 — the loading code:**

| Part | Load |
|---|---|
| **IS 875 (Part 1)** | **DEAD loads — unit weights of materials and stored materials** |
| **IS 875 (Part 2)** | **IMPOSED (LIVE) loads** ← |
| **IS 875 (Part 3)** | **WIND loads** |
| **IS 875 (Part 4)** | **SNOW loads** |
| **IS 875 (Part 5)** | **SPECIAL loads and LOAD COMBINATIONS** |

> **1 dead, 2 live, 3 wind, 4 snow, 5 special and combinations.** That ordering is the whole question, and it is asked in one form or another almost every sitting.

> **Note the terminology: "imposed load" and "live load" mean the same thing**, and the code's own title uses "imposed". The two terms are interchangeable, and the question says so explicitly.

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **IS 456: 2** | **IS 456 has NO PARTS. It is a single document: "Plain and Reinforced Concrete - Code of Practice"** |
| **IS 875: 2** | ✓ |
| **IS 875: 3** | **WIND load — the neighbouring part, and the commonest wrong answer** |
| **IS 456: 3** | **Again, IS 456 has no parts** |

> **Options (a) and (d) can be eliminated on a structural fact rather than on recall: IS 456 is not a multi-part code.** Recognising that halves the question instantly and leaves a two-way choice between Part 2 and Part 3.

> **Then the ordering settles it: dead comes first, live second, wind third.** **Wind is Part 3, which is the number most often misremembered as Part 2** because Part 3 (wind) is the part engineers use most often and most consciously.

**The codes a civil engineer must be able to name on sight:**

| Code | Subject |
|---|---|
| **IS 456: 2000** | **Plain and reinforced CONCRETE — the central design code** |
| **IS 875 (Parts 1-5)** | **LOADS** ← |
| **IS 1893 (Part 1)** | **EARTHQUAKE resistant design** |
| **IS 800: 2007** | **STEEL structures (limit state)** |
| **IS 383** | **Coarse and fine AGGREGATE** |
| **IS 269 / 1489 / 8112 / 12269** | **Cement — OPC 33, PPC, OPC 43, OPC 53** |
| **IS 10262** | **Concrete MIX DESIGN** |
| **IS 2720** | Methods of test for SOILS (many parts) |
| **IS 1905** | **Unreinforced MASONRY** |
| **IS 883** | Timber structures |
| **IS 3370** | Liquid-retaining structures |
| **IS 1200** | **Method of MEASUREMENT of building works** |
| **SP 16** | **Design AIDS to IS 456 — charts and tables** |

> **IS 456, IS 875, IS 1893 and IS 800 are the four that carry a design**, and confusing their numbers in an answer script suggests unfamiliarity more damaging than the lost mark.

**And the Nepali equivalents, which govern in Nepal and are examined alongside:**

| Nepali code | Subject |
|---|---|
| **NBC 102** | **Unit weights of materials** |
| **NBC 103** | **Occupancy load (IMPOSED load) — the Nepali counterpart of IS 875 Part 2** |
| **NBC 104** | **Wind load** |
| **NBC 105** | **SEISMIC design of buildings in Nepal** |
| **NBC 106** | **Snow load** |

> **The parallel is close and worth noticing: NBC 103 is to imposed load what IS 875 Part 2 is.** A question may be asked in either the Indian or the Nepali frame, and **NBC 103 for imposed load, NBC 104 for wind, NBC 105 for seismic** is the set to hold.

> **In Nepal the NBC governs, with the IS codes used where the NBC is silent** — which is common in detailed design, since the NBC is a loading and general-requirements code rather than a full design code.

examTip.trick: **IS 875: Part 1 dead, Part 2 IMPOSED/LIVE, Part 3 wind, Part 4 snow, Part 5 special and combinations.** "Imposed" and "live" are the same thing.
examTip.trap: **IS 456 has NO PARTS** — it is a single document. That fact eliminates options (a) and (d) instantly, without recalling anything about loads.
examTip.mnemonic: **Nepali parallel: NBC 103 imposed, NBC 104 wind, NBC 105 seismic, NBC 106 snow, NBC 102 unit weights.** A question may be asked in either frame, so hold both sets.

questions.stem: Chlorine usage in the treatment of 25000 m³/day of water is 9 kg/day. The residual chlorine after 10 min of contact is 0.2 mg/l. Calculate the dosage in milligram per litre and the chlorine demand of the water.
questions.solution:
**Dosage 0.36 mg/l, chlorine demand 0.16 mg/l.**

**Step 1 — convert the water treated to litres:**

> **25,000 m³/day × 1000 L/m³ = 25 × 10⁶ L/day**

**Step 2 — convert the chlorine used to milligrams:**

> **9 kg/day = 9 × 10⁶ mg/day**

> **(1 kg = 10⁶ mg — two factors of a thousand, and this is where slips happen.)**

**Step 3 — the DOSAGE is chlorine applied per litre of water:**

> **Dosage = 9 × 10⁶ mg/day ÷ 25 × 10⁶ L/day**

> **= 0.36 mg/l**

**Step 4 — apply the definition that the whole question turns on:**

> **CHLORINE DOSAGE = CHLORINE DEMAND + RESIDUAL CHLORINE**

> **0.36 = demand + 0.2**

> **Chlorine DEMAND = 0.36 − 0.2 = 0.16 mg/l** ✓

**The three terms, since confusing them is the only way to fail this question:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **DOSAGE (applied chlorine)** | **The TOTAL chlorine added per litre** |
| **DEMAND (chlorine consumed)** | **The part CONSUMED by organic matter, ammonia, iron, manganese and pathogens** |
| **RESIDUAL** | **The part LEFT OVER after the contact period — the protection carried into the distribution system** |

> **Dosage = demand + residual.** The demand is what the water eats; the residual is what survives.

> **A question can give any two and ask for the third, so the relation matters more than the arithmetic.**

**Why the distractor structure is instructive:**

| Option | What the candidate did |
|---|---|
| **0.36, 0.16** | ✓ |
| **0.36, 0.36** | **Got the dosage right, then confused demand WITH dosage — forgot to subtract the residual** |
| **0.16, 0.36** | **Correct numbers, ANSWERS TRANSPOSED** ← the classic |
| **0.16, 0.16** | Subtracted, then reported the demand twice |

> **Option (c) is the designed trap and the commonest error in questions of this shape: both numbers are right and the labels are swapped.** The defence is to read what is asked FIRST and in what ORDER — here "the dosage ... and the chlorine demand", so dosage comes first.

> **Notice also that the 10-minute contact time is given and is not needed.** It is context, establishing that the residual is measured after the standard contact period. **A question containing an unused datum is testing whether you can identify what is relevant** — and an unused number often prompts candidates to invent a use for it.

**Why the residual is kept at all, since the water is already disinfected:**

> **The residual protects against RECONTAMINATION IN THE DISTRIBUTION SYSTEM** — through a leaking joint, a repair, a back-siphonage, or a cross-connection.

| Standard | Value |
|---|---|
| **Residual at the far end of the network** | **0.2 mg/l minimum** |
| **Residual after treatment (leaving the works)** | **0.5 mg/l typical** |
| **Contact time required** | **At least 30 minutes at pH < 8** |
| **Break-point chlorination residual type** | **FREE residual — the effective form** |

> **The 0.2 mg/l figure in this question is exactly the standard minimum residual**, which is why it was chosen.

**The break-point chlorination curve, which explains why demand is not simply proportional to dose:**

> **As chlorine is added to water containing ammonia, four things happen in sequence:**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Chlorine is destroyed by reducing agents — NO residual at all** |
| **2** | **CHLORAMINES form (combined residual) — residual rises** |
| **3** | **Chloramines are DESTROYED — the residual FALLS to the BREAK POINT** |
| **4** | **Beyond the break point, FREE residual chlorine appears and rises linearly** |

> **Chlorination is practised BEYOND the break point**, because only free residual chlorine is a reliable disinfectant — **combined (chloramine) residual is far weaker.**

> **The counter-intuitive consequence is important: adding MORE chlorine can REDUCE the residual**, in stage 3. **A plant operator who responds to a low residual by adding a little more chlorine can make it worse**, and the only way out is to dose well past the break point.

examTip.trick: **DOSAGE = DEMAND + RESIDUAL.** Dosage = 9×10⁶ mg ÷ 25×10⁶ L = 0.36 mg/l; demand = 0.36 − 0.2 = 0.16 mg/l.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) has both correct numbers TRANSPOSED** — the classic trap in two-answer questions. Read what is asked and in what order before computing. Note also that the 10-minute contact time is not needed.
examTip.mnemonic: **Chlorinate BEYOND the break point**, because only FREE residual disinfects reliably. The counter-intuitive consequence: in stage 3, adding MORE chlorine REDUCES the residual.

questions.stem: Determine the shear stress required to move a single grain on the side slopes, if the critical shear stress required to move a similar grain on the horizontal bed is 2.91 N/m². Take the angle of the side slope with the horizontal as 30° and the angle of repose of the soil as 37°.
questions.solution:
**1.61 N/m².**

**The formula for tractive force on a side slope:**

> **τ′ = τ_c √(1 − sin²θ / sin²φ)**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value here |
|---|---|---|
| **τ_c** | **Critical shear stress on the HORIZONTAL bed** | **2.91 N/m²** |
| **θ** | **Angle of the SIDE SLOPE with the horizontal** | **30°** |
| **φ** | **ANGLE OF REPOSE of the soil** | **37°** |

**The computation:**

> **sin 30° = 0.5000**  →  **sin²30° = 0.2500**

> **sin 37° = 0.6018**  →  **sin²37° = 0.3622**

> **sin²θ / sin²φ = 0.2500 / 0.3622 = 0.6903**

> **1 − 0.6903 = 0.3097**

> **√0.3097 = 0.5565**

> **τ′ = 2.91 × 0.5565 = 1.6195 ≈ 1.61 N/m²** ✓

**Why the side slope value is LOWER — the physical reason, which is the point of the question:**

> **A grain on the BED is held down by its own submerged weight acting perpendicular to the bed.** The flow must overcome friction alone.

> **A grain on a SIDE SLOPE has a COMPONENT OF ITS OWN WEIGHT acting DOWN THE SLOPE**, already trying to move it.

> **So part of the grain's available friction is already used up resisting gravity, and less remains to resist the flow.**

> **The grain on the slope is therefore easier to dislodge, and the permissible shear stress is lower.**

> **Hence a lined or unlined canal's SIDE SLOPES are more vulnerable to erosion than its bed** — which is the design conclusion, and the reason side-slope protection is provided where the bed needs none.

**The two limiting checks that confirm the formula:**

> **CHECK 1 — a horizontal "slope" (θ = 0):** τ′ = τ_c √(1 − 0) = **τ_c.** Correct: no slope, no reduction.

> **CHECK 2 — the slope at the angle of repose (θ = φ):** τ′ = τ_c √(1 − 1) = **ZERO.**

> **The second check is the striking one and is worth dwelling on: at the angle of repose the grain is on the verge of sliding under its own weight, so ANY flow at all will move it.**

> **This is exactly why a canal's side slope must be flatter than the angle of repose**, and why a slope built at the angle of repose has no margin whatever against erosion.

> **Here θ = 30° against φ = 37°, so the slope is comfortably flatter than the repose angle** and the reduction factor is 0.56 rather than zero.

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **1.61 N/m²** | ✓ |
| **2.61 N/m²** | **Close to the given bed value 2.91 — what a candidate reports who applies only a small correction, or who computes √(1 − sinθ/sinφ) without the squares** |
| **1.61 N** | **RIGHT NUMBER, WRONG UNIT.** Newtons is a force; shear STRESS is force per unit area, N/m² ← the trap |
| **All of the above** | Cannot hold, since the options are mutually inconsistent |

> **Option (c) is the designed trap and an excellent one, because the arithmetic is complete and correct.** The candidate has done all the work and then thrown the mark away on the unit.

> **A stress is never in newtons.** N/m² = Pa; kN/m² = kPa. **Checking the unit of the final answer costs one second and catches this whole class of error.**

**Where the tractive-force approach sits in canal design:**

| Method | Basis |
|---|---|
| **PERMISSIBLE VELOCITY method** | Keep the mean velocity below a tabulated maximum for the soil — simple, empirical |
| **TRACTIVE FORCE (shear stress) method** | **Keep the boundary shear below the critical value for the grain — rational, and treats bed and sides separately** ← |
| **Regime theory (Kennedy, Lacey)** | Silt-transporting equilibrium |

> **The tractive-force method is the physically sound one** because scour is caused by the shear the flow exerts on individual grains, not by the mean velocity of the section. **And it is the only one of the three that distinguishes the bed from the side slopes** — which this question is precisely about.

> **The bed shear in a wide channel is τ = γ R S ≈ γ y S**, and comparing that with the critical shear for the soil is the check that decides whether a canal needs lining.

examTip.trap: **Option (c) is the same number in NEWTONS.** A stress is never in newtons — N/m² or kPa. Checking the unit of the answer costs a second and catches this whole class of error.
examTip.mnemonic: **At θ = φ the formula gives ZERO** — a grain on a slope at the angle of repose is already on the verge of sliding, so any flow moves it. That is why canal side slopes must be flatter than the repose angle.

questions.stem: The branch of science which deals with the occurrence, circulation and distribution of the waters of the earth and its atmosphere is:
questions.solution:
**Hydrology.**

**The definition, essentially as the question states it:**

> **HYDROLOGY is the science of the occurrence, circulation and distribution of WATER on and below the earth's surface and in its atmosphere** — including its physical and chemical properties and its interaction with the environment and with living things.

> **The key word in the question is "waters".** Every option names a science, and only one of them has water as its subject.

**Why each distractor is wrong, and each is a genuinely different thing:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **PRECIPITATION** | **Not a science at all — it is a PROCESS, one component of the hydrologic cycle** |
| **CLIMATOLOGY** | **The study of climate — LONG-TERM average weather patterns over decades** |
| **HYDROLOGY** | ✓ **The waters of the earth** |
| **METEOROLOGY** | **The study of the ATMOSPHERE and SHORT-TERM weather** |

> **Option (a) can be eliminated on a category error alone: the question asks for a branch of science, and precipitation is a phenomenon.**

> **Options (b) and (d) are the pair worth separating properly**, because both concern the atmosphere and both are neighbours of hydrology:

| | **METEOROLOGY** | **CLIMATOLOGY** |
|---|---|---|
| **Timescale** | **HOURS to days — weather** | **DECADES — climate** |
| **Question answered** | **"Will it rain tomorrow?"** | **"What is the annual rainfall pattern of this region?"** |
| **Method** | Forecasting from current state | Statistics of long records |

> **The useful compression: meteorology is weather, climatology is the STATISTICS of weather, hydrology is what the water does once it arrives.**

**The hydrologic cycle, since hydrology is the study of it:**

| Process | Description |
|---|---|
| **EVAPORATION** | Liquid water to vapour from water bodies and soil |
| **TRANSPIRATION** | Water released by plants (together: EVAPOTRANSPIRATION) |
| **CONDENSATION** | Vapour to cloud droplets |
| **PRECIPITATION** | **Rain, snow, hail — water returning to the surface** |
| **INTERCEPTION** | Caught by vegetation before reaching the ground |
| **INFILTRATION** | Water entering the soil |
| **PERCOLATION** | Downward movement to groundwater |
| **RUNOFF** | Overland and channel flow |
| **Groundwater flow** | Sub-surface movement to streams and the sea |

> **The cycle has NO beginning and NO end, and the total quantity of water on earth is essentially CONSTANT.** What hydrology studies is its distribution and its timing — **and timing is the whole engineering problem, since a year's rain falling in three months is a flood followed by a drought.**

**The water balance equation, which is hydrology's central tool:**

> **P = R + E + T + I + ΔS**

> **Precipitation = runoff + evaporation + transpiration + infiltration + change in storage.**

> **Every hydrological calculation is a version of this, applied to a defined catchment over a defined period.** The art lies in knowing which terms can be neglected: **over a long period ΔS → 0; over a single storm, E and T are negligible.**

**What a civil engineer uses hydrology for:**

| Application | The hydrological question |
|---|---|
| **Bridge and culvert design** | **What is the DESIGN FLOOD for a chosen return period?** |
| **Spillway design** | **What is the probable maximum flood?** |
| **Reservoir sizing** | **How much water arrives, and when?** |
| **Water supply** | Is the yield reliable in the driest year on record? |
| **Irrigation** | Crop water requirement against available supply |
| **Urban drainage** | Peak runoff from a rainfall of stated intensity |

> **Return period is the concept that binds these together: T = 1/p, so a 100-year flood has a 1 per cent chance in any given year.**

> **And the point most often misunderstood: a 100-year flood is not one that occurs every hundred years.** The probability of at least one such flood in a 100-year design life is **1 − (0.99)¹⁰⁰ = 63 per cent** — so a structure designed for the 100-year flood is more likely than not to meet it. **That is why important structures are designed for much longer return periods.**

examTip.trick: **The key word is "waters".** Every option names a field, but only hydrology has water as its subject. Precipitation is not a science at all — it is a process.
examTip.trap: **Meteorology is WEATHER (hours to days); climatology is the STATISTICS of weather (decades).** Both concern the atmosphere and both neighbour hydrology, which is what makes them plausible.
examTip.mnemonic: **A 100-year flood is not one per century.** Over a 100-year life the chance of at least one is 1 − 0.99¹⁰⁰ = **63 %** — more likely than not. Which is why important structures use far longer return periods.

questions.stem: How often is the regular inspection done for engineering institutions provided with permanent approval?
questions.solution:
**Every two years.**

**The Nepal Engineering Council inspection schedule:**

| Programme | Approval status | Inspection interval |
|---|---|---|
| **Bachelor** | **PERMANENT approval** | **Every 2 years** ← |
| **Bachelor** | **TEMPORARY approval** | **Every 1 year** |
| **Master** | **Temporary approval** | **Every 1 year** |
| **Master** | **Permanent approval** | **Every 18 months** |

> **The logic of the schedule is straightforward and worth reading rather than memorising blindly:**

> **TEMPORARY approval means the institution has not yet demonstrated sustained compliance, so it is watched more closely — annually.**

> **PERMANENT approval means it has, so the interval lengthens.**

> **Note that every one of the four intervals appears among the options**, which is what makes the question demanding: **the candidate must match the right pair of attributes (level of programme AND type of approval), not merely recall one number.**

**Why accreditation of institutions is part of a licensing council's work at all:**

> **The council's central function is to decide who may practise.** A graduate's degree is the primary evidence of competence.

> **So the council must satisfy itself that the DEGREE means something — which requires inspecting the institution that awards it.**

| What an inspection examines | Note |
|---|---|
| **Faculty — numbers, qualifications, permanence** | **The single most important input** |
| **Laboratories and equipment** | Engineering cannot be taught without them |
| **Library and learning resources** | — |
| **Curriculum and its delivery** | Against the recognised syllabus |
| **Student intake against sanctioned capacity** | **Over-enrolment dilutes everything else** |
| Physical infrastructure | Classrooms, workshops |

> **Faculty and laboratories are what an inspection is really about**, because they are the two things that cannot be produced quickly for a visit and cannot be substituted for.

**The consequence of recognition, which is why the process has teeth:**

> **A graduate of an unrecognised programme CANNOT REGISTER with the council, and therefore cannot practise as an engineer in Nepal.**

> **That is a severe consequence for a student who has already spent four years and a great deal of money**, and it falls on the student rather than on the institution. **Which is why the council publishes the list of recognised programmes, and why checking it before enrolling is genuine practical advice.**

> **Recognition of FOREIGN degrees works through the same power**: the council assesses the qualification, and may require an examination or additional study before permitting registration.

**And the wider structure this sits in:**

| Function | Body |
|---|---|
| **University-level academic accreditation** | **The UNIVERSITY and the University Grants Commission** |
| **PROFESSIONAL recognition for licensing** | **NEPAL ENGINEERING COUNCIL** ← |
| Institutional affiliation | The affiliating university |

> **Two separate approvals are needed, and they answer different questions.** The university asks whether the institution can award its degree; **the council asks whether that degree qualifies its holder to practise engineering on the public.**

> **An institution can hold the first and not the second**, and a student who assumes university affiliation implies council recognition has made an expensive mistake. **The two are related but independent, and the council's inspection cycle set out above is the mechanism by which the second is maintained.**

examTip.trick: **Bachelor permanent: 2 years. Bachelor or Master temporary: 1 year. Master permanent: 18 months.** All four intervals appear among the options, so the pair of attributes must be matched, not one number recalled.
examTip.trap: **The logic is that temporary approval is watched more closely.** Unproven compliance → annual; demonstrated compliance → longer interval. Reasoning it out beats memorising four numbers.
examTip.mnemonic: **A graduate of an unrecognised programme cannot REGISTER, so cannot practise** — and that falls on the student, not the institution. University affiliation does NOT imply council recognition; the two are independent.

questions.stem: The average anchorage value of hooks is:
questions.solution:
**16 times the bar diameter (16φ).**

**The anchorage values from IS 456:2000 clause 26.2.2.1(b):**

| Detail | Anchorage value |
|---|---|
| **BEND through 45°** | **4φ** |
| **BEND through 90°** | **8φ** |
| **BEND through 135°** | **12φ** |
| **U-type HOOK (180° bend)** | **16φ** ← |

> **The pattern is exactly 4φ for every 45° of bend**, up to a maximum of 16φ. **That single rule generates the whole table**, and it is far easier than memorising four numbers:

> **45° → 4φ, 90° → 8φ, 135° → 12φ, 180° → 16φ.**

> **A hook is a 180° bend, so it earns the full 16φ.**

**What anchorage value MEANS, since the concept is more useful than the number:**

> **A bar in tension must be held in the concrete by a DEVELOPMENT LENGTH L_d of straight bar.**

> **If there is not enough room for the full straight length, a bend or hook is provided, and the bend is CREDITED with being equivalent to a stated length of straight bar.**

> **So: straight length provided + anchorage value of the bend ≥ L_d.**

> **The hook does not create anchorage out of nothing** — it works by bearing on the concrete inside the bend and by the mechanical interlock of the turned-back end. **It substitutes for straight length, which is why it is measured in bar diameters.**

**The development length itself, since the two are always used together:**

> **L_d = φ σ_s / (4 τ_bd)**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **σ_s** | **Stress in the bar (0.87 f_y at design strength)** |
| **τ_bd** | **Design bond stress — 1.2, 1.4, 1.5, 1.7, 1.9 N/mm² for M20 to M40** |

> **Two modifications apply and both are examinable:**

| Case | Factor on τ_bd |
|---|---|
| **DEFORMED bars** | **× 1.6 — the ribs give mechanical bond** |
| **Bars in COMPRESSION** | **× 1.25 — end bearing helps** |

> **For Fe415 deformed bars in M20 concrete, L_d works out to about 47φ**, commonly rounded to **47 times the diameter** — and the figure to remember is that **L_d is roughly 47φ for the standard combination.**

> **Compare that with a hook's 16φ and the proportion becomes clear: a hook supplies about a third of the required anchorage.** It is a useful supplement, never a substitute for development length.

**The bend geometry, which the anchorage value depends on:**

| Requirement | Value |
|---|---|
| **Minimum internal radius of bend** | **2φ for mild steel, 4φ for HYSD** |
| **Minimum straight length beyond a 180° hook** | **4φ** |
| **Minimum straight length beyond a 90° bend** | **4φ** |

> **The straight tail beyond the bend is not optional.** Without it the bar can straighten out under load and the anchorage is lost — **and "a hook with no tail" is a common site defect that looks correct on a drawing.**

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **16 dia** | ✓ **180° hook** |
| **20 dia** | Not a standard anchorage value |
| **32 dia** | Not standard — but is roughly the LAP length order of magnitude, so it feels plausible |
| **12 dia** | **The anchorage value of a 135° BEND** ← the trap |

> **Option (d) is the designed trap** because 12φ is a genuine value from the same table. **The question asks for a HOOK (180°), not a bend, and the two words are used precisely in the code** — a "bend" turns the bar through less than 180°, a "hook" turns it right back.

**And the modern practice note:** **hooks are much less used than they once were**, because deformed HYSD bars develop bond in a shorter straight length than plain mild steel did. **Hooks now appear mainly in stirrups and ties (where they are essential for confinement, at 135° in seismic detailing) rather than as tension anchorage for main bars.**

> **The 135° stirrup hook in seismic design is worth the emphasis: a 90° hook opens out when the concrete cover spalls in an earthquake, and the confinement is lost exactly when it is needed.** IS 13920 requires 135° hooks with a 10φ tail on stirrups in ductile detailing for precisely that reason.

examTip.trick: **4φ for every 45° of bend: 45°→4φ, 90°→8φ, 135°→12φ, 180° hook→16φ.** One rule generates the whole table.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) 12φ is the 135° BEND value.** The code uses "bend" and "hook" precisely — a hook turns the bar right back through 180°.
examTip.mnemonic: **L_d ≈ 47φ for Fe415 in M20**, so a 16φ hook supplies about a THIRD of the anchorage needed — a supplement, never a substitute. And **seismic stirrups need 135° hooks with a 10φ tail**, since a 90° hook opens out when cover spalls.

questions.stem: The width of standard A-series drawing paper such as A4, A3, A2 ... is:
options: 1/3 times the length of the paper
1/√2 times the length of the paper
1/2 times the length of the paper
1/√3 times the length of the paper
questions.solution:
**1/√2 times the length — the aspect ratio is 1 : √2.**

**Why √2 and nothing else — the requirement generates the number:**

> **The A series is designed so that FOLDING A SHEET IN HALF gives the next size down WITH THE SAME PROPORTIONS.** That is the whole specification, and it forces the ratio.

> **Let the sheet be w wide and l long, with l/w = r.**

> **Halving it across the long side gives a sheet w wide and l/2 long, whose long side is now w.** So the new ratio is **w / (l/2) = 2w/l = 2/r.**

> **For the proportions to be unchanged: r = 2/r  ⟹  r² = 2  ⟹  r = √2.**

> **So width = length / √2 = 0.7071 × length.** The ratio is not a convention chosen by committee; **it is the only number that makes the halving property possible.**

**The series itself, and how it is anchored:**

> **A0 is defined as the sheet of AREA ONE SQUARE METRE with the 1 : √2 ratio.** From w × √2 w = 1 m², w = 841 mm and l = 1189 mm.

| Size | Dimensions (mm) | Area |
|---|---|---|
| **A0** | **841 × 1189** | **1 m²** |
| **A1** | **594 × 841** | **0.5 m²** |
| **A2** | **420 × 594** | 0.25 m² |
| **A3** | **297 × 420** | 0.125 m² |
| **A4** | **210 × 297** | **1/16 m²** |
| A5 | 148 × 210 | 1/32 m² |

> **Each size has HALF the area of the one above**, and the long side of one is the short side of the next. **Note how the numbers recur: 841 is A0's width and A1's length; 297 is A3's width and A4's length.**

> **A0 = 1 m² and A4 = 210 × 297 are the two anchors** — from either, the whole series can be reconstructed by halving or doubling.

**Why the property matters in practice, since it is not merely elegant:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Scaling between sizes needs no cropping** | **An A3 drawing photocopies to A4 at 71 % with nothing lost** ← |
| **Enlargement factor is always the same** | **A4 → A3 is 141 % (√2); A3 → A4 is 71 % (1/√2)** |
| **Paper weight in GSM is per square metre** | **So one A0 sheet of 80 gsm paper weighs exactly 80 g, and an A4 sheet 5 g** |
| **Folding for filing is systematic** | Any size folds down to A4 |

> **The 71 % and 141 % buttons on every photocopier exist because of this ratio**, and knowing why they are those numbers is more useful than knowing that they are.

**Why the distractors are wrong — test each against the halving requirement:**

| Option | Ratio | Halve it and the new ratio is | Same? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1/3** | 1 : 3 | 1 : 1.5 | **No** |
| **1/√2** | **1 : 1.414** | **1 : 1.414** | **YES** ✓ |
| **1/2** | 1 : 2 | **1 : 1 (a square)** | **No — and dramatically so** |
| **1/√3** | 1 : 1.732 | 1 : 1.155 | **No** |

> **Option (c) is the interesting failure: a 1 : 2 sheet halved becomes a SQUARE.** The next halving would return to 1 : 2, so the series would alternate between two shapes rather than keeping one. **That is exactly the defect the √2 ratio was designed to avoid.**

**The drawing conventions that accompany this in the syllabus:**

| Item | Standard |
|---|---|
| **Border margin** | **10 mm on three sides, 20 mm on the FILING (left) side** |
| **Title block** | **Bottom RIGHT corner** |
| **Standard scales** | **1:1, 1:2, 1:5, 1:10, 1:20, 1:50, 1:100, 1:200, 1:500, 1:1000** |
| **Reduced / enlarged** | Reduced for buildings; enlarged (2:1, 5:1) for details |
| **Lettering height** | 2.5, 3.5, 5, 7, 10, 14, 20 mm |

> **The 20 mm left margin is the one with a reason worth stating: it is the filing margin**, wide enough that punched holes or a binding do not obscure the drawing. **Which is why the title block goes bottom RIGHT — it stays visible when a folded set is bound at the left.**

examTip.trick: **The ratio must be unchanged by halving: r = 2/r, so r = √2.** It is the only number with that property — not a convention but a consequence.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) 1:2 halved becomes a SQUARE**, so the series would alternate between two shapes. That is precisely the defect √2 avoids.
examTip.mnemonic: **A0 = 1 m², A4 = 210 × 297 mm** — from either anchor the whole series follows by halving. And 80 gsm means one A0 sheet weighs exactly 80 g, an A4 sheet 5 g.

questions.stem: The formula to calculate maximum normal stress is:
questions.solution:
**σ_max = σx/2 + ½√(σx² + 4τxy²).**

**Where the formula comes from — the general principal stress result:**

> **For a general two-dimensional stress state (σx, σy, τxy):**

> **σ₁,₂ = (σx + σy)/2 ± √[((σx − σy)/2)² + τxy²]**

> **The question's case has σy = 0** — a single direct stress with shear, which is the commonest practical case (a shaft in combined bending and torsion, a beam web, a bolt in shear and tension).

> **Substituting σy = 0:**

> **σ_max = σx/2 + √[(σx/2)² + τxy²]**

> **= σx/2 + √[σx²/4 + τxy²]**

> **Take the 1/4 outside the root:**

> **= σx/2 + ½√[σx² + 4τxy²]** ✓

> **That factor of 4 is where the whole question lives.** It appears because the σx²/4 inside the root must be scaled up by 4 when the ½ is pulled out — so the τxy² must be scaled by 4 as well.

**The dimensional and limiting checks, which settle it without the algebra:**

> **CHECK 1 — set τxy = 0 (pure direct stress).** Then σ_max should equal σx.

| Option | At τxy = 0 | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **(a) σx/2 + ½√(σx²)** | **σx/2 + σx/2 = σx** ✓ | **Passes** |
| (b) σx/2 + ½√(σx²) | **σx** ✓ | Passes |
| (c) σx/2 + ½√(σx²) | **σx** ✓ | Passes |
| (d) σx/2 + ½√(σx²) + 0 | **σx** ✓ | Passes |

> **All four pass — so this check does not discriminate, and that is worth knowing rather than discovering mid-exam.**

> **CHECK 2 — set σx = 0 (PURE SHEAR).** For pure shear the principal stresses are known to be **± τxy** exactly. That is a standard result, and it is the discriminating test:

| Option | At σx = 0 | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **(a) ½√(4τxy²) = τxy** ✓ | **τxy** | **CORRECT** |
| (b) ½√(τxy²) = τxy/2 | **Half the right value** | **Fails** |
| (c) ½√(2τxy²) = 0.707 τxy | Wrong | **Fails** |
| (d) 0 + τxy² | **Wrong DIMENSIONS — a stress squared** | **Fails** |

> **The pure-shear check is decisive and takes ten seconds.** It is the check to reach for whenever a principal-stress formula must be identified from options.

> **And option (d) fails on dimensions alone**, since τxy² is a stress squared and cannot be added to a stress. **Look for a dimensional mismatch first — it is free.**

**The companion results, since they are asked together:**

| Quantity | Formula (for σy = 0) |
|---|---|
| **σ_max (major principal)** | **σx/2 + ½√(σx² + 4τxy²)** ← |
| **σ_min (minor principal)** | **σx/2 − ½√(σx² + 4τxy²)** |
| **MAXIMUM SHEAR stress** | **τ_max = ½√(σx² + 4τxy²) = (σ₁ − σ₂)/2** |
| **Orientation of principal planes** | **tan 2θ = 2τxy / (σx − σy)** |

> **Notice that τ_max is exactly the RADICAL TERM**, and that it equals half the difference of the principal stresses. **On Mohr's circle, that is simply the RADIUS** — and σ_max, σ_min are the centre plus and minus the radius.

> **Which is the fastest way to hold all of this: Mohr's circle has centre (σx+σy)/2 and radius √[((σx−σy)/2)² + τxy²].** Everything else is read off it.

**Two further facts worth having:**

> **PRINCIPAL PLANES CARRY NO SHEAR — that is their definition**, and it is why the principal stresses are the extremes of direct stress.

> **The planes of maximum shear are at 45° to the principal planes**, and they carry a direct stress of (σ₁+σ₂)/2, not zero. **A common error is to assume the maximum-shear plane is free of direct stress; it is not.**

**Where this is used:**

> **A shaft under combined bending moment M and torque T** has σx = 32M/πd³ and τxy = 16T/πd³, and substituting gives the **equivalent bending moment M_e = ½(M + √(M² + T²))** and **equivalent torque T_e = √(M² + T²).** **Those two expressions are this formula in disguise**, and recognising that saves learning them separately.

examTip.trick: **Start from σ₁,₂ = (σx+σy)/2 ± √[((σx−σy)/2)² + τxy²] with σy = 0**, then pull the ½ out of the root — which scales τxy² by 4. That factor of 4 is the whole question.
examTip.trap: **Setting τxy = 0 does NOT discriminate — all four options pass.** Use PURE SHEAR (σx = 0) instead: the principal stresses must be exactly ± τxy, and only (a) gives that.
examTip.mnemonic: **Mohr's circle: centre (σx+σy)/2, radius √[((σx−σy)/2)² + τxy²].** σ_max and σ_min are centre ± radius, and **τ_max IS the radius.** Everything is read off one circle.

questions.stem: Select the correct formula for horizontal thrust when there is a temperature increase (T) and the effect of rib shortening is considered:
questions.solution:
**H = ∫(Myds/EI + LαT) / ∫(y²ds/EI + L/AE).**

**Where the expression comes from — the two-hinged arch in one line:**

> **A two-hinged arch is statically indeterminate to the FIRST degree.** The redundant is the horizontal thrust H.

> **The compatibility condition is that the horizontal distance between the two hinges does not change.** Apply Castigliano's theorem or the unit-load method to that condition, and H falls out as a ratio:

> **H = (total horizontal displacement that WOULD occur if H were absent) ÷ (horizontal displacement per unit H)**

> **Numerator: the effects that PUSH THE SPRINGINGS APART** — the applied loading (∫Myds/EI) and the thermal expansion (LαT).

> **Denominator: the FLEXIBILITY of the arch against a unit horizontal force** — bending flexibility (∫y²ds/EI) plus axial flexibility from rib shortening (L/AE).

**Why every sign is a PLUS, which is the whole question:**

| Term | Sign | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **∫Myds/EI** | **+** | The loading tends to spread the arch |
| **LαT** | **+** | **A temperature RISE EXPANDS the arch, spreading it further — so it ADDS to the numerator and INCREASES H** |
| **∫y²ds/EI** | **+** | Bending flexibility resists H |
| **L/AE** | **+** | **Rib shortening is ADDITIONAL flexibility — the arch also squashes axially, so it is EASIER to push in** |

> **The physical reasoning to hold onto:**

> **A temperature RISE increases H** — the arch wants to grow, the abutments will not let it, so the thrust rises. **A temperature FALL reduces H** (and can even reverse the sign of the moments).

> **RIB SHORTENING reduces H.** The arch is not rigid axially; part of the applied thrust is absorbed in simply compressing the rib. **So allowing for rib shortening puts a LARGER number in the denominator and gives a SMALLER H.**

> **That second point is the discriminating one against options (b) and (d), which subtract L/AE.** Subtracting would make the denominator smaller and H larger — **claiming that an arch which can squash axially develops MORE thrust, which is backwards.**

**Reasoning out each distractor:**

| Option | The error |
|---|---|
| **(a) both +** | ✓ |
| **(b) numerator +, denominator −** | **Rib shortening treated as reducing flexibility** |
| **(c) numerator −, denominator +** | **Temperature RISE treated as reducing H — that is the FALL case** ← |
| **(d) both −** | Both errors together |

> **Option (c) is the near-miss to guard against, because −LαT is the correct expression for a temperature DROP.** So (c) is not nonsense; it is the right formula for the other case. **The stem says "temperature increase", which selects the plus sign.**

**The three effects on an arch besides the applied load — worth knowing as a set:**

| Effect | Consequence for H |
|---|---|
| **Temperature RISE** | **INCREASES H** |
| **Temperature FALL** | **DECREASES H** |
| **RIB SHORTENING (axial compression)** | **DECREASES H** |
| **SUPPORT (yielding) of the abutments** | **DECREASES H — this is the k term in the full expression** |
| Shrinkage of a concrete arch | **Acts like a temperature fall — DECREASES H** |

> **Note that support yielding appears as an additional flexibility k in the denominator**, exactly parallel to rib shortening — **the source's own note names it.** Any mechanism that lets the springings move toward each other reduces the thrust.

> **This is why a three-hinged arch is often preferred on poor ground:** being determinate, **it develops NO stresses at all from temperature change, rib shortening, shrinkage or support settlement.** All four of these effects vanish for a determinate structure, since it can accommodate the movement without straining.

**The arch comparison, since it follows directly:**

| Arch | Degree of indeterminacy | Sensitive to temperature/settlement? |
|---|---|---|
| **THREE-HINGED** | **0 — determinate** | **NO — completely insensitive** |
| **TWO-HINGED** | **1** | **YES** ← this question |
| **FIXED** | **3** | **MOST sensitive** |

> **The trade-off is clean: more restraint gives smaller moments under load but larger stresses from movement.** A fixed arch is the most efficient under its design load and the most vulnerable to a settling abutment.

> **And for a two-hinged PARABOLIC arch under udl, the classic simplification is H = wL²/8h**, obtained by neglecting rib shortening — which the same source's later question exploits when it asks for the bending moment (zero).

examTip.trick: **Numerator = what spreads the arch (load + thermal expansion); denominator = flexibility against H (bending + axial).** All four terms are PLUS for a temperature RISE.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) with −LαT is the correct formula for a temperature FALL** — not nonsense, just the other case. The stem's word "increase" selects the sign.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rib shortening is EXTRA flexibility, so it goes in the denominator with a PLUS and REDUCES H.** Same for support yielding (the k term). And a **THREE-hinged arch is immune to all of temperature, rib shortening, shrinkage and settlement.**

questions.stem: What is the unit of highway capacity?
questions.solution:
**PCU per hour.**

**Why the unit must be PCU and not vehicles:**

> **CAPACITY is the maximum traffic flow a road can accommodate in a stated period under prevailing roadway, traffic and control conditions.**

> **A road carrying 1000 buses per hour and a road carrying 1000 motorcycles per hour are not equally loaded**, so counting vehicles tells you almost nothing about how full a road is.

> **The PASSENGER CAR UNIT converts every vehicle to an equivalent number of cars**, so that mixed traffic can be added up meaningfully.

> **Hence capacity is expressed in PCU/hour, not vehicles/hour.**

**Typical PCU equivalency factors (IRC 106):**

| Vehicle | PCU |
|---|---|
| **Passenger CAR, taxi, van** | **1.0 — the reference** |
| **Motorcycle / scooter** | **0.5** |
| **Bicycle** | **0.5** |
| **Auto-rickshaw** | **1.2** |
| **Light commercial vehicle** | **1.4** |
| **TRUCK or BUS** | **2.2 to 3.0** |
| **Truck-trailer, agricultural tractor-trailer** | **4.0 to 4.5** |
| Cycle rickshaw | 2.0 |
| **Animal-drawn cart** | **6.0 to 8.0** |

> **The factors depend on the proportion of that vehicle in the stream**, which is why they are given as ranges — a single truck in light traffic obstructs less than a truck in a dense stream, because there is room to overtake.

> **The animal-drawn cart at 6-8 PCU is worth noticing**: a slow vehicle on a two-lane road with limited overtaking blocks the flow far out of proportion to the space it occupies. **PCU measures OBSTRUCTION, not size.**

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Veh/hr** | **A rate, and it is how a traffic COUNT is reported — but it cannot express capacity for MIXED traffic** ← the near-miss |
| **PCU/hr** | ✓ |
| **Veh/hr/section of road** | **Not a unit of anything. "Per section of road" is not a measurable quantity — capacity is per LANE or per DIRECTION, both of which are definite** |
| **PCU/section of road** | **Not a rate at all — no time dimension, so it cannot be a flow** |

> **Option (a) is the genuine near-miss and the one worth arguing.** Vehicles per hour is a perfectly good unit of *flow* and is what a counting station records. **But capacity is a design quantity for mixed traffic, and mixed traffic must be homogenised before it can be compared with a capacity figure.**

> **Options (c) and (d) fail on the phrase "per section of road", which specifies nothing.** Capacity is quoted per lane, or for a carriageway, or for a direction — **all definite; "a section" is not.**

**Design service volumes worth having (IRC 64 / IRC 106):**

| Road | Capacity |
|---|---|
| **Single lane (3.75 m), both directions** | **~1000-2000 PCU/day** |
| **Two-lane two-way, plain terrain** | **~2400 PCU/hour total, both directions** |
| **Two-lane, design service volume** | **~15,000 PCU/day** |
| **Four-lane divided, per direction** | **~1800 PCU/hour per lane** |
| **Ideal single lane, theoretical** | **~2000 PCU/hour per lane** |
| Urban road, at-grade intersections | Much lower — the junction governs |

> **The 1800-2000 PCU/hour per lane figure is the anchor**, and it is remarkably stable across countries — because it is set by human reaction time and the resulting headway, not by the pavement.

**The theoretical basis, which explains that stability:**

> **Capacity C = 1000 V / S**, where V is the speed in km/h and S the average centre-to-centre spacing in metres.

> **The spacing must include the stopping distance, so S grows with V — and the two effects fight each other.**

> **The result is a MAXIMUM capacity at a moderate speed, not at high speed.** Capacity peaks at around 30-50 km/h and falls off both above and below it.

> **That is genuinely counter-intuitive and it is the key result of traffic flow theory: a faster road does not carry more vehicles.** Above the optimum, the headway needed for safe stopping grows faster than the speed, so throughput drops.

| Relation | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Fundamental equation** | **q = k × v  (flow = density × speed)** |
| **At maximum flow** | **Speed and density are both about HALF their free-flow / jam values** |
| **Above capacity** | **Flow FALLS as density rises — congested regime** |

> **The last row is why a motorway jam clears slowly: once density passes the critical value, the road carries LESS than its capacity**, and it stays in that regime until the demand drops well below capacity.

examTip.trick: **1000 buses and 1000 motorcycles do not load a road equally**, so mixed traffic must be homogenised to PASSENGER CAR UNITS before it can be compared with a capacity. Hence PCU/hour.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) veh/hr is a real unit** — it is how a traffic count is reported. But capacity is a mixed-traffic design quantity, so it needs PCU. And "per section of road" in (c) and (d) specifies nothing measurable.
examTip.mnemonic: **~1800-2000 PCU/hour per lane**, and the figure is stable worldwide because it is set by reaction time, not pavement. **Capacity PEAKS at 30-50 km/h** — a faster road does not carry more vehicles.

questions.stem: A two-hinged parabolic arch with a udl throughout the span has a bending moment of:
questions.solution:
**Zero — everywhere along the arch.**

**Why the bending moment vanishes — the two contributions cancel exactly:**

> **The bending moment at any section of an arch is:**

> **M = M_beam − H·y**

> **where M_beam is the moment the same span would have as a simply supported BEAM, H is the horizontal thrust, and y the rise of the arch at that section.**

> **For a udl w on a span L, the beam moment at distance x is:**

> **M_beam = (w/2)(Lx − x²)**

> **For a two-hinged parabolic arch of rise h, the thrust (neglecting rib shortening) is:**

> **H = wL²/(8h)**

> **And the parabolic shape is:**

> **y = (4h/L²)(Lx − x²)**

> **Now form H·y:**

> **H·y = [wL²/(8h)] × [(4h/L²)(Lx − x²)] = (w/2)(Lx − x²)**

> **Which is EXACTLY M_beam.**

> **So M = M_beam − H·y = 0 at every section.** ✓

**Why this is not a coincidence — the underlying principle:**
