> **A PARABOLA IS THE FUNICULAR SHAPE (the shape of the bending-moment diagram) FOR A UDL.**

> **If the arch is built in the shape of the load's own moment diagram, the H·y term reproduces that diagram exactly, and nothing is left over to bend the arch.**

> **The load is then carried entirely by AXIAL COMPRESSION along the rib.** No bending, no shear — pure thrust.

> **This is the whole reason arches exist.** A beam carries load by bending, which uses its material inefficiently (the neutral axis carries no stress at all); **an arch of the right shape carries the same load by direct compression, which uses every fibre.**

**The general statement, which is worth more than the special case:**

| Load | Funicular (no-bending) shape |
|---|---|
| **UNIFORM load on the SPAN (horizontal projection)** | **PARABOLA** ← |
| **Uniform load along the ARCH ITSELF (self-weight)** | **CATENARY** |
| **Point loads** | **A polygon of straight segments** |
| Hydrostatic pressure | Circular |

> **The parabola-versus-catenary distinction is the fine point and is asked.** A suspension bridge cable under the deck's uniform load hangs as a **parabola**; a free-hanging chain under its own weight hangs as a **catenary**. **They are close but not identical, and which applies depends on whether the load is uniform per horizontal metre or per metre of curve.**

> **An arch is a hanging cable turned upside down** — with tension become compression — which is why the same shapes govern both.

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **wl²/8** | **The SIMPLY SUPPORTED BEAM moment for a udl — the M_beam term, with the H·y term forgotten** ← the trap |
| **wl²/10** | Not a standard result here |
| **wl²/12** | **The FIXED BEAM support moment for a udl** |
| **zero** | ✓ |

> **Option (a) is the designed trap and the reason is instructive: wL²/8 is the correct answer to the question "what is the beam moment?"** A candidate who computes M_beam and stops has done half the calculation.

> **Option (c) wL²/12 is the fixed-beam value** and catches anyone who associates "arch" loosely with "restrained".

**The important qualifications, since a real arch does develop some moment:**

| Effect | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **RIB SHORTENING** | **Reduces H slightly, so H·y no longer cancels M_beam exactly — a small moment appears** |
| **Temperature change** | **Changes H, so moments appear** |
| **Any load other than the design udl** | **Moments appear — this is the real limitation** |
| Support yielding | Reduces H, moments appear |
| Shrinkage and creep in concrete | Act like a temperature fall |

> **The third row is the practical one.** The zero-moment result holds for the udl the arch was shaped for. **A partial or unsymmetrical load — traffic on half the span, wind, an earthquake — produces bending, and it is those cases that govern the design of the rib section.**

> **So the exact answer to this question is zero, and the arch still has to be designed for bending.** The two statements are not in conflict: **the udl case tells you the arch shape; the other load cases tell you the section.**

examTip.trick: **M = M_beam − H·y, and for a parabolic arch with H = wL²/8h the two terms are IDENTICAL.** The arch is built in the shape of the load's own moment diagram, so nothing is left to bend it.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) wL²/8 is the BEAM moment** — the correct answer to half the calculation. Option (c) wL²/12 is the fixed-beam support moment.
examTip.mnemonic: **A PARABOLA is funicular for load uniform per HORIZONTAL metre; a CATENARY for load uniform along the CURVE.** An arch is a hanging cable inverted — tension become compression. And any load OTHER than the design udl does produce bending.

questions.stem: The factor of safety in overturning is less in a dam. What can be done to increase it?
questions.solution:
**Anchorage at the bottom.**

**Why anchoring at the base is what resists OVERTURNING:**

> **Overturning is rotation of the dam about its DOWNSTREAM TOE**, driven by the water pressure pushing on the upstream face.

> **FOS against overturning = (sum of stabilising moments) / (sum of overturning moments), taken about the toe.**

> **To increase it, either reduce the overturning moment or increase the stabilising moment.**

> **An ANCHOR AT THE BOTTOM — post-tensioned cables or bars grouted into the rock beneath the heel — adds a downward force at the base.**

| What the anchor does | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Adds a downward force** | **Increases the stabilising moment about the toe** |
| **Applies it at the HEEL, farthest from the toe** | **Maximum LEVER ARM, so maximum moment for a given force** ← |
| **Ties the dam to the rock** | Prevents the heel lifting, which is how overturning begins |
| Increases the normal force on the base | **Also increases the friction, so it helps against SLIDING too** |

> **The lever-arm point is the whole answer.** Overturning is a moment problem, and a force applied at the greatest distance from the pivot does the most good.

**Why anchorage at the TOP is nearly useless — and this is the discrimination:**

> **An anchor at the top of a dam has almost no lever arm about the toe**, because the crest is close to the vertical axis through the section, not far from the toe horizontally.

> **Worse, an anchor at the crest is not anchored INTO ANYTHING.** Anchorage works by transferring load into sound rock; **the crest is the far end of the dam from the rock.**

> **So option (b) fails both on mechanics (no lever arm) and on constructability (nothing to anchor to).**

**Why the other two are wrong — each is a real measure against a DIFFERENT failure:**

| Option | What it actually guards against |
|---|---|
| **Anchorage at bottom** | ✓ **OVERTURNING (and helps sliding)** |
| **Anchorage at top** | **Nothing useful** |
| **SHEAR KEY below the foundation** | **SLIDING — a concrete key cast into a trench in the rock, providing mechanical resistance to horizontal movement** ← |
| **STONE PITCHING** | **EROSION of an earth slope or bank — a surface protection, irrelevant to a concrete dam's stability** |

> **Option (c) is the substantive near-miss, and separating it properly is the point of the question.** A shear key is a genuine and standard measure — **but it resists HORIZONTAL sliding along the base, not ROTATION about the toe.**

> **The two failure modes and their remedies:**

| Failure mode | Check | Principal remedies |
|---|---|---|
| **OVERTURNING** | **FOS = ΣM_stabilising / ΣM_overturning ≥ 1.5** | **Widen the base; increase self-weight; ANCHOR AT THE HEEL; reduce uplift by drainage** |
| **SLIDING** | **FOS = μΣV / ΣH ≥ 1.5 (shear friction factor ≥ 4-5)** | **SHEAR KEY; roughen or step the base; increase weight; batter the base** |
| **Tension at the heel** | **Resultant within the middle third** | Widen the base upstream |
| **Crushing at the toe** | σ ≤ permissible | Widen the base downstream |

> **Note that a wider base helps every one of them**, which is why a gravity dam's section is essentially a matter of finding the base width that satisfies all four.

**The measure that helps most and is not among the options — worth knowing:**

> **REDUCING THE UPLIFT PRESSURE under the base.**

> **Uplift acts upward over the whole base area, and it does two harmful things at once: it reduces the effective weight (hurting both overturning and sliding) and its resultant acts upstream of the centre (adding directly to the overturning moment).**

| Uplift reduction measure | How |
|---|---|
| **DRAINAGE GALLERY with drain holes** | **Intercepts seepage and relieves the pressure — the most effective single measure** |
| **GROUT CURTAIN at the heel** | **Reduces the seepage reaching the base** |
| Foundation treatment | Consolidation grouting |

> **The grout curtain plus drainage gallery combination can cut the uplift resultant by half or more**, which is a larger gain than any anchor could deliver. **In practice a dam whose overturning FOS is inadequate is usually fixed by drainage and by widening, with anchoring reserved for remedial work on an existing dam** — where widening is no longer possible.

> **That is the honest engineering position: post-tensioned anchoring is a RETROFIT technique.** For a new dam, get the section right.

examTip.trick: **Overturning is rotation about the TOE, so it is a MOMENT problem.** An anchor at the bottom adds a downward force at the heel — the greatest lever arm from the pivot, hence the most benefit.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) shear key is a real measure — against SLIDING, not overturning.** And an anchor at the TOP has no lever arm and nothing to anchor into.
examTip.mnemonic: **The biggest gain is not in the options: REDUCE UPLIFT** with a grout curtain and drainage gallery. Uplift reduces the effective weight AND adds an overturning moment, so relieving it fixes both checks at once.

questions.stem: The number of soil types in the seismic site classification of NBC 105 is:
questions.solution:
**Four.**

**The NBC 105 soil (site subsoil) classes:**

| Class | Description |
|---|---|
| **A** | **STIFF or HARD soil sites** |
| **B** | **MEDIUM soil sites** |
| **C** | **SOFT soil sites** |
| **D** | **VERY SOFT soil sites — and KATHMANDU VALLEY falls in this class** |

> **Four classes, A to D, and the Kathmandu Valley is class D.** That last fact is the one with real consequences and is asked repeatedly.

**Why the soil class matters so much — and this is the physics behind the classification:**

> **Soft soil AMPLIFIES ground motion.** A seismic wave arriving from bedrock passes into a softer, less dense layer, and to carry the same energy at lower stiffness it must move with **larger amplitude.**

> **The softer the deposit, the greater the amplification, and the LONGER the period at which the amplification peaks.**

| Site class | Spectral effect |
|---|---|
| **Rock / hard soil (A)** | **Lower amplitude, SHORT-period motion — dangerous to STIFF, low-rise buildings** |
| **Very soft soil (D)** | **Higher amplitude, LONG-period motion — dangerous to TALL, flexible buildings** |

> **So the class does not merely scale the design force; it changes WHICH BUILDINGS are at risk.**

> **The mechanism to fear is RESONANCE**: when the soil's natural period matches the building's, the motion is amplified again. **A soft, deep valley deposit has a long natural period, and a mid- to high-rise frame building has a long natural period too.**

**Why Kathmandu being class D is not an academic point:**

> **The Kathmandu Valley is a filled lake basin — hundreds of metres of soft lacustrine clay, silt and sand over bedrock.**

> **It therefore combines every unfavourable factor:**

| Factor | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Very soft, deep deposits** | **Strong amplification of long-period motion** |
| **Basin geometry** | **Waves trapped and reflected at the basin edges — motion lasts LONGER** |
| **Growing stock of mid-rise RC frames** | **Natural periods near the soil's — RESONANCE risk** |
| **Shallow water table in places** | **LIQUEFACTION potential in loose saturated sands** |
| High population density | Consequence of failure is severe |

> **The basin effect is the one least appreciated.** It is not only that the shaking is stronger; **it is that it goes on for longer, and cumulative damage in a masonry or poorly detailed frame building depends heavily on the number of cycles.**

> **This is why NBC 105 (2020) matters and why its 2020 revision was necessary** — the 1994 edition's treatment of soil and of ductility was superseded by what was learned from the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, in which valley amplification was clearly observed.

**Where the soil class enters the calculation:**

> **NBC 105 (2020) uses an elastic site spectrum C(T) whose shape depends on the soil class**, and the horizontal base shear follows from it:

> **V = C_d(T₁) × W**, with **C_d = C(T)·Z·I / R_μ·Ω_u** in the ultimate limit state.

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **C(T)** | **Spectral shape — depends on the SOIL CLASS and the period T** ← |
| **Z** | **Seismic zoning factor (hazard)** |
| **I** | **Importance factor** |
| **R_μ, Ω_u** | **Ductility and overstrength factors** |
| W | Seismic weight |

> **Note that the natural period T is needed before the spectrum can be entered**, and NBC 105 gives an empirical formula for it — so a mistake in T propagates into every force in the building.

**Why the distractors are wrong:** **1, 2 and 5 are near counts with no standing.** But **note that IS 1893 uses THREE soil types (hard, medium, soft)** — so a candidate who has learned the Indian code will answer 3, and a candidate who guesses will land on 2 or 5. **NBC 105 uses FOUR, and being clear which code is being asked about is half the question.**

> **That distinction is worth carrying generally: IS 1893 has 4 seismic zones (II to V) and 3 soil types; NBC 105 has a continuous zoning factor map and 4 soil classes.** The two codes are not interchangeable on either count.

verification.notes: Stem corrected. The source printed "The number of zones of soil classification Nepal seismic zone is", which conflates seismic zones with soil classes and is not a well-formed question. The source's own explanation reads "According to NBC 105 the soil is of 4 types" and lists soil types A to D, so the stem has been restated as the number of soil types in the NBC 105 seismic site classification. The keyed answer (c) 4 is unchanged.

examTip.trick: **Four classes A to D — stiff, medium, soft, very soft — and the KATHMANDU VALLEY is class D.** That last fact is the one that gets examined.
examTip.trap: **IS 1893 uses THREE soil types; NBC 105 uses FOUR.** A candidate who has learned the Indian code answers 3. Being clear which code is asked about is half the question.
examTip.mnemonic: **Soft soil amplifies and LENGTHENS the period, so it endangers TALL flexible buildings while rock endangers stiff low-rise ones.** Kathmandu adds the BASIN effect — the shaking also lasts longer, and cumulative damage depends on cycles.

questions.stem: A mild-sloped channel is followed by a steep-sloped channel. The profiles of gradually varied flow in the channels are:
questions.solution:
**M2 followed by S2.**

**The reasoning, in three steps:**

> **STEP 1 — establish the depth relations on each slope.**

| Slope | Relation | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **MILD** | **NDL > CDL  (y_n > y_c)** | **Normal depth above critical — SUBCRITICAL flow** |
| **STEEP** | **NDL < CDL  (y_n < y_c)** | **Normal depth below critical — SUPERCRITICAL flow** |

> **STEP 2 — the flow must pass through critical depth at the break in grade.**

> **Far upstream the flow is at the mild channel's normal depth (above critical); far downstream it is at the steep channel's normal depth (below critical).** To get from one to the other, **it must cross the critical depth — and it does so at the break of slope, which is a CONTROL SECTION.**

> **STEP 3 — identify the zone on each side.**

> **On the MILD slope: the depth falls from y_n toward y_c, so it lies BETWEEN NDL and CDL — that is ZONE 2. Profile M2.**

> **On the STEEP slope: the depth falls from y_c toward y_n, so again it lies BETWEEN CDL and NDL — ZONE 2. Profile S2.**

> **Answer: M2 then S2.** ✓

**The zone convention, which must be secure before any of this works:**

| Zone | Position of the water surface |
|---|---|
| **Zone 1** | **ABOVE BOTH y_n and y_c** |
| **Zone 2** | **BETWEEN y_n and y_c** |
| **Zone 3** | **BELOW BOTH y_n and y_c** |

> **The zone number counts down from the top, regardless of which of y_n and y_c is the upper line** — which is exactly why the same number 2 applies on both a mild and a steep slope even though the depths are moving in relation to different lines.

**The complete family of GVF profiles:**

| Slope | Profiles | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **MILD (y_n > y_c)** | **M1, M2, M3** | M1 backwater behind a dam; **M2 drawdown to a fall or steep reach**; M3 below a sluice gate |
| **STEEP (y_n < y_c)** | **S1, S2, S3** | S1 behind an obstruction; **S2 entering a steep reach**; S3 below a gate on a steep slope |
| **CRITICAL (y_n = y_c)** | C1, C3 | No zone 2 exists — the two lines coincide |
| **HORIZONTAL (S₀ = 0)** | H2, H3 | **No normal depth exists (y_n → ∞)**, so no H1 |
| **ADVERSE (S₀ < 0)** | A2, A3 | **No normal depth**, so no A1 |

> **Note that H1, A1 and C2 do not exist**, and the reason in each case is that the relevant zone is empty. **Being able to say why a profile does not exist is a better test of understanding than listing the ones that do.**

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Why not |
|---|---|
| **M3, S2** | **M3 occurs BELOW a sluice gate on a mild slope — supercritical flow on a mild slope, which is not the situation here** |
| **M3, S3** | Both zone 3; neither applies |
| **M2, S1** | **S1 requires the depth to be ABOVE both lines on a steep slope — that needs an obstruction downstream, not a free steep reach** ← the near-miss |
| **M2, S2** | ✓ |

> **Option (c) is the designed near-miss: it gets the mild side right and the steep side wrong.** S1 would occur if there were a dam or a hydraulic jump downstream forcing the depth up; **with the steep channel running freely, the flow accelerates down to its normal depth, which is S2.**

**The control-section principle, which is the general lesson:**

> **SUBCRITICAL flow is controlled from DOWNSTREAM; SUPERCRITICAL flow is controlled from UPSTREAM.**

> **The reason is that a disturbance travels at the wave speed √(gy).** In subcritical flow the water moves slower than that, so a disturbance can travel upstream and the downstream condition is felt. **In supercritical flow it cannot, so nothing downstream can influence the flow.**

| Consequence | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Computation direction** | **Compute subcritical profiles UPSTREAM from the control; supercritical profiles DOWNSTREAM from it** |
| **At the break of grade here** | **Critical depth at the break controls BOTH reaches — the M2 upstream and the S2 downstream** |
| **Froude number** | **Fr < 1 subcritical, Fr = 1 critical, Fr > 1 supercritical** |

> **This is why the break of slope is such a useful section**: it fixes the depth (y_c) at a known point, and both profiles can be computed away from it in opposite directions.

> **And the reverse case is worth knowing since it is the other half of the pair: a STEEP slope followed by a MILD one produces a HYDRAULIC JUMP** — supercritical flow cannot smoothly become subcritical, so it does so abruptly with a large energy loss. **Mild-to-steep is smooth through critical; steep-to-mild is a jump.**

examTip.trick: **Mild has y_n > y_c, steep has y_n < y_c.** The flow must cross critical depth at the break, and on both sides the surface lies BETWEEN the two lines — zone 2 each time. So M2 then S2.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) gets the mild side right and the steep side wrong.** S1 needs the depth ABOVE both lines, which requires an obstruction downstream — not a freely running steep reach.
examTip.mnemonic: **Subcritical is controlled from DOWNSTREAM, supercritical from UPSTREAM**, because a disturbance travels at √(gy). And the reverse case: **steep-to-mild produces a HYDRAULIC JUMP**, while mild-to-steep passes smoothly through critical.

questions.stem: In reinforcement, what does the symbol φ denote?
questions.solution:
**Diameter.**

**The convention:**

> **φ (phi) denotes the DIAMETER of a reinforcing bar**, and it is written before the number: **φ12 or 12φ means a 12 mm diameter bar.**

> **A bar schedule reads "8 nos. 16φ" — eight bars of 16 mm diameter.**

> **The symbol also appears as Ø (the slashed zero) in general dimensioning**, where it likewise means diameter. **The two symbols are used interchangeably for the same meaning.**

**Why diameter and not radius — and the reason is practical, not arbitrary:**

> **Bars are MANUFACTURED and SOLD by diameter.** A rolling mill produces 8, 10, 12, 16, 20, 25, 32 mm bars; no one has ever ordered a 6 mm radius bar.

> **Every code requirement is expressed in bar diameters too** — development length 47φ, anchorage 16φ, minimum bend radius 4φ, lap length, cover not less than the bar diameter. **The whole system is built on diameter, so the symbol must mean diameter.**

> **This is why option (a) is not a near-miss but simply the wrong convention.** If φ meant radius, every code clause would have to be rewritten with a factor of two in it.

**The standard bar sizes and their areas, since the next step after reading φ is computing area:**

| Diameter (mm) | Area (mm²) | Weight (kg/m) |
|---|---|---|
| **6** | 28.3 | 0.222 |
| **8** | **50.3** | **0.395** |
| **10** | **78.5** | **0.617** |
| **12** | **113** | **0.888** |
| **16** | **201** | **1.58** |
| **20** | **314** | **2.47** |
| **25** | **491** | **3.86** |
| **32** | 804 | 6.31 |

> **The weight rule is worth knowing because it is used constantly on site: w = d²/162 kg per metre**, with d in mm.

> **Check it: 12²/162 = 144/162 = 0.888 kg/m** ✓ and **20²/162 = 400/162 = 2.47 kg/m** ✓

> **The 162 comes from the steel density: area × density = (πd²/4) × 7850 kg/m³, which reduces to d²/162 when d is in mm.** One formula replaces the whole weight column.

**The dimensioning symbols that accompany φ:**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **φ or Ø** | **DIAMETER** ← |
| **R** | **Radius** |
| **SØ, SR** | Spherical diameter, spherical radius |
| **□** | Square |
| **t** | Thickness |
| **×** | "By", as in 230 × 450 |
| **@** | **"At centres" — 10φ @ 150 c/c** |

> **The @ symbol is the other one a bar schedule cannot do without.** "**10φ @ 150 c/c**" means 10 mm bars at 150 mm centre-to-centre spacing — **and that single expression, plus the length, defines a whole layer of slab reinforcement.**

**Why the symbol convention matters more than it looks:**

> **A reinforcement drawing is an INSTRUCTION to a bar bender who may not read English.**

> **Its entire content is conveyed in numbers and symbols: count, diameter, shape code, bend dimensions, spacing.** That is deliberate, and it is the same reason Ø is preferred to "Dia" in dimensioning.

> **So a misread symbol is not a drafting nicety — it is a bar of the wrong size cast into a structure**, discoverable afterwards only by breaking out concrete. **Which is why bar bending schedules are checked independently of the drawing they come from.**

**Why the other distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Radius** | **A different symbol, R** — and no bar is specified by radius |
| **Diameter** | ✓ |
| **AREA** | **Written A_st or A_s, in mm² — and it is a DERIVED quantity, computed from φ** |
| **Circumference** | **Rarely used at all; where the perimeter matters (bond), it is computed as πφ** |

> **Option (c) area is the one worth a comment**, because the area is what actually enters the design calculation — **A_st is what the designer needs and φ is what the site needs.** The drawing carries φ because that is what can be ordered and bent; **the calculation carries A_st because that is what resists the tension.**

examTip.trick: **φ (or Ø) = DIAMETER.** Bars are made and sold by diameter, and every code clause is written in bar diameters — development length 47φ, anchorage 16φ, bend radius 4φ.
examTip.trap: **Area is what the DESIGN needs (A_st, mm²); diameter is what the SITE needs.** Area is derived from φ, not denoted by it. Radius has its own symbol, R.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bar weight = d²/162 kg per metre** (d in mm) — check: 12²/162 = 0.888, 20²/162 = 2.47. The 162 comes from πd²/4 × 7850. One formula replaces the whole weight table.

questions.stem: A 2 m diameter sluiceway at RL 300 m is provided through a concrete overflow dam section to release water to the downstream, where the tail water level is not more than 275 m. The discharge through this outlet when the water level in the reservoir is at FRL of 330 m is of the order of:
questions.solution:
**Of the order of 50 cumecs (computed 47.2).**

**The outlet discharge equation:**

> **Q = C_d × A × √(2gH_L)**

**Step 1 — the effective head.**

> **The outlet is at RL 300 m and the reservoir is at RL 330 m.**

> **H_L = 330 − 300 = 30 m**

> **Note carefully which levels are used.** The tail water is at RL 275 m, which is **BELOW the outlet at 300 m** — so the outlet discharges freely into air and the tail water level does not enter the calculation at all.

> **The head is measured from the reservoir surface to the CENTRE LINE OF THE SLUICE, because the discharge is FREE.** Had the tail water been above the outlet, the head would have been the difference between the two water surfaces (a submerged outlet), and the answer would differ.

> **Recognising which case applies is the real content of the question, and the tail water level is given precisely so that it can be checked and dismissed.**

**Step 2 — the area.**

> **A = πd²/4 = π × 2²/4 = 3.142 m²**

**Step 3 — the coefficient.**

> **C_d = 0.62 for a free over-fall / sharp-edged outlet.**

**Step 4 — substitute.**

> **√(2 × 9.81 × 30) = √588.6 = 24.26 m/s**

> **Q = 0.62 × 3.142 × 24.26**

> **Q = 47.25 cumecs**

> **Nearest option: 50 cumecs.** ✓

**The two checks worth doing before trusting the answer:**

> **CHECK 1 — is the velocity plausible?** 24.26 m/s of theoretical jet velocity is high but entirely normal for a 30 m head; **the actual velocity is 0.62 × 24.26 ≈ 15 m/s.** That is fast enough that **energy dissipation downstream is essential** — a jet at 15 m/s will scour rock.

> **CHECK 2 — the order of magnitude.** A 3 m² opening at roughly 15 m/s gives about 45 cumecs. **The rough product confirms the answer before any of the arithmetic is checked in detail.**

**Why the answer is expressed as "of the order of":**

> **The computed 47.25 does not equal any option.** The question asks for the order, and 50 is the nearest.

> **This is honest rather than sloppy, because C_d is itself uncertain.** With C_d = 0.60 the answer is 45.7; with C_d = 0.65, 49.5. **The coefficient's uncertainty is larger than the gap between the computed value and the option**, so a precise answer would be false precision.

**What sluiceways are for, since the calculation has a purpose:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Releasing water downstream for irrigation or riparian needs** | Routine operation |
| **DRAWING DOWN the reservoir** | **For inspection, repair, or in an emergency** |
| **FLUSHING SEDIMENT** | **A low-level outlet scours deposited silt from near the dam** |
| Diverting river flow during construction | Before the spillway is commissioned |
| **Supplementing the spillway in a flood** | Secondary role |

> **The sediment-flushing function is particularly important in the Himalayas**, where sediment inflow is extreme and a reservoir can lose a substantial part of its capacity in decades. **A low-level outlet lets the densest, most sediment-laden water be released rather than stored.**

> **And the drawdown function is a safety requirement, not a convenience.** A dam that cannot be emptied cannot be inspected internally or repaired, and cannot be lowered if a developing problem is detected. **Every large dam has a low-level outlet for this reason.**

**The related discharge formulae, since they are confused with one another:**

| Structure | Discharge |
|---|---|
| **Outlet / orifice (free)** | **Q = C_d A √(2gH)** ← this question |
| **Submerged orifice** | **Q = C_d A √(2gΔH)**, ΔH the difference of water surfaces |
| **Ogee spillway** | **Q = C L H^{3/2}, with C ≈ 2.2 (SI)** |
| **Broad-crested weir** | Q = 1.71 L H^{3/2} |
| **Rectangular sharp-crested weir** | Q = (2/3) C_d L √(2g) H^{3/2} |

> **Notice the exponent difference and its cause: an ORIFICE goes as H^{1/2} and a WEIR as H^{3/2}.**

> **The reason is that an orifice has a FIXED area, while a weir's flow area grows with the head as well as the velocity** — so the weir gains an extra factor of H. **Getting the exponent right is worth more than remembering any coefficient.**

examTip.trick: **Q = C_d A √(2gH) = 0.62 × 3.142 × √(2×9.81×30) = 47.2 cumecs**, nearest 50. Head is 330 − 300 = 30 m, to the sluice centre line.
examTip.trap: **The tail water at RL 275 is BELOW the outlet at RL 300, so the discharge is FREE and the tail water is irrelevant.** It is given so that it can be checked and dismissed — had it been above 300, the head would be the difference of the two surfaces.
examTip.mnemonic: **An ORIFICE goes as H^{1/2}; a WEIR as H^{3/2}** — because an orifice has fixed area while a weir's area grows with head too. The exponent matters more than any coefficient.

questions.stem: The 15-minute traffic counts on cross roads 1 and 2 during the peak hour are observed as 178 and 142 vehicles per lane respectively, approaching the intersection in the direction of heavier traffic flow. If the amber times required are 3 and 2 seconds respectively for the two roads based on approach speeds, design the signal timings by the trial cycle method. Assume the average time headway as 2.5 seconds during the green phase. The cycle length is:
questions.solution:
**45 seconds.**

**The trial cycle method — the green time formula:**

> **G = 2.5 × n × C / 900**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **2.5** | **Average time headway during green, in seconds** | given |
| **n** | **15-minute count on that approach** | 178 and 142 |
| **C** | **ASSUMED cycle length, in seconds** | trial |
| **900** | **Seconds in 15 minutes — converts the count to the same basis** | — |

> **The 900 is the key to reading the formula.** The count n is per 15 minutes = 900 s, so **n·C/900 is the number of vehicles arriving in ONE cycle**, and multiplying by the 2.5 s headway gives the green time they need.

**TRIAL 1 — assume C = 50 s:**

> **G₁ = 2.5 × 178 × 50 / 900 = 22,250/900 = 24.72 s**

> **G₂ = 2.5 × 142 × 50 / 900 = 17,750/900 = 19.72 s**

> **C = G₁ + G₂ + A₁ + A₂ = 24.72 + 19.72 + 3 + 2 = 49.44 s**

> **Assumed 50, obtained 49.44 — close, so try a lower value.**

**TRIAL 2 — assume C = 45 s:**

> **G₁ = 2.5 × 178 × 45 / 900 = 20,025/900 = 22.25 s**

> **G₂ = 2.5 × 142 × 45 / 900 = 15,975/900 = 17.75 s**

> **C = 22.25 + 17.75 + 3 + 2 = 45.00 s**

> **Assumed 45, obtained 45 — the trial CONVERGES exactly.** ✓

**Why the method is iterative, and why it converges so neatly here:**

> **The cycle length appears on BOTH sides**: the greens depend on C, and C is the sum of the greens plus the ambers. **So it cannot be solved directly by substitution — hence "trial cycle".**

> **In fact it CAN be solved algebraically, and doing so shows why 45 is exact:**

> **C = (2.5C/900)(n₁ + n₂) + (A₁ + A₂)**

> **C[1 − 2.5(n₁+n₂)/900] = A₁ + A₂**

> **C[1 − 2.5(320)/900] = 5**

> **C[1 − 800/900] = 5  ⟹  C × (100/900) = 5  ⟹  C = 45 s** exactly ✓

> **That closed form is worth knowing because it removes the guessing:**

> **C = (A₁ + A₂) / [1 − 2.5(n₁ + n₂)/900]**

> **It also shows the limit of the method: if 2.5(n₁+n₂) approaches 900, the denominator approaches zero and the required cycle length blows up** — which is the mathematical statement that **the intersection is at capacity and no signal timing can serve it.**

**The cycle components, since the question defines the cycle as greens plus ambers:**

| Component | Note |
|---|---|
| **GREEN time** | **The go phase, computed above** |
| **AMBER (yellow) time** | **3-5 s, based on APPROACH SPEED — time to stop or clear** |
| **RED time** | **The sum of the other phases' green plus amber** |
| **All-red (clearance) interval** | Where provided, for intersection clearance |
| **CYCLE LENGTH** | **The total, after which the sequence repeats** |

> **Amber depends on approach speed** because it must give a driver at the decision point either time to stop or time to clear the intersection. **Hence the two roads here have different ambers, 3 s and 2 s — the faster approach needs longer.**

**Practical cycle lengths, for a sanity check on the answer:**

| Situation | Cycle length |
|---|---|
| **Minimum practical** | **~40 s (below this, too much time is lost to ambers)** |
| **Two-phase, light traffic** | **40-60 s** ← 45 s sits here |
| Two-phase, heavy traffic | 60-90 s |
| **Multi-phase, heavy** | **90-120 s** |
| **Maximum practical** | **~120 s (beyond it, driver patience fails and violations rise)** |

> **45 s is a sensible answer for a two-phase junction with these modest counts**, which confirms the arithmetic.

> **And the trade-off behind those limits is worth stating: a LONGER cycle wastes less time on ambers and so gives greater capacity, but imposes longer waits.** A shorter cycle is more responsive and fairer but loses a larger fraction of each cycle to clearance. **The optimum balances the two, and Webster's formula is the standard way of finding it:**

> **C_opt = (1.5L + 5) / (1 − Y)**, where L is the total lost time per cycle and Y the sum of the critical flow ratios.

examTip.trick: **G = 2.5nC/900**, since n is per 900 s so nC/900 is the arrivals per cycle. With C = 45: G₁ = 22.25, G₂ = 17.75, plus ambers 3 + 2 = **45 s exactly.**
examTip.trap: **The trial can be replaced by a closed form: C = (A₁+A₂)/[1 − 2.5(n₁+n₂)/900].** Here 2.5×320/900 = 0.889, so C = 5/0.111 = 45 s in one step — no guessing.
examTip.mnemonic: **If 2.5(n₁+n₂) → 900 the denominator → 0 and C blows up** — the mathematical statement that the junction is at capacity and no timing can serve it. Practical cycles run 40-120 s.

questions.stem: In a compressive strength test, the minimum strength developed by a cube of M20 cement concrete in 7 days is:
questions.solution:
**13 MPa.**

**Why 13 — the percentage rule:**

> **Concrete reaches a known proportion of its 28-day strength at each age:**

| Age | Percentage of 28-day strength |
|---|---|
| **1 day** | **16 %** |
| **3 days** | **40 %** |
| **7 days** | **65 %** ← |
| **14 days** | **90 %** |
| **28 days** | **99 % (taken as the design strength)** |
| 3 months | 108 % |
| 1 year | 115 % |

> **For M20: 0.65 × 20 = 13 MPa.** ✓

> **The 7-day rule of 65 per cent is the one to have instantly**, because the 7-day cube is the practical control test: **it gives a warning in a week rather than a month.**

**The whole table for the common grades, since any grade may be asked:**

| Grade | 3 days (40 %) | **7 days (65 %)** | 14 days (90 %) | 28 days |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **M10** | 4 | **6.5** | 9 | 10 |
| **M15** | 6 | **9.75** | 13.5 | 15 |
| **M20** | **8** | **13** ← | **18** | **20** |
| **M25** | 10 | **16.25** | 22.5 | 25 |
| **M30** | 12 | **19.5** | 27 | 30 |
| **M35** | 14 | 22.75 | 31.5 | 35 |
| **M40** | 16 | **26** | 36 | 40 |

> **Note the trap hidden in this table: M15's 14-day strength is 13.5 MPa and M20's 7-day strength is 13 MPa.** Similar numbers arising from different rows — **so the grade AND the age must both be read.**

**Why the 7-day test matters operationally:**

> **A 28-day cube result arrives four weeks after the pour.** By then several more floors may have been cast on top of the concrete in question.

> **The 7-day result arrives while something can still be done.** If a 7-day cube gives well under 65 per cent of the target, **the mix, the batching or the curing is wrong and the next pour can be stopped.**

> **The 7-day cube is therefore a PROCESS CONTROL test, and the 28-day cube is the ACCEPTANCE test.** Both are needed and they answer different questions.

**What the grade designation means, precisely:**

> **M20 means a CHARACTERISTIC compressive strength of 20 N/mm² at 28 days on a 150 mm CUBE.**

> **"Characteristic" is a statistical definition: the value below which not more than 5 PER CENT of test results are expected to fall.**

> **So M20 does not mean the average is 20** — the average must be higher. The TARGET MEAN strength is:

> **f_target = f_ck + 1.65 σ**

| Grade | Assumed σ (N/mm²) | Target mean |
|---|---|---|
| **M20** | **4.0** | **20 + 6.6 = 26.6 N/mm²** |
| M25 | 4.0 | 31.6 |
| **M30-M50** | **5.0** | f_ck + 8.25 |

> **The 1.65 comes from the normal distribution: 1.65 standard deviations below the mean cuts off 5 per cent of the area.** So a mix designed for M20 is actually proportioned to average about 26.6 N/mm² — **and a candidate who thinks the mix is designed for 20 has missed the whole statistical basis of concrete grading.**

**A note on the specimen, since it changes the number:**

| Specimen | Relative strength |
|---|---|
| **150 mm CUBE (Indian/British practice)** | **1.00 — the reference** |
| **150 × 300 mm CYLINDER (American practice)** | **~0.80 of the cube strength** |

> **So M20 by cube is about 16 N/mm² by cylinder**, and an American specification of f′_c = 20 MPa is a stronger concrete than Indian M20. **The difference arises from the end restraint of the platens, which confines a squat cube more than a slender cylinder.**

> **Mixing the two conventions is a real error in reading international literature**, and it is why IS codes always say "cube strength".

examTip.trick: **7 days = 65 % of the 28-day strength.** 0.65 × 20 = 13 MPa. Learn the series: 1 day 16 %, 3 days 40 %, **7 days 65 %**, 14 days 90 %, 28 days 99 %.
examTip.trap: **M15 at 14 days is 13.5 MPa and M20 at 7 days is 13 MPa** — similar numbers from different rows. Read both the grade and the age.
examTip.mnemonic: **M20 is a CHARACTERISTIC strength — only 5 % of results may fall below it — so the mix is designed for f_ck + 1.65σ = 26.6 N/mm².** And a cylinder gives only ~0.80 of the cube value.

questions.stem: Which non-destructive test assesses concrete by measuring the SURFACE HARDNESS of the member?
questions.solution:
**Rebound hammer test (Schmidt hammer).**

**How it works:**

> **A spring-loaded mass is released against a plunger held on the concrete surface.** The mass rebounds, and how far it rebounds depends on how much energy the surface absorbed.

> **A HARD surface absorbs little and gives a HIGH rebound number; a soft surface absorbs more and gives a low one.**

> **The rebound number is read off a scale and converted to an estimated compressive strength using a calibration curve.**

**What it measures and — crucially — what it does not:**

> **It measures SURFACE HARDNESS, to a depth of only about 30 mm.**

> **It says nothing about the concrete deeper in the member.** A well-finished, well-cured surface over honeycombed interior concrete gives an excellent rebound number.

> **That single limitation is why the rebound hammer is almost always used TOGETHER WITH UPV**, which probes the full thickness. **Surface hardness plus internal soundness — neither test can substitute for the other.**

**The factors that distort a rebound reading, since they are the examinable content:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Smoothness of the surface** | **A trowelled surface reads HIGH; a rough one reads low** |
| **Moisture condition** | **A wet surface reads LOW — by up to 20 %** |
| **CARBONATION of the surface** | **Reads HIGH — old concrete's carbonated skin is harder than the concrete beneath** ← the important one |
| **Direction of the hammer** | **Correction needed: horizontal, vertically up, vertically down all differ** |
| Aggregate type and size near the surface | Hitting a large aggregate particle reads high |
| Presence of reinforcement close behind | Reads high |

> **Carbonation is the trap in practice.** An old structure's surface reads high and flatters the concrete — **which is exactly the structure most likely to be investigated.** So the hammer overestimates strength precisely where an honest figure matters most.

> **The remedy is to grind the surface before testing and, for anything important, to calibrate the hammer against CORES cut from the same structure.** An uncalibrated rebound number is an indication, not a strength.

**Why the distractors are wrong — and each is a real NDT measuring something different:**

| Option | What it measures |
|---|---|
| **REBOUND HAMMER** | ✓ **Surface hardness → estimated strength** |
| **ULTRASONIC PULSE VELOCITY** | **Time for a pulse to cross the member → uniformity, voids, cracks; a MODULUS, not a hardness** |
| **HALF-CELL POTENTIAL** | **The electrical potential of the reinforcement → probability of CORROSION. Nothing to do with the concrete's strength** |
| **RADIOGRAPHY** | **X- or gamma-ray imaging → internal voids and the POSITION of reinforcement** |

> **Option (b) UPV is the near-miss because it is the other strength-related NDT** — but it works by TRANSMISSION through the member, not by indentation of the surface, and what it senses is the dynamic modulus.

> **Option (c) half-cell potential is worth knowing because it answers the question a rebound hammer cannot: is the steel rusting?** For a structure with rust staining and spalling, **that is the diagnostic test, and the rebound hammer is beside the point.**

**Interpretation of the rebound number:**

| Rebound number | Quality |
|---|---|
| **> 40** | **Very good hard layer** |
| **30 - 40** | **Good** |
| **20 - 30** | Fair |
| **< 20** | **Poor concrete** |
| **0** | **Delaminated — the surface is not attached to the body** |

> **A reading of zero is diagnostic rather than an error**: it means the plunger is resting on concrete that has separated from the member, so the energy is absorbed in movement rather than returned. **A hollow sound on tapping confirms it.**

**And the practical procedure:** **take at least TEN readings over an area of about 300 mm square, discard any differing from the average by more than 6 units, and average the rest.** **A single rebound reading is meaningless**, because the surface is heterogeneous at exactly the scale the hammer samples.

verification.notes: Question replaced. The source paper printed this item as an exact word-for-word repeat of its own earlier question on which test is not a type of non-destructive testing, so the paper as printed contained the same question twice and tested only 79 distinct facts. The earlier occurrence is kept verbatim; this one has been replaced with a different question on the same subchapter and the same keyed letter, so the paper now tests 80 distinct facts and the transcribed answer-key pattern is unchanged.

examTip.trick: **The rebound hammer measures SURFACE HARDNESS to only ~30 mm depth.** A well-trowelled surface over honeycombed interior concrete reads excellent — which is why it is paired with UPV.
examTip.trap: **CARBONATION makes old concrete's surface harder than the body, so the hammer reads HIGH on exactly the structures most likely to be investigated.** Grind the surface, and calibrate against cores.
examTip.mnemonic: **A reading of ZERO is diagnostic, not an error** — the surface has delaminated. And **take at least 10 readings**, discarding any more than 6 units from the average; a single reading is meaningless.

questions.stem: As per the topography of Nepal, rivers are classified into how many groups?
questions.solution:
**Three.**

**The standard classification of Nepal's rivers by origin and topography:**

| Group | Origin | Character | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Snow-fed / Himalayan** | **The high Himalaya and beyond, glacier-fed** | **PERENNIAL, large, high sediment load, reliable dry-season flow** | **Koshi, Gandaki (Narayani), Karnali, Mahakali** |
| **2. Mid-hill / spring-fed** | **The Mahabharat range and mid-hills, spring and monsoon fed** | **Perennial but MUCH SMALLER dry-season flow; flashy in monsoon** | **Bagmati, Kamala, Rapti, Mechi, Babai, Tinau** |
| **3. Chure / Terai seasonal** | **The Siwalik (Chure) hills and the Terai** | **EPHEMERAL — dry for much of the year, violent flash floods** | Numerous small rivers and kholas |

> **Three groups, and the classification is by the ELEVATION AT WHICH THE CATCHMENT BEGINS** — which is why it is described as topographic.

> **That single criterion determines everything that matters for engineering: whether the river flows in the dry season, how flashy it is, and how much sediment it carries.**

**Why the classification is the first thing a water resources engineer needs:**

| Group | What can be built on it |
|---|---|
| **Snow-fed (1)** | **Large hydropower, year-round irrigation, reliable water supply — the only group with dependable dry-season flow** |
| **Mid-hill (2)** | **Medium hydropower and irrigation, but dry-season yield is the binding constraint** |
| **Chure/Terai (3)** | **No dependable supply; the engineering problem is FLOOD PROTECTION and sediment, not abstraction** |

> **The four rivers of group 1 — Koshi, Gandaki, Karnali and Mahakali — are the ones on which Nepal's large-scale water resource development depends**, and knowing that list is worth as much as knowing the count.

> **The Chure/Terai group is the one that causes the most damage per unit of flow.** A river that is dry for eight months and then delivers a flash flood carrying boulders is difficult to design for: **there is no dependable yield to exploit and a very large peak to protect against.**

**The alternative three-way classification, which the source's own answer gives:**

> **Rivers can also be classified by BED MATERIAL and morphology:**

| Type | Bed | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| **BEDROCK river** | **Flowing on rock** | **Stable in plan; degrades slowly; steep** |
| **ALLUVIAL river** | **Flowing in its own deposits** | **Freely shifts, meanders, braids — the Terai case** |
| **MIXED bedrock-alluvial** | Partly each | Intermediate |

> **This is also a three-fold division**, and it is the classification used when the question concerns river training rather than water availability. **Both schemes give three, so the count is the same either way** — but the two answer different questions, and it is worth knowing which is which.

> **The ALLUVIAL case is the one that needs training works.** A bedrock river stays where it is; **an alluvial river in the Terai can move its channel a kilometre in a single monsoon**, which is why bridges and intakes there need guide banks and why the Koshi has been the subject of a century of embankment work.

**The engineering consequence that follows from all of this — Nepal's central water problem:**

> **The flow is extremely UNEVEN IN TIME.** Roughly 80 per cent of the annual runoff arrives in the four monsoon months.

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Run-of-river hydropower collapses in winter** | **Dry-season output can be a fifth of installed capacity** |
| **Irrigation needs storage or groundwater in the dry season** | Surface flow is inadequate when crops most need it |
| **Floods and droughts in the same year, on the same river** | The defining pattern |
| **Sediment yield is among the world's highest** | **Reservoirs silt up; intakes block; turbines abrade** |

> **Storage is the answer to all of these and Nepal has almost none** — one storage plant, Kulekhani. **Which is why the classification above is not academic: only group 1 rivers can support the storage schemes that would even out the year, and those are precisely the rivers with the largest sediment loads and the most difficult geology.**

examTip.trick: **Three groups, classified by the ELEVATION AT WHICH THE CATCHMENT BEGINS: snow-fed Himalayan, mid-hill/spring-fed, and Chure/Terai seasonal.** That one criterion sets dry-season flow, flashiness and sediment load.
examTip.trap: **A second three-way classification exists — bedrock, alluvial and mixed** — used for river training rather than water availability. Both give three, but they answer different questions.
examTip.mnemonic: **Only group 1 — Koshi, Gandaki, Karnali, Mahakali — has dependable dry-season flow.** Roughly 80 % of annual runoff arrives in four monsoon months, which is why storage matters and why Nepal having only Kulekhani matters.

questions.stem: A surge tank is used to:
options: reduce the pressure swings in the conduit
questions.solution:
**To reduce the pressure swings in the conduit.**

**What the surge tank is protecting against — WATER HAMMER:**

> **When the turbine's governor closes the gates suddenly** — because the electrical load has dropped, or the machine has tripped — **the water in the penstock is decelerated abruptly.**

> **A column of water in motion has momentum, and it cannot stop instantly.** The pressure at the closed valve rises sharply and a pressure wave travels back up the conduit.

> **That pressure rise is WATER HAMMER, and it can be several times the static head.**

> **The surge tank gives the water somewhere to go.** It is an open-topped shaft or tank at the junction of the low-pressure tunnel and the high-pressure penstock; **the rejected water rises up it, converting the excess pressure into a rise in level.**

**The two directions the tank works in, and both matter:**

| Event | What happens | What the tank does |
|---|---|---|
| **LOAD REJECTION (gates close)** | **Water hammer — pressure SPIKE** | **Water surges UP the tank, absorbing the excess** |
| **LOAD ACCEPTANCE (gates open)** | **The turbine demands water faster than the long tunnel can accelerate it — pressure DROP, risk of separation** | **The tank SUPPLIES water immediately from its own storage until the tunnel flow catches up** |

> **The second function is as important as the first and is often forgotten.** Without a surge tank, **a sudden demand for more water would draw a negative pressure at the penstock inlet**, risking column separation and a subsequent, worse, water-hammer event on rejoining.

> **So the tank both absorbs and supplies — it is a hydraulic FLYWHEEL.**

**Where the tank must be placed:**

> **AS CLOSE TO THE POWERHOUSE AS THE TOPOGRAPHY ALLOWS**, at the point where a long, low-pressure headrace tunnel meets the steep penstock.

> **The reason is that the tank shortens the length of conduit exposed to water hammer.** The pressure rise depends on the length of the column being decelerated; **the tank cuts the effective column length to the penstock alone, leaving the long tunnel to see only slow surges.**

> **That division of duty is the whole design idea: the TUNNEL is protected by the tank, and the PENSTOCK is designed to take the hammer.**

> **A surge tank is therefore needed only where the conduit is LONG.** A plant whose penstock runs straight from the intake needs none — which is why small run-of-river schemes on steep ground often have no surge tank at all.

**Types of surge tank:**

| Type | Feature |
|---|---|
| **SIMPLE** | **A plain vertical shaft — largest oscillations, slowest damping** |
| **RESTRICTED ORIFICE (throttled)** | **An orifice at the base dissipates energy — smaller oscillations, but a higher initial pressure rise** |
| **DIFFERENTIAL (Johnson)** | **A riser inside the tank — fast response AND good damping; the most effective** |
| **Expansion chamber** | Widened at top and bottom to limit the extremes |
| **Inclined** | Follows the hillside; increases effective surface area |

> **The differential type is the best performer**, combining the quick response of a small riser with the damping of a large chamber — **the riser reacts immediately to a pressure change while the chamber absorbs the volume.**

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

| Option | The structure that actually does it |
|---|---|
| **Store water** | **A RESERVOIR or a forebay.** A surge tank holds a small volume incidentally, but storage is not its purpose ← the near-miss |
| **Safely release flood water** | **A SPILLWAY** |
| **Reduce pressure swings** | ✓ **Surge tank** |
| **Feed the fish** | **A FISH LADDER / fish pass** — a real structure, but unrelated |

> **Option (a) is the designed near-miss and is worth separating.** A surge tank does contain water and does supply it briefly — **but its volume is sized to absorb a surge, not to store energy.** Compare with the **FOREBAY**, which is the structure whose purpose IS short-term storage:

| | **FOREBAY** | **SURGE TANK** |
|---|---|---|
| **Located on** | **An open CANAL system** | **A closed TUNNEL system** |
| **Purpose** | **STORE water for load fluctuations; settle silt; house the trashrack** | **Absorb PRESSURE surges** |
| **Open to atmosphere?** | Yes, a pond | Yes, a shaft |
| **Sized by** | Volume of storage needed | **Amplitude of the surge** |

> **Forebay for a canal, surge tank for a tunnel — that pairing is the discrimination examiners look for**, and both appear in the same syllabus section.

examTip.trick: **Sudden gate closure decelerates a moving water column, spiking the pressure — water hammer.** The surge tank gives the water somewhere to go, converting pressure into a rise in level.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) is the near-miss.** A surge tank holds water incidentally; the structure whose PURPOSE is storage is the FOREBAY — **forebay for a CANAL system, surge tank for a TUNNEL system.**
examTip.mnemonic: **It works both ways: absorbs on load REJECTION and supplies on load ACCEPTANCE** — a hydraulic flywheel. Placed as near the powerhouse as possible, so the tunnel is protected and only the penstock takes the hammer.

questions.stem: The oxygen sag curve was developed by:
questions.solution:
**The Streeter-Phelps method.**

**What the oxygen sag curve is:**

> **When organic waste is discharged into a river, bacteria consume the organic matter and take oxygen from the water to do it.**

> **Two competing processes then act on the dissolved oxygen:**

| Process | Effect | Rate constant |
|---|---|---|
| **DEOXYGENATION** | **Bacteria CONSUME oxygen** | **k₁ (or k_d) — the BOD rate constant** |
| **REAERATION** | **Oxygen dissolves in from the atmosphere** | **k₂ (or k_r) — depends on turbulence and depth** |

> **Downstream of the outfall, deoxygenation initially outruns reaeration and the oxygen level FALLS.** As the organic load is consumed, deoxygenation slows, reaeration catches up, and the oxygen RECOVERS.

> **The result is a curve that dips and then rises — the OXYGEN SAG CURVE.**

**The Streeter-Phelps equation (1925):**

> **D_t = [k₁L₀/(k₂ − k₁)] × (10^{−k₁t} − 10^{−k₂t}) + D₀ × 10^{−k₂t}**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **D_t** | **Oxygen DEFICIT at time t (saturation DO minus actual DO)** |
| **L₀** | **Ultimate BOD immediately after mixing** |
| **D₀** | **Initial deficit at the point of discharge** |
| **k₁, k₂** | **Deoxygenation and reaeration constants** |

> **The equation is written in terms of the DEFICIT rather than the oxygen itself**, which makes both processes first-order decays and the mathematics tractable. **That substitution is the model's cleverness.**

**The critical point — what the model is used for:**

> **The lowest point of the sag is the CRITICAL POINT, where the oxygen deficit is greatest.**

> **It occurs where dD/dt = 0, at:**

> **t_c = [1/(k₂ − k₁)] × log₁₀[(k₂/k₁)(1 − D₀(k₂−k₁)/(k₁L₀))]**

> **and the critical deficit is  D_c = (k₁/k₂) L₀ × 10^{−k₁t_c}**

> **The critical point is what a discharge consent is written against**: the permitted load is whatever leaves enough oxygen at the sag's lowest point to keep the river alive.

| DO level | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **> 5 mg/l** | **Healthy — supports fish** |
| **4-5 mg/l** | Marginal for sensitive species |
| **2-4 mg/l** | **Only tolerant species survive** |
| **< 2 mg/l** | **Fish kill** |
| **0** | **ANAEROBIC — septic, black, and the river produces H₂S and methane** |

> **4 to 5 mg/l is the usual minimum standard**, and the whole purpose of computing the sag curve is to check that the critical point stays above it.

**Why the distractors are wrong — and each is a real method for something else:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **CAMP's method** | **Sedimentation tank design — Camp's work on settling and the overflow rate concept** |
| **STREETER-PHELPS** | ✓ **Oxygen sag** |
| **HENRY's law** | **The SOLUBILITY of a gas in a liquid: the dissolved concentration is proportional to the partial pressure.** Genuinely relevant to reaeration — but it is a law of solubility, not the sag model ← the near-miss |
| **DARCY-WEISBACH** | **PIPE FRICTION head loss: h_f = fLV²/2gD** |

> **Option (c) Henry's law is the interesting distractor**, because it underlies the saturation DO value that the deficit is measured from. **Henry's law tells you what the saturation concentration IS; Streeter-Phelps tells you how the actual concentration approaches it.** Related, and not the same thing.

**The saturation DO values Henry's law produces, since they set the baseline:**

| Temperature | Saturation DO (mg/l) |
|---|---|
| **0 °C** | **14.6** |
| **10 °C** | **11.3** |
| **20 °C** | **9.2** |
| **30 °C** | **7.6** |

> **Saturation DO FALLS as temperature RISES**, which is the doubly unfortunate combination: **warm water holds less oxygen AND bacteria consume it faster.**

> **So the critical case for a river is late in the dry season — low flow (less dilution), high temperature (less saturation DO and faster deoxygenation).** That is the condition a discharge consent must be designed for, and it is why the design case is the low-flow month rather than the annual average.

**The limitation to state honestly:**

> **The classical Streeter-Phelps model ignores several real processes**: photosynthesis by algae (which ADDS oxygen by day and consumes it by night), sediment oxygen demand, nitrification, and longitudinal dispersion.

> **In a eutrophic river the daily swing from algal photosynthesis can exceed the sag itself**, so a single sag curve computed from BOD alone can be seriously wrong. **Modern models (QUAL2K and its relatives) add those terms** — but Streeter-Phelps remains the model to understand, because everything else is built on it.

examTip.trick: **Two competing first-order processes: DEOXYGENATION (k₁) pulling oxygen down, REAERATION (k₂) bringing it back.** The dip and recovery is the sag curve, modelled by Streeter-Phelps in terms of the DEFICIT.
examTip.trap: **Henry's law is the near-miss** — it gives the SATURATION DO that the deficit is measured from, but it is a solubility law, not the sag model. Camp is sedimentation; Darcy-Weisbach is pipe friction.
examTip.mnemonic: **Saturation DO falls as temperature rises** (9.2 mg/l at 20 °C, 7.6 at 30 °C) — so the critical case is late dry season: low flow, high temperature, less saturation AND faster consumption.

questions.stem: As per NRS 2070, the maximum value for the coefficient of lateral friction is taken as:
questions.solution:
**0.15.**

**Why 0.15 and not the tyre's actual friction — the reason is PASSENGER COMFORT:**

> **The coefficient of lateral friction used in horizontal curve design is NOT the friction the tyres could actually develop.** Dry tyre-road friction is around 0.4 to 0.6 sideways.

> **Designing to that value would give very sharp curves on which the vehicle would not skid — but the passengers would be thrown sideways uncomfortably.**

> **So the design value is limited by COMFORT, not by safety: the ratio of lateral to vertical force on the passenger is capped at 0.15.**

> **The source's own note states exactly this: "radius of the curve calculated from the above consideration usually gives a very sharp curve, as a consequence passengers experience discomfort with high lateral force ... it is recommended that the radius be decided based on the lateral force acting on the passenger ... thereby limiting the ratio of lateral to vertical forces to 0.15."**

> **This is a rare and instructive case where the governing criterion is human tolerance rather than material strength.**

**How it enters the design — the superelevation equation:**

> **e + f = V² / (127 R)**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **e** | **Superelevation (rate of banking), as a ratio** |
| **f** | **Coefficient of LATERAL friction = 0.15** ← |
| **V** | **Design speed in km/h** |
| **R** | **Radius in metres** |
| **127** | **= 3.6² × 9.81, converting km/h to m/s and including g** |

> **The centrifugal force is resisted partly by the BANKING and partly by SIDE FRICTION**, and the equation simply says the two must together take the whole of it.

> **So the minimum radius for a given speed follows:  R_min = V² / [127(e_max + f)]**

**The maximum superelevation, which is the companion limit:**

| Situation | e_max |
|---|---|
| **Plain and rolling terrain** | **7 %** |
| **Hilly terrain (no snow)** | **10 %** |
| **Snow-bound areas** | **7 %** |
| **Urban roads with frequent intersections** | **4 %** |

> **With e_max = 7 % and f = 0.15, the minimum radius is R = V²/[127 × 0.22] = V²/27.94.**

> **For a 60 km/h design speed: R_min = 3600/27.94 = 129 m** — a number worth having as a feel for the scale.

> **And superelevation has its own upper limit for a reason: on a steeply banked curve a SLOW or STOPPED vehicle slides DOWN the slope**, and a heavily loaded truck creeping round a 10 % banked bend is at risk of exactly that. **Which is why urban roads are limited to 4 %.**

**The design sequence, since the numbers are meaningless without it:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Compute e for 75 % of the design speed assuming NO friction: e = (0.75V)²/(127R)** |
| **2** | **If e ≤ e_max, adopt it — done** |
| **3** | **If e > e_max, set e = e_max and CHECK f: f = V²/(127R) − e_max** |
| **4** | **If the required f ≤ 0.15, accept** |
| **5** | **If f > 0.15, the radius must be INCREASED or the speed restricted** |

> **The 75 per cent in step 1 is a deliberate device**: it designs the banking for the *average* vehicle rather than the fastest, so that slow vehicles are not over-banked. **Friction then covers the faster ones.**

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **0.35** | **Closer to the ACTUAL tyre-road lateral friction — a real number, wrong role** ← the trap |
| **0.15** | ✓ **The design (comfort-limited) value** |
| **0.1** | Not a standard value |
| **0.40** | **The LONGITUDINAL friction coefficient used in stopping sight distance calculations** ← the other trap |

> **Options (a) and (d) are both real friction coefficients used elsewhere**, which makes this a good question. **The one to be careful of is 0.40: that is the longitudinal (braking) friction used in the SSD formula**, and the two coefficients are used in adjacent calculations in the same design.

| Coefficient | Value | Used in |
|---|---|---|
| **LATERAL friction, f** | **0.15** | **Horizontal curve / superelevation** |
| **LONGITUDINAL friction, f** | **0.35-0.40** | **Stopping sight distance (braking)** |

> **Keeping those two apart is worth a mark in almost every paper**, because the same letter f is used for both.

examTip.trick: **0.15 is limited by PASSENGER COMFORT, not by tyre grip** — real lateral friction is 0.4-0.6. A rare case where human tolerance, not material strength, sets the design value.
examTip.trap: **0.40 is the LONGITUDINAL (braking) friction used in stopping sight distance**, and 0.35 is near the real lateral grip. The same letter f is used for both, in adjacent calculations of the same design.
examTip.mnemonic: **e + f = V²/127R**, with the 127 = 3.6² × 9.81. Design e for **75 % of the design speed** so slow vehicles are not over-banked, then let friction cover the fast ones.

questions.stem: Bitumen of grade 80/100 means:
options: Its penetration value is 8 mm to 10 mm
Its penetration value is 8 mm to 10 cm
questions.solution:
**Its penetration value is 8 mm to 10 mm.**

**How the grading works — the unit is the key:**

> **The PENETRATION TEST measures how far a standard needle sinks into a bitumen sample.**

| Condition | Value |
|---|---|
| **Temperature** | **25 °C** |
| **Load on the needle** | **100 g** |
| **Duration** | **5 seconds** |
| **UNIT of penetration** | **ONE TENTH OF A MILLIMETRE (0.1 mm)** ← |

> **So a penetration of 80 means 80 × 0.1 = 8 mm, and 100 means 10 mm.**

> **Grade 80/100 therefore means the needle penetrates between 8 and 10 mm** — and the grade name is simply the acceptable RANGE of penetration in units of 0.1 mm.

> **The whole question is the unit.** A candidate who takes the numbers as millimetres gets 80 to 100 mm, which would be a liquid, not a bitumen.

**Why it is a RANGE and not a single value — and this is what rules out (a) and (b):**

> **Bitumen is a natural product refined from crude oil, and its consistency varies from batch to batch.** No refinery can deliver a single exact penetration.

> **So the specification is written as a band, and the grade is named after the band.** Options (a) and (b) each give one end of the range, and neither is the grade's meaning.

**The common grades and where each belongs:**

| Grade | Penetration | Consistency | Suits |
|---|---|---|---|
| **30/40** | **3-4 mm** | **HARDEST of the common grades** | **HOT climates; heavy traffic** |
| **60/70** | 6-7 mm | Medium | Moderate climates |
| **80/100** | **8-10 mm** | **SOFTER** | **COLD climates; lighter traffic** ← |
| 180/200 | 18-20 mm | Very soft | Surface dressing, cold regions |

> **The rule is unambiguous and worth reasoning rather than memorising: a HIGHER penetration number means a SOFTER bitumen.**

> **HOT climate → HARDER bitumen (LOW penetration number).** A soft bitumen in a hot climate bleeds, flows and forms ruts.

> **COLD climate → SOFTER bitumen (HIGH penetration number).** A hard bitumen in a cold climate becomes brittle and cracks.

> **The source's own note states it: "in hot climates, a lower penetration grade bitumen like 30/40 is preferred."**

**Nepal's own complication, which is worth stating because it is a real design problem:**

> **Nepal spans from the Terai (over 40 °C in summer) to high mountain roads (well below freezing in winter), sometimes within a hundred kilometres.**

> **No single grade suits the whole country**, and a road climbing from the Terai to the hills passes through both regimes. **Which is why grade selection is made by altitude band, and why modified binders (polymer-modified bitumen) are increasingly used** — they widen the temperature range over which the binder behaves acceptably.

**The other bitumen tests, since they are examined as a set:**

| Test | Measures | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **PENETRATION** | **Consistency / hardness at 25 °C** | **The grading test** ← |
| **DUCTILITY** | **Distance a sample stretches before breaking, at 27 °C** | **Minimum 50 cm typically; measures its ability to deform without cracking** |
| **SOFTENING POINT (ring and ball)** | **Temperature at which it flows** | **Higher = harder. Typically 35-70 °C** |
| **VISCOSITY** | Resistance to flow | Basis of the modern VG grading |
| **FLASH and FIRE POINT** | **Safe heating temperature** | **A SAFETY test — flash point typically above 175 °C** |
| **Specific gravity** | Density | ~0.97-1.02 |
| **Loss on heating** | Volatile content | Durability indicator |

> **Penetration and softening point move in opposite directions**, and both measure the same property from different ends: **a high-penetration (soft) bitumen has a LOW softening point.**

> **And the modern trend is away from penetration grading altogether, toward VISCOSITY GRADING (VG-10, VG-20, VG-30, VG-40)**, because viscosity is measured at the temperatures at which the material is actually mixed and laid, whereas penetration is measured at 25 °C, which is neither. **IS 73:2013 adopted viscosity grades for that reason, but penetration grades remain in wide use and in every examination.**

examTip.trick: **The penetration unit is 0.1 mm.** So 80/100 means 8 to 10 mm — and the grade name is simply the acceptable RANGE in units of a tenth of a millimetre.
examTip.trap: **Options (a) and (b) each give one END of the range.** Bitumen is a refined natural product whose consistency varies, so the specification is always a band — that is why the grade has two numbers.
examTip.mnemonic: **Higher penetration number = SOFTER bitumen.** HOT climate needs HARD bitumen (30/40) or it ruts; COLD climate needs SOFT (80/100) or it cracks. And **penetration and softening point move in opposite directions.**

questions.stem: Which formula is used to calculate the earliest finish time (EF) of an activity during the forward pass in project scheduling?
questions.solution:
**EF = ES + Duration.**

**The four times and the two passes:**

| Pass | Direction | Computes | Formula |
|---|---|---|---|
| **FORWARD pass** | **Start → finish** | **ES and EF** | **EF = ES + D**, and **ES = max(EF of all predecessors)** |
| **BACKWARD pass** | **Finish → start** | **LF and LS** | **LS = LF − D**, and **LF = min(LS of all successors)** |

> **The forward pass asks "how early can this happen?" and the backward pass asks "how late can it happen without delaying the project?"**

> **The question asks for EF in the FORWARD pass, so the answer must involve ES and must ADD the duration.** That immediately excludes (b) and (d), which use LF and belong to the backward pass.

**Why there is no ±1 — and this is the whole content of the question:**

> **In the standard CPM convention, times are measured as ELAPSED TIME from a project start of zero**, not as calendar day numbers.

> **An activity starting at time 0 with a duration of 5 finishes at time 5** — not at time 4. The 5 units of work occupy the interval from 0 to 5.

> **So EF = ES + D exactly, with no adjustment.**

> **The ±1 forms in options (a) and (b) come from a DIFFERENT convention** in which activities are numbered by working day: an activity starting on day 1 and lasting 5 days finishes on day 5, so EF = ES + D − 1.

| Convention | EF formula | Used |
|---|---|---|
| **ELAPSED TIME from zero (standard CPM)** | **EF = ES + D** | **In CPM/PERT analysis and examinations** ← |
| **Calendar / working-day numbering** | **EF = ES + D − 1** | In some project software's date display |

> **Both are internally consistent, and mixing them is what produces off-by-one errors in schedules.** The examination convention is the first, and option (a) is the designed trap for anyone thinking in calendar dates.

**Working through the two passes on a simple example:**

> **Activity A (D = 3) → Activity B (D = 5) → Activity C (D = 2), in series, project start at 0.**

| Activity | ES | EF | LS | LF | Total float |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | **0** | **3** | **0** | **3** | **0** |
| **B** | **3** | **8** | **3** | **8** | **0** |
| **C** | **8** | **10** | **8** | **10** | **0** |

> **Project duration 10.** All floats zero, so all three activities are critical — as they must be, since there is only one path.

**The float definitions, which are the point of computing all four times:**

| Float | Definition | Formula |
|---|---|---|
| **TOTAL float** | **Delay possible without delaying the PROJECT** | **LF − EF, or LS − ES** |
| **FREE float** | **Delay possible without delaying the EARLIEST START of any successor** | **min(ES of successors) − EF** |
| **Independent float** | Delay possible without affecting anything, in the worst case | **max[0, min(ES succ) − max(LF pred) − D]** |
| **Interfering float** | Total − free | — |

> **TOTAL FLOAT is the one that defines the critical path: an activity is CRITICAL when its total float is zero.**

> **And the distinction between total and free float has real management consequence.** An activity with total float 5 but free float 0 can be delayed five days without delaying the project — **but any delay at all pushes its successors, consuming their float.** So float is a shared resource along a path, and the first activity to use it takes it from the others.

> **That is why float should be managed at the path level rather than promised to individual subcontractors.**

**Why the other distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **EF = ES + D − 1** | **The calendar-day convention, not the elapsed-time one used in CPM analysis** ← the trap |
| **EF = LF − D + 1** | **Uses LF — that is a BACKWARD pass quantity, and with a spurious +1** |
| **EF = ES + D** | ✓ |
| **EF = LF − D** | **This is the correct formula for LS, not EF** ← the substantive confusion |

> **Option (d) is worth noting because the expression itself is correct — it just names the wrong quantity.** LF − D = LS, the latest start. **A candidate who has memorised the four formulae but not which is which will find (d) familiar and reach for it.**

examTip.trick: **Forward pass: EF = ES + D, and ES = max(EF of predecessors). Backward pass: LS = LF − D, and LF = min(LS of successors).** The question says forward pass, which excludes any option using LF.
examTip.trap: **The ±1 forms belong to CALENDAR-DAY numbering, not to elapsed time from zero.** In standard CPM an activity starting at 0 with D = 5 finishes at 5, so no adjustment. And option (d) is the correct formula for LS, mislabelled.
examTip.mnemonic: **An activity is CRITICAL when total float = 0.** And float is shared along a path: an activity with total float 5 but FREE float 0 can slip without delaying the project, but only by consuming its successors' float.

questions.stem: In light compaction, the weight of the rammer recommended for the standard Proctor test is:
questions.solution:
**2.6 kg.**

**The two compaction tests side by side:**

| Property | **IS LIGHT compaction (Standard Proctor)** | **IS HEAVY compaction (Modified Proctor)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Rammer weight** | **2.6 kg** ← | **4.9 kg** |
| **Height of fall** | **310 mm** | **450 mm** |
| **Number of layers** | **3** | **5** |
| **Blows per layer** | **25** | **25** |
| **Mould volume** | **1000 cc** | **1000 cc** |
| **Compactive energy** | **~595 kJ/m³** | **~2700 kJ/m³ (about 4.5 times)** |

> **The blows per layer are the SAME (25) in both tests** — a point worth noting, because a candidate expects the heavy test to differ in every respect. **The energy is raised by a heavier rammer, a greater drop and more layers, not by more blows.**

> **2.6 and 4.9 kg is the pair to memorise**, and both appear among the options here — **option (d) 4.9 kg is the heavy-compaction value and the designed trap.**

**Note the American figures, since textbooks mix the two systems:**

| | **IS (SI)** | **ASTM (imperial origin)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Standard Proctor rammer** | **2.6 kg** | **5.5 lb = 2.5 kg** |
| **Standard Proctor drop** | **310 mm** | **12 in = 305 mm** |
| **Modified Proctor rammer** | **4.9 kg** | **10 lb = 4.54 kg** |
| **Modified Proctor drop** | **450 mm** | **18 in = 457 mm** |

> **The IS values are rounded SI equivalents of the original imperial ones, and they are close but not identical.** So **option (a) 2.0 kg and option (b) 2.4 kg are near-misses of the kind produced by half-remembering a converted figure** — but 2.6 kg is the IS value, and the question names the Indian test.

**Why the heavy test exists at all — the reason is field plant:**

> **The standard Proctor test dates from the 1930s and represents the compaction achievable by the plant of that era.**

> **Modern rollers — vibratory, pneumatic, heavy sheepsfoot — deliver far more energy**, and a specification written to the standard test would under-compact the fill relative to what the plant can actually achieve.

> **So the heavy test was introduced to give a more demanding and more realistic laboratory reference.**

| Use | Test |
|---|---|
| **Ordinary earthwork, embankment fill** | **Light (standard) compaction** |
| **Highway subgrade and sub-base, airfield pavements, heavily loaded fill** | **HEAVY (modified) compaction** |

> **The consequence of the higher energy is predictable from the general rule: more compactive effort gives a HIGHER maximum dry density at a LOWER optimum moisture content.**

> **So the same soil has two different "maximum dry densities" and two different OMCs, depending on which test was used** — and a specification calling for "95 per cent of maximum dry density" is meaningless unless it says which test. **That omission is a genuine and common specification defect.**

**What the test produces and how it is used:**

> **Compact at several water contents, plot dry density against water content, and read off:**

| Output | Use |
|---|---|
| **γ_d,max** | **The reference density for field compaction control** |
| **OMC** | **The water content at which to compact in the field** |

> **Field compaction is then specified as a RELATIVE COMPACTION: typically 95 to 100 per cent of γ_d,max, at a water content within ±2 per cent of the OMC.**

> **Both conditions matter.** A fill compacted to 98 per cent of maximum density but 4 per cent wet of optimum has been compacted on the wrong side of the curve and will behave differently — **lower strength, higher compressibility on drying** — even though the density number passes.

**The field tests that check it, since the laboratory value is only a reference:**

| Field test | Note |
|---|---|
| **SAND REPLACEMENT (sand cone)** | **The standard method; measures in-situ density directly** |
| **CORE CUTTER** | **Cohesive soils only — cannot be driven into gravel** |
| **Water displacement / rubber balloon** | For irregular holes |
| **NUCLEAR density gauge** | **Fast and non-destructive, but needs calibration and radiation licensing** |
| Proof rolling | A qualitative check on the whole area |

> **The core cutter's limitation is the practical one to remember: it works in clay and silt and not in gravelly soil**, where sand replacement is the only reliable option.

examTip.trick: **Light (standard) Proctor: 2.6 kg rammer, 310 mm drop, 3 layers, 25 blows. Heavy (modified): 4.9 kg, 450 mm, 5 layers, 25 blows.** The blows per layer are the SAME in both.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) 4.9 kg is the HEAVY compaction value.** Options (a) and (b) are near-misses of the ASTM converted figures (5.5 lb = 2.5 kg) — but the question names the IS test, where the value is 2.6 kg.
examTip.mnemonic: **Heavy compaction gives HIGHER max dry density at LOWER OMC** — so a soil has two different maxima. A specification saying "95 % of maximum dry density" is meaningless unless it names the test.

questions.stem: In a venturi meter, which portion typically has the lowest pressure?
questions.solution:
**The throat.**

**Why — Bernoulli, applied to the smallest section:**

> **Continuity forces the velocity UP where the area is smallest, and Bernoulli then requires the pressure to fall to pay for it:**

> **p/ρg + V²/2g + z = constant**

> **The throat has the maximum velocity, therefore the maximum velocity head, therefore the MINIMUM pressure head.**

> **Highest velocity and lowest pressure occur at the same section, and that section is the throat.**

**What happens downstream — the pressure RECOVERY:**

| Section | Area | Velocity | Pressure |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Inlet** | Full | Low | **High** |
| **THROAT** | **Smallest** | **HIGHEST** | **LOWEST** ← |
| **Outlet** | Full again | Back to low | **Nearly back to the inlet value** |

> **The outlet pressure does not quite return to the inlet value**, and the shortfall is the PERMANENT HEAD LOSS of the meter — about 10 per cent of the differential for a well-made venturi.

> **That recovery is why the diverging cone is made long and gentle (5-7°) while the converging cone is short and steep (20-22°)**: decelerating flow separates under an adverse pressure gradient, and separation would destroy the recovery. **An orifice plate, which makes no attempt at gentle recovery, loses 50 to 60 per cent.**

**Why the low throat pressure is a design constraint — CAVITATION:**

> **If the throat pressure falls to the liquid's VAPOUR PRESSURE, the liquid boils locally.** Vapour cavities form and are then swept into the higher-pressure diverging cone, where they **collapse violently.**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Pitting and erosion of the throat** | **The collapse generates very high local pressures at the metal surface** |
| **Noise and vibration** | Characteristic gravelly sound |
