| **The measurement becomes meaningless** | **The flow is no longer single-phase, so the discharge equation does not apply** |

> **So the throat cannot be made arbitrarily small.** The area ratio is limited by the requirement that the throat pressure stay comfortably above vapour pressure at the maximum flow.

> **The same limit governs a pump's suction lift and a reaction turbine's setting**, where it is expressed as the NET POSITIVE SUCTION HEAD and Thoma's cavitation number respectively. **One piece of physics, three applications.**

> **Typical throat-to-inlet diameter ratio is therefore held between 1/3 and 3/4**, most often about 1/2.

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Inlet** | **Where the pressure is HIGHEST** — the opposite end of the scale |
| **Throat** | ✓ |
| **Outlet** | **Pressure recovers here, back to nearly the inlet value** ← the near-miss for anyone who assumes pressure falls monotonically along a pipe |
| **None of the above** | — |

> **Option (c) is the interesting distractor.** In an ordinary pipe the pressure does fall continuously in the direction of flow, so "the outlet has the lowest pressure" is a reasonable general instinct. **A venturi is the exception because its area varies**, and the area change dominates the friction loss over such a short length.

**Where else the same reasoning is used:**

| Device | The low-pressure section |
|---|---|
| **Venturi meter** | **Throat** |
| **Orifice meter** | **The VENA CONTRACTA, slightly downstream of the plate — not at the plate itself** |
| **Nozzle** | Exit |
| **Aircraft wing / aerofoil** | Upper surface, where the flow is fastest |
| **Carburettor and venturi scrubber** | **The throat's suction is used to draw in fuel or scrubbing liquid** |

> **The vena contracta point is the one worth remembering as a contrast**: for an orifice the minimum area, and therefore the minimum pressure, is a little way DOWNSTREAM of the plate, where the jet has finished contracting. **A venturi's throat is a physical constriction; an orifice's is a property of the jet.**

verification.notes: Stem restated. As printed, this question ("which portion typically has the highest velocity?") tested the same single fact as the earlier question in the same paper on whether throat velocity is higher than inlet velocity, so the paper asked one fact twice. The stem now asks for the section of LOWEST PRESSURE - the companion half of the same Bernoulli argument and a distinct fact - with the options and the keyed letter (b) Throat unchanged.

examTip.trick: **Highest velocity and lowest pressure occur at the SAME section — the throat.** Continuity raises the velocity at the smallest area; Bernoulli makes the pressure pay for it.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) outlet appeals to the instinct that pressure falls continuously along a pipe.** It does in a uniform pipe — but a venturi's area change dominates friction over so short a length, and the outlet RECOVERS to near the inlet value.
examTip.mnemonic: **The low throat pressure limits the area ratio: fall to vapour pressure and it CAVITATES.** Same physics as a pump's NPSH and a turbine's Thoma number. And note an orifice's minimum is at the VENA CONTRACTA, downstream of the plate.

questions.stem: What is the term for the sheet of water flowing over a weir?
questions.solution:
**Nappe (also called the vein).**

**The terminology of a weir, which is what the question tests:**

| Term | What it is |
|---|---|
| **CREST or SILL** | **The TOP EDGE of the weir, over which the water passes** |
| **HEAD (H)** | **The height of the upstream water surface ABOVE the crest** |
| **NAPPE / VEIN** | **The SHEET OF WATER itself, after it leaves the crest** ← |
| Ventilation | Admitting air beneath the nappe |
| Drowned / submerged | When the downstream level rises above the crest |

> **Note that CREST and SILL are the same thing**, so options (a) and (c) are two names for one wrong answer. **A candidate who eliminates one has eliminated both**, which reduces this to a two-way choice immediately.

> **The distinction the question draws is between the STRUCTURE (crest/sill), the HYDRAULIC CONDITION (head) and the WATER ITSELF (nappe).** Only one of those is a sheet of water.

**Why the nappe matters — the ventilation problem:**

> **A free nappe springs clear of the weir and encloses a pocket of air beneath it.**

> **The falling sheet ENTRAINS that air and carries it away.** If air cannot get back in, the pocket is progressively evacuated.

| Consequence of an unventilated nappe | Note |
|---|---|
| **Sub-atmospheric pressure under the nappe** | **The sheet is sucked toward the weir face** |
| **The nappe CLINGS to the downstream face** | It no longer springs clear |
| **The effective head changes, so the DISCHARGE COEFFICIENT changes** | **The weir is no longer a reliable measuring device** ← |
| **Fluctuation and vibration** | The nappe oscillates between clinging and springing |

> **So a measuring weir MUST BE VENTILATED**, by air vents through the weir wall or by making the weir narrower than the channel so air reaches the underside from the sides.

> **This is a real and frequently overlooked source of error in field measurement**: a weir installed across the full channel width with no air path reads high, and no amount of careful head measurement corrects it.

**The three nappe conditions, which change the discharge formula:**

| Condition | Description |
|---|---|
| **FREE (aerated)** | **Nappe springs clear, atmospheric pressure underneath — the design condition** |
| **DEPRESSED / clinging** | **Partial vacuum underneath; nappe drawn in — coefficient increases** |
| **DROWNED (submerged)** | **Downstream water level above the crest — discharge REDUCED and depends on BOTH levels** |

> **The drowned condition is the one that destroys a measurement most completely**, because the discharge then depends on the tailwater as well as the head — and a single upstream reading no longer determines the flow. **Which is why a measuring weir needs a free fall downstream, and why the drop must be maintained by design rather than assumed.**

**The weir discharge relations, since they follow directly:**

| Weir | Discharge |
|---|---|
| **Rectangular sharp-crested** | **Q = (2/3) C_d L √(2g) H^{3/2}** |
| **Triangular (V-notch), angle θ** | **Q = (8/15) C_d √(2g) tan(θ/2) H^{5/2}** |
| **Ogee spillway** | **Q = C L H^{3/2}, C ≈ 2.2 in SI** |
| **Broad-crested** | Q = 1.71 L H^{3/2} |
| **Cipolletti (trapezoidal)** | Q = 1.86 L H^{3/2} |

> **Note the exponents: 3/2 for a rectangular weir, 5/2 for a V-notch.**

> **The V-notch's higher exponent is exactly why it is preferred for SMALL flows**: as H falls, the flow area of a V-notch shrinks in both dimensions, so the head varies far more for a given change in discharge. **A rectangular weir's head becomes too small to read accurately at low flow; a V-notch's does not.**

> **And the corollary: a V-notch is poor at high flow**, because the head then becomes inconveniently large. **Rectangular for large flows, V-notch for small ones** — which is the practical selection rule.

**One further correction worth knowing:** **the effective length of a rectangular weir is reduced by END CONTRACTIONS**, L_eff = L − 0.1nH, with n the number of contracted ends. **A weir spanning the full channel width has no end contractions — one of the few advantages of the unventilated arrangement, and not enough to justify it.**

examTip.trick: **CREST and SILL are the SAME thing**, so options (a) and (c) are one wrong answer twice — eliminating either eliminates both. The nappe is the sheet of water itself.
examTip.trap: **An unventilated nappe clings to the weir face, changing the discharge coefficient** — so the weir reads high and no care in measuring the head corrects it. Measuring weirs must be aerated.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rectangular weir goes as H^{3/2}; V-notch as H^{5/2}.** The higher exponent is why a V-notch suits SMALL flows — the head changes far more per unit of discharge, so it can still be read accurately.

questions.stem: What is the Shields diagram used for in sediment transport?
options: Calculating the volume of transported sediment
questions.solution:
**Predicting incipient motion.**

**What the Shields diagram answers — one question only:**

> **"At what bed shear stress does a sediment grain of a given size BEGIN TO MOVE?"**

> **That threshold condition is called INCIPIENT MOTION (or the threshold of motion, or critical condition).**

> **The diagram plots the dimensionless SHIELDS PARAMETER against the grain Reynolds number:**

> **θ_c = τ_c / [(γ_s − γ) d]**   against   **R* = u* d / ν**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **τ_c** | **CRITICAL bed shear stress — the answer sought** |
| **γ_s, γ** | Unit weights of sediment and water |
| **d** | **Grain diameter** |
| **u\*** | **Shear velocity = √(τ/ρ)** |
| **ν** | Kinematic viscosity |

> **For coarse sediment (large R*) the curve flattens to θ_c ≈ 0.06**, which is the value most often quoted and used.

> **The diagram is IMPLICIT** — τ_c appears on both axes through u* — **so it must be entered iteratively, or by using one of the modified explicit forms.** That awkwardness is a known feature of the method.

**Why the diagram does NOT do what options (a) and (c) claim, and this is the key discrimination:**

> **Incipient motion is a THRESHOLD, not a RATE.** The diagram tells you WHETHER the bed moves. It says nothing about HOW MUCH sediment moves once it does.

| Question | Tool |
|---|---|
| **Does the bed start to move?** | **SHIELDS diagram** ← |
| **How much bed load is transported?** | **Meyer-Peter Müller, Einstein-Brown, Bagnold, Van Rijn** |
| **How much suspended load?** | **Rouse profile, Einstein's method, Lane-Kalinske** |
| **How much total sediment volume in a reservoir?** | **Sediment yield estimates, trap efficiency (Brune's curve)** |

> **So option (c) names the job of a bed-load TRANSPORT formula, not of Shields.** And option (a), estimating sediment volume, is a catchment-yield question answered from measurements or from empirical yield relations. **Option (d) fails because it includes both.**

> **The distinction between a THRESHOLD criterion and a TRANSPORT RATE formula is the substance of this question**, and it is worth carrying: the two answer different questions and neither substitutes for the other.

**Where incipient motion is used in design:**

| Application | The design question |
|---|---|
| **Unlined canal design (tractive force method)** | **Will the bed and banks scour? Keep τ below τ_c** |
| **RIPRAP and stone protection sizing** | **How large must a stone be to stay in place? Solve Shields for d** ← |
| **Gravel-bed river stability** | Is the bed mobile at this discharge? |
| **Launching apron stone size** | Same as riprap |
| Fish-habitat and ecological flow studies | Will spawning gravel be disturbed? |

> **The riprap application is the inverse use of the diagram and the commonest in practice**: instead of asking whether a given grain moves, **you specify that it must not move and solve for the required stone size.**

> **A useful approximation follows from θ_c ≈ 0.06:  d ≈ τ / [0.06(γ_s − γ)]**, which for stone of relative density 2.65 in water gives **d ≈ τ/(0.06 × 16,200) ≈ τ/970 with τ in N/m² and d in metres.**

> **So a bed shear of 100 N/m² needs roughly a 100 mm stone** — a figure worth having as a feel for the scale.

**Why grain size alone does not settle it — the honest complications:**

| Complication | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Bed slope** | **A grain on a slope is easier to move — the side-slope correction of the tractive force method** |
| **Grain SHAPE and packing** | Angular, interlocked grains resist more than rounded loose ones |
| **ARMOURING** | **A mixed bed loses its fines, leaving a coarse surface layer that protects what is beneath** |
| **Cohesion in fine sediment** | **Clay resists far more than Shields predicts — Shields is for NON-COHESIVE sediment** |
| Turbulence and burst events | Motion begins intermittently, not at a sharp threshold |

> **The armouring effect is the one with the largest practical consequence.** A gravel-bed river degrades until the surface layer is coarse enough to resist the flow, and then stops — **so a Shields calculation using the mean grain size of the whole bed will overpredict scour.**

> **And the cohesion limit must be stated plainly: Shields does not apply to clay.** A cohesive bed's resistance comes from inter-particle bonds, not from grain weight, and can be an order of magnitude greater than the grain size would suggest.

examTip.trick: **Shields answers one question: does the bed START to move?** It is a THRESHOLD criterion, not a transport rate. For coarse sediment θ_c ≈ 0.06.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) names the job of a bed-load TRANSPORT formula** (Meyer-Peter Müller and the rest), and (a) is a catchment-yield question. A threshold and a rate answer different questions.
examTip.mnemonic: **The practical use is INVERSE — specify that the stone must not move and solve for its size.** From θ_c ≈ 0.06, roughly **d(m) ≈ τ/970** for stone in water: 100 N/m² of shear needs about a 100 mm stone.

questions.stem: An L-section stands on its base with the corner of the base as the origin. The vertical leg is 20 mm wide and 120 mm tall; the horizontal foot is 80 mm long overall and 20 mm deep. Find the centroid (x̄, ȳ) of the section in mm.
questions.solution:
**(23.3, 43.3) mm.**

**Split the L into two non-overlapping rectangles.**

> **The important step is to divide the shape so that no area is counted twice.** Take the vertical leg over its full height, and the foot only over the part that is NOT already in the leg.

| Part | Dimensions | Area A | x from origin | y from origin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1 — vertical leg** | **20 wide × 120 tall** | **2400 mm²** | **20/2 = 10** | **120/2 = 60** |
| **2 — foot, beyond the leg** | **(80 − 20) = 60 wide × 20 deep** | **1200 mm²** | **20 + 60/2 = 50** | **20/2 = 10** |
| **Total** | | **3600 mm²** | | |

> **Note the second row carefully: the foot's width is 60, not 80**, because the leftmost 20 mm of the foot is already inside the vertical leg. **Using 80 would double-count 400 mm² and is the standard error in this calculation.**

**Take moments of area about each axis:**

> **x̄ = (A₁x₁ + A₂x₂) / (A₁ + A₂)**

> **= (2400 × 10 + 1200 × 50) / 3600**

> **= (24,000 + 60,000) / 3600 = 84,000 / 3600 = 23.33 mm** ✓

> **ȳ = (A₁y₁ + A₂y₂) / (A₁ + A₂)**

> **= (2400 × 60 + 1200 × 10) / 3600**

> **= (144,000 + 12,000) / 3600 = 156,000 / 3600 = 43.33 mm** ✓

> **Centroid = (23.33, 43.33) mm.**

**The checks that catch a wrong answer in seconds:**

> **CHECK 1 — the centroid must lie INSIDE the bounding box, 0 to 80 in x and 0 to 120 in y.** All four options pass, so this does not discriminate.

> **CHECK 2 — is it in the right half?** The tall leg is on the LEFT and carries two thirds of the area, so **x̄ must be well left of the mid-width (40).** 23.3 qualifies; **43.3 does not** — which eliminates option (c) immediately.

> **CHECK 3 — is it in the right half vertically?** The tall leg dominates, so **ȳ must be well ABOVE the mid-height of the foot but BELOW the mid-height of the leg (60).** 43.3 sits sensibly between; **33.3 is too low** for a section two thirds of whose area is a 120 mm tall leg — which eliminates option (d).

> **That leaves (a) and (b), differing only in x̄: 23.3 against 33.3.** The remaining discrimination is the double-counting error:

> **If the foot is wrongly taken as the FULL 80 × 20 = 1600 mm² at x = 40, then x̄ = (24,000 + 64,000)/4000 = 22.0** — not 33.3 either. **33.3 arises from a different slip, and (a) is confirmed by the clean calculation.**

**Why the centroid must be found first:**

> **Every second moment of area is referred to the CENTROIDAL axis**, so nothing else about the section can be computed until the centroid is known.

> **For this L-section the next step would be the parallel axis theorem:**

> **I_xx = Σ[I_own + A·d²]**, with d the distance from each part's own centroid to the section centroid.

| Part | I_own about its own horizontal axis | d = y_part − ȳ | A·d² |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Leg** | **20 × 120³/12 = 2.88 × 10⁶** | **60 − 43.33 = 16.67** | **2400 × 277.9 = 0.667 × 10⁶** |
| **Foot** | **60 × 20³/12 = 0.04 × 10⁶** | **10 − 43.33 = −33.33** | **1200 × 1111 = 1.333 × 10⁶** |
| **Total I_xx** | | | **≈ 4.92 × 10⁶ mm⁴** |

> **Notice how large the A·d² terms are compared with the parts' own I values** — for the foot, 1.333 × 10⁶ against 0.04 × 10⁶, a factor of thirty. **In a compound section the transfer terms usually dominate**, which is why an error in the centroid propagates so strongly.

**And why an L-section behaves awkwardly, worth knowing:**

> **An L (angle) section is UNSYMMETRICAL about both axes**, so its principal axes are INCLINED to the legs.

> **A load applied vertically therefore produces bending about an inclined axis, and the section deflects sideways as well as downward — UNSYMMETRICAL BENDING.**

> **This is why a single angle used as a beam twists and sags out of plane**, and why angles are used in pairs (back to back) or as struts and ties in trusses rather than as beams. **The centroid calculation above is the first step in the analysis that reveals it.**

verification.notes: Figure-dependent question rewritten in text. The source stem read only "Find the CG o following section" and referred to a figure that the scanned question pages omit. The figure appears on the source's own answer page and gives the dimensions used here - a vertical leg 20 wide by 120 tall and a horizontal foot 80 overall by 20 deep - and the source's working (A1 = 2400 at x = 10, y = 60; A2 = 1200 at x = 50, y = 10; x = 23.33, y = 43.33) confirms both the geometry and the keyed answer (a). Options and answer are unchanged.

examTip.trap: **Taking the foot as the full 80 × 20 double-counts 400 mm²** — the standard error here. And check the halves: the tall left leg holds two thirds of the area, so x̄ must be well LEFT of 40, which kills option (c) at once.
examTip.mnemonic: **In a compound section the A·d² transfer terms usually DOMINATE the parts' own I values** — here by a factor of thirty for the foot. Which is why an error in the centroid propagates so strongly into I.

questions.stem: The stiffness of a member if the farther end is hinged is:
questions.solution:
**3EI/L.**

**The four stiffness values, one for each far-end condition:**

| Far end | Stiffness | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **FIXED** | **4EI/L** | **The reference case — the stiffest** |
| **HINGED (pinned)** | **3EI/L** ← | **Three quarters of the fixed value** |
| **GUIDED ROLLER** | **EI/L** | One quarter of the fixed value |
| **FREE** | **0** | Nothing to rotate against |

> **STIFFNESS is defined as the moment required at a joint to produce UNIT ROTATION there.**

> **So the sequence 4 : 3 : 1 : 0 (in units of EI/L) is the whole answer, and every option in the question is one member of it.**

**Why the hinged case gives exactly three quarters — the derivation is short and worth knowing:**

> **For a member AB with A rotating by θ and B fixed, the slope-deflection equations give:**

> **M_AB = (4EI/L)θ  and  M_BA = (2EI/L)θ**

> **The carry-over factor is 1/2** — half the applied moment appears at the far end.

> **Now release the far end (make B a hinge).** B can no longer carry a moment, so **M_BA must be released to zero.** Releasing it carries half of it back to A:

> **Carry-back to A = ½ × (2EI/L)θ = (EI/L)θ, and it OPPOSES the applied moment.**

> **So the net moment needed at A is  4EI/L − EI/L = 3EI/L.** ✓

> **That is why the factor is exactly 3/4, and it also explains the second key fact: for a member hinged at the far end, the CARRY-OVER FACTOR IS ZERO.** There is nowhere for a moment to be carried to.

**The distribution factor consequence, which is where this is actually used:**

> **DF for a member at a joint = (its stiffness) / (sum of stiffnesses of all members at that joint)**, and ΣDF at any joint = 1.

> **Using the MODIFIED stiffness 3EI/L for a member hinged at its far end is the standard shortcut in moment distribution**: the hinged member then needs no further balancing, because no moment carries to it.

| Approach | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Use 4EI/L and distribute the far-end moment each cycle** | Correct, but wastes cycles |
| **Use 3EI/L once, with zero carry-over** | **Correct and finishes the hinge in one step — the standard method** ← |

> **The relative stiffness form is often used instead**, dividing by 4EI/L throughout:

| Far end | Relative stiffness |
|---|---|
| **Fixed** | **1** |
| **Hinged** | **3/4** |
| Guided roller | 1/4 |
| Free | 0 |

> **The source's own note gives exactly these: relative stiffness 1 if fixed, 3/4 if hinged.**

**Why each distractor is a real value, wrongly placed:**

| Option | Whose value it is |
|---|---|
| **0** | **FREE far end — and also the DF of a hinge joint itself** ← |
| **EI/L** | **Guided roller far end** |
| **3EI/L** | ✓ **Hinged far end** |
| **4EI/L** | **FIXED far end — the value everyone learns first** ← the trap |

> **Option (d) is the designed trap** because 4EI/L is the stiffness a candidate meets first and remembers best. **The question deliberately asks for the modified value.**

> **Option (a) zero is worth a second look**, because it is the correct answer to a neighbouring question: **the stiffness of a member whose far end is FREE is zero**, there being nothing to rotate against.

> **It is also, separately, the DISTRIBUTION FACTOR of a member framing into a FIXED support** - the support is infinitely stiff, so it absorbs the whole moment and the member gets none of it.

**A caution on distribution factors at supports, because the circulating notes state this badly:**

| Support at the joint | Distribution factor of the member there |
|---|---|
| **FIXED support** | **0** - the support is infinitely stiff and takes everything |
| **HINGED or ROLLER END support** | **1** - the support takes no moment, so the member takes all of it |

> **Those two are the standard convention and they are the way round shown here.** Some circulating solutions assert instead that "the distribution factor of a hinge joint is always zero", which is misleading: **it is true of a member running into a fixed support and false of a member at a hinged END support, where the factor is 1.**

> **The underlying rule settles it without memorising either case: DF = (member stiffness) / (sum of stiffnesses at the joint).** A fixed support contributes infinite stiffness to that sum, driving the member fraction to zero; **a hinged end support contributes none, leaving the member as the only term and its fraction equal to one.**

> **So the two facts to keep apart are: stiffness of a member HINGED AT ITS FAR END is 3EI/L, and DF of a member AT a hinged end support is 1.** Both concern hinges and they answer different questions.

**The related quantities, since they are asked together:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **Stiffness, far end fixed** | **4EI/L** |
| **Stiffness, far end hinged** | **3EI/L** |
| **CARRY-OVER factor, far end fixed** | **+1/2** |
| **Carry-over factor, far end hinged** | **0** |
| **FEM, udl, both ends fixed** | **wL²/12** |
| **FEM, udl, one end hinged** | **wL²/8 at the fixed end** |
| **FEM, central point load, both fixed** | **WL/8** |

> **Notice the pattern in the fixed-end moments: releasing one end RAISES the moment at the other from wL²/12 to wL²/8** — a 50 per cent increase, since the released end's moment has to go somewhere. **The same logic that gives 3EI/L gives these.**

examTip.trick: **The sequence is 4 : 3 : 1 : 0 in units of EI/L** for far end fixed, hinged, guided roller, free. Stiffness = moment for unit rotation at the joint.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) 4EI/L is the FIXED value, the one learned first.** And option (a) zero is the stiffness for a FREE far end - and separately the distribution factor of a member running into a FIXED support.
examTip.mnemonic: **Releasing the far end carries back half of 2EI/L, opposing the applied moment: 4 - 1 = 3.** Hence also **carry-over to a hinged far end is ZERO.** Keep DF straight from the rule DF = member stiffness / joint stiffness: **fixed support DF = 0, hinged END support DF = 1.**

questions.stem: Which of the following cannot be obtained by using an un-drained test?
questions.solution:
**The effective stress failure envelope.**

**Why an undrained test cannot give the effective stress envelope:**

> **An EFFECTIVE STRESS envelope requires the effective stresses at failure to be known**, which means the PORE PRESSURE at failure must be known: **σ′ = σ − u.**

> **In an unconsolidated undrained (UU) test on a SATURATED specimen, no drainage is permitted at either stage — so the pore pressure adjusts itself to whatever the confining pressure demands.**

> **The consequence is the striking result: raising the cell pressure raises the pore pressure by the SAME amount, so the EFFECTIVE stress is unchanged.**

> **Every specimen therefore fails at the SAME effective stress, and every Mohr circle in effective-stress terms is THE SAME CIRCLE.**

> **One circle cannot define an envelope.** An envelope is a line tangent to a family of circles, and here the family has only one member. **That is the source's own reasoning: "since only one Mohr circle in terms of effective stresses is obtained from all un-drained tests, an effective stress failure envelope cannot be obtained."**

**What the UU test DOES give:**

> **In TOTAL stress terms the circles are different — each specimen was tested at a different cell pressure — and the envelope is HORIZONTAL:**

> **φ_u = 0,  and  τ = c_u**

> **This is the famous "φ = 0 analysis" for saturated clay, and c_u (the undrained cohesion) is exactly what the UU test is for.**

| Test | Envelope obtained |
|---|---|
| **UU on saturated clay** | **TOTAL stress: φ_u = 0, c = c_u** |
| **CU without pore pressure measurement** | **Total stress: c_cu, φ_cu** |
| **CU WITH pore pressure measurement** | **EFFECTIVE stress: c′, φ′** ← the practical route |
| **CD (drained)** | **EFFECTIVE stress: c′, φ′ directly** |

> **Note row three carefully: a CONSOLIDATED undrained test WITH pore pressure measurement DOES give effective parameters**, because the pore pressure is measured rather than unknown, and the specimens were consolidated to different effective stresses before shearing.

> **So the impossibility in this question belongs specifically to the UNCONSOLIDATED undrained test on a saturated soil**, where the specimens all start at the same effective stress. **The consolidation stage is what spreads them out.**

**Why options (b) and (c) ARE obtainable:**

> **SHEAR STRENGTH (b) — obtainable, and it is the test's whole purpose.** The undrained shear strength c_u = q_u/2 in an unconfined test, or the radius of the total-stress Mohr circle in a UU triaxial test.

> **SENSITIVITY (c) — obtainable, and it is defined entirely in terms of undrained strengths:**

> **Sensitivity S_t = (undrained strength UNDISTURBED) / (undrained strength REMOULDED at the same water content)**

| Sensitivity | Classification |
|---|---|
| **~1** | **Insensitive** |
| **1 - 4** | **Normal / low sensitivity** |
| **4 - 8** | **Sensitive** |
| **8 - 16** | **Extra sensitive** |
| **> 16** | **QUICK CLAY — loses nearly all strength on remoulding** |

> **Sensitivity measures how much strength a clay loses when its structure is destroyed**, and both numerator and denominator come from undrained tests. **So option (c) is not merely obtainable from an undrained test — it can be obtained from nothing else.**

> **QUICK CLAYS are the dramatic case: a sensitivity above 16 means the remoulded clay is almost a liquid.** They cause flow slides in which a whole hillside liquefies and runs — the Scandinavian and Canadian landslide mechanism. **The relevance is that any disturbance during sampling or construction destroys strength that cannot be recovered.**

**And the companion concept, THIXOTROPY, since it is often confused with sensitivity:**

> **A remoulded clay left undisturbed at constant water content REGAINS part of its strength over time.** That is thixotropy.

> **Sensitivity is the strength LOST on remoulding; thixotropy is the part of it RECOVERED with rest.**

> **The practical consequence is real: a driven pile in soft clay carries much more load a month after driving than the day after**, because the clay remoulded by driving recovers thixotropically and reconsolidates. **This "set-up" or "freeze" is why pile tests are not done immediately after driving.**

**Why option (d) is wrong:** it requires all three to be unobtainable, and two of them plainly are obtainable. **A candidate uncertain about (a) may reach for (d), but any one clear case defeats it — and shear strength being obtainable from a shear test is as clear as it gets.**

examTip.trick: **In a saturated UU test, raising the cell pressure raises the pore pressure equally — so the EFFECTIVE stress never changes and every specimen gives the SAME effective-stress Mohr circle.** One circle cannot define an envelope.
examTip.trap: **A CU test WITH pore pressure measurement DOES give c′ and φ′** — the consolidation stage spreads the specimens to different effective stresses. The impossibility belongs specifically to the UNCONSOLIDATED undrained test.
examTip.mnemonic: **Sensitivity is defined entirely from undrained strengths** (undisturbed ÷ remoulded), so it is obtainable from nothing else. Above 16 is QUICK CLAY. And **thixotropy is the part of that lost strength recovered with rest** — why driven piles gain capacity for weeks.

questions.stem: In geotechnical engineering, a vane shear test is typically conducted to determine the shear strength of which of the following soil types?
questions.solution:
**Soft clays.**

**How the test works:**

> **A four-bladed vane on a rod is pushed into the soil and rotated at a slow constant rate (about 0.1° per second) until the soil fails on a cylindrical surface.** The torque at failure gives the strength:

> **c_u = T / [π D²(H/2 + D/6)]**  for a vane shearing on both ends

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **T** | **Torque at failure** |
| **D** | Vane diameter |
| **H** | **Vane height (usually H = 2D)** |

> **The term H/2 accounts for the cylindrical side surface and D/6 for the two circular ends** — so the formula is simply the sum of the resisting moments of the three surfaces.

**Why it works only in SOFT COHESIVE soil:**

> **The vane must be PUSHED IN without excessive disturbance and must then shear the soil on a clean cylindrical surface.**

| Soil | Why the test fails |
|---|---|
| **SOFT CLAY** | ✓ **Vane penetrates easily; failure surface is clean; the undrained condition is genuine** |
| **Stiff clay** | **The vane may not penetrate, and may crack rather than shear the soil** |
| **Coarse SAND, SHINGLE, GRAVEL** | **The vane cannot be pushed in at all; and any shearing would be DRAINED, so no undrained strength exists to measure** ← |

> **Options (b), (c) and (d) are all coarse-grained and fail for the same two reasons — the vane cannot penetrate, and their high permeability means shear is drained, so "undrained shear strength" is not a property they have.**

> **That single observation disposes of three options at once**, which is worth noticing: the question is really asking whether the candidate understands that undrained strength is a concept for fine-grained soil.

**Why the test is valuable — the case for it:**

> **It measures the strength IN SITU, on soil that has not been sampled, transported or trimmed.**

> **Soft and very soft clays are exactly the soils most damaged by sampling.** A soft clay pushed into a tube, carried to a laboratory and extruded has lost part of the strength it had in the ground.

> **So for a soft clay the vane test may be MORE RELIABLE than a laboratory test on a "good" sample**, and it is the reference method for soft-clay strength profiles.

> **It is also quick**: a full strength-depth profile can be taken through a soft deposit in a day.

**The correction that must be applied, and it is substantial:**

> **The vane test OVERESTIMATES the strength relevant to design**, and the correction is not small.

> **c_u(design) = μ × c_u(vane)**, with Bjerrum's correction factor μ depending on the plasticity index:

| Plasticity index | μ |
|---|---|
| **20** | **~1.0** |
| **40** | **~0.85** |
| **60** | **~0.75** |
| **100** | **~0.6** |

> **The reason for the correction is a combination of the fast shearing rate (the standard rate is still far faster than a real embankment loads the ground) and anisotropy (the vane shears mostly on a vertical surface, while a foundation failure is largely horizontal).**

> **Highly plastic clays need the largest correction** — up to a 40 per cent reduction. **Using an uncorrected vane strength for a highly plastic clay is unsafe**, and the discovery that this was happening came from back-analysing embankment failures that the uncorrected strengths said should have been stable.

**The related in-situ tests, and which soil each suits:**

| Test | Suits | Gives |
|---|---|---|
| **VANE SHEAR** | **SOFT CLAY** | **c_u in situ, plus SENSITIVITY (rotate to remould, retest)** ← |
| **SPT (standard penetration)** | **SAND, and stiff soils** | N value → φ, relative density |
| **CPT (cone penetration)** | **Any soil; continuous profile** | Tip resistance and sleeve friction |
| **Pressuremeter** | Any | Stress-strain and modulus |
| **Plate load** | Any at foundation level | Bearing capacity, settlement |

> **A useful pairing to hold: SPT for sand, VANE for soft clay.** They are complementary, and neither works in the other's ground.

> **And a valuable extra from the vane: after the peak, continue rotating rapidly through several revolutions to REMOULD the soil, then retest.** The ratio of the two readings is the **SENSITIVITY**, measured in situ — which no laboratory test on a disturbed sample can give as directly.

examTip.trick: **Coarse sand, shingle and gravel all fail for the SAME two reasons** — the vane cannot be pushed in, and shearing them would be DRAINED, so they have no undrained strength to measure. One observation kills three options.
examTip.trap: **The vane OVERESTIMATES design strength** — apply Bjerrum's μ, which falls to about 0.6 for a plasticity index of 100. Using an uncorrected vane strength in highly plastic clay is unsafe, as back-analysed embankment failures showed.
examTip.mnemonic: **SPT for sand, VANE for soft clay** — complementary, neither works in the other's ground. And the vane's bonus: rotate rapidly to remould, retest, and the ratio gives **SENSITIVITY measured in situ.**

questions.stem: The ratio of the maximum deflection due to a udl throughout the span for a fixed beam and a simply supported beam of similar dimensions is:
questions.solution:
**1 : 5.**

**The two standard deflections:**

> **Simply supported beam, udl w over span L:**

> **Δ_SSB = 5wL⁴ / (384 EI)**

> **Fixed (both ends) beam, same udl and span:**

> **Δ_fixed = wL⁴ / (384 EI)**

> **The ratio:**

> **Δ_fixed / Δ_SSB = [wL⁴/384EI] ÷ [5wL⁴/384EI] = 1/5** ✓

> **The denominators are the same 384EI in both**, so the entire ratio is the numerator: **1 against 5.** That is why this pair is so convenient to remember.

**Reading the question in the right order — which is where marks are lost:**

> **The stem asks for "fixed beam AND simply supported beam", in that order.**

> **So the ratio is Δ_fixed : Δ_SSB = 1 : 5**, not 5 : 1.

> **Option (d) 5:1 is the same numbers reversed, and it is the designed trap.** The physics is unambiguous — **a fixed beam is STIFFER, so its deflection must be SMALLER, so the first number must be the smaller one.**

> **That sanity check settles the direction without any recall: more restraint, less deflection.**

**Why exactly five — the physical reason, which makes the number memorable:**

> **Fixing the ends applies a HOGGING moment at each support that opposes the sagging caused by the load.**

| Beam | Support moment | Mid-span moment |
|---|---|---|
| **Simply supported** | **0** | **wL²/8** |
| **FIXED** | **wL²/12 (hogging)** | **wL²/24 (sagging)** |

> **Notice that fixing reduces the maximum moment only from wL²/8 to wL²/12 — a factor of 1.5 — but reduces the DEFLECTION by a factor of 5.**

> **The restraint is far more effective against deflection than against moment**, because deflection depends on the moment distributed over the whole span (a double integration), not merely on its peak value. **Fixing flattens the whole curvature diagram, not just its maximum.**

> **This is the general and useful lesson: END RESTRAINT buys much more stiffness than strength.**

**The full family, since any pair may be asked:**

| Beam, udl w | Max deflection | Relative to SSB |
|---|---|---|
| **Cantilever** | **wL⁴/8EI = 48wL⁴/384EI** | **9.6 ×** |
| **Simply supported** | **5wL⁴/384EI** | **1.0** |
| **Propped cantilever** | **wL⁴/185EI ≈ 2.08wL⁴/384EI** | **0.42 ×** |
| **FIXED both ends** | **wL⁴/384EI** | **0.2 ×** |

> **The sequence 48 : 5 : 2.08 : 1 (in units of wL⁴/384EI) shows the whole effect of restraint on a udl-loaded beam** — from a cantilever to a fixed beam is a factor of 48.

> **And for a CENTRAL POINT LOAD the corresponding pair is Δ_SSB = WL³/48EI and Δ_fixed = WL³/192EI, again a ratio of 1 : 4.**

> **Note that the ratio is 1:5 for a udl but 1:4 for a point load** — the two are different, and assuming one applies to the other is a genuine error.

**Why deflection matters as much as strength — the serviceability point:**

> **IS 456 limits deflection by span-to-depth ratio rather than by calculation for ordinary cases:**

| Support condition | Basic span/depth |
|---|---|
| **Cantilever** | **7** |
| **Simply supported** | **20** |
| **Continuous** | **26** |

> **Notice that the code's ratios reflect exactly the stiffness sequence above**: a continuous (partly restrained) beam is allowed to be more slender than a simply supported one, and a cantilever much less.

> **The absolute limits are span/250 for total deflection, and span/350 or 20 mm (whichever is less) for the deflection after partition construction** — the second being the one that cracks masonry and jams doors, which is usually what a building owner actually complains about.

> **So the 1:5 ratio is not an arithmetic curiosity: it is why continuity is worth building in.** A continuous slab can be thinner than a series of simply supported ones spanning the same distances, and the saving is in every floor of the building.

examTip.trick: **Both have 384EI in the denominator: Δ_SSB = 5wL⁴/384EI, Δ_fixed = wL⁴/384EI.** So the ratio is just the numerators — 1 : 5.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) 5:1 is the reversal, and the stem's order ("fixed and simply supported") decides it.** Sanity check without recall: a fixed beam is STIFFER, so its deflection is SMALLER, so the first number is the smaller.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fixing cuts the moment by only 1.5× (wL²/8 → wL²/12) but the deflection by 5×** — restraint buys far more stiffness than strength. And the point-load ratio is **1:4, not 1:5.**

questions.stem: What is the full form of BES?
questions.solution:
**Brief Environmental Study.**

**Where BES sits in Nepal's environmental assessment framework:**

> **Nepal's Environment Protection Act 2076 (2019) and Environment Protection Rules 2077 (2020) introduced a THREE-TIER system**, replacing the earlier two-tier arrangement:

| Tier | Scope | Approved by |
|---|---|---|
| **BES — Brief Environmental Study** | **The SMALLEST projects — a short screening-level study** | **The concerned body / local level** |
| **IEE — Initial Environmental Examination** | **Medium projects** | **The concerned ministry** |
| **EIA — Environmental Impact Assessment** | **The LARGEST or most sensitive projects — the fullest study** | **Ministry of Forests and Environment** |

> **BES is the newest of the three and the addition made by the 2076 Act.** Before it, small projects either needed a full IEE or nothing at all — **so BES fills a real gap: a proportionate assessment for a small project.**

> **The principle is PROPORTIONALITY: the depth of the assessment should match the scale of the likely impact.** Requiring a full EIA of a village water supply wastes everyone's effort; requiring nothing of it is negligent.

**What distinguishes the three in practice:**

| Feature | **BES** | **IEE** | **EIA** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Scoping document and terms of reference** | Not required | **Not required** | **REQUIRED, and approved before the study** |
| **PUBLIC HEARING** | Not required | **Not required** | **REQUIRED** |
| **Public notice** | Limited | Required | **Required, in a national daily** |
| **Alternatives analysis** | Minimal | Limited | **Full** |
| **Duration and cost** | **Weeks** | Months | **Many months to years** |

> **The public hearing requirement is the most consequential difference.** An EIA must be presented to the affected community and their views recorded; **an IEE or BES need not be.**

> **Which is why the SCHEDULE that decides a project's tier matters so much politically as well as technically** — the tier determines whether the affected people get a formal say.

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Brief Environmental Study** | ✓ |
| **British Environmental study** | **"British" has no place in Nepali environmental law** ← |
| **British Engineering study** | Likewise |
| **None** | — |

> **Options (b) and (c) are eliminated by a single observation: this is a term from NEPALI legislation, so "British" cannot be right.** That is worth noting as a technique — **an acronym question can often be answered by asking which words could plausibly appear in the relevant statute.**

> **The real discrimination is between BES, IEE and EIA**, and a better-set question would have offered those. **As printed, the question is answerable by elimination alone.**

**The EIA process, since it is the tier that carries the syllabus content:**

| Stage | Note |
|---|---|
| **SCREENING** | **Which tier applies? Decided from the Rules' schedules by project type and size** |
| **SCOPING** | **What issues must the study cover? Produces the Terms of Reference** |
| **ToR approval** | By the ministry, before the study begins |
| **Baseline study** | **Physical, biological, socio-economic and cultural environment** |
| **IMPACT PREDICTION** | **By MAGNITUDE, EXTENT and DURATION** |
| **MITIGATION** | **Avoid → minimise → mitigate → COMPENSATE, in that order of preference** |
| **EMP — Environmental Management Plan** | Mitigation, monitoring, institutional arrangements, cost |
| **Public hearing and report submission** | — |
| **Review and approval** | — |
| **MONITORING and AUDITING** | **Compliance, impact and audit after two years of operation** |

> **The mitigation hierarchy is the single most useful idea in the whole topic: AVOID the impact if you can, MINIMISE it if you cannot avoid it, MITIGATE what remains, and COMPENSATE only for what is left.**

> **Compensation is last for a reason — it is an admission that the impact will happen.** A design change that avoids a wetland is worth more than any payment for destroying it, and an assessment that jumps straight to compensation has skipped the part where engineering can help.

> **And the monitoring stage is the one most often neglected in practice.** An EIA that is approved and then filed has cost money and protected nothing; **the commitments in the EMP are only worth what the monitoring enforces.**

examTip.trick: **Three tiers under the Environment Protection Act 2076: BES (smallest) → IEE (medium) → EIA (largest).** BES is the tier the 2076 Act added, filling the gap below IEE.
examTip.trap: **Options (b) and (c) say "British" — impossible in Nepali legislation.** An acronym question can often be answered by asking which words could plausibly appear in the relevant statute.
examTip.mnemonic: **Only an EIA requires SCOPING, a ToR and a PUBLIC HEARING** — so the tier decides whether affected people get a formal say. And the mitigation hierarchy: **AVOID → MINIMISE → MITIGATE → COMPENSATE**, compensation last.

questions.stem: An overhanging beam carries a uniformly distributed load of 10 kN/m over its whole length of 6 m. It is supported by a pin at the left-hand end and by a roller 4 m from that end, leaving a 2 m overhang. Calculate the maximum negative bending moment.
questions.solution:
**20 kNm.**

**Where the maximum negative moment occurs — and why no reactions are needed:**

> **The maximum NEGATIVE (hogging) moment in an overhanging beam occurs AT THE SUPPORT that has the overhang beyond it** — here the roller at 4 m.

> **To find it, take moments of the OVERHANG ALONE**, working from the free end inward. **Nothing to the left of the roller enters the calculation, so the reactions never have to be computed.**

**The calculation:**

> **The overhang is 2 m long, carrying 10 kN/m.**

> **Load on the overhang = 10 × 2 = 20 kN, acting at its centroid, 1 m from the roller.**

> **M = w x² / 2 = 10 × 2² / 2 = 10 × 4 / 2 = 20 kNm** ✓

> **Or equivalently: 20 kN × 1 m = 20 kNm.** The two routes are the same arithmetic.

> **The moment is HOGGING (negative) because the overhang's load bends the beam concave DOWNWARD at the support** — the top fibres are in tension there.

**Why the shear force changes sign at the roller, which is the source's own observation:**

> **The maximum moment on any span occurs where the shear force is zero or changes sign, since dM/dx = V.**

> **At a support with an overhang, the shear jumps by the amount of the reaction, and here it changes sign at the roller** — which locates the hogging maximum without any search.

> **A well-set problem of this type therefore has TWO candidate maxima:**

| Location | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **At the roller** | **NEGATIVE (hogging)** | **wx²/2 = 20 kNm** ← asked |
| **Somewhere in the 4 m span** | **POSITIVE (sagging)** | Where the span shear crosses zero |

> **Let us compute the sagging maximum too, since it confirms the picture.** Taking moments about the roller for the whole beam:

> **Total load = 10 × 6 = 60 kN at 3 m from the left end.**

> **R_A × 4 = 60 × (4 − 3) ... ** more directly, ΣM about the roller: **R_A × 4 = 10 × 6 × (3 − 0) − ...**

> **Cleanest route — ΣM about A: R_B × 4 = 60 × 3 = 180, so R_B = 45 kN, and R_A = 60 − 45 = 15 kN.**

> **Shear in the span: V(x) = 15 − 10x, which is zero at x = 1.5 m.**

> **M_sagging = 15 × 1.5 − 10 × 1.5²/2 = 22.5 − 11.25 = 11.25 kNm.**

| Moment | Value |
|---|---|
| **Maximum HOGGING, at the roller** | **20 kNm** ← the answer |
| **Maximum SAGGING, at 1.5 m from A** | **11.25 kNm** |

> **So the hogging moment is the LARGER of the two here**, which is typical of a beam with a substantial overhang and is the reason such beams are reinforced at the TOP over the support.

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| **10 kNm** | **Half the answer — using wx²/4, or forgetting the factor** |
| **20 kNm** | ✓ |
| **30 kNm** | — |
| **40 kNm** | **wx² = 10 × 4 = 40 — the /2 omitted entirely** ← the trap |

> **Option (d) is the designed trap: it is exactly wx² without the division by two.** The factor of 2 comes from the load resultant acting at the MIDPOINT of the overhang, and dropping it is the standard slip.

> **Note also the printed unit of option (d): "40 kN" rather than kNm.** A bending moment is never in kN. **That alone rules it out, and it is worth checking the units of the options before computing anything.**

**The design consequence — where the steel goes:**

> **NEGATIVE (hogging) moment means TENSION AT THE TOP**, so the main reinforcement over the support must be in the TOP of the section, and it must extend far enough into the span to cover the point of contraflexure.

> **The POINT OF CONTRAFLEXURE is where the bending moment passes through zero**, and it is the point at which the tension steel must change from top to bottom.

> **In this beam, setting the span moment expression to zero: 15x − 5x² = 0 gives x = 0 and x = 3 m.** So the moment is sagging from A to 3 m and hogging from 3 m to the roller and out along the overhang.

> **Top steel is therefore needed from 3 m onward, plus the development length beyond that point.**

> **Getting the top steel wrong — or stopping it too soon — is one of the commonest and most dangerous detailing errors in cantilever and overhanging construction**, because the failure is brittle and gives no warning. **A cantilever balcony with its main steel placed at the bottom collapses the first time it is loaded.**

verification.notes: Figure-dependent question rewritten in text. The source stem read only "Calculate the maximum negative BM in given overhang beam" and referred to a figure the scanned question pages omit. The figure appears on the source's own answer page and shows a 10 kN/m udl over a 6 m beam with a pin at the left end, a roller 4 m along and a 2 m overhang; the source's working (wx2/2 = 10 x 4/2 = 20 kNm at the roller, where the shear changes sign) confirms both the geometry and the keyed answer (b). Options and answer are unchanged, except that option (d)'s printed unit "40 kN" is retained as "40 kNm" for consistency of the option list.

examTip.trick: **The maximum hogging moment is at the support with the overhang, and it comes from the OVERHANG ALONE: M = wx²/2 = 10 × 4/2 = 20 kNm.** The reactions never need computing.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) 40 kNm is wx² with the /2 dropped** — the factor comes from the load resultant acting at the overhang's midpoint. Note also that the source printed it as "40 kN": a bending moment is never in kN.
examTip.mnemonic: **Hogging means TENSION AT THE TOP**, so top steel over the support must extend past the POINT OF CONTRAFLEXURE (here x = 3 m) plus development length. Stopping it too soon fails brittly, with no warning.

questions.stem: In a closed traverse the sum of the latitudes is +0.42 m and the sum of the departures is −0.56 m. The closing error is:
questions.solution:
**0.70 m.**

**The closing error is the resultant of the two misclosures:**

> **In a CLOSED traverse the survey returns to its starting point, so in a perfect survey:**

> **ΣLatitudes = 0  and  ΣDepartures = 0**

> **Any non-zero sums are the misclosure, and the CLOSING ERROR is their vector resultant:**

> **e = √[(ΣL)² + (ΣD)²]**

> **e = √[(0.42)² + (−0.56)²] = √[0.1764 + 0.3136] = √0.49 = 0.70 m** ✓

> **Note the sign of the departure is irrelevant — it is squared.** What the signs give is the DIRECTION of the error, not its size.

**Recognise the triangle and the arithmetic is instant:**

> **0.42 and 0.56 are 0.14 × 3 and 0.14 × 4.**

> **So this is a 3-4-5 triangle scaled by 0.14, and the hypotenuse is 0.14 × 5 = 0.70 m.**

> **Spotting a Pythagorean triple saves the whole calculation**, and examiners choose such numbers precisely because they are clean — which makes the triple a useful thing to look for.

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

| Option | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| **0.14 m** | **The DIFFERENCE 0.56 − 0.42 — subtracting instead of combining as vectors** |
| **0.49 m** | **The SUM OF SQUARES, with the square root forgotten** ← the trap |
| **0.98 m** | **The arithmetic sum 0.42 + 0.56 — adding two perpendicular components directly** |
| **0.70 m** | ✓ |

> **Option (b) 0.49 is the designed trap: it is the value under the root sign.** Anyone who computes 0.1764 + 0.3136 and stops has done all the work and thrown the answer away. **Option (c) is the other classic — adding perpendicular components as if they were collinear.**

**The direction of the closing error, since it is asked alongside:**

> **tan θ = ΣD / ΣL = −0.56 / +0.42 = −1.333, so θ = 53°08′.**

> **With ΣL positive and ΣD negative the error lies in the NORTH-WEST quadrant**, so the bearing of the closing error is **N 53°08′ W** — or equivalently 306°52′.

> **The CORRECTION is applied in the opposite direction to the error**, which is the point of computing the bearing.

**The relative accuracy, which is how a traverse is judged:**

> **Relative precision = closing error / total perimeter of the traverse**, expressed as 1 in N.

| Class of survey | Acceptable relative precision |
|---|---|
| **Rough / reconnaissance** | **1 in 300 to 1 in 600** |
| **Ordinary chain or compass traverse** | **1 in 1000** |
| **Theodolite traverse, ordinary work** | **1 in 3000 to 1 in 5000** |
| **Precise traverse** | **1 in 10,000 or better** |

> **A 0.70 m error is acceptable on a 3 km traverse (1 in 4300) and disgraceful on a 300 m one (1 in 430).** So the closing error alone means nothing — **it must always be quoted against the traverse length**, and a question that gives only the error is testing the arithmetic, not the judgement.

**The two methods of adjusting the traverse, since the error must then be distributed:**

| Method | Distributes the error in proportion to | Assumes |
|---|---|---|
| **BOWDITCH (compass) rule** | **The LENGTH of each line** | **Angles and lengths are of EQUAL precision — as in a compass traverse** |
| **TRANSIT rule** | **The LATITUDE and DEPARTURE of each line** | **ANGLES are more precise than lengths — as in a theodolite traverse** |

> **The choice follows from the instrument.** A theodolite measures angles far more accurately than a tape or stadia measures distance, **so the error is presumed to lie in the lengths and the transit rule is used.** A compass measures both roughly, so Bowditch applies.

> **Bowditch's correction to any latitude = total ΣL × (length of that line / perimeter)**, and similarly for departures — which is the version most often examined.

> **And the check afterwards: after adjustment, ΣL and ΣD must both be exactly zero.** If they are not, the distribution was arithmetically wrong, and that check costs nothing.

examTip.trick: **e = √[(ΣL)² + (ΣD)²] = √(0.1764 + 0.3136) = √0.49 = 0.70 m.** And spot the triple: 0.42 and 0.56 are 3 and 4 units of 0.14, so the answer is 5 × 0.14 = 0.70.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) 0.49 is the value UNDER the root** — all the work done, the answer thrown away. Option (c) 0.98 adds two perpendicular components as if collinear.
examTip.mnemonic: **A closing error means nothing without the traverse length** — 0.70 m is fine over 3 km (1 in 4300) and disgraceful over 300 m. Then adjust by **BOWDITCH** (compass: angles and lengths equally precise) or **TRANSIT** (theodolite: angles better).

questions.stem: A damp proof course (DPC) in a load-bearing masonry wall is provided:
options: at the top of the plinth beam only, to protect the floor finish
immediately below ground level, so that it is protected from damage
at plinth level, at least 150 mm above the finished ground level
at the top of the foundation footing, below all the masonry
questions.solution:
**At plinth level, at least 150 mm above the finished ground level.**

**Why that particular position — it must interrupt a path:**

> **A DPC is a CONTINUOUS IMPERVIOUS BARRIER whose only job is to break the capillary path by which ground moisture rises through the masonry.**

> **Moisture rises by CAPILLARY ACTION through the fine pores of bricks and mortar — a phenomenon known as RISING DAMP.** It can climb a metre or more in porous brickwork.

> **To stop it, the barrier must lie ABOVE the highest level at which water can reach the wall from outside.**

| Requirement | Reason |
|---|---|
| **ABOVE finished ground level** | **Below it, splash and surface water would wet the wall ABOVE the barrier and defeat it** |
| **At least 150 mm above** | **Clear of RAIN SPLASH off the ground and of any shallow ponding** |
| **CONTINUOUS, and linked to the floor DPC** | **A gap of a single brick is a bypass — the damp simply goes round it** |
| **Turned up at door openings and junctions** | So the path is broken everywhere, not just in the plain wall |

> **The continuity requirement is what makes DPC work difficult on site rather than merely a material to be laid.** A DPC broken at one pilaster, or not lapped into the floor membrane, protects nothing along that line — **and the resulting damp patch appears in one place, which makes it look like a local defect rather than a design failure.**

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Why not |
|---|---|
| **Top of plinth beam only, for the floor finish** | **Too narrow a purpose.** A DPC protects the WALL from rising damp; protecting the floor finish is incidental |
| **Immediately BELOW ground level** | **Self-defeating — moisture and splash reach the wall above the barrier and rise from there** ← the substantive error |
| **At plinth level, ≥ 150 mm above ground** | ✓ |
| **At the top of the footing, below all masonry** | **Far too low.** The masonry between the footing and the ground would wick moisture, and the barrier would be bypassed entirely |

> **Option (b) is the instructive wrong answer** because it sounds protective — putting the membrane where it cannot be damaged. **But a DPC does not need protecting; it needs to be in the right place.** Burying it below ground puts it below the water it is meant to exclude.

**The materials used, since the choice affects the detail:**

| Material | Note |
|---|---|
| **Cement concrete, 1:1½:3, 40-75 mm thick, with a waterproofing compound** | **The commonest in Nepal and India — placed as a course of the wall** |
| **Rich cement mortar 1:2 with waterproofer** | Thin sections |
| **Bitumen felt / mastic asphalt** | **FLEXIBLE — accommodates slight settlement without cracking** |
| **Polythene / HDPE sheet** | Cheap and effective; must be lapped generously |
| **Metal sheet (lead, copper)** | Durable and expensive; used in restoration |
| Dense engineering brick in cement mortar | Two or three courses; traditional |

> **The rigid-versus-flexible choice matters.** A concrete DPC is rigid and CRACKS if the wall settles differentially — **and a cracked DPC is no DPC at all**, since capillary water needs only a hairline path.

> **So where settlement is expected, a flexible membrane is right**; where the ground is sound, a concrete course is simpler and is integral with the wall.

**What happens when it is omitted or bridged, which is why the topic matters:**

| Symptom | Note |
|---|---|
| **A horizontal TIDE MARK on the wall, about 0.5-1 m up** | **The classic signature of rising damp — the height at which evaporation balances capillary rise** |
| **EFFLORESCENCE — white salt deposits** | **Salts carried up in solution and left behind as the water evaporates** |
| **Plaster and paint failure, blistering** | Immediately above the tide mark |
| **Timber decay** | Skirtings, joist ends, door frames |
| **Persistent damp smell and mould** | A health matter, not only a building one |

> **The tide mark is diagnostic and worth being able to read**: rising damp produces a roughly LEVEL line, because it is governed by the balance between capillary rise and evaporation. **Damp from a leaking pipe or a defective roof does not — it makes a patch or a run.**

> **So the shape of a damp patch tells you where to look, and a level line low on a ground-floor wall points at the DPC and nowhere else.**

**The related barriers, for completeness:**

| Barrier | Position and purpose |
|---|---|
| **DPC (horizontal)** | **In the wall at plinth level — stops RISING damp** ← |
| **Vertical DPC** | **On the earth face of a basement or retaining wall — stops LATERAL penetration** |
| **Floor DPC / membrane** | **Under the floor slab — must LAP with the wall DPC** |
| **Cavity wall** | **An air gap breaks the path without a membrane** |
| **Plinth protection / apron** | Sheds rainwater away from the wall base |

> **The lap between the floor membrane and the wall DPC is the junction most often missed**, and it is the one that determines whether the two barriers act as one continuous envelope or as two separate and bypassable pieces.

examTip.trick: **The barrier must lie ABOVE the highest level water can reach the wall from outside** — hence at plinth level, at least 150 mm clear of finished ground to escape rain splash.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) "below ground level, protected from damage" sounds sensible and is self-defeating** — it puts the membrane below the water it is meant to exclude. A DPC does not need protecting; it needs to be in the right place.
examTip.mnemonic: **A level TIDE MARK 0.5-1 m up a wall, with efflorescence, is rising damp** — the height where capillary rise balances evaporation. A leak makes a patch or a run, not a level line. And the wall DPC must LAP the floor membrane.

questions.stem: A flow net is drawn for seepage beneath a sheet pile wall. The flow net has 5 flow channels and 12 equipotential drops, and the coefficient of permeability is 4 × 10⁻⁵ m/s. If the total head loss is 6 m, the seepage discharge per metre run of wall is:
questions.solution:
**1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³/s per metre run.**

**The flow net discharge formula:**

> **q = k H (N_f / N_d)**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **k** | **Coefficient of permeability** | **4 × 10⁻⁵ m/s** |
| **H** | **TOTAL head loss across the flow net** | **6 m** |
| **N_f** | **Number of FLOW CHANNELS (spaces between flow lines)** | **5** |
| **N_d** | **Number of EQUIPOTENTIAL DROPS (spaces between equipotential lines)** | **12** |

**The calculation:**

> **q = 4 × 10⁻⁵ × 6 × (5/12)**

> **= 4 × 10⁻⁵ × 6 × 0.41667**

> **= 4 × 10⁻⁵ × 2.5**

> **= 10 × 10⁻⁵ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³/s per metre run** ✓

> **The arithmetic is clean because 6 × 5/12 = 2.5 exactly** — worth doing the fraction first, before touching the permeability.

**Why it is CHANNELS and DROPS, not lines — and this is where most errors arise:**

> **N_f and N_d count the SPACES, not the LINES.**

> **Six flow lines bound FIVE flow channels; thirteen equipotential lines bound TWELVE drops.**

> **A question that says "5 flow channels and 12 drops" has already done that conversion**, and a question that gives numbers of LINES has not. **Reading which is given is worth the mark.**

> **The reason the formula uses spaces is that each channel carries an equal share Δq of the flow, and each drop takes an equal share Δh of the head** — so the discharge is (number of channels) × (flow per channel), and the flow per channel depends on the head per drop.

**Where the formula comes from, in two lines:**

> **Each equipotential drop takes Δh = H/N_d.**

> **In a properly drawn flow net every field is a curvilinear SQUARE (b = l), so by Darcy's law each channel carries Δq = k Δh × (b/l) = k Δh.**

> **Total q = N_f × Δq = N_f × k H / N_d = k H (N_f/N_d).** ✓

> **So the "square fields" rule is not a drafting nicety — it is what makes b/l = 1 and lets the formula be so simple.** A flow net with rectangular fields needs the b/l ratio carried through.

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| **1.2 × 10⁻⁴** | **Using N_f/N_d = 1/2, or otherwise mis-forming the ratio** |
| **5.8 × 10⁻⁴** | **INVERTING the ratio: 4 × 10⁻⁵ × 6 × 12/5 = 5.76 × 10⁻⁴** ← the trap |
| **2.4 × 10⁻⁴** | **k H alone, with the ratio omitted entirely** |
| **1.0 × 10⁻⁴** | ✓ |

> **Option (b) is the designed trap — the shape factor turned upside down.** The defence is physical rather than algebraic: **more equipotential drops means the head is dissipated in more steps, so LESS flow. N_d must be in the denominator.**

> **A sanity check confirms it: 12 drops against 5 channels means the ratio is less than 1, so q must be LESS than kH = 2.4 × 10⁻⁴.** Options (b) and (c) both fail that test at a glance.

**The other outputs of the same flow net, since the discharge is rarely the only thing wanted:**

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Seepage discharge** | **q = kH(N_f/N_d)** ← |
| **Head at any point** | **h = H(1 − n_d/N_d)**, n_d being the drops passed |
| **Pore pressure at a point** | **u = γ_w × (pressure head there)** |
| **EXIT GRADIENT** | **i_exit = Δh / l**, with l the length of the smallest field at the exit |
| **Factor of safety against PIPING** | **FOS = i_critical / i_exit, with i_critical = (G−1)/(1+e)** |

> **The exit gradient is the output that matters most for safety**, and note that it depends on the SMALLEST FIELD at the exit — **so the flow net must be drawn carefully precisely where the fields are smallest, which is where the drawing is hardest.**

> **The critical hydraulic gradient i_c = (G−1)/(1+e) is about 1.0 for most soils** (G = 2.65, e = 0.65 gives 1.0), which is why a computed exit gradient of, say, 0.25 corresponds to a factor of safety of 4 — **and why the tabulated "safe exit gradients" of Khosla's method are of that order.**

**The properties a valid flow net must have, since the answer is only as good as the drawing:**

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **Flow lines and equipotentials meet at RIGHT ANGLES** | Because flow is normal to the equipotential |
| **Fields are curvilinear SQUARES** | **What makes b/l = 1** |
| **Impervious boundaries are FLOW LINES** | No flow crosses them |
| **Permeable boundaries are EQUIPOTENTIALS** | Constant head along them |
| Quantity of flow between any two adjacent flow lines is equal | By construction |

> **The last row is the assumption the whole method rests on**, and it is why the channels can simply be counted.

examTip.trick: **q = kH(N_f/N_d) = 4×10⁻⁵ × 6 × 5/12 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³/s per metre.** Do the fraction first: 6 × 5/12 = 2.5 exactly.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) inverts the shape factor.** Check it physically: MORE equipotential drops means the head is dissipated in more steps, so LESS flow — N_d belongs in the denominator. And since 5/12 < 1, q must be below kH = 2.4 × 10⁻⁴.
examTip.mnemonic: **N_f and N_d count SPACES, not LINES** — six flow lines bound five channels. And the fields must be curvilinear SQUARES, because that is what makes b/l = 1 and the formula so simple.

questions.stem: The property of a fluid by virtue of which it offers resistance to shear is:
questions.solution:
**Viscosity.**

**The definition — Newton's law of viscosity:**

> **τ = μ (du/dy)**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **τ** | **Shear stress** |
| **μ** | **DYNAMIC (absolute) viscosity** |
| **du/dy** | **VELOCITY GRADIENT (rate of shear strain)** |

> **The statement to hold onto is the contrast with a solid:**

> **A SOLID's shear stress is proportional to the shear STRAIN. A FLUID's is proportional to the RATE of shear strain.**

> **That is what distinguishes a fluid from a solid.** A solid resists being deformed; **a fluid resists being deformed QUICKLY, and offers no resistance at all to being deformed slowly enough.**

> **Hence a fluid at rest can sustain no shear stress**, which is the starting point of hydrostatics.

**The two viscosities, since both are used:**

| Viscosity | Definition | SI unit | CGS unit |
|---|---|---|---|
| **DYNAMIC, μ** | **τ/(du/dy)** | **N·s/m² = Pa·s** | **POISE (1 Pa·s = 10 poise)** |
| **KINEMATIC, ν** | **μ/ρ** | **m²/s** | **STOKES (1 m²/s = 10⁴ stokes)** |

> **For water at 20 °C: μ ≈ 1 × 10⁻³ Pa·s and ν ≈ 1 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s.** Those two round numbers are worth memorising — **almost every Reynolds number calculation uses ν = 10⁻⁶ m²/s for water.**

> **Kinematic viscosity appears wherever inertia competes with viscosity**, which is why it is the one in Re = VD/ν.

**How viscosity varies with temperature — and the two fluids behave OPPOSITELY:**

| Fluid | Effect of rising temperature | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **LIQUIDS** | **Viscosity DECREASES** | **Cohesive forces between molecules weaken** |
| **GASES** | **Viscosity INCREASES** | **Molecular momentum transfer intensifies** |

> **This opposite behaviour is a favourite examination point** and it follows from the different mechanism: **in a liquid, viscosity is intermolecular attraction; in a gas, it is molecules carrying momentum across the shear layer.** Heat weakens the first and strengthens the second.

> **The practical consequence is familiar: engine oil thins when hot, and bitumen must be heated to be pumped and sprayed.**

**Why the distractors are wrong — each is a real fluid property doing a different job:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **SURFACE TENSION (σ)** | **The tensile force per unit length in a liquid SURFACE, caused by unbalanced cohesion at the interface. Units N/m. Explains droplets, soap bubbles, the pressure inside a bubble** |
| **CAPILLARITY** | **The rise or fall of a liquid in a fine tube — a CONSEQUENCE of surface tension and of adhesion versus cohesion, not an independent property** ← |
| **VISCOSITY** | ✓ **Resistance to shear** |
| **COMPRESSIBILITY** | **The change in VOLUME under pressure — the reciprocal of the bulk modulus K. Governs water hammer and acoustic wave speed** |

> **Option (b) capillarity is worth a note because it is a phenomenon rather than a property**: it arises from surface tension acting at a contact angle. **Water RISES in a glass tube (adhesion beats cohesion, contact angle < 90°) while mercury FALLS (cohesion beats adhesion, contact angle > 90°).**

> **Option (d) compressibility is the one whose neglect defines most of hydraulics**: treating water as incompressible is what makes the continuity equation so simple, **and the assumption fails in exactly one important place — water hammer, where the compressibility of the water and the elasticity of the pipe together set the wave speed.**

**The classification of fluids by their shear behaviour, which follows from the definition:**

| Type | τ versus du/dy | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **IDEAL fluid** | **τ = 0 always — zero viscosity** | **A useful fiction; no real fluid** |
| **NEWTONIAN** | **LINEAR through the origin** | **Water, air, thin oils, most fluids of engineering interest** |
| **Dilatant (shear-thickening)** | Slope INCREASES with shear rate | Thick slurry, wet sand, cornflour paste |
| **Pseudoplastic (shear-thinning)** | Slope DECREASES | Paint, blood, polymer solutions |
| **BINGHAM plastic** | **Needs a YIELD stress before it flows at all** | **Toothpaste, sewage sludge, FRESH CONCRETE, drilling mud** |

> **Fresh concrete as a Bingham plastic is the entry with the most engineering content**: it does not flow until a yield stress is exceeded, **which is exactly why it holds a slump, why it needs vibration to flow into formwork, and why the slump test measures anything at all.**

> **A Newtonian fluid would simply level out**, and there would be no slump to measure.

examTip.trick: **τ = μ(du/dy).** A SOLID's shear stress is proportional to STRAIN; a FLUID's to the RATE of strain. Which is why a fluid at rest can carry no shear at all.
examTip.trap: **Capillarity is a PHENOMENON, not a property** — it follows from surface tension and the contact angle. Water rises in glass (adhesion wins), mercury falls (cohesion wins).
examTip.mnemonic: **Heating THINS a liquid but THICKENS a gas** — liquid viscosity is intermolecular attraction, gas viscosity is momentum transfer. And remember **ν = 10⁻⁶ m²/s for water**, the number in every Reynolds calculation.

questions.stem: A plane truss has 15 members and 9 joints, with 3 support reactions. The truss is:
questions.solution:
**Indeterminate to the second degree.**

**The test for a plane truss:**

> **m + r  compared with  2j**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **m** | **Number of MEMBERS** | **15** |
| **r** | **Number of support REACTIONS** | **3** |
| **j** | **Number of JOINTS** | **9** |

> **m + r = 15 + 3 = 18**

> **2j = 2 × 9 = 18**

> **These are EQUAL, so the count says the truss is determinate...**

> **but the question's answer is indeterminate to the second degree, so the count must be read more carefully. Let us set the criterion out properly.**

**The correct criterion and where the degree comes from:**

> **The equation-counting test compares UNKNOWNS with EQUATIONS.**

> **UNKNOWNS = m member forces + r reactions = 15 + 3 = 18.**

> **EQUATIONS = 2 per joint (ΣH = 0 and ΣV = 0 at each pin) = 2 × 9 = 18.**

> **Degree of static indeterminacy D_s = (m + r) − 2j = 18 − 18 = 0.**

> **On the standard count this truss is JUST DETERMINATE — and that is option (b), not the keyed answer.**

> **This is the point at which the honest thing to do is say so plainly: the numbers 15, 9 and 3 give a determinate truss, and any claim of second-degree indeterminacy would require m + r − 2j = 2, that is m = 17 with the same j and r, or j = 8.**

> **So the correct answer to the question AS THE NUMBERS STAND is (b) determinate. The item is recorded with the corrected key, and the reasoning is set out here in full so the candidate can see the criterion rather than a result.**

**The full classification, which is the content worth taking away:**

| Condition | Classification |
|---|---|
| **m + r < 2j** | **UNSTABLE — a mechanism. Fewer unknowns than equations means it cannot equilibrate all loads** |
| **m + r = 2j** | **JUST DETERMINATE (if properly arranged)** ← this truss |
| **m + r > 2j** | **INDETERMINATE, to degree (m + r − 2j)** |

> **And the indeterminacy splits into two parts:**

> **D_s = D_se + D_si**, where

| Part | Expression | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **EXTERNAL, D_se** | **r − 3** | **Redundant SUPPORTS** |
| **INTERNAL, D_si** | **m − (2j − 3)** | **Redundant MEMBERS** |

> **For this truss: D_se = 3 − 3 = 0 (statically determinate supports) and D_si = 15 − (18 − 3) = 15 − 15 = 0.** Both zero, consistent with D_s = 0.

**The critical qualification — counting is NECESSARY but not SUFFICIENT:**

> **A truss can satisfy m + r = 2j and still be UNSTABLE**, if the members are badly arranged.

| Defect | Example |
|---|---|
| **A panel left as an unbraced RECTANGLE while another is over-braced** | **The count balances but one panel is a mechanism and the other is redundant** |
| **Three collinear support reactions** | **Cannot resist a force along that line — externally unstable regardless of the count** |
| **Three parallel reactions** | Cannot resist a force perpendicular to them |
| **A joint with two collinear members and a load** | Local mechanism |

> **So the count identifies the ARITHMETIC of stability, and the arrangement must then be checked by inspection.** The classic demonstration is a truss with one square panel left undiagonalised and another panel given two diagonals: **m + r = 2j exactly, and the structure folds up.**

> **This is why option (a) "unstable" can never be ruled out by counting alone**, and why a well-set question of this type either gives a figure or states that the arrangement is proper.

**The method of analysis, since determinacy is what makes it possible:**

| Method | Use |
|---|---|
| **Method of JOINTS** | **All member forces; start at a joint with no more than two unknowns** |
| **Method of SECTIONS** | **A FEW specific members, quickly — cut through no more than three unknowns** |
| **Zero-force member identification** | **Do this FIRST — it removes members from the problem before any arithmetic** |

> **The zero-force rules are worth having instantly:**

> **Two non-collinear members at an unloaded joint: BOTH are zero.**

> **Three members at an unloaded joint, two collinear: the THIRD is zero.**

> **Spotting these before starting can remove a third of the members of a typical truss from the calculation**, and in an examination that is the difference between finishing and not.

verification.notes: Answer corrected from (d) to (b). With m = 15, j = 9 and r = 3 the standard plane-truss criterion gives m + r = 18 and 2j = 18, so the degree of static indeterminacy is (m + r) - 2j = 0 and the truss is just determinate. Second-degree indeterminacy would require m + r - 2j = 2, that is 17 members for the same 9 joints and 3 reactions. The corrected answer is (b) determinate, and the solution sets out the criterion and its split into external and internal indeterminacy in full, together with the reason that counting is necessary but not sufficient for stability.

examTip.trick: **Unknowns = m + r; equations = 2j. D_s = (m + r) − 2j.** Here 15 + 3 = 18 and 2 × 9 = 18, so D_s = 0 — just determinate.
examTip.trap: **Counting is NECESSARY but not SUFFICIENT.** A truss with one unbraced square panel and another double-braced satisfies m + r = 2j exactly and still folds up. Three collinear or parallel reactions are unstable whatever the count.
examTip.mnemonic: **Split it: D_se = r − 3 (redundant supports), D_si = m − (2j − 3) (redundant members).** And identify **ZERO-FORCE members first** — two non-collinear at an unloaded joint are both zero; with three, two collinear, the third is zero.

questions.stem: In a bolted steel connection, the phenomenon in which the bolt shank is pulled out through the bolt hole because of insufficient plate thickness is:
questions.solution:
**Bearing failure of the plate.**

**What bearing failure is:**

> **The bolt bears on the edge of the hole and CRUSHES the plate material ahead of it**, elongating the hole into a slot. In the limit the bolt tears out through the edge of the plate.

> **It is a failure of the PLATE at the hole, not of the bolt** — and it happens when the plate is too thin to spread the bolt's force over enough material.

> **The bearing capacity is proportional to the PLATE THICKNESS**, which is why insufficient thickness is the stated cause:

> **V_dpb = 2.5 k_b d t f_u / γ_mb**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **d** | **Bolt diameter** |
| **t** | **PLATE THICKNESS (the thinner of the connected plates)** ← |
| **f_u** | **Ultimate tensile strength of the PLATE** |
| **k_b** | **Factor for edge distance, pitch and bolt strength — the smallest of e/3d₀, p/3d₀ − 0.25, f_ub/f_u, and 1.0** |

> **Note that k_b brings the EDGE DISTANCE into the bearing capacity.** A bolt too close to the edge tears out through it, so a minimum edge distance is specified — **typically 1.5 times the hole diameter for a machine-cut edge and 1.7 for a hand-flame-cut one.**

**The failure modes of a bolted connection, which is what the question sets against one another:**

| Failure | Where | Governed by |
|---|---|---|
| **SHEAR of the bolt** | **Across the bolt shank, on one or two planes** | **Bolt area and bolt grade** |
| **BEARING on the plate** | **At the hole — the plate crushes** | **PLATE THICKNESS, edge distance, f_u of the plate** ← |
| **TENSION of the plate** | **Across the NET SECTION between holes** | **Net area = (b − n d₀)t** |
| **BLOCK SHEAR** | **A block of plate tears out — tension on one plane, shear on another** | **Combination of gross shear and net tension areas** |
| **Tension in the bolt** | Bolt pulled along its axis | Net tensile area of the bolt |

> **A connection's capacity is the LEAST of all of these**, so every one must be checked. **A design that checks bolt shear only is incomplete, and bearing on a thin plate is the check most often found to govern.**

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

> **Option (a) shear of the bolt** is failure of the BOLT, not the plate, and depends on the bolt's area and grade — **plate thickness does not enter it.** The stem's cause (insufficient plate thickness) rules it out.

> **Option (c) tension failure of the plate** happens across the NET SECTION away from any single bolt, and is a tearing of the plate in the direction of the load — **not a bolt pulling through a hole.**

> **Option (d) BLOCK SHEAR is worth separating carefully**, because it is the subtle one and is often the governing mode in a short end connection:

| | **BEARING** | **BLOCK SHEAR** |
|---|---|---|
