| **What moves** | **The BOLT, through an elongated hole** | **A BLOCK of the plate, containing the bolts, tears out entirely** |
| **Failure surfaces** | Local crushing at one hole | **Two surfaces: TENSION across one line, SHEAR along another** |
| **Governed by** | **Plate thickness** | **Edge distances and bolt group geometry** |
| **Warning** | Hole elongation — visible | Sudden |

> **Block shear is the mode that codes added relatively recently**, after connections failed at loads their bolt-shear and bearing checks said were safe. **It is why generous end distances matter beyond the bearing requirement.**

**The detailing rules that prevent these failures:**

| Requirement | Value (IS 800:2007) |
|---|---|
| **Minimum PITCH (spacing along the load)** | **2.5 d** |
| **Maximum pitch** | **32 t or 300 mm, whichever is less** |
| **Minimum EDGE / end distance** | **1.5 d₀ (machine cut), 1.7 d₀ (hand flame cut)** |
| **Maximum edge distance** | **12 t ε, or 40 mm + 4t in corrosive exposure** |
| Hole diameter d₀ | **d + 1 to 3 mm** by bolt size |

> **The minimum pitch of 2.5d prevents the bearing zones of adjacent bolts from overlapping**, and the maximum pitch prevents the plates buckling apart between bolts or moisture entering the joint.

> **And the maximum edge distance has a purpose worth stating**: it keeps the plate edges clamped so they cannot lift and admit water. **In corrosive conditions an unclamped edge corrodes from the inside of the joint outward, where it cannot be seen or painted.**

**The two categories of bolted connection, since bearing is central to one of them:**

| Type | How load is transferred |
|---|---|
| **BEARING type** | **The bolt bears on the hole and shears — slip occurs first, then bearing** |
| **FRICTION (HSFG) type** | **A high-strength bolt is pre-tensioned so that FRICTION between the plates carries the load and NO SLIP occurs** |

> **In a friction-grip connection the bolt ideally never bears at all**, which is why HSFG bolts are used where slip cannot be tolerated — **bridge girders, connections subject to load reversal or fatigue, and anywhere alignment must be maintained.**

examTip.trick: **Bearing capacity is proportional to PLATE THICKNESS** (V = 2.5 k_b d t f_u/γ), so "insufficient plate thickness" names bearing directly. It is a failure of the PLATE at the hole, not of the bolt.
examTip.trap: **Block shear (d) is the subtle near-miss** — a whole BLOCK of plate tears out, on a tension plane and a shear plane together. Codes added it after connections failed at loads their bolt-shear and bearing checks called safe.
examTip.mnemonic: **A connection's capacity is the LEAST of bolt shear, plate bearing, net-section tension and block shear** — all four must be checked. Minimum pitch 2.5d, minimum edge distance 1.5d₀.

questions.stem: In the design of a two-way slab by IS 456, torsional reinforcement is required at a corner:
options: at every corner of every two-way slab
only where the slab is simply supported on all four sides and free to lift
only at a corner where the slab is continuous over both edges
at a corner where the slab is discontinuous (not continuous) over both edges meeting there
questions.solution:
**At a corner where the slab is DISCONTINUOUS over both edges meeting there.**

**Why a corner needs torsional steel at all — the mechanism:**

> **A two-way slab supported on all four edges tends to LIFT AT ITS CORNERS when it deflects under load.** The slab dishes downward in the middle, and the corners want to curl upward.

> **If the corner is held down — as it is by the wall, by the slab's own weight, or by a beam — the restraint produces TWISTING (torsional) moments in the corner region.**

> **Those twisting moments cause TENSION on the top of the slab in one diagonal direction and on the bottom in the other.**

| Direction | Where the tension is |
|---|---|
| **Along the diagonal FROM the corner** | **TOP of the slab** |
| **Perpendicular to that diagonal** | **BOTTOM of the slab** |

> **So torsional reinforcement must be provided in BOTH the top and the bottom of the slab**, and in both directions — a mesh in each face.

> **Without it, a diagonal crack opens at the corner, running perpendicular to the corner diagonal on the top surface.** That crack is the recognisable signature of missing corner steel.

**Why only a DISCONTINUOUS corner needs it — and this is the whole question:**

> **Where a slab panel is CONTINUOUS over an edge, the adjacent panel restrains it.** The two panels deflect together, the corner cannot curl, and the negative moment steel already provided for continuity handles what twisting there is.

> **Where BOTH edges at a corner are discontinuous — an external corner of the building, or a single isolated panel — there is nothing to restrain the curl, and the torsional moments are at their largest.**

> **IS 456 Table 26 and clause D-1.8 therefore require torsional reinforcement only where the slab is simply supported (discontinuous) on both edges meeting at that corner.**

| Corner condition | Torsional steel |
|---|---|
| **Both edges DISCONTINUOUS** | **FULL torsional reinforcement required** ← |
| **One edge continuous, one discontinuous** | **HALF the above** |
| **Both edges continuous** | **NONE required** |

> **Note that the code does provide for the intermediate case at half the amount**, which is why option (b) — restricting it to slabs simply supported on ALL FOUR sides — is too narrow, and option (a) — every corner of every slab — is too broad.

**The quantity and extent, since the detail is specific:**

| Requirement | Value |
|---|---|
| **AREA per layer, per direction** | **0.75 × the maximum mid-span steel of the shorter span** |
| **Layers** | **FOUR — two directions in the TOP face, two in the BOTTOM face** |
| **EXTENT from the corner** | **One FIFTH of the SHORTER span, in each direction** |
| **Arrangement** | A square mesh in each face |

> **The 0.75 and the L/5 are the two numbers to remember**, and note that both are keyed to the SHORTER span.

> **Four layers is the detail most often short-changed on site**, because providing a mesh in the top face of a slab at its corners is fiddly and looks unnecessary to anyone who has not seen a corner crack.

**The related corner effect, which is asked alongside:**

> **CORNERS HELD DOWN versus CORNERS FREE TO LIFT is a distinction that changes the design moments themselves.**

| Case | Moment coefficients | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Corners HELD DOWN (torsionally restrained)** | **IS 456 Table 26** | **LOWER moments — the corner restraint helps carry the load** |
| **Corners FREE TO LIFT (unrestrained)** | **IS 456 Table 27 (Rankine-Grashoff)** | **HIGHER moments — no help from the corners** |

> **So the corner restraint that CAUSES the torsional moments also REDUCES the mid-span moments**, and the two tables reflect the two assumptions.

> **The design must be consistent: if Table 26 is used, the torsional steel it depends on MUST be provided.** Using the lower moments of Table 26 and then omitting the corner steel takes the benefit without the price — **and that combination is a genuine design error, not merely a detailing lapse.**

**And the definition that decides whether any of this applies:**

> **A slab is TWO-WAY when L_y/L_x ≤ 2, and ONE-WAY when L_y/L_x > 2.**

> **The reason is that beyond a ratio of about 2 the load carried in the long direction becomes negligible** — the share carried each way goes roughly as the fourth power of the inverse span, so a 1:2 slab already sends about 94 per cent of its load across the short span.

> **A one-way slab has no corner-lifting behaviour to speak of and needs no torsional reinforcement** — only distribution steel of 0.12 per cent (HYSD) across the span.

examTip.trick: **Corners curl UP as the slab dishes down; restraining them creates twisting moments** — tension on the TOP along the diagonal and on the BOTTOM across it. Hence a mesh in BOTH faces, four layers.
examTip.trap: **Both edges discontinuous → FULL steel; one continuous → HALF; both continuous → NONE.** Option (a) is too broad and (b) too narrow; the code covers the intermediate case as well.
examTip.mnemonic: **0.75 × the maximum short-span mid-span steel, extending L/5 from the corner** (both keyed to the SHORTER span). And note: **Table 26's lower moments DEPEND on that steel** — taking the benefit and omitting the steel is a design error.

questions.stem: A town of population 40,000 has an average water demand of 135 litres per capita per day. Taking a peak factor of 2.5, the maximum hourly demand is:
questions.solution:
**13.5 MLD.**

**Step 1 — the average daily demand:**

> **Q_avg = population × per capita demand**

> **= 40,000 × 135 litres/day**

> **= 5,400,000 litres/day = 5.4 MLD**

**Step 2 — apply the peak factor:**

> **Q_max hourly = peak factor × Q_avg**

> **= 2.5 × 5.4 = 13.5 MLD** ✓

> **The arithmetic is trivial; the question is testing whether the candidate knows which quantity the peak factor multiplies and reads which demand is asked for.**

**Why each distractor is wrong — and every one is a real quantity in the same problem:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **13.5 MLD** | ✓ **Maximum hourly demand** |
| **5.4 MLD** | **The AVERAGE daily demand — the peak factor not applied** ← the trap |
| **10.8 MLD** | **2.0 × average — the maximum DAILY demand, using the wrong factor** |
| **2.16 MLD** | 0.4 × average — no standard meaning |

> **Option (b) is the designed trap: it is the intermediate result.** Anyone who computes the average and stops has done the arithmetic and answered a different question.

> **Option (c) is the more interesting error** because 2.0 is itself a standard peak factor — **for the maximum DAILY demand rather than the maximum HOURLY.** So (c) is the right calculation with the wrong factor.

**The peak factors, which is the substance of the topic:**

| Demand | Factor × average | Used to size |
|---|---|---|
| **Average daily** | **1.0** | **The SOURCE — total quantity needed over a year** |
| **Maximum DAILY** | **1.8 to 2.0** | **Treatment plant, pumps, transmission main** |
| **Maximum HOURLY** | **2.5 to 3.0** | **DISTRIBUTION network and service reservoir** ← |
| Maximum hourly of the maximum day | **2.7 (= 1.8 × 1.5)** | Distribution, by the compounded route |
| Minimum hourly | ~0.4 to 0.5 | Checking for stagnation and excess pressure |

> **The essential idea is that different components are sized on different peaks**, and it follows from where storage sits in the system:

> **A SERVICE RESERVOIR absorbs the hourly variation.** So the treatment plant and the main feeding it need only meet the maximum DAILY demand, running steadily; **the reservoir supplies the hourly peaks from storage, and the distribution mains downstream of it must carry those peaks.**

> **That is why the plant is sized on 1.8-2.0 and the distribution network on 2.5-3.0.** Sizing the plant for the hourly peak would mean building a plant 50 per cent larger than necessary and running it at part load almost always.

**Why smaller towns have larger peak factors — a point worth knowing:**

> **The peak factor DECREASES as population increases.**

| Population | Typical peak factor (hourly) |
|---|---|
| **< 50,000** | **3.0** |
| **50,000 - 200,000** | **2.5** |
| **> 200,000** | **2.0** |

> **The reason is STATISTICAL SMOOTHING.** In a small town everyone bathes, cooks and washes at much the same time, so the demands coincide. **In a large city the habits of a million people average out, and the peak is a smaller multiple of the mean.**

> **This is the same principle as diversity factor in electrical load estimation**, and it is why per capita design figures cannot simply be scaled between town sizes.

**The per capita figures themselves, since 135 lpcd is a standard value:**

| Use | lpcd |
|---|---|
| **Domestic** | **135 (CPHEEO standard for a piped supply with sewerage)** |
| **Domestic, without sewerage** | **70-100** |
| **Industrial and commercial** | 20-25 |
| **Public / institutional** | 10-25 |
| **Fire fighting** | 1-5 |
| **LOSSES AND WASTAGE (unaccounted for water)** | **15 % of total — often far more in practice** |
| **Total, design** | **~200-270 lpcd for a large town** |

> **The unaccounted-for-water allowance is the line that deserves attention.** A nominal 15 per cent is standard in design; **real losses in many South Asian systems run from 30 to over 50 per cent.**

> **Which means that in a leaky network, reducing losses is a far cheaper way to increase supply than building new source works** — the water is already being abstracted and treated, and it is simply not arriving. **That is a genuine engineering conclusion and not a platitude: leak detection is a capacity project.**

examTip.trick: **Average = 40,000 × 135 = 5.4 MLD; maximum hourly = 2.5 × 5.4 = 13.5 MLD.** The whole question is which demand is asked for.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) 5.4 is the intermediate result** — the average, with the factor not applied. Option (c) uses 2.0, which is the real factor for maximum DAILY demand, not hourly.
examTip.mnemonic: **Plant and transmission on maximum DAILY (1.8-2.0); distribution and service reservoir on maximum HOURLY (2.5-3.0)** — because the reservoir absorbs the hourly swing. And the peak factor FALLS as population rises: statistical smoothing.

questions.stem: In a water distribution network, the Hardy Cross method of analysis proceeds by:
options: assuming heads at each node and correcting them until continuity is satisfied at every pipe
solving the network directly, since the equations are linear
assuming pipe diameters and correcting them until the pressures are acceptable
assuming a flow distribution satisfying continuity, then correcting it until the head loss round each loop sums to zero
questions.solution:
**Assume a flow distribution satisfying continuity, then correct it until the head loss round each loop sums to zero.**

**The two conditions a solved network must satisfy:**

| Condition | Statement | Analogy |
|---|---|---|
| **CONTINUITY at each junction** | **Inflow = outflow at every node** | **Kirchhoff's CURRENT law** |
| **HEAD LOSS round each loop** | **Σh_f = 0 going round any closed loop** | **Kirchhoff's VOLTAGE law** |

> **The Hardy Cross method satisfies the FIRST exactly from the start, by choosing the assumed flows to balance at every node, and then iterates to satisfy the SECOND.**

> **That is the whole structure of the method, and it is what option (d) states.**

**The correction formula:**

> **ΔQ = − Σh_f / [n Σ(h_f / Q)]**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Σh_f** | **Algebraic sum of head losses round the loop (clockwise positive, anticlockwise negative)** |
| **n** | **The EXPONENT of Q in the head loss law — 2 for Darcy-Weisbach, 1.85 for Hazen-Williams** |
| **Σ(h_f/Q)** | **Sum of the ABSOLUTE values of h_f/Q for the loop** |

> **Note the two different treatments in one formula: the numerator is a SIGNED sum, the denominator an sum of MAGNITUDES.** Getting that wrong is the standard error in the method.

> **The correction ΔQ is then applied to EVERY pipe in the loop, in the same rotational sense** — which is precisely what preserves the continuity that was established at the start. **Adding the same ΔQ round a loop changes no node's balance.**

> **A pipe shared between two loops receives BOTH corrections.**

**Why the method has to be iterative — the reason option (b) is wrong:**

> **The head loss varies as Q^n with n ≈ 2, so the equations are NON-LINEAR.**

> **A set of non-linear simultaneous equations cannot be solved by direct elimination**, so a successive-approximation scheme is used. **Hardy Cross's contribution in 1936 was a hand-computable one.**

> **Convergence is judged by Σh_f in each loop approaching zero — commonly to within about 0.3 m, or ΔQ becoming a small fraction of the flow.**

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Assume HEADS at nodes, correct until continuity holds** | **This is a REAL method — the NODAL (Cornish) method, the dual of Hardy Cross.** But it is not Hardy Cross ← the substantive near-miss |
| **Solve directly, equations are linear** | **They are NON-LINEAR (h_f ∝ Q^{1.85-2})** |
| **Assume DIAMETERS and correct them** | **That is DESIGN, not ANALYSIS.** Hardy Cross analyses a network of known pipes |
| **Assume flows satisfying continuity, correct for loop head loss** | ✓ |

> **Option (a) is worth taking seriously because it describes a genuine and useful technique.** The two methods are duals:

| | **HARDY CROSS (loop method)** | **NODAL (Cornish) method** |
|---|---|---|
| **Assume** | **FLOWS (satisfying continuity)** | **HEADS at nodes** |
| **Correct until** | **Σh_f = 0 round each loop** | **Continuity satisfied at each node** |
| **Number of equations** | **One per LOOP** | **One per NODE** |
| **Better when** | **Loops are few** | **Nodes are few, or the network is branched** |

> **The choice between them is a matter of which count is smaller**, and for a typical grid network with many nodes and few loops, Hardy Cross wins — which is why it became the standard hand method.

> **Option (c) points at the real distinction between ANALYSIS and DESIGN.** Analysis takes the pipes as given and finds the flows; **design chooses the pipes to achieve required pressures.** Design is done by analysing a trial network, adjusting, and analysing again — **so Hardy Cross is a tool used inside a design loop, not a design method itself.**

**The requirements a distribution network must meet, since the analysis exists to check them:**

| Requirement | Typical value |
|---|---|
| **Minimum residual pressure at the consumer** | **7 m (single storey) to 17-22 m (multi-storey)** |
| **Maximum pressure** | **~70 m, or fittings and pipes are overstressed and leakage rises** |
| **Velocity** | **0.6 to 3 m/s — above the self-cleansing minimum, below the scouring maximum** |
| **Residual chlorine at the extremity** | **0.2 mg/l** |

> **The maximum pressure limit is the one most often overlooked**, and it matters because **leakage from a distribution system rises steeply with pressure.** Pressure management — deliberately holding pressure down to the minimum acceptable — is one of the most cost-effective loss-reduction measures available, and it is a direct application of the network analysis this question is about.

**And the modern position, stated honestly:** **Hardy Cross is no longer used for real networks** — software solving the full non-linear system by the Newton-Raphson or gradient method (EPANET and its commercial relatives) handles thousands of pipes at once.

> **It remains on the syllabus because it makes the two governing conditions explicit**, and an engineer who understands why loops must balance and nodes must conserve can read a software result critically. **One who has only ever pressed a button cannot.**

examTip.trick: **Continuity is satisfied from the START by the assumed flows; the iteration fixes the LOOP head loss.** ΔQ = −Σh_f/[nΣ(h_f/Q)], with n = 2 for Darcy-Weisbach and 1.85 for Hazen-Williams.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) is a genuine method — the NODAL (Cornish) method, the dual of Hardy Cross.** Assume heads, correct for continuity. Choose whichever has the smaller count: one equation per loop, or one per node.
examTip.mnemonic: **Numerator is a SIGNED sum, denominator a sum of MAGNITUDES** — the standard error in the formula. And the correction is applied to EVERY pipe in the loop, which is exactly what preserves node continuity.

questions.stem: In an activated sludge process, a persistently high sludge volume index (SVI) above about 150 ml/g indicates:
options: excessive dissolved oxygen in the aeration tank
a sludge that settles too rapidly, leaving the effluent turbid
sludge bulking, in which the sludge settles poorly and is carried over in the effluent
that the sludge age is too short for nitrification
questions.solution:
**Sludge bulking — the sludge settles poorly and is carried over in the effluent.**

**What SVI measures:**

> **SVI = (volume of settled sludge in ml after 30 minutes × 1000) / (suspended solids concentration in mg/l)**

> **It is the volume in millilitres occupied by ONE GRAM of sludge after settling for 30 minutes.**

| SVI (ml/g) | Settling |
|---|---|
| **< 80** | **Excellent — dense, compact sludge** |
| **80 - 100** | **Good** |
| **100 - 150** | Acceptable |
| **> 150** | **BULKING — poor settling** ← |
| **> 250** | Severe bulking; plant failure imminent |

> **A HIGH SVI means the sludge is BULKY — it occupies a large volume per unit mass, so it settles slowly and incompletely.**

> **The number is a volume per gram, so "high" means "fluffy", and fluffy sludge does not settle.**

**Why bulking is so damaging — the consequence chain:**

> **The secondary clarifier depends on the sludge settling out so that clarified effluent can be drawn off the top and the sludge returned to the aeration tank.**

| Consequence of bulking | Note |
|---|---|
| **Sludge blanket rises in the clarifier** | Less and less clear water above it |
| **Solids CARRY OVER in the effluent** | **The plant fails its suspended solids and BOD consent** |
| **Return sludge is thin, so the MLSS in the aeration tank falls** | **The process loses biomass — and the problem worsens** |
| **In the extreme, total loss of biomass (washout)** | Weeks to recover |

> **The self-worsening loop is what makes bulking urgent.** Poor settling means thin return sludge, which means less biomass, which stresses the process further and encourages the very organisms causing the bulking.

**The cause, and it is specific:**

> **Bulking is usually caused by FILAMENTOUS ORGANISMS** — *Sphaerotilus natans*, *Microthrix*, *Nocardia*, type 021N and others.

> **Filaments bridge between floc particles and hold them apart**, producing an open, fluffy structure that traps water and will not compact.

| Condition that favours filaments | Remedy |
|---|---|
| **LOW dissolved oxygen (< 1-2 mg/l)** | **Increase aeration** ← the commonest cause |
| **Low F/M ratio (over-aerated, starved sludge)** | Adjust loading or wasting rate |
| **NUTRIENT deficiency (low N or P)** | **Dose nutrients — the BOD:N:P ratio should be about 100:5:1** |
| **Low pH (< 6.5)** | Correct pH |
| **Septic, high-sulphide influent** | Pre-aerate; reduce sewer detention |
| Highly soluble carbohydrate waste | Selector zone at the tank inlet |

> **Low DO is the first thing to check**, and it is the reason option (a) is exactly backwards: **excessive dissolved oxygen does not cause bulking; INSUFFICIENT oxygen does.**

> **The nutrient point is worth remembering because it is counter-intuitive: a wastewater can be DEFICIENT in nitrogen and phosphorus**, particularly an industrial one, and then nutrients must be ADDED to a treatment plant whose whole purpose elsewhere is removing them.

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Excessive DO** | **The reverse — LOW DO favours filaments** |
| **Settles too rapidly, turbid effluent** | **That is PIN FLOC (deflocculation), and it corresponds to a LOW SVI** ← the interesting distractor |
| **Sludge bulking** | ✓ |
| **Sludge age too short for nitrification** | **A real problem, measured by SLUDGE AGE (SRT), not by SVI** |

> **Option (b) describes a genuine and opposite condition.** **PIN FLOC** is small, dense, over-oxidised floc that settles fast but leaves a turbid supernatant because the fine particles never flocculate. **It gives a LOW SVI and a poor effluent — so a good SVI is not by itself proof of a good effluent.**

> **Option (d) names the right kind of problem measured by the wrong index.** Nitrification needs a sludge age of about 8 to 15 days at 20 °C; **that is set by the wasting rate and read from the SRT, not from a settling test.**

**The related operating parameters, since SVI is meaningless in isolation:**

| Parameter | Expression | Typical |
|---|---|---|
| **MLSS** | Mixed liquor suspended solids | **1500-3000 mg/l (conventional)** |
| **F/M ratio** | **BOD load / MLVSS mass** | **0.2-0.5 per day (conventional)** |
| **SLUDGE AGE (SRT)** | **MLSS mass in tank / MLSS wasted per day** | **5-15 days** |
| **RETURN sludge ratio** | Q_r/Q | **0.25-0.5 (up to 1.0)** |
| **SVI** | **Settled volume × 1000 / SS** | **< 150 ml/g** ← |
| Aeration period | — | **4-8 hours** |

> **F/M and sludge age are the two control handles**, and they are inversely related — **wasting more sludge raises F/M and lowers sludge age.**

> **The extremes define the process variants: EXTENDED AERATION runs at very low F/M and long sludge age** (stable, tolerant, produces little sludge, needs a big tank); **HIGH-RATE runs at high F/M and short sludge age** (small tank, more sludge, less stable, no nitrification).

> **So the choice of F/M is the choice of process**, and SVI is the measurement that tells you whether the choice is working.

examTip.trick: **SVI is a VOLUME PER GRAM, so high means fluffy — and fluffy sludge does not settle.** Above 150 ml/g the sludge is bulking and solids carry over in the effluent.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) describes PIN FLOC, the opposite condition — a LOW SVI with a turbid effluent.** So a good SVI is not by itself proof of a good effluent. And option (a) is backwards: LOW DO favours filaments, not high.
examTip.mnemonic: **Check DO first** — under 1-2 mg/l is the commonest cause of filamentous bulking. Then nutrients: **BOD:N:P should be about 100:5:1**, and an industrial waste can be genuinely DEFICIENT in N and P.

questions.stem: A crop has a base period of 120 days and a delta of 60 cm. The duty of water for this crop, in hectares per cumec, is:
questions.solution:
**1728 hectares per cumec.**

**The relation between duty and delta:**

> **Δ = 8.64 B / D**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Δ** | **DELTA — total depth of water required, in METRES** | **0.60 m** |
| **B** | **BASE PERIOD, in days** | **120** |
| **D** | **DUTY, in hectares per cumec** | **?** |
| **8.64** | **The unit-conversion constant** | — |

> **Rearranging:  D = 8.64 B / Δ**

> **D = 8.64 × 120 / 0.60 = 1036.8 / 0.60 = 1728 ha/cumec** ✓

**Where the 8.64 comes from — deriving it removes the need to remember it:**

> **One cumec flowing for one day delivers 1 × 86,400 = 86,400 m³ of water.**

> **Over B days: 86,400 B m³.**

> **That volume irrigates D hectares = 10,000 D m².**

> **So the depth applied is  Δ = 86,400 B / (10,000 D) = 8.64 B / D** metres. ✓

> **The constant is simply 86,400 seconds in a day divided by 10,000 m² in a hectare.** Knowing that, the formula can be rebuilt from scratch in ten seconds — **and, more importantly, the units can never be muddled.**

**The check that catches every error in this calculation:**

> **Duty and delta are INVERSELY related.** A crop needing more water (a large delta) can have less land served by a given flow (a small duty).

> **So verify the direction: rice has a large delta (~125 cm) and therefore a SMALL duty; wheat has a small delta (~40 cm) and a LARGE duty.**

| Crop | Base period (days) | Delta (cm) | Duty (ha/cumec) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RICE** | **120** | **125** | **~830 — the LOWEST, the thirstiest crop** |
| **Sugarcane** | **320** | **90** | ~3070 (long base period) |
| **Wheat** | **120** | **40** | **~2590** |
| **Cotton** | 200 | 50 | ~3456 |
| **Maize** | 100 | 25 | ~3456 |

> **Notice the trap the table reveals: DUTY depends on BOTH the delta AND the base period**, so a crop with a large delta can still have a high duty if it grows over a long season — as sugarcane does. **The duty is a rate; the delta is a total.**

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| **1728** | ✓ |
| **864** | **Using Δ = 1.2 m, or dividing by 2 — half the answer** |
| **3456** | **DOUBLE the answer: using Δ = 0.30 m, or reading the delta as 30 cm** |
| **172.8** | **A factor of ten out — the classic consequence of putting the delta in CENTIMETRES instead of METRES** ← the trap |

> **Option (d) is the designed trap and it is the commonest real error: Δ must be in METRES.** Substituting 60 instead of 0.60 gives 17.28, and substituting 6 gives 172.8. **The formula's 8.64 constant is defined for metres, and the question gives the delta in centimetres deliberately.**

**The definitions, since these terms are used together and confused:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **DELTA (Δ)** | **The TOTAL DEPTH of water required by a crop over its whole base period** |
| **DUTY (D)** | **The AREA that a unit discharge, run continuously, can irrigate — ha/cumec** |
| **BASE PERIOD (B)** | **The whole period of crop growth, from first to last watering** |
| **CROP PERIOD** | **From sowing to harvest — slightly LONGER than the base period** |
| **KOR depth and KOR period** | **The single most critical watering, soon after sowing, and its duration** |
| **OUTLET FACTOR** | Duty at the outlet head |
| **INTENSITY of irrigation** | **Percentage of the culturable area actually cropped in a season** |

> **The base-period/crop-period distinction is small and is examined**: the crop period is longer, because the crop continues to ripen after the last watering.

> **The KOR watering is the one that determines the canal's CAPACITY**, because it is the peak demand: the whole command needs its first critical watering within a short window, so the canal must be sized for that rather than for the average seasonal demand. **A canal sized on the average delta would be too small in the KOR period and idle for much of the rest of the season.**

**And the efficiency chain, which is why the field delta is not the delta at the head:**

| Efficiency | Typical | Loss to |
|---|---|---|
| **Conveyance efficiency** | **60-80 %** | **SEEPAGE and evaporation in the canals — the largest loss** |
| **Field application efficiency** | **60-80 %** | Deep percolation and runoff at the field |
| **OVERALL project efficiency** | **~40-60 %** | The product of the two |

> **So the discharge required at the canal HEAD is roughly TWICE what the crops actually consume**, and the duty at the head is correspondingly about half the duty at the field. **Lining the canals attacks the largest single loss in the chain**, which is why it is the standard first improvement to an existing scheme.

examTip.trick: **Δ = 8.64B/D, so D = 8.64 × 120 / 0.60 = 1728 ha/cumec.** The 8.64 is just 86,400 s/day ÷ 10,000 m²/ha — derive it and the units can never be muddled.
examTip.trap: **Δ must be in METRES.** Putting 60 cm in as 60 gives a factor-of-a-hundred error; option (d) is the factor-of-ten version. The question gives centimetres deliberately.
examTip.mnemonic: **Duty and delta are INVERSE — but duty depends on the base period too**, so long-season sugarcane has a high duty despite a large delta. And the **KOR watering** sets the canal capacity, not the average demand.

questions.stem: A cross-drainage work in which the canal is carried over the natural drain, with the drain flowing under the canal in a barrel, is called:
questions.solution:
**An aqueduct.**

**The rule that resolves the whole family:**

> **Name the structure after WHAT IS CARRIED ON TOP.**

> **CANAL over drain → AQUEDUCT.  DRAIN over canal → SUPER PASSAGE.**

> **And if the lower channel is forced to run under PRESSURE, the word "siphon" is added.**

| Structure | Canal | Drain | Lower channel flows |
|---|---|---|---|
| **AQUEDUCT** | **ON TOP** | **Underneath, in a barrel** | **FREE (gravity)** ← |
| **SIPHON AQUEDUCT** | **ON TOP** | **Underneath** | **UNDER PRESSURE** |
| **SUPER PASSAGE** | **Underneath** | **ON TOP** | **FREE** |
| **CANAL SIPHON (siphon)** | **Underneath, under PRESSURE** | **ON TOP** | Canal is pressurised |
| **LEVEL CROSSING** | \- | \- | **The two MIX, then separate again** |
| Inlet and outlet | \- | \- | Drain admitted into the canal and taken out downstream |

> **The mnemonic that follows: the FIRST word of the name tells you what is on top.** An aqueDUCT carries the canal (as a Roman aqueduct carries water over a valley); a SUPER passage has the drain SUPERior, on top.

**Why the aqueduct-versus-siphon-aqueduct distinction matters more than the name:**

| | **AQUEDUCT** | **SIPHON AQUEDUCT** |
|---|---|---|
| **Drain's HFL relative to the canal trough bottom** | **BELOW it — the drain has clear headroom** | **ABOVE it — the drain must be pressurised to get through** |
| **Barrel flows** | **Part full, at atmospheric pressure** | **FULL, under pressure** |
| **Needs** | Simple barrel | **Impervious floor, cut-offs, energy dissipation downstream** |
| **Silting risk** | Low | **HIGH — velocity varies, silt deposits in the barrel** |
| Cost | Lower | Higher |

> **The choice is not the designer's: it is decided by the LEVELS.** If the drain's high flood level is above the underside of the canal trough, a siphon aqueduct is unavoidable.

> **And the siphon aqueduct's problems are real.** Because the barrel runs under pressure, **an impervious floor with upstream and downstream cut-offs is needed** — the same uplift and exit-gradient analysis as for a weir. **And silt deposited in the barrel during low flows must be flushed out**, or the capacity is progressively lost.

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **Super passage** | **The EXACT REVERSE — drain carried over the canal** ← the mirror trap |
| **Level crossing** | **The canal and drain are allowed to MIX in a common pool, then separated by regulators.** Used where the drain is large and the canal small |
| **Aqueduct** | ✓ |
| **Canal siphon** | **The canal passes UNDER the drain, under pressure — the reverse again, and pressurised** |

> **Option (a) is the designed trap because it is the exact mirror image**, and the two words give no help unless the naming rule is known. **This is a question where knowing one rule answers it and knowing four definitions separately does not.**

**When each is chosen — the selection logic, which is the substantive content:**

| Situation | Structure |
|---|---|
| **Canal bed well above the drain bed; drain flood level low** | **AQUEDUCT** |
| **Canal bed above the drain bed but the drain's HFL is high** | **SIPHON AQUEDUCT** |
| **Drain bed well above the canal FSL** | **SUPER PASSAGE** |
| **Drain bed above the canal but canal FSL is higher** | **CANAL SIPHON** |
| **Drain is LARGE and the canal SMALL, and the levels are similar** | **LEVEL CROSSING** |
| **Drain is very small** | **INLET (admit it into the canal) and OUTLET** |

> **Notice that the whole selection is a matter of comparing four levels: canal bed, canal FSL, drain bed, drain HFL.** No judgement is involved once those are surveyed — **which is why an accurate levelling survey at every drainage crossing is the first task in canal alignment, and why a mistake there is expensive to discover later.**

> **The economic reality behind it: an aqueduct is the cheapest of the four and a canal siphon the most troublesome**, because a pressurised canal barrel silts and cannot easily be inspected. **So a canal alignment is chosen, where the ground allows, to keep the canal ABOVE the drains it crosses** — and that preference shapes the route of the whole scheme.

examTip.trick: **Name the structure after WHAT IS ON TOP.** Canal on top = aqueduct; drain on top = super passage. Add "siphon" when the lower channel must run under pressure.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) super passage is the exact MIRROR IMAGE**, and the words give no help without the naming rule. One rule answers this; four memorised definitions do not.
examTip.mnemonic: **The choice is decided by four surveyed levels** — canal bed, canal FSL, drain bed, drain HFL — not by judgement. Which is why accurate levelling at every crossing is the first task in canal alignment.

questions.stem: A hydropower plant has an installed capacity of 40 MW and generates 175.2 GWh in a year. Its annual capacity factor is:
questions.solution:
**50 per cent.**

**The definition:**

> **Capacity factor = (actual energy generated in a period) / (energy that would be generated at FULL capacity throughout that period)**

**Step 1 — the energy possible at full capacity for a year:**

> **Hours in a year = 365 × 24 = 8760 h**

> **E_max = 40 MW × 8760 h = 350,400 MWh = 350.4 GWh**

**Step 2 — the ratio:**

> **Capacity factor = 175.2 / 350.4 = 0.50 = 50 %** ✓

> **The numbers are chosen so the answer is exactly half**, which is a useful sign that the arithmetic is right: **175.2 is precisely half of 350.4.**

> **A quicker route: 175,200 MWh ÷ 40 MW = 4380 hours of full-capacity equivalent operation, and 4380/8760 = 0.5.** That intermediate figure — **4380 EQUIVALENT FULL-LOAD HOURS** — is often more informative than the percentage, because it says directly how long the plant effectively ran flat out.

**What the capacity factor tells you, and what it does not:**

> **A LOW capacity factor is not necessarily a fault.** It has two quite different causes, and distinguishing them is the whole value of the number:

| Cause of a low capacity factor | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| **The plant is UNAVAILABLE — breakdowns, outages** | **A PROBLEM — measured separately by the plant use factor** |
| **The WATER is not there — dry-season flow is a fraction of installed capacity** | **NORMAL for a run-of-river plant, and designed in** |
| **The plant is a PEAKING plant, run only at peak demand** | **BY DESIGN — a storage plant deliberately idles off-peak** |

> **The last row is important: a low capacity factor can be a sign of a VALUABLE plant.** A storage or peaking plant that runs only when demand and prices are highest has a low capacity factor by intent, and its energy is worth more per unit.

**The related factors, which are constantly confused:**

| Factor | Definition |
|---|---|
| **LOAD factor** | **Average load / PEAK LOAD over the period** |
| **CAPACITY factor (plant factor)** | **Average load / INSTALLED CAPACITY** ← |
| **UTILISATION factor** | **Maximum load used / installed capacity** |
| **PLANT USE factor** | **Energy produced / (capacity × hours the plant was ACTUALLY IN OPERATION)** |
| **DIVERSITY factor** | Sum of individual peaks / system peak |

> **The distinction between LOAD factor and CAPACITY factor is the one to get right: load factor is against the PEAK LOAD, capacity factor against the INSTALLED CAPACITY.**

> **They are equal only when the peak load equals the installed capacity** — that is, when the plant is exactly the right size for its load. **A plant with spare capacity has a load factor higher than its capacity factor**, and the gap between the two measures how much spare capacity it carries.

> **And the plant use factor is the one that isolates availability**, because it counts only the hours the plant was running. **A plant with a low capacity factor and a high plant use factor was short of water, not broken.**

**Typical capacity factors, for orientation:**

| Plant | Capacity factor |
|---|---|
| **Run-of-river hydro (Nepal)** | **40-60 %** ← where this plant sits |
| **Storage hydro, peaking** | **20-40 % by design** |
| **Storage hydro, base load** | 50-70 % |
| **Solar PV** | **15-25 %** |
| **Wind** | 25-40 % |
| **Thermal base load** | **60-85 %** |
| **Nuclear** | **80-90 %** |

> **Nepal's run-of-river plants sit at 40-60 per cent, and the reason is the monsoon**: at full flow they generate at capacity, and in the dry season their output falls to a fraction. **50 per cent is a normal and respectable figure for such a plant.**

> **This is exactly why capacity in megawatts is a misleading way to compare Nepali hydropower projects.** A 40 MW run-of-river plant and a 40 MW storage plant deliver very different amounts of energy and very different value — **the storage plant's energy arrives when it is needed, and the run-of-river plant's arrives when the river decides.**

> **So the honest comparison is on ENERGY (GWh per year) and on DRY-SEASON energy in particular**, not on installed capacity. **A candidate who understands that has understood the topic rather than the formula.**

examTip.trick: **8760 hours in a year. 40 MW × 8760 = 350.4 GWh possible, and 175.2/350.4 = 50 %.** Or divide energy by capacity: 4380 equivalent full-load hours out of 8760.
examTip.trap: **LOAD factor is against the PEAK LOAD; CAPACITY factor against the INSTALLED CAPACITY.** They coincide only when the plant is exactly sized for its load, and the gap measures the spare capacity.
examTip.mnemonic: **A low capacity factor can mean a broken plant OR a valuable peaking plant OR simply a dry season** — the PLANT USE FACTOR separates them, since it counts only the hours actually run. Compare hydro projects on GWh, not MW.

questions.stem: In a run-of-river hydropower scheme in a steep Himalayan river, the principal purpose of a settling basin immediately downstream of the intake is to:
options: raise the water level so that the headrace can be fed by gravity
provide storage so that the plant can operate through the dry season
dissipate the energy of the diverted flow before it enters the tunnel
remove suspended sediment coarse enough to abrade the turbine runners
questions.solution:
**To remove suspended sediment coarse enough to abrade the turbine runners.**

**Why sediment removal is the governing problem in Himalayan hydropower:**

> **Himalayan rivers carry among the highest sediment loads in the world** — the young, rapidly uplifting, poorly consolidated geology delivers enormous quantities of sand and silt, most of it in the monsoon.

> **The sediment that matters is the HARD, ANGULAR, coarse fraction — chiefly QUARTZ, with a Mohs hardness of 7.**

> **Passed through a turbine at high velocity, quartz particles ABRADE the runner, the guide vanes and the liners.**

| Consequence of abrasion | Note |
|---|---|
| **Loss of EFFICIENCY** | **The runner profile is eroded away, so the machine no longer matches its design geometry** |
| **Loss of generation during repairs** | **Runner replacement or repair takes the unit out for weeks** |
| **Cavitation, once the surface roughens** | **The two damage mechanisms then reinforce each other** |
| Shortened plant life | Major overhauls far earlier than designed |

> **The interaction between abrasion and cavitation is the point worth understanding: abrasion roughens and pits the surface, roughness triggers local flow separation, separation lowers the local pressure, and cavitation begins.** Each then accelerates the other.

> **So a settling basin is not an optional refinement in this setting — it protects the single most expensive component of the plant.**

**How a settling basin works:**

> **The flow is spread into a wide, deep basin so that its VELOCITY FALLS FAR ENOUGH for particles above a target size to settle out.**

| Design parameter | Typical |
|---|---|
| **Target particle size to remove** | **Commonly 0.2 to 0.3 mm and coarser (down to 0.15 mm for high-head plants)** |
| **Flow-through velocity** | **0.2 to 0.5 m/s — low enough for settling, high enough to avoid depositing everywhere** |
| **Basin length** | Enough that the settling time exceeds the transit time |
| **Flushing** | **Continuous or periodic, through a flushing conduit to the river** |

> **The governing relation is simply that the particle must reach the floor before the water reaches the outlet:  L / V ≥ D / w**, where w is the particle's settling velocity, giving **L ≥ V·D/w.**

> **The finer the particle to be removed, the smaller w, and the longer the basin must be.** Which is why the target size is an economic decision: **removing everything is impossible, and removing very fine silt would need an impossibly large basin.**

> **Fine silt is therefore allowed through deliberately** — it is softer in effect and its abrasive damage is tolerable — **while the coarse quartz that does the real damage is caught.**

**Why the distractors are wrong — each names a real structure's job:**

| Option | The structure that does it |
|---|---|
| **Raise the water level to feed the headrace** | **The DIVERSION WEIR at the intake** |
| **Storage for dry-season operation** | **A RESERVOIR — and a run-of-river scheme by definition HAS NONE** ← |
| **Dissipate energy of the diverted flow** | **A stilling basin, plunge pool or baffle — an energy dissipator, a different structure with a confusingly similar name** ← the trap |
| **Remove abrasive sediment** | ✓ **SETTLING BASIN** |

> **Option (b) is self-contradicting and worth noticing as a technique**: the stem says "run-of-river", and a run-of-river scheme is defined by having no meaningful storage. **A question that contains its own contradiction can be answered from the stem alone.**

> **Option (c) is the designed trap because "settling basin" and "stilling basin" differ by one letter and do entirely different jobs:**

| | **SETTLING basin** | **STILLING basin** |
|---|---|---|
| **Purpose** | **Remove SEDIMENT** | **Dissipate ENERGY** |
| **Mechanism** | **Low velocity, long residence time** | **Forced HYDRAULIC JUMP** |
| **Located** | **Downstream of the intake, on the water conveyance side** | **Downstream of a spillway or weir, on the river side** |
| **Wants velocity** | **LOW** | **HIGH entering, low leaving** |

> **They want opposite things of the flow**, which makes the near-identical names genuinely unhelpful. **Reading the word carefully is part of the answer.**

**The full sediment-handling chain of a Himalayan run-of-river scheme, since the basin is only one part:**

| Structure | Removes |
|---|---|
| **TRASH RACK** | Floating debris, branches, plastic |
| **BOULDER TRAP / gravel trap at the intake** | **Boulders and gravel — the coarsest fraction** |
| **Undersluice and silt excluder at the weir** | **Keeps bed load out of the intake in the first place** |
| **SETTLING BASIN** | **Sand — the abrasive fraction** ← |
| Forebay | A final settling opportunity |

> **The principle running through the chain is to exclude sediment as EARLY and as HIGH UP as possible.** Every particle kept out at the weir is one that need not be settled, flushed and disposed of later — **and the undersluice, which uses the river's own energy to keep bed load moving past the intake, is the cheapest device in the whole sequence.**

examTip.trick: **The damaging fraction is hard, angular QUARTZ (Mohs 7)**, which abrades runners and guide vanes. Abrasion roughens the surface, roughness triggers CAVITATION, and the two then accelerate each other.
examTip.trap: **SETTLING basin and STILLING basin differ by one letter and want OPPOSITE things of the flow** — low velocity to settle sediment, a forced hydraulic jump to kill energy. And option (b) contradicts the stem: run-of-river means no storage.
examTip.mnemonic: **L ≥ V·D/w** — the particle must reach the floor before the water reaches the outlet. Fine silt is let through deliberately, because catching it would need an impossibly long basin. Exclude sediment as EARLY and HIGH as possible.

questions.stem: The specific speed of a turbine is defined as the speed of a geometrically similar turbine that would:
options: develop unit power under unit head
pass unit discharge under unit head
develop unit power at unit speed
have unit runner diameter under unit head
questions.solution:
**Develop unit power under unit head.**

**The definition and the formula:**

> **The specific speed of a TURBINE is the speed at which a geometrically similar turbine would run to develop UNIT POWER under UNIT HEAD.**

> **N_s = N √P / H^{5/4}**

| Symbol | Meaning | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| **N** | Rotational speed | **rpm** |
| **P** | **POWER developed** | **kW** |
| **H** | Net head | **m** |

> **The 5/4 exponent on the head is the part most often misremembered**, and it follows from the similarity laws: **P ∝ H^{3/2} and N ∝ H^{1/2} for a given machine, so N√P/H^{5/4} is the combination that is invariant.**

**The crucial contrast with a PUMP — the two definitions are different:**

| Machine | Specific speed | Based on |
|---|---|---|
| **TURBINE** | **N_s = N√P / H^{5/4}** | **POWER** ← |
| **PUMP** | **N_s = N√Q / H^{3/4}** | **DISCHARGE** |

> **This is exactly the trap the question sets: option (b) — unit DISCHARGE under unit head — is the PUMP definition.**

> **The reason for the difference is what each machine is for.** A turbine's output is POWER, and its rating is in kilowatts; **a pump's output is FLOW, and its rating is in litres per second.** So each specific speed is built on the quantity the machine is bought to deliver.

> **Confusing the two is a real error, because a pump's and a turbine's specific speeds are not comparable numbers at all** — they have different dimensions and different numerical ranges.

**Why specific speed is the most useful single number about a turbine:**

> **It identifies the TYPE of machine, independently of its size.**

| Specific speed (metric, kW) | Turbine | Head |
|---|---|---|
| **8 - 30** | **PELTON, single jet** | **Very high (above ~250 m)** |
| **30 - 50** | Pelton, multi-jet | High |
| **50 - 250** | **FRANCIS** | **Medium (45-400 m)** |
| **250 - 850** | **KAPLAN / propeller** | **Low (below ~60 m)** |

> **The trend to hold onto: LOW specific speed goes with HIGH head, and HIGH specific speed with LOW head.**

> **The physical reason is worth stating.** A high-head machine extracts a great deal of energy from a small flow, so it can be small and slow-turning relative to its power; **a low-head machine must pass a large flow to develop the same power, so it must be large in flow area and runs fast for its head.**

> **So specific speed is really a shape parameter: it tells you how the runner must be proportioned**, and the three turbine families are simply the three shapes that work at the three ends of the range.

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

| Option | What it actually defines |
|---|---|
| **Unit power under unit head** | ✓ **Turbine specific speed** |
| **Unit DISCHARGE under unit head** | **PUMP specific speed** ← the designed trap |
| **Unit power at unit SPEED** | **Not a standard definition — and it inverts the roles, since SPEED is what the definition solves for** |
| **Unit runner DIAMETER under unit head** | **Not a specific speed at all; diameter is a size, and the point of specific speed is to be independent of size** |

> **Option (c) is subtly self-defeating: specific speed IS a speed, so it cannot be defined at a specified unit speed.** Noticing that disposes of it without any recall.

**The related unit quantities, since they come from the same similarity analysis:**

| Quantity | Definition | Expression |
|---|---|---|
| **UNIT SPEED** | Speed under unit head | **N_u = N/√H** |
| **UNIT DISCHARGE** | Discharge under unit head | **Q_u = Q/√H** |
| **UNIT POWER** | Power under unit head | **P_u = P/H^{3/2}** |

> **These three let a machine tested at one head be predicted at another**, which is their purpose: **a model test at 3 m of head predicts the prototype at 300 m.**

> **And they are what makes model testing of turbines possible at all** — a full-size Francis runner cannot be tested in a laboratory, but a one-tenth scale model can, and the similarity laws carry the result across.

**One honest caveat, since it matters in practice:** **efficiency does NOT scale by these laws.** A model is always less efficient than its prototype, because the relative roughness and the relative clearances are larger at small scale. **A "step-up" formula (Moody's) is applied to predict the prototype efficiency from the model's**, and it is an empirical correction rather than a similarity result — which is why guaranteed efficiencies are confirmed by field tests on the built machine, not by model tests alone.

examTip.trick: **Turbine: N_s = N√P/H^{5/4}, based on POWER. Pump: N_s = N√Q/H^{3/4}, based on DISCHARGE.** Each is built on the quantity the machine is bought to deliver.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) is the PUMP definition** — the designed trap. And option (c) is self-defeating: specific speed IS a speed, so it cannot be defined at a specified unit speed.
examTip.mnemonic: **LOW specific speed = HIGH head (Pelton 8-30); HIGH specific speed = LOW head (Kaplan 250-850); Francis in between (50-250).** It is really a shape parameter. And note **efficiency does NOT scale** — Moody's step-up is empirical.

questions.stem: In a penstock, the thickness of the steel shell is governed principally by:
options: the weight of the water it carries
the external soil pressure where it is buried
the internal pressure, including the water hammer rise above static head
questions.solution:
**The internal pressure, including the water hammer rise above the static head.**

**Why internal pressure governs:**

> **A penstock is a thin-walled cylinder under internal pressure, and the CIRCUMFERENTIAL (hoop) stress governs:**

> **σ_h = p D / (2 t)**   ⟹   **t = p D / (2 σ_allowable)**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **p** | **DESIGN internal pressure = static head + water hammer rise** |
| **D** | Internal diameter |
| **t** | **Shell thickness — what is being designed** |
| **σ_allowable** | Permissible stress in the steel |

> **Note that the hoop stress is TWICE the longitudinal stress in a thin cylinder** (σ_l = pD/4t), which is why the circumferential direction governs and why a pressure vessel splits along its length rather than across it.

**Why the water hammer term is the substance of the answer:**

> **The static head alone is not the design pressure.** When the turbine gates close, the pressure rises above static — sometimes greatly.

> **The maximum rise for INSTANTANEOUS closure is given by the Joukowsky (waterhammer) equation:**

> **Δh = (a / g) × V**

> **where a is the pressure wave speed, typically 900 to 1200 m/s in a steel penstock.**

> **So for a flow velocity of 4 m/s and a = 1000 m/s:  Δh = (1000/9.81) × 4 ≈ 408 m.**

> **That is a pressure rise of 400 metres of head from a 4 m/s flow** — comparable with or greater than the static head on many plants. **Which is exactly why the design pressure, not the static pressure, sets the thickness.**

> **A penstock designed for the static head alone would burst on the first load rejection.**

**How the rise is actually limited in design:**

| Measure | Effect |
|---|---|
| **SLOW the gate closure** | **If the closure time exceeds 2L/a, the closure is "slow" and the rise is much less than Joukowsky** ← the primary control |
| **SURGE TANK** | **Shortens the effective column length to the penstock alone** |
| **Pressure relief valve / synchronous bypass** | Releases water as the gates close |
| **Flywheel effect of the generator** | Slows the speed rise, allowing slower gate closure |
| Larger diameter (lower velocity) | Δh is proportional to V |

> **The critical time 2L/a is the concept to hold: it is the time for the pressure wave to travel to the reservoir and back.** Close faster than that and the full Joukowsky rise develops; close slower and the returning wave relieves the pressure while closure is still in progress.

> **For a 500 m penstock with a = 1000 m/s, the critical time is 1 second** — so any closure taking more than a second is "slow", which is why governor closure times of 3 to 10 seconds are specified.

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Weight of the water carried** | **A real load — it produces longitudinal bending between supports and is why anchor and saddle spacing is designed. But it does not govern the SHELL THICKNESS** |
| **External soil pressure** | **Matters for a buried penstock, and governs BUCKLING when the pipe is EMPTY (or under vacuum) — a genuine check, but a secondary one** ← |
| **Temperature range** | **Produces longitudinal forces, handled by EXPANSION JOINTS and anchor blocks, not by thickness** |
| **Internal pressure with water hammer** | ✓ |

> **Option (b) is the most interesting distractor because it names a real and sometimes critical check.** An empty buried penstock, or one subjected to a vacuum by a downstream break, **can COLLAPSE inward under external pressure** — and the thickness needed to resist buckling can exceed that needed for internal pressure in a large, low-head pipe.

> **But for the normal high-head case the internal pressure governs by a wide margin**, and the external check is made afterwards. **The honest statement is: internal pressure governs, and the empty/vacuum case must still be checked.**

> **The vacuum case is also why an AIR VALVE is fitted at the high point of a penstock** — to admit air when the pipe drains and prevent exactly that collapse.

**The other components of penstock design, for completeness:**

| Component | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **ANCHOR BLOCKS** | **Take the thrust at bends and the longitudinal force; fix the pipe at intervals** |
| **SADDLE / ring supports** | Carry the weight between anchors, allowing axial movement |
| **EXPANSION JOINTS** | **Absorb thermal movement between anchors** |
| **AIR VALVE at high points** | **Admits air on draining — prevents collapse; releases air on filling** |
| **Butterfly or spherical inlet valve** | Isolates the penstock |
| **Corrosion protection** | Coating inside and out; cathodic protection where buried |

> **The anchor block at a BEND is the one that carries the largest force, and it is easy to underestimate.** The thrust is the vector change in momentum plus pressure force: **for a 90° bend at 400 m of head on a 2 m pipe, the resultant thrust is of the order of several thousand kilonewtons** — which is why anchor blocks are massive concrete structures rather than brackets.

> **And the economic diameter of a penstock is a genuine optimisation**: a larger diameter costs more steel but loses less head to friction, so the total of capital cost plus the capitalised value of lost energy has a minimum. **That optimisation, not the hydraulics alone, sets the diameter — and the diameter then sets the thickness through the hoop-stress formula above.**

examTip.trick: **t = pD/2σ from hoop stress, with p the DESIGN pressure = static head PLUS water hammer rise.** Hoop stress is twice the longitudinal, which is why a pressure pipe splits lengthwise.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) names a real check** — an EMPTY or vacuum-subjected buried penstock can buckle inward, which is why an air valve sits at the high point. But internal pressure governs the normal case by a wide margin.
examTip.mnemonic: **Joukowsky: Δh = aV/g.** At a = 1000 m/s and V = 4 m/s that is 400 m of head — often more than the static head. The control is the critical time **2L/a**: close slower than that and the returning wave relieves the pressure.

questions.stem: In a flexible pavement, alligator (fatigue) cracking originates:
options: at the surface, from ultraviolet ageing of the binder
at the surface, from excessive bitumen content
at the BOTTOM of the bituminous layer, from repeated tensile strain, and propagates upward
in the subgrade, and appears only after the subgrade has failed completely
questions.solution:
**At the BOTTOM of the bituminous layer, from repeated tensile strain, propagating upward.**

**Why the bottom — the strain picture in a flexible pavement:**

> **A wheel load bends the bituminous layer like a slab on an elastic foundation.**

> **The layer is therefore in COMPRESSION at the top and in TENSION at the BOTTOM.**

> **The critical HORIZONTAL TENSILE STRAIN occurs at the UNDERSIDE of the bituminous layer, directly beneath the wheel.**

> **Bitumen is weak in tension and fails by FATIGUE — not from one load, but from the accumulation of millions of small tensile strains.**

> **So the crack starts at the bottom where the strain is greatest, and works its way UP through the layer until it reaches the surface.**

> **By the time an interconnected pattern of cracks resembling alligator hide is visible at the surface, the layer has been cracked through most of its depth for some time.** That is the practically important consequence: **the visible damage lags the actual damage considerably.**

**The two critical strains that govern flexible pavement design:**

| Strain | Location | Failure it causes |
|---|---|---|
| **Horizontal TENSILE strain** | **BOTTOM of the bituminous layer** | **FATIGUE (alligator) cracking** ← |
| **Vertical COMPRESSIVE strain** | **TOP of the SUBGRADE** | **RUTTING (permanent deformation)** |

> **Those two, and only those two, are the design criteria of a mechanistic flexible pavement design (IRC 37).** Everything else in the design serves to keep them within limits.

> **The design equations are of the form N = k(1/ε)^n**, with the exponent n around 3.9 for fatigue and 4.5 for rutting — **which is why a small increase in strain shortens the life so dramatically, and is the same fourth-power sensitivity that makes axle load so important.**

**How each failure is remedied — and the remedies are different, which is why the diagnosis matters:**

| Failure | Remedy |
|---|---|
| **FATIGUE cracking** | **A thicker or stiffer BITUMINOUS layer** — the bending is in that layer |
| **RUTTING from subgrade** | **A thicker GRANULAR base/sub-base**, to spread the load and reduce subgrade strain |
| Rutting within the bituminous layer | A stiffer, better-graded mix; harder binder |

> **Diagnosing which failure has occurred determines what to build.** Overlaying a rutted pavement with more bitumen does not reduce the subgrade strain much; **thickening the granular layers does little for fatigue in the bituminous layer.** The wrong remedy is money spent for no gain.

**Why the distractors are wrong — and two of them describe real, different distresses:**

| Option | The distress it actually describes |
|---|---|
| **Surface, from UV ageing of binder** | **Real — but that causes RAVELLING and BLOCK cracking (a rectangular pattern unrelated to wheel paths), not alligator cracking** ← |
| **Surface, from excessive bitumen** | **Real — excess binder causes BLEEDING and a slippery surface, and contributes to rutting. Not fatigue cracking** |
| **Bottom of bituminous layer, tensile fatigue, upward** | ✓ |
| **In the subgrade, only after complete failure** | **Wrong location and wrong sequence** — fatigue is a distress of the bituminous layer |

> **Option (a) is the instructive distractor because BLOCK CRACKING is genuinely a surface-initiated, age-related crack pattern** — and telling the two apart in the field is a real skill:

| | **ALLIGATOR (fatigue) cracking** | **BLOCK cracking** |
|---|---|---|
| **Pattern** | **Interconnected, irregular, small pieces — like alligator hide** | **Large RECTANGULAR blocks, roughly 0.3-3 m** |
| **Location** | **CONFINED TO THE WHEEL PATHS** ← the diagnostic | **Over the WHOLE surface, including areas with no traffic** |
| **Cause** | **Repeated traffic loading** | **Binder ageing and shrinkage; temperature cycling** |
| **Indicates** | **Structural inadequacy — needs a strengthening overlay** | **Ageing of the surfacing — needs resurfacing, not strengthening** |

> **The location is the diagnostic: fatigue cracking follows the wheel paths, block cracking does not.** Which means a walk along the road answers the question that a laboratory test would take weeks to settle.

**The other common flexible pavement distresses, for completeness:**

| Distress | Cause |
|---|---|
| **RUTTING** | Permanent deformation in the wheel paths, from subgrade or mix |
| **RAVELLING** | **Loss of aggregate from the surface — binder ageing, poor compaction, or stripping** |
| **POTHOLES** | Progression of cracking plus water ingress |
| **STRIPPING** | **Loss of ADHESION between bitumen and aggregate, caused by WATER — the underlying mechanism of much surface failure** |
| **Corrugation and shoving** | Unstable mix, too much fine aggregate or binder |
| Edge failure | Inadequate lateral support from the shoulder |

> **Water is the common factor behind most of these**, directly or indirectly. **Stripping in particular is water attacking the bitumen-aggregate bond**, and it is worse with hydrophilic (siliceous) aggregates — **which is why an anti-stripping agent or hydrated lime is added where such aggregates must be used.**

> **And it is why the single most cost-effective maintenance activity on a flexible pavement is keeping the side drains clear.** A blocked drain saturates the subgrade, the subgrade weakens, the strains rise, and every one of the distresses above accelerates.

examTip.trick: **A wheel load bends the bituminous layer: compression on top, TENSION at the bottom.** Fatigue cracks start at the bottom where the tensile strain is greatest and propagate UPWARD — so visible damage lags real damage.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) describes BLOCK cracking, which IS surface-initiated and age-related.** The diagnostic is location: **fatigue cracking follows the WHEEL PATHS; block cracking covers the whole surface, traffic or not.**
examTip.mnemonic: **Two critical strains only: tensile at the bottom of the bitumen (fatigue) and compressive at the top of the subgrade (rutting).** Fatigue needs a thicker BITUMINOUS layer; rutting needs thicker GRANULAR layers. The wrong remedy buys nothing.

questions.stem: A machine costs Rs 500,000, has a salvage value of Rs 50,000 and a useful life of 10 years. By the straight line method, the book value at the end of the fourth year is:
questions.solution:
**Rs 320,000.**

**Step 1 — the annual depreciation by the straight line method:**

> **D = (Cost − Salvage value) / Useful life**

> **= (500,000 − 50,000) / 10**

> **= 450,000 / 10 = Rs 45,000 per year**

> **The depreciable amount is the cost MINUS the salvage value, not the cost itself.** That is the step most often missed — **an asset expected to be worth Rs 50,000 at the end has only lost Rs 450,000 of value, not Rs 500,000.**

**Step 2 — the book value after four years:**

> **BV₄ = Cost − 4 × D**

> **= 500,000 − 4 × 45,000**

> **= 500,000 − 180,000 = Rs 320,000** ✓

**The check that confirms it:**

> **After 10 years: BV₁₀ = 500,000 − 10 × 45,000 = 500,000 − 450,000 = Rs 50,000 = the salvage value.** ✓

> **A straight-line schedule must land exactly on the salvage value at the end of the life**, and testing that takes one line. **Any method whose final book value is not the salvage value has been set up wrongly.**

**Where each distractor comes from:**

| Option | The slip |
|---|---|
| **Rs 300,000** | **Depreciating the FULL COST: D = 500,000/10 = 50,000, so BV = 500,000 minus 200,000. The salvage value ignored entirely** <- the commonest error |
| **Rs 275,000** | Depreciating the full cost over a shorter assumed life |
| **Rs 180,000** | **The ACCUMULATED DEPRECIATION (4 x 45,000), reported instead of the book value** <- the other trap |
| **Rs 320,000** | correct |

> **Option (a) is caught by the end-of-life check: 500,000 minus 10 x 50,000 = 0, which contradicts the stated salvage value of Rs 50,000.** So that depreciation rate cannot be right, and the check catches it immediately.

> **Option (c) is the classic case of answering a different question.** 4 x 45,000 = 180,000 is how much value has been LOST; the book value is what REMAINS. **Reading whether the question asks for the depreciation or for the book value is the whole of it.**

**The depreciation methods, since any may be asked:**

| Method | Annual charge | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **STRAIGHT LINE** | **(C − S)/n — CONSTANT each year** | **Simplest; assumes uniform loss of value** ← |
| **DECLINING BALANCE (constant percentage)** | **A fixed PERCENTAGE of the reducing book value** | **ACCELERATED — most depreciation in the early years** |
| **Double declining balance** | **2/n of the book value each year** | Accelerated; ignores salvage until the floor is reached |
| **SUM OF YEARS DIGITS** | **(remaining life / Σ years) × (C − S)** | Accelerated, but linearly declining |
| **SINKING FUND** | **A uniform annual deposit that, with interest, accumulates to (C − S)** | **The only method that recognises the TIME VALUE of money** |
| Service output / production unit | Per unit produced | Matches usage rather than time |

> **The accelerated methods reflect economic reality better than the straight line does**, because most assets lose more value in their first years — a new machine becomes a used machine the day it is commissioned.

> **And the SINKING FUND method is the conceptually distinct one:** the others merely allocate a past cost across years, **while a sinking fund actually sets money aside at interest to buy the replacement.** It is the only method that connects depreciation accounting to the cash that will be needed.

**Why depreciation matters to an engineer, not only to an accountant:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **Equipment hire rates and plant costing** | **The owning cost of plant is depreciation plus interest, insurance and taxes** |
| **Life-cycle cost comparison of alternatives** | Which machine is cheaper over its life, not to buy |
| **Replacement timing** | **When does rising maintenance outweigh the remaining value?** |
| **Tender rate analysis** | Plant charges in a bill of quantities |

> **The plant-costing application is the everyday one.** A contractor's rate for excavation must recover the excavator's depreciation, and getting that wrong makes a tender either uncompetitive or loss-making.

> **And the replacement decision is where the accounting meets the engineering.** An old machine's depreciation charge is low (it has little value left to lose) but its **maintenance and downtime costs are rising** — the economic life ends at the year where the total of the two is least, which is generally well before the machine stops working.

**The distinction worth keeping clear, since it is examined:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **DEPRECIATION** | **Loss of value from USE, AGE and WEAR — a normal, predictable decline** |
| **OBSOLESCENCE** | **Loss of value because something BETTER exists, though the asset is undamaged** |
| **SALVAGE / scrap value** | **What it fetches at the end of its useful life** |
| **Book value** | **Cost less accumulated depreciation — an accounting figure, not a market price** |

> **Obsolescence is the one that catches engineers out**, because it has nothing to do with the asset's condition. **A perfectly serviceable machine can be worth scrap value the day a better one is marketed**, and no maintenance regime protects against it.

examTip.trick: **Depreciate (Cost − Salvage), not Cost.** D = 450,000/10 = 45,000 per year, so BV₄ = 500,000 − 180,000 = **Rs 320,000.**
examTip.trap: **Forgetting the salvage value gives D = 50,000 and BV = Rs 300,000** - caught by the end-of-life check, since 500,000 minus 10 x 50,000 = 0 contradicts the stated salvage. And **Rs 180,000 is the ACCUMULATED DEPRECIATION, not the book value.**
examTip.mnemonic: **A straight-line schedule must land exactly on the salvage value in year n** — one line to verify. And know that **SINKING FUND is the only method recognising the time value of money**; the rest merely allocate a past cost.

questions.stem: An engineer is instructed by a client to certify work that the engineer knows has not been completed to the specification. The engineer's primary obligation under an engineering code of ethics is to:
options: hold the safety, health and welfare of the public paramount, and decline to issue the false certificate
comply with the client's instruction, since the client is paying for the service
issue the certificate but record a private note of disagreement in the engineer's own file
resign from the commission without informing anyone of the defect
questions.solution:
**Hold the safety, health and welfare of the public paramount, and decline to issue the false certificate.**

**The fundamental canon:**

> **Every engineering code of ethics — the Nepal Engineering Council's included — places the same obligation first:**

> **"Engineers shall hold PARAMOUNT the safety, health and welfare of the PUBLIC in the performance of their professional duties."**

> **The word PARAMOUNT is doing precise work.** It does not mean "important among other things"; **it means it OVERRIDES every other obligation, including the duty to the client and the engineer's own interest.**

> **That is what makes engineering a profession rather than a trade.** A trader's duty runs to whoever pays; **a professional's duty runs first to those who will be affected by the work and who never had a say in it.**

**Why a certificate is a special case — the reason this scenario is the standard ethics question:**

> **A CERTIFICATE is a statement made by a professional on which others RELY.**

| Who relies on it | For what |
|---|---|
| **The client** | To release payment |
| **The owner or a purchaser** | To believe the work is sound |
| **The lender or insurer** | To advance funds or accept risk |
| **The public authority** | **To permit occupation or use** |
| **The eventual OCCUPANTS** | **Their safety** |

> **The engineer's signature is the whole value of the document.** A certificate signed by someone who knows it to be untrue is not merely a lie — **it is a lie designed to be relied upon by people who cannot check it themselves.**

> **That is why false certification is treated as among the gravest professional offences, and why it is grounds for removal from the register under the NEC Act.**

> **It is also, separately, likely to be a criminal fraud and a civil wrong** — the professional consequence is not the only one.

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

| Option | Why not |
|---|---|
| **Public paramount; decline** | ✓ |
| **Comply — the client is paying** | **The clearest possible statement of the error.** Payment buys competent professional service; it does not buy the engineer's signature on a falsehood ← |
| **Certify, but note disagreement privately** | **The certificate still goes out and is still relied upon. A private note protects the engineer's conscience and no one's safety** ← the seductive option |
| **Resign silently** | **Removes the engineer from the problem and leaves the defect in the building.** The next engineer may not know, and the public certainly will not |

> **Option (c) is the one worth thinking hardest about, because it is the compromise a real person under pressure is most tempted by.** It feels like a middle path: do as asked, but leave a record.

> **It fails completely, and the reason is worth stating: the harm is done by the certificate, not by the engineer's state of mind.** The document still circulates; the payment is still released; the occupants are still at risk. **A private note changes nothing except the engineer's later ability to say "I knew".**

> **Which in fact makes the position worse, not better — a documented awareness of the defect at the time of certifying is evidence of knowing misrepresentation.**

> **Option (d) is worth taking seriously too, because resignation IS sometimes the right final step** — but silent resignation is not. **The obligation is to the public, and it does not end when the engagement does.** If the defect endangers people, the appropriate authority must be informed.

**What the engineer should actually do, in order — since the question deserves a constructive answer:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Record the facts in writing: what is not to specification, and how it was established** |
| **2** | **Inform the client IN WRITING that the certificate cannot be issued, with the reasons** |
| **3** | **Offer the constructive route: what remedial work would allow certification** |
| **4** | **Escalate within the client's organisation if the instruction is repeated** |
| **5** | **If there is a DANGER to the public, inform the relevant authority** |
| **6** | **Withdraw from the commission if the position is untenable — but not silently** |
| **7** | Seek guidance from the professional body |

> **Step 3 matters as much as step 2.** Refusing is necessary but not sufficient; **the professional contribution is to say what would make certification possible.** An engineer who only says no has done half the job.

> **And step 1 is what makes the rest survivable.** Ethics questions in practice are rarely decided in the moment; they are decided months later by what is on the record. **A contemporaneous written record of the defect and of the refusal protects both the public and the engineer.**

**The other canons that sit beneath the first, since they are examined together:**

| Canon | Note |
|---|---|
| **Public safety PARAMOUNT** | The overriding duty ← |
| **Perform services only in areas of COMPETENCE** | Do not certify what you are not qualified to judge |
| **Issue statements that are OBJECTIVE and TRUTHFUL** | Directly engaged here |
| **Act as a FAITHFUL AGENT of the client — and DISCLOSE conflicts of interest** | **Subordinate to the first canon** |
| **Avoid deceptive acts** | — |
| **Conduct oneself honourably; uphold the profession's integrity** | — |
| **Continue professional development** | — |

> **The fourth canon is the one in tension here, and the resolution is in the ordering: the duty of faithful agency is real but SUBORDINATE.** An engineer is the client's faithful agent in everything that does not put the public at risk — **and the moment those conflict, the ordering of the canons decides it, which is exactly why they are ordered.**

examTip.trick: **PARAMOUNT means it OVERRIDES every other duty** — including the duty to the client. The canons are ORDERED for exactly this situation, and public safety is first.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) is the seductive compromise** — certify but note it privately. It fails because the HARM is done by the certificate, not by the engineer's state of mind. And a documented awareness while certifying is evidence of knowing misrepresentation.
examTip.mnemonic: **Refusing is necessary but not sufficient** — say in writing what remedial work WOULD allow certification. And resignation may be right, but never SILENT resignation: the duty to the public does not end with the engagement.

questions.stem: In a construction contract, a retention money provision allows the employer to:
options: recover liquidated damages for late completion
pay the contractor in advance for materials brought to site
adjust the contract price for changes in the cost of labour and materials
withhold a percentage of each payment as security for the completion of defects
questions.solution:
**Withhold a percentage of each payment as security for the completion of defects.**

**How retention works:**

> **A stated percentage of each interim payment is withheld by the employer rather than paid to the contractor.**

| Stage | Typical treatment |
|---|---|
| **Deduction from each interim certificate** | **5 to 10 % of the amount certified** |
| **LIMIT (retention ceiling)** | **Commonly 5 % of the contract price** |
| **On substantial completion (taking over)** | **HALF the retention is released** |
| **On expiry of the DEFECTS LIABILITY PERIOD** | **The remaining half is released** |
| Defects liability period | **Commonly 12 months from completion** |

> **The two-stage release is the essential feature.** The first half is released when the works are usable; **the second half is held through the defects liability period, and it is that residue which secures the making good of defects.**

**Why retention exists — the commercial logic:**

> **The employer's leverage over a contractor falls to almost nothing once the final payment is made and the contractor has left the site.**
