> **Defects, however, tend to appear AFTER completion** — a leaking roof shows itself in the first monsoon, settlement over the first year, a failed damp course when the plaster blisters.

> **Retention keeps a sum of the contractor's own money in the employer's hands throughout that period**, which is a far more effective incentive to return and fix a defect than any contractual right to sue.

> **The alternative is a DEFECTS LIABILITY BOND or bank guarantee**, which serves the same purpose without depriving the contractor of working capital — and many contractors prefer it for exactly that reason.

**Why each distractor is wrong — and every one names a real and different contract provision:**

| Option | The provision that actually does it |
|---|---|
| **Recover damages for late completion** | **LIQUIDATED DAMAGES — a pre-agreed sum per day or week of delay** |
| **Pay in advance for materials on site** | **ADVANCE PAYMENT, or "materials on site" payment / secured advance** |
| **Adjust the price for cost changes** | **PRICE ADJUSTMENT (escalation) clause, usually formula-based on published indices** |
| **Withhold a percentage as security for defects** | ✓ **RETENTION MONEY** |

> **This is a clean four-way match, and the four provisions are worth holding as a set** because a question can be asked from any of them:

| Provision | Protects | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| **RETENTION** | **Employer, against DEFECTS** | **Withhold a % of each payment** ← |
| **PERFORMANCE BOND / security** | **Employer, against NON-PERFORMANCE or abandonment** | **Bank guarantee, typically 5-10 % of the contract price** |
| **LIQUIDATED DAMAGES** | **Employer, against DELAY** | **Pre-agreed sum per day, capped (commonly 10 % of contract price)** |
| **ADVANCE PAYMENT (with a bond)** | **Contractor's CASH FLOW at the start** | **10-20 %, recovered from interim payments** |
| **PRICE ADJUSTMENT** | **Both parties, against INFLATION risk** | Index-based formula |
| **MOBILISATION advance** | Contractor's start-up | Against a bank guarantee |

> **Note the direction each provision runs in.** Most protect the employer, but **advance payment and price adjustment protect the contractor** — and a contract that carries only the first kind is unbalanced, tends to attract higher tender prices, and produces claims.

**A note on LIQUIDATED DAMAGES, since it is the most-confused provision here:**

> **Liquidated damages must be a GENUINE PRE-ESTIMATE of the employer's loss from delay, agreed at the time of contracting.**

> **If the sum is set punitively high, it becomes a PENALTY and is unenforceable in most legal systems** — the employer then falls back on proving actual loss, which is far harder.

> **So an unreasonably high LD rate is against the employer's own interest**, which is a genuinely counter-intuitive point and a favourite examination one.

> **And liquidated damages are the employer's EXCLUSIVE remedy for delay**: having agreed a rate, the employer cannot also claim actual losses beyond it.

**The interim payment mechanism, since retention operates within it:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Contractor submits a monthly statement of work done** | Measured against the bill of quantities |
| **Engineer measures and CERTIFIES the amount due** | **The engineer's independent function** |
| **Deductions applied** | **RETENTION, advance recovery, taxes, any LDs due** |
| **Employer pays within the stated period** | **Late payment usually attracts interest** |
| Final account and final certificate | After the defects liability period |

> **The engineer's certifying role is the pivot of the whole mechanism**, and it is why the ethics of certification matter so much: **the certificate is what causes money to move.**

> **Which connects this question directly to the ethical one about false certification: retention, liquidated damages and payment all operate through certificates that an engineer signs.** The contract's protections are only as good as the honesty of the person certifying.

examTip.trick: **5-10 % withheld from each interim payment, capped at about 5 % of the contract price; HALF released at completion and half at the end of the defects liability period (usually 12 months).** The second half is what secures defects.
examTip.trap: **Clean four-way match** — the other options name liquidated damages (delay), advance payment (cash flow) and price adjustment (inflation). Hold all four as a set, plus the performance bond (non-performance).
examTip.mnemonic: **Liquidated damages must be a GENUINE pre-estimate of loss** — set punitively high they become an unenforceable PENALTY, which is against the employer's own interest. And they are the EXCLUSIVE remedy for delay.
